title: Preface
content: Preface Sets, Relations, and Cardinality is volume F2 of the series. It is followed by Number Systems: From \nN to \nR.

title: Sets, Functions, Images and Preimages
content:
Sets, Functions, Images and Preimages Every definition of analysis is a sentence about sets and functions. “The supremum of A is the least element of the set of upper bounds of A.” “A function is continuous if the preimage of every open set is open.” Logic and Proof, Chapters 1 to 5 supplied the grammar of such sentences: the connectives, the quantifiers, and the prose that carries their rules. This chapter supplies the nouns: sets and subsets, unions and intersections of whole families of sets, ordered pairs and products, relations, functions, inverses, images and preimages. It is also where the logic of the first five chapters becomes visible inside mathematics. Inclusion is a “for every” around an “implies”, a union is an “or”, the union of a family is a “there exists”, and a function is a “for every there exists exactly one”. The laws of sets are the laws of logic, read through membership, and the chapter uses this from its second section to its last. Two surprises drive the chapter. The first is that the naive rule “any property defines a set” is contradictory (Russell’s paradox), so we must say which sets exist, and every set in this book is cut out of a set already given. The second is the chapter’s motivating problem. For f(x) = x^2, is f(A \cap B) = f(A) \cap f(B)? Is f^{-1}(C \cap D) = f^{-1}(C) \cap f^{-1}(D)? Why is the second always true and the first not? The answer is a single quantifier: membership in an image hides a “there exists”, and membership in a preimage hides nothing. Preimages therefore respect every set operation, and images only unions. This asymmetry is why analysis defines continuity by preimages. What you need. Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–5. From Logic and Proof, Chapters 1 and 2: the rules for the connectives and the derived laws used as rules, above all distributivity (@fd1:prp-distributivity), De Morgan’s laws (@fd1:prp-de-morgan), an iff as two implications (@fd1:prp-iff-two-implications), the contrapositive (@fd1:prp-contrapositive), vacuous implication (@fd1:prp-vacuous-implication), and derived rules (@fd1:def-derived-rule). From Logic and Proof, Chapter 3: the standard equivalences (@fd1:prp-standard-equivalences) and completeness (@fd1:thm-completeness). From Logic and Proof, Chapter 4: the rules for “for every” and “there exists”, bounded quantifiers (@fd1:def-bounded-quantifier) and their rules (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-rules), the rules for equality (@fd1:def-rules-equality), unique existence (@fd1:def-unique-existence, @fd1:prp-unique-existence-use), and the laws for negating quantifiers. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 5: plain-prose proofs, the convention on which steps may be silent, and the catalogue of what is not allowed. The number sets 
N, 
Z, 
Q, 
R are used as familiar sets, with their school arithmetic and order. Time. About 35 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 45 hours for everything. Roadmap - Sets, subsets and Russell’s paradox. What a set is allowed to be, equality by elements, the subset relation and the element-chasing proofs that establish it, describing sets by a property cut out of an ambient set, the empty set, and why no set contains every set. - Unions, intersections, complements and families. The set operations as the connectives read through membership, the algebra of sets as propositional logic, power sets, unions and intersections of arbitrary families, and De Morgan’s laws for families, including the empty one. - Ordered pairs, products and relations. An object that remembers order, the product A 	imes B and how it interacts with the set operations, and relations as sets of pairs. - Functions, composition, injections and surjections. A function as a graph with a declared target, when two functions are equal, composition, and the two questions of injectivity and surjectivity, with the squaring map as three different functions. - Left, right and two-sided inverses. A left inverse exists exactly for injective maps (on a nonempty domain), a right inverse forces surjectivity, bijections are the maps with a two-sided inverse, and the question whether every surjection has a right inverse, which needs a new principle. - Images and preimages. What a function does to sets, why preimages respect every operation and images only unions, where injectivity and surjectivity repair the failures, and sets of numbers such as -A and A + B as images. Named moves - Element-chasing. To prove A \subseteq B: “let x \in A”, unwind the definition of A, and rewind into the definition of B. To prove A = B: two inclusions. - Unwind the image. “y \in f(A)” means “there is a \in A with f(a) = y”: name the witness before using it. A preimage has no witness to name. - Refute with a small witness. A two- or three-element set, the map x \mapsto x^2, the empty set. - Build the inverse from the definition. For a left inverse, send f(x) back to x and everything else to one fixed point.

title: 1.1 Sets, Subsets and Russell's Paradox
content:
Sets, Subsets and Russell’s Paradox Logic and Proof, Chapters 1 to 5 built the grammar of mathematical statements: the connectives, the quantifiers, and the prose that carries their rules. The statements themselves have so far been about numbers, and occasionally about “collections” taken in their everyday sense. Analysis talks about collections all the time: the set of upper bounds of a set of numbers, the set of points where a function is positive, the set of all formulas. This section says what a set is allowed to be, what it means for one set to lie inside another, and how sets are described. One new notion carries the weight, the subset; the rest is the vocabulary it needs. We begin with the simplest possible idea of a set, and we will see it fail. A naive idea, and what goes wrong with it In everyday speech a collection is given by a property. “The students in this room”, “the even numbers”, “the prime numbers below 100”: in each case we say what an object must satisfy, and the collection is everything that satisfies it. The naive rule is: For every property, there is a set whose elements are exactly the objects having that property. It sounds harmless, and for the properties of everyday mathematics it gives the right answer. But a property may talk about sets themselves, and then the rule can be turned against itself. A set may be an element of another set: the set \{ 
N, 
Z \} has two elements, and each of them is a set. So it makes sense to ask of a set x whether x \in x, and the property “x 
otin x” is a property like any other. Most sets we know have it: the set of even numbers is not an even number, so it is not an element of itself. Apply the naive rule to this property. It promises a set R = 	ext{the set of all } x 	ext{ with } x 
otin x . Now ask whether R \in R. By the way R was made, an object belongs to R exactly when it is not an element of itself; applied to the object R, this says R \in R exactly when R 
otin R. A statement that is equivalent to its own negation leads to a contradiction by the rules of Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 alone; lines 4–11 of the derivation after Russell’s theorem, at the end of this section, carry out exactly this argument, with an extra conjunct carried along. So the naive rule is contradictory: it cannot be part of mathematics. This is Russell’s paradox. We hold it until the end of the section, where it becomes a theorem, Russell’s theorem, about the sets that do exist. First we set out what does work. Sets and membership We do not define “set” or “element”. They are the primitive notions of this chapter, in the way that “statement” was primitive in Logic and Proof, Chapter 1: we say how they are used, not what they are made of. A set is a collection of objects, its elements, and we write x \in A for “x is an element of A”, or “x belongs to A”, or “x lies in A”. Its negation is written x 
otin A. The objects may be numbers, or sets, or (later in this chapter) pairs and functions. In the language of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4, “\in” is a two-place predicate: x \in A is a statement about the two objects x and A, true or false like x < y. So everything Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 says about predicates, quantifiers, and their rules applies to it unchanged. A statement such as “every element of A is positive” is  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x > 0), which the bounded notation of @fd1:def-bounded-quantifier shortens to  orall x \in A\ (x > 0). Two conventions fix what kind of objects we deal with. First, the number sets 
N, 
Z, 
Q, and 
R are given: we use them as familiar sets, with their school arithmetic and order, as the earlier chapters did. (Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 turns the facts we use about 
R into consequences of axioms.) Second, numbers are not sets: a number has no elements, and no number is equal to a set. So 1 
e \{1\}, and z \in 5 is false for every z. The optional Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 1, 2 and 7 explain how numbers can be built out of sets; nothing in the main line depends on how that is done, and nothing here uses it. The single most important fact about sets is that a set is determined by its elements. It has no other features: no order in which the elements come, no count of how often each is listed, no color. Two sets with the same elements are the same set. [Equality of Sets] Sets A and B are equal, A = B, if and only if they have the same elements:  orall x\, (x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B). In words: every element of A is an element of B, and every element of B is an element of A. This principle is called extensionality: a set is fixed by its extension, the things it contains, and not by the words used to describe it. The sign = here is not new: it is the equality of @fd1:def-rules-equality, “names of the same object”. The direction from A = B to the same elements is ulename{{=}E}, with \varphi the formula x \in z and z the variable replaced (and symmetry, @fd1:prp-equality-symmetric-transitive, for the way back from B to A). The converse direction is the principle just stated, that a set has no features beyond its elements; it is what lets an equation proved from “same elements” be used with ulename{{=}E} like any other. The principle is an “if and only if”, so it is used in both directions: to prove A = B, prove the  orall statement; from A = B, conclude x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B for any x we like. Sets with finitely many elements can be written by listing their elements between braces: \{1, 2, 3\} is the set whose elements are 1, 2, and 3, and nothing else. Extensionality has two immediate consequences for such lists. - Repetition does not matter. \{1, 1, 2\} = \{1, 2\}. An object x belongs to the left side exactly when x = 1 or x = 1 or x = 2, and to the right side exactly when x = 1 or x = 2; the two conditions are equivalent, since “x = 1 or x = 1” says no more than “x = 1”. - Order does not matter. \{1, 2\} = \{2, 1\}. Here the two conditions are “x = 1 or x = 2” and “x = 2 or x = 1”, which are equivalent because \vee commutes (@fd1:exm-disjunction-first-derivations). Order and repetition are exactly what a list has and a set does not. When order matters we will need a different object, the ordered pair of Section 1.3. A set with one element, \{a\}, is a singleton. A singleton and its element are different things: \{1\} is a set, and 1 is a number, so 1 
e \{1\} by our convention. For sets the difference is just as real. The set \{
N\} has exactly one element, namely 
N, while 
N has infinitely many; so they differ, by extensionality, as 2 \in 
N and 2 
otin \{
N\}. Are the sets \{1, 2, 2, 3\}, \{3, 2, 1\}, and \{1, \{2\}, 3\} equal? The first two are equal: each has exactly the elements 1, 2, 3, and repetition and order do not count. The third is different: its elements are 1, \{2\}, and 3. The number 2 lies in the first set, but not in the third, since 2 
e 1, 2 
e 3, and 2 
e \{2\} (a number is not a set). So by @def-set-equality the third set differs from the other two. Subsets Most statements about sets in analysis are not equalities but inclusions: every Cauchy sequence converges, every continuous function on [a, b] is bounded, every upper bound of a set is at least its supremum. Each has the shape “everything of this kind is also of that kind”. Before a definition, look at one such statement in the language of sets. The multiples of 6 and the multiples of 3 form sets S = \{ \dots, -12, -6, 0, 6, 12, \dots \}, \qquad T = \{ \dots, -6, -3, 0, 3, 6, \dots \}, and every element of S is an element of T, because 6k = 3 \cdot (2k). The sets are not equal (3 \in T but 3 
otin S), yet one sits inside the other. This relation between sets deserves a name. A set is a subset of another if everything in the first is also in the second. [Subset] Let A and B be sets. A is a subset of B, written A \subseteq B, if every element of A is an element of B:  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x \in B). We also say that A is contained in B, or that B contains A. If A \subseteq B and A 
e B, then A is a proper subset of B, written A \subsetneq B. In words, clause by clause. The quantifier  orall x ranges over every object whatsoever, not over the elements of A only; the implication x \in A 	o x \in B restricts attention to the elements of A, and says nothing about objects outside A. With the bounded notation of @fd1:def-bounded-quantifier, the same condition is  orall x \in A\ (x \in B): “for every x in A, x is in B”. The symbol \subseteq allows equality, as \le does for numbers; the symbol \subsetneq excludes it, as < does. This book never writes \subset, which some books use for \subseteq and others for \subsetneq. The definition is a  orall around an 	o, and its rules are the rules of those two symbols. To prove A \subseteq B, we prove the  orall statement: by the rule ulename{ orall I} of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 we open a box for an arbitrary x (in prose, “let x be arbitrary”), and inside it we prove x \in A 	o x \in B by ulename{{	o}I} (@fd1:def-rules-implication): assume x \in A and reach x \in B. The two openings are always written together, as “let x \in A”. To use A \subseteq B, we apply ulename{ orall E} (Logic and Proof, Chapter 4) at the element we care about, and then ulename{{	o}E}: from A \subseteq B and a \in A, conclude a \in B. This gives the chapter’s first named move. To show A \subseteq B, take an arbitrary element of A and show that it lies in B. We call this element-chasing: we follow one element from A to B, unwinding the definition of A to find out what we know about it, and rewinding the definition of B to see what we must show. Here is the move three times: two ordinary inclusions, then the degenerate one. In each, the first sentence is the pair of openings, ulename{ orall I} and ulename{{	o}I}, and the rest reaches x \in B. [Three inclusions] 1. Show that [1, 2] \subseteq [0, 3]. 2. Let S be the set of integer multiples of 6 and T the set of integer multiples of 3, as above. Show that S \subseteq T. Here d \mid n, “d divides n”, means that n = dk for some integer k, so S consists of the integers x with 6 \mid x, and T of those with 3 \mid x. 3. Let A be any set. Show that A \subseteq A. (a) Let x \in [1, 2]. Then 1 \le x \le 2, by the meaning of the interval. Hence 0 \le 1 \le x and x \le 2 \le 3, so 0 \le x \le 3, that is, x \in [0, 3]. Since x was arbitrary, [1, 2] \subseteq [0, 3]. (b) Let x \in S, that is, let x be an integer with 6 \mid x. By the definition of \mid, there is an integer k with x = 6k; choose such a k (this is ulename{\exists E} of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4, and the name k is new). Then x = 3 \cdot (2k), and 2k is an integer, so 3 \mid x, with 2k as the witness (ulename{\exists I}). Hence x \in T. Since x was arbitrary, S \subseteq T. (c) Let x \in A. Then x \in A. Since x was arbitrary, A \subseteq A. The box of ulename{{	o}I} opens on x \in A and closes on the same line; in a derivation it is the one-line box that proves x \in A 	o x \in A. Part (c) is the degenerate case: every set is a subset of itself. It matters because it shows that \subseteq allows equality, and so “A \subseteq B” alone never tells us that B has anything A lacks. To say that A is a proper subset, A \subsetneq B, we also need an element of B outside A. In part (b) that element is 3: it lies in T, not in S. A nonexample by minimal change. Replace 6 by 4 and 3 by 6 in (b): is the set of multiples of 4 a subset of the set of multiples of 6? The first sentence of the proof still works (let x = 4k), but the last step fails: 4k need not be 6 times an integer. One element is enough to show the failure: 4 is a multiple of 4, and it is not a multiple of 6. What fails is the clause “every element of A” of @def-subset; here it fails at the element 4. That last observation is worth recording in symbols, because it is how every inclusion is refuted. By the negation laws of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 (
eg orall x\, \varphi is equivalent to \exists x\, 
eg\varphi, and 
eg(\varphi 	o \psi) to \varphi \wedge 
eg\psi), A 
ot\subseteq B \quad	ext{means}\quad \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge x 
otin B). To refute an inclusion, exhibit one element of the first set that is not in the second. Why this definition. The definition says nothing about objects outside A; that is the implication doing its job. If the 	o were replaced by \wedge, the condition  orall x\, (x \in A \wedge x \in B) would say that every object lies in A and in B, which is false for every set we will meet (Russell’s theorem at the end of this section shows that no set contains every set). This is the reason why a bounded “for every” always unfolds to an implication (@fd1:def-bounded-quantifier). Element or subset? The symbols \in and \subseteq relate different things. x \in A says that x is one of the objects collected in A; B \subseteq A says that every object collected in B is also collected in A. For example 1 \in \{1\} and \{1\} \subseteq \{1\}, but \{1\} 
otin \{1\}: the only element of \{1\} is the number 1, which is not the set \{1\}. And “1 \subseteq \{1\}” is not a comparison worth making: 1 is a number, not a set, so the definition of \subseteq does not apply to it. Before writing either symbol, ask whether the thing on the left is one of the objects in the set on the right, or a collection of such objects. Sometimes a set is both an element and a subset of the same set. In C = \{1, \{1\}\}, the set \{1\} is an element (it is listed) and also a subset (its only element, 1, is listed too). Change one entry: in \{1, 2\}, the set \{1\} is still a subset, but it is no longer an element, since the two elements are the numbers 1 and 2. Whether \{1\} \in D and whether \{1\} \subseteq D are two separate questions, and each is answered by looking at the elements of D. Checking some elements proves nothing about all of them. To prove A \subseteq B, checking that a few elements of A lie in B is not enough, however many are checked. “The integers 0, 12, 24 and -12 are multiples of 4 and of 3” does not prove that the set of multiples of 4 is a subset of the set of multiples of 3, and that inclusion is false (4 is a witness). The error is entry (N1) of the catalogue of Logic and Proof, Chapter 5: verifying instances and concluding a  orall. The rule ulename{ orall I} needs an arbitrary element, one about which nothing is known except that it lies in A. Two inclusions make an equality The first payoff of the definition connects it with equality. An equality of sets is an \leftrightarrow under a  orall, and by @fd1:prp-iff-two-implications an \leftrightarrow is two implications. So an equality should be two inclusions. [Equality Is Two Inclusions] For all sets A and B, A = B if and only if A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A. Unwind all three definitions. A = B is  orall x\, (x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B); the right side is  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x \in B) and  orall x\, (x \in B 	o x \in A). Inside the  orall, the statements are P \leftrightarrow Q on one side and P 	o Q, Q 	o P on the other, with P the statement x \in A and Q the statement x \in B; @fd1:prp-iff-two-implications says exactly that these are interchangeable. So the proof is that proposition applied at an arbitrary x, once in each direction. (\Rightarrow) Suppose A = B. Let x be arbitrary. By @def-set-equality, x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B, so by the first half of @fd1:prp-iff-two-implications (with P the statement x \in A and Q the statement x \in B, used as a derived rule, @fd1:def-derived-rule), x \in A 	o x \in B and x \in B 	o x \in A. Since x was arbitrary,  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x \in B) and  orall x\, (x \in B 	o x \in A); by @def-subset, A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A. (\Leftarrow) Suppose A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A. Let x be arbitrary. By @def-subset, x \in A 	o x \in B and x \in B 	o x \in A, so by the second half of @fd1:prp-iff-two-implications, x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B. Since x was arbitrary, A = B by @def-set-equality. The name of the proposition in words is antisymmetry of \subseteq: as for \le on numbers, A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A together force equality. It licenses the move that proves almost every set identity in this chapter. To show A = B, show A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A: two element-chases, one in each direction. A proof of this kind is written in two paragraphs, labeled (\subseteq) and (\supseteq), exactly as a proof of an “if and only if” is written in two paragraphs labeled (\Rightarrow) and (\Leftarrow) (Logic and Proof, Section 2.4). The two paragraphs are two separate boxes: neither may use the other’s assumption. Transitivity, rule by rule The second payoff is that inclusions chain, as \le does. Its proof is the first element-chase of the chapter written with every rule named, and we give it at two levels: first as a derivation, then as prose in which each sentence carries its rule in brackets. (These are levels 0 and 2 of Logic and Proof, Chapter 5; from here on the book writes level-3 prose; after one more fully tagged proof, in Section 1.2, brackets appear only on the step a proof is about.) [Inclusion Is Transitive] For all sets A, B, and C, if A \subseteq B and B \subseteq C, then A \subseteq C. The goal A \subseteq C is a  orall around an 	o, so the goal-directed moves open two boxes: a box for an arbitrary x_0, and inside it a box on x_0 \in A. The new goal is x_0 \in C. Each hypothesis is a  orall around an 	o too, and we use each at x_0: the first carries x_0 from A into B, the second from B into C. Unwound by @def-subset, the hypotheses are  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x \in B) and  orall x\, (x \in B 	o x \in C), and the goal is  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x \in C). The following is a derivation of the goal from the hypotheses. The outer box, flagged x_0, is the box of ulename{ orall I} (Logic and Proof, Chapter 4); it has no assumption line. The same proof in prose, with each step’s rule in brackets: Suppose A \subseteq B and B \subseteq C. Let x be arbitrary [ulename{ orall I}, opening], and suppose x \in A [ulename{{	o}I}, opening]. Since A \subseteq B, in particular x \in A 	o x \in B [ulename{ orall E}], so x \in B [ulename{{	o}E}]. Since B \subseteq C, in particular x \in B 	o x \in C [ulename{ orall E}], so x \in C [ulename{{	o}E}]. Hence x \in A 	o x \in C [ulename{{	o}I}, closing], and since x was arbitrary, A \subseteq C [ulename{ orall I}, closing]. This proves the proposition. At level 3, the prose a mathematician writes, the same proof is one line: let x \in A; then x \in B since A \subseteq B, and x \in C since B \subseteq C. The silent steps are those Logic and Proof, Chapter 5’s convention allows: the two instances of ulename{ orall E} at the obvious term x, and the two closing sentences. What may never be silent is the opening “let x \in A”, and the two citations, “since A \subseteq B” and “since B \subseteq C”. Let A = \{1, 2\}, B = \{1, 2, 3\}, and C = \{1, 3\}. Which of the six statements A \subseteq B, B \subseteq A, A \subseteq C, C \subseteq A, B \subseteq C, C \subseteq B are true? For each false one, name a witness. True: A \subseteq B and C \subseteq B (every listed element of A, and of C, is listed in B). False: B \subseteq A (witness 3 \in B, 3 
otin A); A \subseteq C (witness 2); C \subseteq A (witness 3); B \subseteq C (witness 2). Both A and C are proper subsets of B, and neither of A, C is a subset of the other. Describing sets: listing and specification Listing works for a handful of elements. For a set such as “the real numbers whose square is less than 2” we need to describe the elements by a property, as the naive rule wanted. The repair of the naive rule is small but essential: we may cut a set out of a set we already have. [Specification] Let A be a set and P(x) a property of objects x. Then there is a set, written \{ x \in A : P(x) \}, whose elements are exactly the elements of A that have the property P: for every y, y \in \{ x \in A : P(x) \} \iff y \in A 	ext{ and } P(y). The notation is read “the set of x in A such that P(x)”; the colon is read “such that” (the book never writes a bar here, so that a bar stays free for divisibility and absolute value). The letter x is a bound variable, like the x of  orall x: \{ x \in A : P(x) \} and \{ t \in A : P(t) \} are the same set. The set A is the ambient set of the description, and every set-builder in this book has one, named or fixed by the context; a set written \{ f(a) : a \in A \} is the image of A under f (Section 1.6), and any other set the book defines is shown to exist by (W1)–(W6) where it is introduced. By @def-set-equality, the equivalence in the definition determines the set completely, so “the” set is justified. In the language of the rules: to show that y belongs to \{ x \in A : P(x) \}, show y \in A and P(y); from y \in \{ x \in A : P(x) \}, conclude both. Each is one ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E} (@fd1:def-rules-biconditional) with the definition, followed or preceded by ulename{\wedge I} or ulename{\wedge E} (@fd1:def-rules-conjunction); at level 3 all of these are silent, and a proof simply writes “by definition” or nothing at all. Specification is one of a short list of working rules that say which sets exist. We state them once, here, and use them from now on without comment. 1. Specification. For a set A and a property P, \{ x \in A : P(x) \} is a set (@def-set-builder). 2. Listing. Any finitely many objects a_1, \dots, a_n form a set \{ a_1, \dots, a_n \}, whose elements are exactly a_1, \dots, a_n. 3. Unions. For sets A and B, there is a set whose elements are exactly the objects lying in A or in B; more generally, for a family of sets indexed by a set, there is a set whose elements are exactly the objects lying in at least one member of the family (Section 1.2). 4. Power sets. For a set X, the subsets of X form a set (Section 1.2). 5. Products. For sets A and B, the ordered pairs (a, b) with a \in A and b \in B form a set; more generally, for a set X and n \in 
N with n \ge 2, the n-tuples (x_1, \dots, x_n) with every x_k \in X form a set (Section 1.3). 6. Numbers. 
N, 
Z, 
Q, and 
R are sets. These rules are enough for everything the book does with sets until Chapter 3, which adds one more: a principle for making infinitely many choices at once (Section 1.5 shows where it is first needed). They are not axioms in the formal sense, and we do not try to derive them from fewer principles; the optional Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 1 states the axioms of set theory behind them and shows how (W1)–(W5) and the set 
N follow from them, and the optional Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapters 2 and 7 build 
Z, 
Q and 
R, which completes (W6). What matters here is what is missing from the list: there is no rule that collects all objects with a property, without an ambient set. The end of this section shows that such a rule would be contradictory. The empty set Among all sets, one is special: the set with nothing in it. It turns up constantly: as the set of real solutions of x^2 = -1, as the intersection of two sets with nothing in common (Section 1.2), as the domain of a function with no inputs (Section 1.4). Without it, “the set of solutions” would not always name a set. [Empty Set] An empty set is a set with no elements: a set E such that  orall x\, (x 
otin E). Such a set exists. Take any set we are given, say 
N, and collect its elements x with x 
e x; by specification (@def-set-builder), this is a set, and since x = x for every x (ulename{{=}I}, @fd1:def-rules-equality), nothing has the property, so the set has no elements. There is also at most one empty set, which justifies the article “the”. [The Empty Set Is Unique] If E and E' are empty sets, then E = E'. Let x be arbitrary. Since E and E' are empty, x 
otin E and x 
otin E'. By @fd1:prp-vacuous-implication, x 
otin E gives x \in E 	o x \in E', and x 
otin E' gives x \in E' 	o x \in E. So x \in E \leftrightarrow x \in E' by @fd1:prp-iff-two-implications. Since x was arbitrary, E = E' by @def-set-equality. We write \emptyset for the empty set. The same vacuous truth gives its most useful property at once: \emptyset \subseteq A for every set A. Indeed, let x be arbitrary; x 
otin \emptyset, so x \in \emptyset 	o x \in A by @fd1:prp-vacuous-implication; since x was arbitrary, \emptyset \subseteq A. In words: to refute \emptyset \subseteq A we would need an element of \emptyset outside A, and \emptyset has no elements at all. The empty set is a set with no elements, and a set containing it is not empty. The set \{\emptyset\} has exactly one element, namely \emptyset; so \{\emptyset\} 
e \emptyset, with \emptyset itself as the witness: \emptyset \in \{\emptyset\} and \emptyset 
otin \emptyset. A box containing an empty box is not an empty box. 1. Is \emptyset \subseteq \emptyset? 2. Is \emptyset \in \emptyset? 3. Which of the sets \emptyset, \{\emptyset\}, \{\{\emptyset\}\} are equal? (a) Yes: \emptyset \subseteq A for every set A, and in particular for A = \emptyset. (It also follows from A \subseteq A.) (b) No: \emptyset has no elements, so nothing, not even \emptyset, belongs to it. (c) None. \emptyset has no elements, and each of the other two has exactly one, so \emptyset differs from both. The only element of \{\emptyset\} is \emptyset, and the only element of \{\{\emptyset\}\} is \{\emptyset\}; these two elements are different by the first observation, so \emptyset \in \{\emptyset\} but \emptyset 
otin \{\{\emptyset\}\}, and the two sets differ by @def-set-equality. Computing with set-builders The next worked example shows how a set-builder is computed: we guess the answer, then prove the guess by two inclusions (@prp-subset-antisymmetric). [Computing sets given by a property] 1. Show that \{ x \in 
Z : x^2 < 5 \} = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}. 2. Show that \{ x \in 
R : x^2 < 0 \} = \emptyset. (a) Write S for the left side. Squaring the integers near 0 suggests the guess: 0^2 = 0, (\pm 1)^2 = 1, (\pm 2)^2 = 4 are below 5, and (\pm 3)^2 = 9 is not. (\subseteq) Let x \in S. Then x \in 
Z and x^2 < 5, by @def-set-builder. We claim \abs{x} \le 2. Otherwise \abs{x} \ge 3, since x is an integer, and then x^2 = \abs{x}^2 \ge 9 > 5, which contradicts x^2 < 5. So \abs{x} \le 2, and the integers with \abs{x} \le 2 are -2, -1, 0, 1, 2. Hence x \in \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}. (\supseteq) Let x \in \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}. Then x is one of five integers, and we check each case: x^2 is 4, 1, 0, 1, 4 respectively, and each is less than 5. So x \in 
Z and x^2 < 5, that is, x \in S. By @prp-subset-antisymmetric, S = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}. (b) (\subseteq) Let x \in \{ x \in 
R : x^2 < 0 \}. Then x is a real number with x^2 < 0; but x^2 \ge 0 for every real x, a contradiction. So this case cannot occur, and x \in \emptyset holds in it vacuously (ulename{ ot E}, @fd1:def-rules-contradiction). (\supseteq) \emptyset \subseteq \{ x \in 
R : x^2 < 0 \}, because \emptyset is a subset of every set. By @prp-subset-antisymmetric, the set is \emptyset. A set-builder with an impossible property is a legitimate description of \emptyset. Two remarks on the example. In (a), the (\supseteq) direction is a proof by cases over a finite list, which is legitimate: the five cases exhaust the set, because the list says exactly which elements it has. That is quite different from the error of the second warning above, where finitely many cases were checked for an infinite set. In (b), the (\supseteq) direction is free, and only (\subseteq) needs an argument. For “S = \emptyset” this is always so: the claim amounts to “S has no elements”. Russell’s paradox as a theorem We return to the contradiction of the opening. The naive rule failed on R = “all x with x 
otin x”. Specification allows only the version with an ambient set: for any set A, R_A \coloneqq \{ x \in A : x 
otin x \} is a set, by (W1). What happens to the paradox now? [Russell’s Theorem] For every set A, the set R_A = \{ x \in A : x 
otin x \} is not an element of A. Hence there is no set of which every set is an element. Try it first (five minutes): suppose R_A \in A. Is R_A \in R_A? Try each answer in turn, and see where each one leads. The attempt runs into the old paradox, but with one extra condition. If R_A \in R_A, then by specification R_A 
otin R_A: the first answer refutes itself. If R_A 
otin R_A, then specification puts R_A into R_A, provided R_A \in A: the second answer refutes itself only under that proviso. So the two answers together are impossible exactly when R_A \in A, and the conclusion is not a contradiction in mathematics but a fact: R_A 
otin A. We do not need to split into the two answers. The first answer is refuted outright, with no proviso, by ulename{
eg I} (@fd1:def-rules-negation); so R_A 
otin R_A holds whenever R_A \in A. That fact, fed back into specification, gives R_A \in R_A, and the two collide. Let A be a set, and write R for R_A. By @def-set-builder, for every y, y \in R \iff y \in A 	ext{ and } y 
otin y. 	ag{$\ast$} Suppose R \in A, for ulename{
eg I}. We first show R 
otin R. Suppose R \in R. Then by (\ast) at y = R, R \in A and R 
otin R; in particular R 
otin R, which contradicts R \in R. Hence R 
otin R, by ulename{
eg I}. Now R \in A and R 
otin R, so R \in R by (\ast) read from right to left. This contradicts R 
otin R. Hence R 
otin A, by ulename{
eg I}. For the second claim, suppose U were a set of which every set is an element. By the first claim with A = U, the set R_U is not an element of U; but R_U is a set, so it is an element of U. This contradiction shows that no such U exists. Here is the first part of the proof as a derivation, with (\ast) as its premise, written as the universal statement it is, and R for R_A: Every rule in it is one of ulename{ orall E}, ulename{{\leftrightarrow}E}, ulename{\wedge E}, ulename{\wedge I}, ulename{
eg E}, and ulename{
eg I}. There is no ulename{RAA}, and no excluded middle: the inner box (lines 4–7) refutes one answer outright instead of splitting into two answers. This is worth noticing. The paradox is not an artifact of classical logic, and cannot be escaped by giving up a classical rule; it is a genuine contradiction in the naive rule, and the only repair is to change which sets exist. What the theorem says about sets. Read with A arbitrary, the theorem says that no set contains everything: for every set A we have produced a set, R_A, outside it. The naive rule “any property defines a set” is exactly specification without the phrase “x \in A”, and the theorem shows that the phrase cannot be dropped: with A ranging over “everything”, R_A would be the paradoxical R. This is why every set-builder in this book has an ambient set, and why (W1)–(W6) contain no “set of all sets”. When we want “all objects with a property”, we first say where to look. The argument has a shape that will return: a set built from A so that it disagrees with each candidate on the candidate itself. Chapter 3 proves by the same shape of argument that no function from a set X to the set of its subsets reaches every subset. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Negate “A \subseteq B” in symbols, and then in words, with the negation pushed through the quantifier and the implication. 2. True or false: \{1\} \in \{\{1\}, 2\}; \{1\} \subseteq \{\{1\}, 2\}; \emptyset \subseteq \emptyset; \{\emptyset\} \subseteq \{1\}. Give a reason for each. 3. List the elements of \{ n \in 
Z : 0 < n^2 \le 9 \}. 4. In an element-chasing proof of A \subseteq B, the first sentence is “let x \in A”. Which rule of logic gives its first clause, and which its second? (a) By @def-subset, A \subseteq B is  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x \in B). By the quantifier negation law of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4, its negation is equivalent to \exists x\, 
eg(x \in A 	o x \in B), and by the law for negated implications (also Logic and Proof, Chapter 4) to \exists x\, (x \in A \wedge x 
otin B). In words: some element of A is not an element of B. (b) True: \{1\} is listed as an element of \{\{1\}, 2\}. False: the only element of \{1\} is 1, and 1 
otin \{\{1\}, 2\}, since 1 
e \{1\} (a number is not a set) and 1 
e 2; so 1 is a witness. True: \emptyset is a subset of every set. False: \emptyset \in \{\emptyset\} but \emptyset 
otin \{1\}, since \emptyset 
e 1; so \emptyset is a witness. (c) \{-3, -2, -1, 1, 2, 3\}. The integer 0 is excluded because 0^2 = 0 is not > 0, and integers with \abs{n} \ge 4 have n^2 \ge 16 > 9. (d) “Let x \in A” opens two boxes. Its first clause, “let x be arbitrary”, is ulename{ orall I} (Logic and Proof, Chapter 4); its second, “suppose x \in A”, is ulename{{	o}I} (@fd1:def-rules-implication). The proof must then reach x \in B inside both boxes. B. Practice [B1: A set given by an equation] Prove that \{ x \in 
R : x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0 \} = \{1, 2\}, by two inclusions. Write S for the left side. (\subseteq) Let x \in S. Then x is real and x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0. Since x^2 - 3x + 2 = (x - 1)(x - 2), we have (x - 1)(x - 2) = 0. A product of two real numbers is zero only if one of the factors is zero, so x - 1 = 0 or x - 2 = 0, that is, x = 1 or x = 2. In either case x \in \{1, 2\}. (\supseteq) Let x \in \{1, 2\}, so x = 1 or x = 2. If x = 1, then x^2 - 3x + 2 = 1 - 3 + 2 = 0. If x = 2, then x^2 - 3x + 2 = 4 - 6 + 2 = 0. In either case x is a real number satisfying the equation, so x \in S. By @prp-subset-antisymmetric, S = \{1, 2\}. [B2: A subset of the empty set] Let A be a set with A \subseteq \emptyset. Prove that A = \emptyset. We have A \subseteq \emptyset by hypothesis, and \emptyset \subseteq A because the empty set is a subset of every set. By @prp-subset-antisymmetric, A = \emptyset. Directly: if x \in A, then x \in \emptyset because A \subseteq \emptyset, which is impossible; so A has no elements, and it is the empty set by @prp-empty-set-unique. [B3: Equal or not?] For each pair, determine whether the two sets are equal. Justify your answer: prove each equality, and give a witness element for each inequality. 1. \{ x \in 
Z : 4 \mid x \} and \{ x \in 
Z : 2 \mid x \}. 2. \{ x \in 
R : x^2 = 4 \} and \{-2, 2\}. 3. \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\} and \{\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset, \emptyset\}. 4. \{ x \in 
Z : x^2 < 2 \} and \{ x \in 
N : x < 2 \}. (a) Not equal. The integer 2 lies in the second set (2 = 2 \cdot 1) but not in the first, since 2 = 4k would need k = 	frac12, which is not an integer. (The first set is a proper subset of the second: x = 4k gives x = 2 \cdot (2k).) (b) Equal. (\subseteq) If x is real with x^2 = 4, then (x - 2)(x + 2) = x^2 - 4 = 0, so x = 2 or x = -2. (\supseteq) 2^2 = 4 and (-2)^2 = 4. (c) Equal. Both sets have exactly the elements \emptyset and \{\emptyset\}: an object lies in the first exactly when it is \emptyset or \{\emptyset\}, and in the second exactly when it is \{\emptyset\} or \emptyset or \emptyset. Order and repetition do not count. (d) Not equal. The first set is \{-1, 0, 1\}: an integer with \abs{x} \ge 2 has x^2 \ge 4, and (-1)^2 = 1, 0^2 = 0, 1^2 = 1 are below 2. The second set is \{0, 1\}, since 
N starts at 0. The witness -1 lies in the first set and not in the second (-1 
otin 
N). C. Going deeper [C1: Every set has something outside it] Let A be a set, and let R_A = \{ x \in A : x 
otin x \} as in @thm-russell. 1. Let A^{+} be the set whose elements are the elements of A together with the object R_A (it exists by (W2) and (W3)). Show that A \subsetneq A^{+}. 2. Deduce from @thm-russell that no set A has the property “every subset of A is an element of A”. [Hint 1] In (a), a proper inclusion needs two things: the inclusion, and a witness in the larger set that is not in the smaller one. The theorem supplies the witness. In (b), look for a subset of A that the theorem says is not an element of A. [Hint 2] For (b): suppose, for ulename{
eg I}, that every subset of A is an element of A. First show that R_A \subseteq A. (a) First, A \subseteq A^{+}: an element of A is an element of A^{+} by the description of A^{+}. Second, A^{+} 
e A: the object R_A lies in A^{+}, and R_A 
otin A by @thm-russell. So R_A is a witness, and A \subsetneq A^{+}. (b) Suppose, for ulename{
eg I}, that A is a set such that every subset of A is an element of A. The set R_A is a subset of A: if y \in R_A, then y \in A (and y 
otin y) by @def-set-builder. So by the assumption, R_A \in A, which contradicts @thm-russell. Hence no set has the property. Part (a) says that no set is “as large as possible”: there is always a set with one more element. Part (b) rules out a set containing all of its own subsets; for instance, no set A has as its elements exactly the subsets of A. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) proves the inclusion A \subseteq A^{+} from the description of A^{+}. - 3: (a) names R_A as the witness to A^{+} 
e A, citing @thm-russell for R_A 
otin A. - 3: (b) proves R_A \subseteq A by element-chasing through @def-set-builder. - 2: (b) combines the assumption with R_A \subseteq A to get R_A \in A, and cites the theorem for the contradiction. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using “the set of all sets” or any set-builder without an ambient set; taking A^{+} 
e A as obvious “because an element was added” (if R_A were already in A, nothing would have been added). [C2: Antisymmetry for sets of sets] Can there be sets A and B, whose elements are themselves sets, such that A \subseteq B, B \subseteq A, and A 
e B? Explain why the answer does not depend on what the elements of A and B are. No. By @prp-subset-antisymmetric, A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A give A = B, for all sets A and B. The answer does not depend on the elements, because nothing in the proof of @prp-subset-antisymmetric looks at them. The proof works with the statements x \in A and x \in B for an arbitrary object x, and uses only @def-subset, @def-set-equality, and the propositional law @fd1:prp-iff-two-implications applied to those two statements. Whether x is a number, a set, or a set of sets never enters. For example, with A = \{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\} and B = \{\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset\}, the two inclusions hold and indeed A = B. The point of the question is a habit: an element-chasing proof treats its element as a black box, and so it proves the statement for sets of anything at all.

title: 1.2 Unions, Intersections, Complements and Families
content:
Unions, Intersections, Complements and Families Section 1.1 said what sets are, when two of them are equal, and when one lies inside another. It gave us ways to describe a single set, by listing or by a property cut out of an ambient set. This section makes new sets from old ones. Each connective of Logic and Proof, Chapter 1 gives a set operation: “or” gives the union, “and” gives the intersection, “and not” gives the difference. That observation is the thesis of the chapter: the laws of sets are the laws of logic, read through membership. We state it, prove the standard laws of set algebra from it, and then take the step analysis needs constantly, from two sets to a whole family of them, where “or” becomes “there exists” and “and” becomes “for all”. Union, intersection and difference Here is the standard example of a new set. Let A be the set of integers divisible by 2 and B the set of integers divisible by 3. Three natural questions about an integer x are: is it divisible by 2 or by 3? by 2 and by 3? by 2 and not by 3? Each question collects integers into a set, and each set is built from A and B by one connective applied to the statements x \in A and x \in B. The pattern does not depend on divisibility at all, so we name the three constructions once, for any sets. The union collects what lies in either set, the intersection what lies in both, the difference what lies in the first and not the second. [Union, Intersection, Difference] Let A and B be sets. 1. The union A \cup B is the set whose elements are exactly the objects lying in A or in B: x \in A \cup B \iff (x \in A \vee x \in B). 2. The intersection A \cap B is the set \{ x \in A : x \in B \}: so x \in A \cap B \iff (x \in A \wedge x \in B). 3. The difference A \setminus B is the set \{ x \in A : x 
otin B \}: so x \in A \setminus B \iff (x \in A \wedge x 
otin B). Sets A and B are disjoint if A \cap B = \emptyset. If A \subseteq X, the difference X \setminus A is called the complement of A in X. In words, clause by clause. The union exists by the working rule (W3) of Section 1.1; it is not cut out of an ambient set, since its elements come from two sets at once. The intersection and the difference are cut out of an ambient set, namely A, so they exist by specification (W1), and the description \{ x \in A : \dots \} names its ambient set as Section 1.1 requires. The “or” of the union is inclusive, as \vee always is: an object in both sets is in the union. “Disjoint” means “no common element”. The complement is always written X \setminus A, with the ambient set X named. Many books write A^c and leave X to the reader, and a reader who guesses X wrongly gets a different set: the complement of [0, 1] in [0, 2] is (1, 2], and in 
R it is (-\infty, 0) \cup (1, \infty). There is no “complement of A” on its own: by Russell’s theorem (@thm-russell) there is no set of everything outside A (such a set, joined with A, would contain every set). So this book never writes A^c. Examples, simplest first, each checked against the membership conditions. - Finite sets. For A = \{1, 2, 3\} and B = \{2, 4\}: A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}, A \cap B = \{2\}, A \setminus B = \{1, 3\}, B \setminus A = \{4\}. For instance 3 \in A \setminus B because 3 \in A and 3 
otin B; and 4 
otin A \setminus B because 4 
otin A. - Intervals. For A = [0, 2] and B = [1, 3]: A \cup B = [0, 3], A \cap B = [1, 2], A \setminus B = [0, 1). The last one shows how an endpoint behaves: 1 \in B, so 1 
otin A \setminus B, while every x with 0 \le x < 1 lies in A and not in B. - Divisibility. With A and B the multiples of 2 and of 3 in 
Z, as in the opening, A \cap B is the set of multiples of 6 (this uses the school fact that an integer divisible by 2 and by 3 is divisible by 6), and 
Z \setminus A is the set of odd integers, the complement of A in 
Z. - Degenerate cases. For every set A: A \cup \emptyset = A, A \cap \emptyset = \emptyset, A \setminus \emptyset = A, and A \setminus A = \emptyset. Each is one line: for example, x \in A \setminus A would mean x \in A and x 
otin A, which is impossible, so A \setminus A has no element. They matter because \emptyset behaves for \cup as 0 does for +, and for \cap as 0 does for 	imes. Three inclusions hold for all sets and are used without comment from now on: A \cap B \subseteq A \subseteq A \cup B, \qquad A \setminus B \subseteq A . Each is one element-chase that drops or adds a disjunct or a conjunct: if x \in A \cap B, then x \in A (ulename{\wedge E}); if x \in A, then x \in A \cup B (ulename{\vee I}); if x \in A \setminus B, then x \in A (ulename{\wedge E}). A nonexample by minimal change: the “difference” of two sets is not “everything in one but not in both”. The set \{ x \in A \cup B : 	ext{not both } x \in A 	ext{ and } x \in B \} is a different set: for A = \{1, 2, 3\} and B = \{2, 4\} it is \{1, 3, 4\}, while A \setminus B = \{1, 3\}. The element 4 is in the first and not in A \setminus B, because the difference keeps only elements of A. The difference is not symmetric. In general A \setminus B 
e B \setminus A. With A = \{1\} and B = \{2\}, A \setminus B = \{1\} and B \setminus A = \{2\}, and the witness 1 lies in the first and not the second. In fact A \setminus B and B \setminus A are always disjoint, since an element of both would lie in A and not in A; they are equal only when both are empty, that is, when A = B. Let X = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}, A = \{1, 2, 3\}, and B = \{2, 4, 6\}. Compute A \cup B, A \cap B, X \setminus (A \cup B), and (X \setminus A) \cap (X \setminus B). A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 6\} and A \cap B = \{2\}. Then X \setminus (A \cup B) = \{5\}. Also X \setminus A = \{4, 5, 6\} and X \setminus B = \{1, 3, 5\}, whose intersection is \{5\}. The last two answers agree. This is the two-set case of De Morgan’s law for sets, which is proved for arbitrary families later in this section. Laws of sets are laws of logic Unwinding the three definitions turns every question about \cup, \cap, and \setminus into a question about \vee, \wedge, and 
eg. Here is the dictionary, with the notions of Section 1.1 included. ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- On sets Unwound through membership Logic ----------------------- ----------------------------------------------- ------------------------------- x \in A \cup B x \in A \vee x \in B \vee x \in A \cap B x \in A \wedge x \in B \wedge x \in A \setminus B x \in A \wedge 
eg(x \in B) \wedge and 
eg A = \emptyset  orall x\, 
eg(x \in A) 
eg under  orall A \subseteq B  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x \in B) 	o under  orall A = B  orall x\, (x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B) \leftrightarrow under  orall ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The dictionary makes an idea precise. Fix an object x and write p, q, r for the statements x \in A, x \in B, x \in C. Then membership of x in any set built from A, B, C by \cup, \cap, \setminus is a propositional formula in p, q, r: for instance, x \in A \cap (B \cup C) \iff p \wedge (q \vee r) . Two such sets are equal if their membership formulas can each be derived from the other, for then x lies in one exactly when it lies in the other, and x was arbitrary. So a law of propositional logic, with letters replaced by membership statements, is a law of sets. That is the thesis of this chapter. The laws of sets are the laws of logic, read through membership. Here are the laws used most. [Algebra of Sets] For all sets A, B, and C: 1. (commutativity) A \cup B = B \cup A and A \cap B = B \cap A; 2. (associativity) (A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C) and (A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C); 3. (distributivity) A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C) and A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C); 4. (differences) A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C) and A \setminus (B \cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C). Each law is a propositional equivalence under  orall x. Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 gives a uniform license for all of them at once: an equivalence that holds in every row of a truth table is derivable in both directions, by completeness, and a derived sequent may be used with its letters replaced by any statements. So one argument covers every law, and the table after the proof names, for each law, the equivalence it comes from. We also write out two laws in full, as element-chases, so that the reader sees what the uniform argument does: the first distributive law, and the second difference law, the one law whose element-chase needs a classical rule (the uniform argument uses one for every law, inside the proof of @fd1:thm-completeness). The uniform argument. Fix one of the eight equations, L = R, and let \varphi and \psi be the propositional formulas in the atoms p, q, r that describe membership in L and in R, as in the dictionary: for the first distributive law, \varphi = p \wedge (q \vee r) and \psi = (p \wedge q) \vee (p \wedge r). For (a)–(c), the semantic equivalence \varphi \equiv \psi is a clause of @fd1:prp-standard-equivalences, with p, q, r in the places of \varphi, \psi, \chi: (f) for (a), (h) for (b), (g) for (c). For (d), it is checked by the truth table displayed below. By @fd1:def-semantic-equivalence, \varphi \models \psi and \psi \models \varphi, so by @fd1:thm-completeness, \varphi \vdash \psi and \psi \vdash \varphi. Now let x be arbitrary. By @fd1:def-derived-rule, each of these two sequents may be used with p, q, r replaced by the statements x \in A, x \in B, x \in C; with @def-set-operations, the first gives x \in L 	o x \in R and the second x \in R 	o x \in L. Hence x \in L \leftrightarrow x \in R, and since x was arbitrary, L = R by @def-set-equality. The truth table for (d), with the atoms in the book’s order (T before F, the last atom alternating fastest):  egin{array}{ccc|cccc} p & q & r & p \wedge 
eg(q \vee r) & (p \wedge 
eg q) \wedge (p \wedge 
eg r) & p \wedge 
eg(q \wedge r) & (p \wedge

The power set of X is the set \powerset{X} whose elements are exactly the subsets of X: S \in \powerset{X} \iff S \subseteq X . The set exists by the working rule (W4) of Section 1.1.
