otin  igcap_{i \in I} A_i into a statement with \exists. What is the correct translation if x \in X is not assumed? (a) The bounded quantifier negation law of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4: 
eg orall i \in I\ \varphi gives \exists i \in I\ 
eg\varphi, with the bound kept. That direction is classical: it rests on the unbounded law 
eg orall x\, \varphi \vdash \exists x\, 
eg\varphi, which needs ulename{RAA}. (b) The left side 
Z \setminus (A_2 \cup A_3) is the set of integers divisible by neither 2 nor 3. The right side (
Z \setminus A_2) \cap (
Z \setminus A_3) is the set of integers that are odd and not multiples of 3. By the theorem they are equal. For instance 1 and 5 (also -1, 7) lie in both, and 3 and 4 (also 6) lie in neither. (c) For I = \emptyset, the empty union is \emptyset and the empty intersection is X. First law: X \setminus \emptyset = X and  igcap_{i \in \emptyset} (X \setminus A_i) = X. Second law: X \setminus X = \emptyset and  igcup_{i \in \emptyset} (X \setminus A_i) = \emptyset. (d) By @def-family-union-intersection, x \in  igcap_{i \in I} A_i means x \in X \wedge  orall i \in I\ (x \in A_i). For x \in X, its negation is 
eg orall i \in I\ (x \in A_i), which by the law of (a) is \exists i \in I\ (x 
otin A_i). Without x \in X, the negation of the conjunction is, by @fd1:prp-de-morgan (d), “x 
otin X or \exists i \in I\ (x 
otin A_i)”: an object may fail to be in the intersection simply because it is not in X, since the intersection is taken inside X. B. Practice [B1: Intersection and difference] Prove that A \cap (B \setminus C) = (A \cap B) \setminus (A \cap C) for all sets A, B, C, and name the propositional equivalence behind it. With p, q, r for x \in A, x \in B, x \in C, the membership conditions are p \wedge (q \wedge 
eg r) and (p \wedge q) \wedge 
eg(p \wedge r), and the equivalence behind the law is p \wedge (q \wedge 
eg r) \equiv (p \wedge q) \wedge 
eg(p \wedge r). Both directions have short direct derivations, which the element-chase follows. (\subseteq) Let x \in A \cap (B \setminus C). Then x \in A, x \in B, and x 
otin C. So x \in A \cap B. If x were in A \cap C, then x \in C, a contradiction; so x 
otin A \cap C. Hence x \in (A \cap B) \setminus (A \cap C). (\supseteq) Let x \in (A \cap B) \setminus (A \cap C). Then x \in A, x \in B, and x 
otin A \cap C. If x were in C, then, since x \in A, x \in A \cap C, a contradiction; so x 
otin C. Hence x \in B \setminus C, and x \in A \cap (B \setminus C). By @prp-subset-antisymmetric the sets are equal. Both halves use ulename{
eg I} and no classical rule. [B2: Three families of intervals] For each family, indexed by t \in (0, \infty), compute the union and the intersection (inside X = 
R), and prove each answer by two inclusions. 1. A_t = [t, 1 + t]; 2. B_t = (-t, 1/t); 3. C_t = (t, 2t). (a) Union (0, \infty). (\subseteq) If x \in [t, 1 + t] for some t > 0, then x \ge t > 0. (\supseteq) If x > 0, take t \coloneqq x: then x \in [x, 1 + x]. Intersection \emptyset. Let x be any real number and take t \coloneqq \abs{x} + 1 > 0. Then x \le \abs{x} < t, so x 
otin [t, 1 + t]. So no real number lies in every A_t. (b) Union 
R. (\subseteq) Every B_t is a set of reals. (\supseteq) Let x \in 
R. If x \le 0, take t \coloneqq 1 - x \ge 1: then -t = x - 1 < x, and 1/t > 0 \ge x, so x \in B_t. If x > 0, take t \coloneqq 1/(2x): then -t < 0 < x and 1/t = 2x > x, so x \in B_t. Intersection \{0\}. (\supseteq) For every t > 0, -t < 0 < 1/t. (\subseteq) Let x lie in every B_t. If x < 0, take t \coloneqq -x > 0: x \in B_t would need -t < x, that is, x < x. If x > 0, take t \coloneqq 1/x: x \in B_t would need x < 1/t = x. Both cases are impossible, so the remaining case of x < 0, x = 0, x > 0 holds: x = 0. (c) Union (0, \infty). (\subseteq) If t < x < 2t for some t > 0, then x > 0. (\supseteq) If x > 0, take t \coloneqq 2x/3: then t = 2x/3 < x and 2t = 4x/3 > x, so x \in C_t. Intersection \emptyset. Already two members are disjoint: C_1 = (1, 2) and C_2 = (2, 4) have no common element, since x < 2 and x > 2 cannot both hold. An element of every C_t would lie in both. In each union the witness t depends on the point x. In the intersections of (a) and (b) the index that excludes x depends on x too; in (c) two fixed disjoint members, C_1 and C_2, already exclude every x. All of these are allowed by the definitions. [B3: Canceling a union] Give sets A, B, C with A \cup B = A \cup C and B 
e C. Then list the properties that any correct answer must have, so that a different answer can be checked against them. Take A = \{1\}, B = \emptyset, C = \{1\}. Then A \cup B = \{1\} = A \cup C, and B 
e C, with the witness 1 \in C, 1 
otin B. Properties of any answer. Call an element odd one out if it lies in exactly one of B and C. - B 
e C holds exactly when there is at least one odd one out (by @def-set-equality; getting such an element from B 
e C uses the classical direction of quantifier negation, Logic and Proof, Chapter 4). - A \cup B = A \cup C holds exactly when every odd one out lies in A. Indeed, if x \in B \setminus C and x 
otin A, then x \in A \cup B but x 
otin A \cup C; symmetrically for x \in C \setminus B. Conversely, if every odd one out lies in A, then an element of A \cup B either lies in A, or lies in B and then, by excluded middle on x \in C (@fd1:prp-excluded-middle), in C or in A; so it lies in A \cup C, and symmetrically. So an answer is correct exactly when some element lies in exactly one of B, C, and every such element lies in A. The union with A “hides” the difference between B and C; the lesson is that \cup cannot be canceled. C. Going deeper [C1: Power sets and operations] Let A and B be sets. 1. Decide whether \powerset{A \setminus B} = \powerset{A} \setminus \powerset{B} can hold. Then prove that every non-empty element of \powerset{A \setminus B} lies in \powerset{A} \setminus \powerset{B}. 2. Show by an example that \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B} = \powerset{A \cup B} can fail. Then prove that it holds if and only if A \subseteq B or B \subseteq A. [Hint 1] In (a), test the empty set against both sides. In (b), one inclusion always holds; for the other, ask which subset of A \cup B could fail to be a subset of A and of B. [Hint 2] For (b) (\Rightarrow), argue by the contrapositive: if A 
ot\subseteq B and B 
ot\subseteq A, choose a \in A \setminus B and b \in B \setminus A. (a) Never. \emptyset \in \powerset{A \setminus B}, since \emptyset is a subset of every set. But \emptyset \in \powerset{B} as well, so \emptyset 
otin \powerset{A} \setminus \powerset{B}. The empty set is a witness for every A and B. Now let S \in \powerset{A \setminus B} be non-empty, and choose s \in S. Since S \subseteq A \setminus B \subseteq A, we have S \in \powerset{A}. Since s \in A \setminus B, s 
otin B; so s is an element of S outside B, and S 
ot\subseteq B, that is, S 
otin \powerset{B}. Hence S \in \powerset{A} \setminus \powerset{B}. (b) Failure. For A = \{1\}, B = \{2\}: \{1, 2\} \in \powerset{A \cup B}, but \{1, 2\} is a subset of neither A nor B, so \{1, 2\} 
otin \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B}. One inclusion always holds. If S \in \powerset{A}, then S \subseteq A \subseteq A \cup B (@prp-subset-transitive), so S \in \powerset{A \cup B}; likewise for S \in \powerset{B}. So \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B} \subseteq \powerset{A \cup B}. (\Leftarrow) Suppose A \subseteq B. Then A \cup B = B (if x \in A \cup B, then x \in A \subseteq B or x \in B; and B \subseteq A \cup B). Let S \in \powerset{A \cup B}. Then S \subseteq B, so S \in \powerset{B} \subseteq \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B}. With the inclusion above, equality holds. The case B \subseteq A is the same with A and B exchanged. (\Rightarrow) We prove the contrapositive. Suppose that neither A \subseteq B nor B \subseteq A. By the negation of \subseteq (@exr-sets-and-subsets-a1 (a) records it), there is a \in A with a 
otin B, and there is b \in B with b 
otin A; choose such a and b. Let S \coloneqq \{a, b\}. Then S \subseteq A \cup B, so S \in \powerset{A \cup B}. But S 
ot\subseteq A, because b \in S and b 
otin A; and S 
ot\subseteq B, because a \in S and a 
otin B. So S 
otin \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B}, and the two sets differ. Two steps here are classical: turning “A 
ot\subseteq B” into a witness uses the classical directions of quantifier negation and of the law for negated implications (Logic and Proof, Chapter 4; see @exr-sets-and-subsets-a1 (a)), and concluding the implication from its contrapositive is @fd1:prp-contrapositive-converse. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) the empty set as the witness that the equality never holds, with both memberships checked. - 2: (a) a non-empty S \subseteq A \setminus B is shown to lie in \powerset{A} and, via an element outside B, not in \powerset{B}. - 1: (b) a counterexample with the offending subset named. - 2: (b) the inclusion \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B} \subseteq \powerset{A \cup B} and the direction (\Leftarrow). - 3: (b) (\Rightarrow): witnesses a \in A \setminus B and b \in B \setminus A named, and \{a, b\} shown to lie in \powerset{A \cup B} and in neither \powerset{A} nor \powerset{B}. A direct proof also earns the 3: assume equality and A 
ot\subseteq B, fix a \in A \setminus B (1 point); for arbitrary b \in B, \{a, b\} \in \powerset{A \cup B} = \powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B}, and \{a, b\} 
ot\subseteq B because a 
otin B, so \{a, b\} \subseteq A and b \in A, giving B \subseteq A (2 points). Both routes also end with a classical step: excluded middle on A \subseteq B in the direct route, the contrapositive in the book’s. Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (a), testing only non-empty subsets and concluding equality; in (b) (\Rightarrow), in the contrapositive route, using one witness a for both failures, or a set such as \{a\} that lies in \powerset{A}. [C2: Find the error] Here is a “proof” that (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C) \subseteq A \cup (B \cap C) for all sets A, B, C. (1) Let x \in (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C). (2) Then x \in A \cup B and x \in A \cup C. (3) We consider two cases, according to x \in A \cup B. (4) Case x \in A. Then x \in A \cup (B \cap C). (5) Case x \in B. Since x \in A \cup C, x \in C. (6) So x \in B \cap C, and hence x \in A \cup (B \cap C). (7) In both cases x \in A \cup (B \cap C), which proves the inclusion. 1. Is the conclusion true? 2. Which line fails, which rule does it break, and which entry of the catalogue of Logic and Proof, Chapter 5 does it commit? 3. Give a counterexample to the illegal step itself: sets and an element for which the line’s premise holds and its conclusion fails. 4. Repair the proof. (a) Yes. It is the (\supseteq) half of the second distributive law of @thm-set-algebra (c). (b) Line (5). From x \in A \cup C, that is, x \in A or x \in C, it concludes x \in C, dropping the case x \in A. A disjunction is used by ulename{\vee E}, which needs both cases; the line uses only one. This is a missing case, entry (N7) of the catalogue of Logic and Proof, Chapter 5. (c) Take A = \{1\}, B = \{1\}, C = \emptyset, and x = 1. Then x \in B (the case of line (5)) and x \in A \cup C (the premise of the line), but x 
otin C. The step is illegal although the conclusion of the whole proof is true: here x \in A, so x \in A \cup (B \cap C) by the other case. (d) Replace lines (5)–(6) by: Case x \in B. Since x \in A \cup C, there are two sub-cases. If x \in A, then x \in A \cup (B \cap C). If x \in C, then x \in B \cap C, so x \in A \cup (B \cap C). In both sub-cases x \in A \cup (B \cap C). The rest of the proof stands.

title: 1.3 Ordered Pairs, Products and Relations
content:
Ordered Pairs, Products and Relations Sections 1.1 and 1.2 built sets and combined them: a set is fixed by its elements, and \cup, \cap, \setminus are \vee, \wedge, \wedge
eg read through membership. None of this can yet say “the point (1, 2) of the plane”, “3 is less than 5”, or “y is the square of x”. Each of these is about two objects in a given order, and a set forgets order. This section adds one new kind of object, the ordered pair (with its longer versions, the n-tuples), and then uses it twice: to build the product A 	imes B of two sets, and to say what a relation between two sets is. The next section needs exactly this much: a function will be given by a relation of a special kind, its graph, together with a declared target set. Order matters: ordered pairs A set remembers which objects are its elements and nothing else. By extensionality (@def-set-equality), \{1, 2\} = \{2, 1\}, since both sets have the elements 1 and 2; and \{1, 1\} = \{1\}, since both have the element 1 and nothing else. For a set that is exactly right. For a point of the plane it is exactly wrong. The point (1, 2) lies one unit to the right of the vertical axis and two units above the horizontal one; the point (2, 1) lies elsewhere. And the point (1, 1) on the diagonal is a perfectly good point, with the same number in both places. So we need an object built from two objects a and b that remembers which came first, and that still has two places when a = b. What we need to know about such an object is one fact: when two of them are equal. An ordered pair is equal to another exactly when they agree in the first place and in the second place. [Ordered pair] For any objects a and b there is an object (a, b), the ordered pair of a and b; we call a its first coordinate and b its second coordinate. Ordered pairs have the characteristic property: for all a, b, c, d, (a, b) = (c, d) \iff a = c 	ext{ and } b = d . In words: to decide whether two pairs are equal, compare first coordinates with first coordinates and second with second; nothing else matters, and both comparisons must succeed. The direction (\Leftarrow) is nothing new: equal inputs give equal pairs, as for any construction (ulename{=E}, @fd1:def-rules-equality). The direction (\Rightarrow) is the content. It says that from the pair we can read off its coordinates, each in its place. We do not say here what the object (a, b) is. Besides the characteristic property, we use one working convention: pairs and n-tuples are a different kind of object from numbers, just as sets are (Section 1.1), so a pair is not a number; and tuples of different lengths are different kinds of object, so a triple is not a pair. Nothing else about pairs is used in this chapter. The optional Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 1 shows that a pair with this property can be built from sets alone, so that nothing new has to be assumed. Until then, the existence of pairs with this property is taken as given, alongside the working rules (W1)–(W6) of Section 1.1. A convention about parentheses. The symbol (a, b) now has two meanings. For real numbers a < b it is also the open interval \{ x \in 
R : a < x < b \}. The book keeps both, and context decides, as it does in every analysis text. In “(0, 1) contains 	frac{1}{2}” it is an interval. In “the point (0, 1) lies on the unit circle” it is a pair. Where both readings are near each other, the text says which is meant. This convention is stated once, here. [Solving an equation between pairs] Find all real numbers x and y with (x + y, x - y) = (3, 1). Then decide whether (1, 2) = (2, 1) and whether (1, 1) = (1, 1). By the characteristic property, (x + y, x - y) = (3, 1) holds if and only if x + y = 3 \quad 	ext{and} \quad x - y = 1 . Adding the two equations gives 2x = 4, so x = 2; subtracting them gives 2y = 2, so y = 1. Conversely, x = 2 and y = 1 give (x + y, x - y) = (3, 1). So there is exactly one solution, x = 2, y = 1. The pairs (1, 2) and (2, 1) are not equal. If they were, the characteristic property would give 1 = 2 for the first coordinates. So (1, 2) 
e (2, 1), by ulename{
eg I}. The same test on (1, 1) and (1, 1) passes in both places, so they are equal; and (1, 1) has two places, although both hold the same number. The first part is typical. One equation between pairs is two equations between coordinates, and this is how pairs are used: an equation of pairs is split by the characteristic property, and the coordinates are compared one at a time. Nonexample by minimal change. Replace the parentheses by braces. The set \{1, 2\} has the same two numbers as the pair (1, 2), but the characteristic property fails for sets: \{1, 2\} = \{2, 1\}, and yet 1 
e 2. What survives is membership: 1 and 2 are both in \{1, 2\}. What is lost is order, the one thing the pair was made to keep. Why this definition. Only (\Rightarrow) carries content. Without it, the pair could forget its coordinates, as \{1, 2\} forgets which number came first. The direction (\Leftarrow) could be dropped from the definition without loss: ulename{=E} already gives it for (a, b), as for any construction. It is stated so that the property reads as a single test for equality of pairs. Longer lists. The same idea gives ordered triples (a, b, c), and more generally ordered n-tuples (x_1, \dots, x_n) for n \in 
N, n \ge 2. Like pairs, n-tuples are taken as given, and the n-tuples with all coordinates in a set form a set, by the working rule (W5) of Section 1.1. Two n-tuples are equal if and only if they agree in every place: (x_1, \dots, x_n) = (y_1, \dots, y_n) means x_k = y_k for every k \in \{1, \dots, n\}. A triple is a new kind of object, not a pair whose first coordinate is a pair (by the convention stated after @def-ordered-pair). The pairs ((1, 2), 3) and (1, (2, 3)) carry the same three numbers in the same order, and it is tempting to call both “the triple (1, 2, 3)”; that is an identification made by convention, and exercise A1 asks whether the two pairs are equal. For which real numbers t is (t^2, t) = (1, -1)? For which is \{t^2, t\} = \{1, -1\}? The pair equation holds if and only if t^2 = 1 and t = -1, so exactly for t = -1. The set equation holds for t = -1 too, since \{1, -1\} = \{1, -1\}. It holds for no other t: the element -1 of the right side must be t^2 or t, and t^2 \ge 0, so t = -1. Here the sets agree exactly where the pairs do, but that is luck. The pair equation (t, 1) = (1, t) holds only for t = 1, while the set equation \{t, 1\} = \{1, t\} holds for every t. Cartesian products With pairs in hand, the plane is the set of all pairs of real numbers. More generally, from any two sets we can collect all pairs whose first coordinate comes from the first set and whose second comes from the second. Taking such a collection is the working rule (W5) of Section 1.1: it is a set. [Cartesian product] Let A and B be sets. Their Cartesian product is the set A 	imes B \coloneqq \{ (a, b) : a \in A, \ b \in B \} of all ordered pairs with first coordinate in A and second coordinate in B. Written out, an object p is an element of A 	imes B if and only if \exists a \in A \ \exists b \in B \ \ p = (a, b) . For a set X we write X^2 \coloneqq X 	imes X, and, for n \in 
N with n \ge 2, X^n is the set of all n-tuples (x_1, \dots, x_n) with every x_k \in X. In words: an element of A 	imes B is a pair, and there exist coordinates, one in A and one in B, from which it is made. The membership condition hides two existential quantifiers, so using it means naming the coordinates, by ulename{\exists E} (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-rules), and then matching them against any other naming by the characteristic property of pairs. That two-step move is the one move of this section; (\ast) below packages it. For a pair the condition simplifies, and we use the simpler form constantly: (x, y) \in A 	imes B \iff x \in A 	ext{ and } y \in B . 	ag{$\ast$} Here is why. If x \in A and y \in B, then x and y themselves are coordinates of the required kind, and (x, y) \in A 	imes B by ulename{\exists I}. Conversely, let (x, y) \in A 	imes B. Then there are a \in A and b \in B with (x, y) = (a, b) [ulename{\exists E}], and the characteristic property (@def-ordered-pair) gives x = a and y = b. So x \in A and y \in B. The characteristic property is used exactly once, in the direction (\Rightarrow); without it, (x, y) might equal (a, b) with the coordinates swapped or lost, and nothing could be concluded. We write (\ast) for this equivalence in the rest of the section. It is the reason a product is easy to work with: membership of a pair in a product is checked one coordinate at a time. Set-builders with a pair pattern. We write \{ (x, y) \in A 	imes B : P(x, y) \} for \{ p \in A 	imes B : 	ext{there are } x, y 	ext{ with } p = (x, y) 	ext{ and } P(x, y) \}, a set-builder in the sense of @def-set-builder. By (\ast) and the characteristic property, (x, y) belongs to it if and only if x \in A, y \in B and P(x, y). The notation \{ (a, b) : a \in A, \ b \in B \} in @def-cartesian-product is different: it names no ambient set, so it is not a set-builder. It is notation for the set that (W5) provides, and the displayed membership condition is its definition. [Products, small and large] (a) Let a, b, c be three different objects, none of them a number. List \{1, 2\} 	imes \{a, b, c\} and \{a, b, c\} 	imes \{1, 2\}. (b) Describe 
R^2 and [0, 1] 	imes [0, 1] as sets of points of the plane. (c) What is \{1, 2\} 	imes \emptyset? (a) Each of the 2 first coordinates is paired with each of the 3 second coordinates: \{1, 2\} 	imes \{a, b, c\} = \{ (1, a), (1, b), (1, c), (2, a), (2, b), (2, c) \}, six pairs, all different by the characteristic property, since 1 
e 2 and a, b, c are different. Swapping the factors gives the six pairs (a, 1), (a, 2), (b, 1), (b, 2), (c, 1), (c, 2). No pair of the first list is in the second: every pair in the first list has a number as its first coordinate, and every pair in the second list has one of a, b, c there, none of which is a number; so by the characteristic property no pair of one list equals a pair of the other. (b) 
R^2 = 
R 	imes 
R is the set of all pairs (x, y) of real numbers: the plane, with x the horizontal and y the vertical coordinate. By (\ast), (x, y) \in [0, 1] 	imes [0, 1] if and only if 0 \le x \le 1 and 0 \le y \le 1: the closed unit square, with its four sides. (c) It is empty. An element p would be (a, b) with b \in \emptyset, and \emptyset has no elements. So \{1, 2\} 	imes \emptyset has no elements, and a set with no elements is \emptyset (@prp-empty-set-unique). Part (c) is the degenerate case, and it matters: a product is empty as soon as one factor is. The general statement is part of the next proposition. List \{0, 1\} 	imes \{0, 1, 2\}. Is (1, 1) \in \{1\} 	imes \emptyset? \{0, 1\} 	imes \{0, 1, 2\} = \{ (0, 0), (0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 0), (1, 1), (1, 2) \}, six pairs. And (1, 1) 
otin \{1\} 	imes \emptyset: by (\ast) it would need 1 \in \emptyset. In fact \{1\} 	imes \emptyset has no elements at all, as in part (c) of the example. The product is not commutative: A 	imes B and B 	imes A are in general different sets. For A = \{1\} and B = \{2\}, A 	imes B = \{(1, 2)\} and B 	imes A = \{(2, 1)\}, and (1, 2) 
e (2, 1) by @exm-pair-equations. The two products have “the same size”, but they do not have the same elements. (They are equal when A = B, and when one of the sets is empty. Exercise C2 finds exactly when even the inclusion A 	imes B \subseteq B 	imes A holds.) Products and the set operations Section 1.2 showed that \cup, \cap, and \setminus obey the laws of \vee, \wedge, and \wedge 
eg. The product interacts with them just as simply, one factor at a time. We use these laws for regions of the plane (exercise B1) and for functions out of the empty set (Section 1.4), so we state them all. [Products and Set Operations] For all sets A, B, C:  egin{aligned} A 	imes (B \cup C) &= (A 	imes B) \cup (A 	imes C), \ A 	imes (B \cap C) &= (A 	imes B) \cap (A 	imes C), \ A 	imes (B \setminus C) &= (A 	imes B) \setminus (A 	imes C), \ A 	imes \emptyset &= \emptyset, \end{aligned} and the mirror-image laws, with the varying factor on the left:  egin{aligned} (B \cup C) 	imes A &= (B 	imes A) \cup (C 	imes A), \ (B \cap C) 	imes A &= (B 	imes A) \cap (C 	imes A), \ (B \setminus C) 	imes A &= (B 	imes A) \setminus (C 	imes A), \ \emptyset 	imes A &= \emptyset . \end{aligned} Every element of each side is a pair, so we name its coordinates by ulename{\exists E} and then test membership one coordinate at a time, by (\ast). The first coordinate lies in A on both sides; the second lies in B \cup C on one side and in “B or C” on the other, which is the same condition by @def-set-operations. Each law is a law of Section 1.2 in the second coordinate, with the first coordinate carried along unchanged. The \cup law. We prove two inclusions and conclude by @prp-subset-antisymmetric. (\subseteq) Let p \in A 	imes (B \cup C). By @def-cartesian-product there are a \in A and d \in B \cup C with p = (a, d) [\( ulename{\exists E} \) (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-rules), with fresh names \( a \), \( d \)]. By @def-set-operations, d \in B or d \in C, and we argue by cases. If d \in B, then p = (a, d) \in A 	imes B by (\ast), so p \in (A 	imes B) \cup (A 	imes C). If d \in C, then likewise p \in A 	imes C \subseteq (A 	imes B) \cup (A 	imes C). In either case p \in (A 	imes B) \cup (A 	imes C). (\supseteq) Let p \in (A 	imes B) \cup (A 	imes C). Then p \in A 	imes B or p \in A 	imes C. If p \in A 	imes B, there are a \in A and b \in B with p = (a, b) [ulename{\exists E}]; since b \in B \subseteq B \cup C, (\ast) gives p \in A 	imes (B \cup C). If p \in A 	imes C, the same argument with C in place of B gives p \in A 	imes (B \cup C). The \cap law. Let p \in A 	imes (B \cap C), so p = (a, d) with a \in A and d \in B \cap C. Then d \in B and d \in C, and (\ast) gives p \in A 	imes B and p \in A 	imes C. Conversely, let p \in (A 	imes B) \cap (A 	imes C). Since p \in A 	imes B, p = (a, b) with a \in A and b \in B. Since also (a, b) = p \in A 	imes C, (\ast) gives b \in C. So b \in B \cap C, and p = (a, b) \in A 	imes (B \cap C). The \setminus law. Let p \in A 	imes (B \setminus C), so p = (a, d) with a \in A, d \in B, and d 
otin C. Then p \in A 	imes B by (\ast). If p were in A 	imes C, then (\ast) would give d \in C, which is false; so p 
otin A 	imes C, and p \in (A 	imes B) \setminus (A 	imes C). Conversely, let p \in (A 	imes B) \setminus (A 	imes C). Then p = (a, b) with a \in A and b \in B, and p 
otin A 	imes C. If b were in C, then (\ast) would give p = (a, b) \in A 	imes C, which is false; so b 
otin C. Hence b \in B \setminus C and p \in A 	imes (B \setminus C). The \emptyset law. An element of A 	imes \emptyset would be a pair (a, b) with b \in \emptyset, and there is no such b. So A 	imes \emptyset has no elements, and it equals \emptyset by @prp-empty-set-unique. The mirror-image laws. The same four arguments, with the roles of the two coordinates exchanged throughout, prove them: the varying set now sits in the first coordinate, and (\ast) is applied to it there. This proves the proposition. The proofs of the \setminus law do not use excluded middle: both “
otin” conclusions are reached by assuming membership and deriving a contradiction, which is ulename{
eg I}. Only the first law was written with every ulename{\exists E} marked; from here on, “p = (a, b) with a \in A and b \in B” is understood to name fresh coordinates. A proof about products usually runs like the one above: take an element, write it as a pair with named coordinates, and work coordinatewise. Here is the pattern on concrete sets. [Two rectangles] Show that ([0, 2] 	imes [0, 1]) \cap ([1, 3] 	imes [0, 2]) = [1, 2] 	imes [0, 1]. Draw the two rectangles first: the first is 2 wide and 1 high, with its lower left corner at the origin; the second is 2 wide and 2 high, with its lower left corner at (1, 0). They overlap in the rectangle over [1, 2] of height 1. Now the proof, by two inclusions. (\subseteq) Let p be in the intersection. Since p \in [0, 2] 	imes [0, 1], p = (x, y) with 0 \le x \le 2 and 0 \le y \le 1. Since also (x, y) = p \in [1, 3] 	imes [0, 2], (\ast) gives 1 \le x \le 3 and 0 \le y \le 2. Together, 1 \le x \le 2 and 0 \le y \le 1, so p = (x, y) \in [1, 2] 	imes [0, 1] by (\ast). (\supseteq) Let p \in [1, 2] 	imes [0, 1], so p = (x, y) with 1 \le x \le 2 and 0 \le y \le 1. Then 0 \le x \le 2, so p \in [0, 2] 	imes [0, 1]; and 1 \le x \le 3, 0 \le y \le 2, so p \in [1, 3] 	imes [0, 2]. Hence p is in the intersection. By @prp-subset-antisymmetric, the two sets are equal. The picture found the answer; the element-chase proved it. The degenerate law of the proposition deserves a second look, because it is easy to misuse. Combining the two \emptyset laws with one more step gives the full description of an empty product: A 	imes B = \emptyset if and only if A = \emptyset or B = \emptyset. The direction (\Leftarrow) is the pair of \emptyset laws. For (\Rightarrow), suppose A 	imes B = \emptyset. If A has an element a and B has an element b, then (a, b) \in A 	imes B = \emptyset, which is impossible. So it is not the case that both sets have an element; by excluded middle (@fd1:prp-excluded-middle) applied to “A has an element”, either A has none, and then A = \emptyset by @prp-empty-set-unique, or A has one, and then B has none, so B = \emptyset. “A 	imes B = \emptyset, so A = \emptyset” misses a case. The product \{1, 2\} 	imes \emptyset is empty, and \{1, 2\} is not. The correct conclusion is the disjunction “A = \emptyset or B = \emptyset” of the remark, and an argument that continues from it must treat both cases. Dropping one is the missing case of the catalogue in Logic and Proof, Chapter 5, entry (N7): a ulename{\vee E} with one of its boxes left out. Relations “Is less than”, “divides”, “is the square of”, “lies on the unit circle with”: each of these connects an object of one set with an object of another, or of the same set. Each can be described by a rule, a formula, or a sentence. But two different descriptions can pick out exactly the same connections: “x < y” and “y - x > 0” are different sentences about real numbers, and they hold for exactly the same pairs (x, y). In mathematics we want these to count as the same relation. The way to make them the same is to forget the description and keep what it picks out: the set of pairs (x, y) for which it holds. Two descriptions that pick out the same pairs then give the same set, by extensionality. A relation is the set of pairs it relates. [Relation] Let A and B be sets. A relation from A to B is a subset R \subseteq A 	imes B. For a \in A and b \in B we write a \mathrel{R} b, read “a is R-related to b”, to mean (a, b) \in R. A relation on A is a relation from A to A, that is, a subset of A^2. The domain of R is the set of first coordinates that occur, \{ a \in A : \exists b \in B \ \ a \mathrel{R} b \}, and its range is the set of second coordinates that occur, \{ b \in B : \exists a \in A \ \ a \mathrel{R} b \}. Turning every pair of R around gives a relation from B to A, the inverse relation R^{-1} \coloneqq \{ (b, a) \in B 	imes A : (a, b) \in R \} . In words: a relation is a set, namely a set of pairs whose coordinates come from the two given sets. The notation a \mathrel{R} b is only a way of writing “(a, b) \in R” that reads like “a < b”. The domain collects the elements of A that are related to at least one element of B; the range collects those of B that something is related to. The inverse relation turns each pair around: b \mathrel{R^{-1}} a exactly when a \mathrel{R} b. Two relations are equal exactly when they relate the same pairs, since relations are sets (@def-set-equality). So the relation “x < y” on 
R and the relation “y - x > 0” on 
R are one relation, as we wanted. That is the whole reason for the definition: a relation is determined by what it relates, not by how it is described. [Relations as sets of pairs] Write each relation as a set, and find its domain and range. (a) The relation < on \{1, 2, 3\}. (b) Divisibility on \{1, \dots, 6\}: a \mathrel{D} b when a \mid b. (c) The unit circle, as a relation on 
R. (d) The graph of squaring, as a relation on 
R. (e) The two extreme relations from A to B: \emptyset and A 	imes B. (a) The pairs (a, b) of elements of \{1, 2, 3\} with a < b are L \coloneqq \{ (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3) \} , three of the nine elements of \{1, 2, 3\}^2. Its domain is \{1, 2\}, since nothing in the set is larger than 3; its range is \{2, 3\}, since nothing is smaller than 1. (b) Write a \mid b when b = ak for some integer k. For each first coordinate a, the second coordinates b \in \{1, \dots, 6\} with a \mid b are the multiples of a up to 6: a the b \in \{1, \dots, 6\} with a \mid b --- ----------------------------------------- 1 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 2 2, 4, 6 3 3, 6 4 4 5 5 6 6 So D has 6 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 14 elements, the pairs (a, b) read off the rows. Its domain and range are both all of \{1, \dots, 6\}, because every a divides itself: (a, a) \in D. (c) The unit circle is S \coloneqq \{ (x, y) \in 
R^2 : x^2 + y^2 = 1 \} , a relation on 
R; for instance 0 \mathrel{S} 1, 0 \mathrel{S} (-1), and 1 \mathrel{S} 0. Its domain is [-1, 1]. If x \mathrel{S} y, then x^2 = 1 - y^2 \le 1, so -1 \le x \le 1. Conversely, for -1 \le x \le 1 the number 1 - x^2 is nonnegative and so has a square root y = \sqrt{1 - x^2}, which satisfies x^2 + y^2 = 1. By the symmetry of the equation, the range is [-1, 1] too. (d) The graph of squaring is Q \coloneqq \{ (x, y) \in 
R^2 : y = x^2 \}. Its domain is all of 
R: every x is related to x^2. Its range is [0, \infty): a square is nonnegative, and every y \ge 0 is the square of \sqrt{y}. (e) Both are subsets of A 	imes B, so both are relations. The empty relation \emptyset relates nothing, and its domain and range are empty. The full relation A 	imes B relates everything to everything. If A and B both have elements, its domain is A and its range is B. The circle and the graph of squaring look alike, both being curves in the plane, but they differ in a way that the next section makes precise. In Q every x is related to exactly one y. In S the number 0 is related to two numbers, 1 and -1, and the number 2 to none. A relation of the first kind will be the graph of a function. Write the inverse relation L^{-1} of part (a) as a set. Which familiar relation on \{1, 2, 3\} is it? Turning each pair of L around gives L^{-1} = \{ (2, 1), (3, 1), (3, 2) \}: the pairs (b, a) with b > a. So L^{-1} is the relation > on \{1, 2, 3\}. Its domain \{2, 3\} is the range of L, and its range \{1, 2\} is the domain of L. Nonexample by minimal change. The set \{ (1, 2), (2, 3), 3 \} looks like the relation “is one less than” on \{1, 2, 3\}, with one pair damaged. It is not a relation on \{1, 2, 3\}: the element 3 is a number, not a pair (the convention after @def-ordered-pair), so the set is not a subset of \{1, 2, 3\}^2. Remove the 3, or replace it by the pair (3, 4) and enlarge the second set to \{1, 2, 3, 4\}, and it becomes a relation. The clause that failed is “R \subseteq A 	imes B”: every element of a relation must be a pair with coordinates in the right sets. Why this definition. A relation could be defined as a rule, a sentence, or a formula. Each of those raises the question of when two rules are “the same”, and that question has no good answer: “x < y” and “y - x > 0” are different sentences. The definition as a set answers it by extensionality. The price is small: a relation may be any set of pairs whatever, such as \{ (1, 3), (2, 2) \} on \{1, 2, 3\}, and the definition never asks for a rule that produces it. That is a gain, not a loss: in analysis we meet relations and functions that no formula describes. A relation “from A to B” has its direction built in: R \subseteq A 	imes B, and the first coordinate comes from A. The relation L of part (a) contains (1, 2) and not (2, 1). Reading a relation backwards, “since 1 \mathrel{L} 2, also 2 \mathrel{L} 1”, treats it as a symmetric relation; relations with that property, and other properties such as transitivity, are studied in Chapter 2. Relating b to a is the job of the inverse relation R^{-1}, a different set. This definition is all the next section needs. The graph of a function from X to Y will be a relation from X to Y in which every element of X is related to exactly one element of Y; the function is that graph together with the declared codomain Y. The graph Q qualifies and the circle S does not. The properties that make a relation an order or an equivalence (reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive) are the subject of Chapter 2. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define A 	imes B in symbols, with its membership condition written out using quantifiers. 2. Is ((1, 2), 3) = (1, (2, 3))? Justify your answer. 3. Write the inverse of the relation < on \{1, 2, 3\} as a set of pairs. 4. Is \emptyset a relation on every set A? Justify your answer. (a) A 	imes B = \{ (a, b) : a \in A, \ b \in B \}; that is, p \in A 	imes B if and only if \exists a \in A \ \exists b \in B \ \ p = (a, b) (@def-cartesian-product). (b) No. Both are ordered pairs, so by the characteristic property (@def-ordered-pair) they are equal if and only if their first coordinates are equal and their second coordinates are equal. The first coordinates are the pair (1, 2) and the number 1. A pair is not a number, by the working convention stated after @def-ordered-pair (the optional Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 1, which builds both from sets, bears it out). So the first coordinates differ, and the pairs are not equal. Calling both “the triple (1, 2, 3)” is an identification made by convention, not an equality. (c) \{ (2, 1), (3, 1), (3, 2) \}, which is the relation > on \{1, 2, 3\}. (d) Yes. A relation on A is a subset of A 	imes A, and \emptyset \subseteq A 	imes A: the condition “x \in \emptyset 	o x \in A 	imes A” holds for every x, because its hypothesis is false (@fd1:prp-vacuous-implication, @def-subset). B. Practice [B1: An L-shaped region] Let E \coloneqq ([0, 1] 	imes [0, 2]) \cup ([1, 2] 	imes [0, 1]). Describe E as a region of the plane. Then use @prp-product-set-laws to write E as ([0, 2] 	imes [0, 1]) \cup (P 	imes Q) for intervals P and Q, and prove the equality. The first rectangle is 1 wide and 2 high, standing on the origin; the second is 1 wide and 1 high, standing on [1, 2]. Together they form an “L”: a bottom strip [0, 2] 	imes [0, 1] of width 2, with a square [0, 1] 	imes [1, 2] on top of its left half. So we expect P = [0, 1] and Q = [1, 2]. Now the proof. Since [0, 2] = [0, 1] \cup [1, 2], the first law of @prp-product-set-laws gives [0, 1] 	imes [0, 2] = ([0, 1] 	imes [0, 1]) \cup ([0, 1] 	imes [1, 2]) , and the mirror-image \cup law gives [0, 2] 	imes [0, 1] = ([0, 1] 	imes [0, 1]) \cup ([1, 2] 	imes [0, 1]) . Substituting the first equation into the definition of E and regrouping the unions (\cup is commutative and associative by @thm-set-algebra),  egin{aligned} E &= ([0, 1] 	imes [0, 1]) \cup ([0, 1] 	imes [1, 2]) \cup ([1, 2] 	imes [0, 1]) \ &= ([0, 2] 	imes [0, 1]) \cup ([0, 1] 	imes [1, 2]), \end{aligned} where the second line uses the mirror-image equation. So P = [0, 1] and Q = [1, 2]. (The equality [0, 2] = [0, 1] \cup [1, 2] is an order fact: 0 \le x \le 2 holds exactly when 0 \le x \le 1 or 1 \le x \le 2.) [B2: The intersection law, written with two pairs] Here is a proof of the inclusion (\supseteq) of A 	imes (B \cap C) = (A 	imes B) \cap (A 	imes C) that works from the definition of the product and the characteristic property directly, without the shortcut (\ast). Its last sentence is blank. Name the move, then complete it. Let p \in (A 	imes B) \cap (A 	imes C). Since p \in A 	imes B, there are a \in A and b \in B with p = (a, b). Since p \in A 	imes C, there are a' \in A and c \in C with p = (a', c); the names a' and c are new, because nothing says that this second pair of coordinates is the first one again. Hence (a, b) = (a', c). \underline{\hspace{8em}} The move is the second half of the section’s move, the characteristic property of pairs (@def-ordered-pair) in the direction (\Rightarrow). An equation between pairs splits into equations between coordinates. The completed last sentence: By the characteristic property, a = a' and b = c; so b \in B and b = c \in C, hence b \in B \cap C, and p = (a, b) \in A 	imes (B \cap C). The names a' and c had to be fresh (a second ulename{\exists E} may not reuse the names of the first), and the characteristic property is what shows, afterwards, that the two namings name the same coordinates. The proof of @prp-product-set-laws took the same step through (\ast), which packages exactly this use of the characteristic property. [B3: Two products crossed] Prove that (A 	imes B) \cap (B 	imes A) = (A \cap B) 	imes (A \cap B) for all sets A and B. We prove two inclusions and conclude by @prp-subset-antisymmetric. (\subseteq) Let p \in (A 	imes B) \cap (B 	imes A). Since p \in A 	imes B, p = (x, y) with x \in A and y \in B. Since also (x, y) = p \in B 	imes A, (\ast) gives x \in B and y \in A. So x \in A \cap B and y \in A \cap B, and p = (x, y) \in (A \cap B) 	imes (A \cap B) by (\ast). (\supseteq) Let p \in (A \cap B) 	imes (A \cap B), so p = (x, y) with x, y \in A \cap B. Then x \in A and y \in B, so p \in A 	imes B; and x \in B and y \in A, so p \in B 	imes A. Hence p \in (A 	imes B) \cap (B 	imes A). C. Going deeper [C1: The square of a union] 1. Determine whether (A \cup B) 	imes (A \cup B) = (A 	imes A) \cup (B 	imes B) for all sets A and B. Justify your answer. 2. Prove the inclusion (A 	imes A) \cup (B 	imes B) \subseteq (A \cup B) 	imes (A \cup B). 3. Prove, from @prp-product-set-laws, that (A \cup B) 	imes (A \cup B) = (A 	imes A) \cup (A 	imes B) \cup (B 	imes A) \cup (B 	imes B) . (a) No. Take A = \{1\} and B = \{2\}. Then (1, 2) \in \{1, 2\} 	imes \{1, 2\} = (A \cup B) 	imes (A \cup B). But (A 	imes A) \cup (B 	imes B) = \{ (1, 1), (2, 2) \}, and (1, 2) is neither (1, 1) nor (2, 2), since in each case the second (or first) coordinates differ. So the two sets are different. (b) Let p \in (A 	imes A) \cup (B 	imes B). If p \in A 	imes A, then p = (x, y) with x, y \in A; so x, y \in A \cup B, and p \in (A \cup B) 	imes (A \cup B) by (\ast). If p \in B 	imes B, the same argument with B in place of A applies. In either case p \in (A \cup B) 	imes (A \cup B). (c) The mirror-image \cup law, with A \cup B as the fixed factor on the right, gives (A \cup B) 	imes (A \cup B) =  igl(A 	imes (A \cup B) igr) \cup  igl(B 	imes (A \cup B) igr) . The first \cup law, applied to each of the two products, gives A 	imes (A \cup B) = (A 	imes A) \cup (A 	imes B), \qquad B 	imes (A \cup B) = (B 	imes A) \cup (B 	imes B) . Substituting, and using that \cup is associative (@thm-set-algebra), so that no brackets are needed, gives the formula. Part (a)’s counterexample is the term A 	imes B at work: (1, 2) \in A 	imes B. [C2: When one inclusion forces equality] Let A and B be sets. Prove that A 	imes B \subseteq B 	imes A if and only if A = B or A = \emptyset or B = \emptyset. [Hint 1] For (\Rightarrow), the empty cases are easy, so assume both sets have elements. To show A \subseteq B, you need to test an element a \in A; put it into a pair that is sure to lie in A 	imes B. [Hint 2] Fix b_0 \in B. For a \in A, the pair (a, b_0) lies in A 	imes B. (\Leftarrow) If A = B, then A 	imes B = B 	imes A, and in particular A 	imes B \subseteq B 	imes A. If A = \emptyset, then A 	imes B = \emptyset by @prp-product-set-laws, and \emptyset is a subset of every set. If B = \emptyset, likewise A 	imes B = A 	imes \emptyset = \emptyset. (\Rightarrow) Suppose A 	imes B \subseteq B 	imes A. By excluded middle (@fd1:prp-excluded-middle), each of A and B either has an element or has none, and a set with no elements is \emptyset (@prp-empty-set-unique). If A = \emptyset or B = \emptyset, we are done. In the remaining case both have elements: fix a_0 \in A and b_0 \in B (ulename{\exists E} twice, with fresh names). A \subseteq B. Let a \in A. Then (a, b_0) \in A 	imes B by (\ast), so (a, b_0) \in B 	imes A by the hypothesis. By (\ast) again, a \in B (and b_0 \in A). B \subseteq A. Let b \in B. Then (a_0, b) \in A 	imes B \subseteq B 	imes A, and (\ast) gives b \in A (and a_0 \in B). By @prp-subset-antisymmetric, A = B. This proves the equivalence. Both witnesses are needed. With B = \emptyset there is no b_0, and indeed then A 	imes B \subseteq B 	imes A holds for every A, including A 
e B: the inclusion \{1\} 	imes \emptyset \subseteq \emptyset 	imes \{1\} is \emptyset \subseteq \emptyset. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (\Leftarrow): all three cases, including that an empty factor makes A 	imes B empty and hence a subset of anything. - 2: (\Rightarrow): splits off the empty cases and, in the remaining case, names witnesses a_0 \in A and b_0 \in B. - 2: A \subseteq B, through a pair (a, b_0) with an arbitrary a \in A. - 2: B \subseteq A, through a pair (a_0, b) with an arbitrary b \in B. - 2: uses the characteristic property (directly or through (\ast)) to read the coordinates off a pair of B 	imes A, and concludes A = B by two inclusions. Fatal errors (0 for the step): testing inclusion on particular elements only (entry (N1) of Logic and Proof, Chapter 5’s catalogue); using b_0 without having shown that B has an element; concluding A = B from A 	imes B = B 	imes A “by canceling” without an element argument. A proof of (\Rightarrow) by contraposition (assume A 
e B and both nonempty, and exhibit a pair of A 	imes B outside B 	imes A) earns full marks if it finds the pair: 2 points for the witnesses and 4 for the pair and the check that it is outside B 	imes A, in place of the two inclusions.

title: 1.4 Functions, Composition, Injections and Surjections
content:
Functions, Composition, Injections and Surjections Section 1.3 made “the pairs a description picks out” into a set: a relation from A to B is a subset of A 	imes B. Among its examples, the graph of squaring relates each real number to exactly one number, and the unit circle relates 0 to two numbers and 2 to none. This section gives the first kind its name, function, and builds the rest on it: we restrict functions, use them to make families, sequences and the set Y^X precise, compose them, and ask the two questions that the rest of the chapter turns on: does a function send different inputs to different outputs, and does it reach every point of its target? What is a function? Everyone has used functions since school, and the everyday definition is “a rule that assigns to each input one output”. Look at the word “rule”. The rules x \mapsto x^2 and x \mapsto (x + 1)^2 - 2x - 1 are different: one squares, the other adds, squares, subtracts, and subtracts again. Yet on every real number they give the same answer, and nobody would call them different functions. Other functions have no rule at all that one could write down. A table of measured temperatures, one per day, assigns to each day one number, and no formula produces it. So the rule is not what matters. What matters is which output goes with which input: the set of input–output pairs. That set is a relation, and Section 1.3 said exactly when two relations are the same, namely when they contain the same pairs. So we forget the rule and keep the pairs. One more piece of data is needed, the set in which the outputs are declared to lie; the reason is given after the definition. A function is its graph, with a declared target. [Function] Let X and Y be sets. A function from X to Y, written f \colon X 	o Y, is given by a relation G \subseteq X 	imes Y, the graph of f, such that 	ext{for every } x \in X 	ext{ there is exactly one } y \in Y 	ext{ with } (x, y) \in G , together with the set Y, the codomain of f. Formally, f is the pair (G, Y). The set X is the domain of f. For x \in X, the unique y with (x, y) \in G is written f(x), the value of f at x. We write (x, y) \in f for (x, y) \in G, and x \mapsto f(x) for the whole function when its domain and codomain are clear. In symbols, the condition on the graph is  orall x \in X \ \ \exists! \, y \in Y \ \ (x, y) \in G , where, as with the bounded quantifiers of @fd1:def-bounded-quantifier, \exists! \, y \in Y \ \psi abbreviates \exists! \, y \, (y \in Y \wedge \psi). The whole definition is the quantifier pattern  orall \exists!. By @fd1:def-unique-existence, “\exists! \, y” is an existence claim and a uniqueness claim, and by @fd1:prp-unique-existence-use the uniqueness claim may be stated without reference to the witness; so the condition on the graph is two clauses: - (Fn1) (existence) for every x \in X there is at least one y \in Y with (x, y) \in G: every input has an output; - (Fn2) (uniqueness) for every x \in X and all y, y' \in Y, if (x, y) \in G and (x, y') \in G, then y = y': no input has two outputs. In words: the graph is a set of input–output pairs, with inputs from X and outputs from Y; (Fn1) says no input is left without an output, and (Fn2) says no input is given two. The codomain Y is where outputs are allowed to lie. It need not consist of outputs: x \mapsto x^2 can be declared as a function from 
R to

e 3. Surjective: the codomain has two points, and a = h(1), b = h(2). For a finite codomain, checking every point is a proof: the instances are all the cases. (d) Injective: the two inputs have the different outputs a 
e c, and there are no other pairs of different inputs to check. Not surjective: b is not an output, since the only outputs are k(1) = a and k(2) = c. Parts (c) and (d) show two more things. A function from a three-element set to a two-element set cannot be injective, and one from a two-element set to a three-element set cannot be surjective: there are too many inputs in the first case and too few in the second. Chapter 3 proves facts of this kind in general, starting from the pigeonhole principle. And the finite pictures are worth drawing: two columns of dots, with an arrow from each input to its output. Injective means no dot on the right receives two arrows; surjective means every dot on the right receives at least one. The key example of the section is one formula read as three different functions. [Squaring, three ways] For each of the three functions, settle both questions: injective or not, surjective or not. (a) q_1 \colon 
R 	o 
R, q_1(x) = x^2. (b) q_2 \colon [0, \infty) 	o 
R, q_2(x) = x^2. (c) q_3 \colon [0, \infty) 	o [0, \infty), q_3(x) = x^2. (a) Not injective: q_1(1) = 1 = q_1(-1) and 1 
e -1. Not surjective: the witness is -1 \in 
R, since x^2 \ge 0 > -1 for every real x. So q_1 is neither. (b) Injective. Let x_1, x_2 \ge 0 with x_1^2 = x_2^2. Then x_1^2 \le x_2^2, so x_1 \le x_2 by @fd1:thm-squares-order, which applies since both numbers are nonnegative; and likewise x_2 \le x_1. Hence x_1 = x_2. Not surjective: the witness -1 still works, for the same reason. (c) Injective, by the same proof as in (b): injectivity concerns only the domain and the values, and these are the same as for q_2. Surjective. Let y \in [0, \infty). A nonnegative real number has a nonnegative square root, so put x \coloneqq \sqrt{y}. Then x \in [0, \infty) and q_3(x) = (\sqrt{y})^2 = y. So q_3 is bijective. The same rule gives three different functions. Shrinking the domain from 
R to [0, \infty) removed the two witnesses \pm 1 against injectivity. Shrinking the codomain to [0, \infty) removed the witness -1 against surjectivity. The graphs of q_2 and q_3 are the same set; only the declared codomain differs, and surjectivity changes with it. Injectivity is not the defining property of a function read backwards. Every function satisfies “if x_1 = x_2, then f(x_1) = f(x_2)”: equal inputs give equal outputs, which is part of f(x) being well defined. Injectivity is the converse, “if f(x_1) = f(x_2), then x_1 = x_2”. A “proof” of injectivity that starts from x_1 = x_2 and reaches f(x_1) = f(x_2) has proved the wrong implication, entry (N5) of Logic and Proof, Chapter 5’s catalogue, and it “proves” q_1 injective, which is false. This is the first theorem about functions whose proof uses the definitions and nothing else, and it shows the two proof shapes of the last subsection working together. Composites of Injections and Surjections Let f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon Y 	o Z be functions. (a) If f and g are injective, then g \circ f is injective. (b) If f and g are surjective, then g \circ f is surjective. (c) If f and g are bijective, then g \circ f is bijective. For (a), start from equal outputs of g \circ f. They are equal outputs of g, at the points f(x_1) and f(x_2); peel off g by its injectivity, then f by its. For (b), work backwards along the chain X 	o Y 	o Z: to reach z \in Z, first find a point of Y that g sends to z, then a point of X that f sends there. Part (c) is (a) and (b) together. (a) Let x_1, x_2 \in X with (g \circ f)(x_1) = (g \circ f)(x_2), that is, g(f(x_1)) = g(f(x_2)) by @def-composition. The points f(x_1) and f(x_2) lie in Y, and g is injective, so f(x_1) = f(x_2) [ulename{ orall E}, ulename{{	o}E}: injectivity of g at f(x_1), f(x_2)]. Since f is injective, x_1 = x_2 [ulename{ orall E}, ulename{{	o}E}: injectivity of f at x_1, x_2]. So g \circ f is injective. (b) Let z \in Z. Since g is surjective, there is y \in Y with g(y) = z [ulename{\exists E}: the name y is fresh]. Since f is surjective, there is x \in X with f(x) = y [ulename{\exists E}: x is fresh]. Then (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) = g(y) = z , so z has the preimage x under g \circ f [ulename{\exists I}, witness x]. Since z \in Z was arbitrary, g \circ f is surjective. (c) If f and g are bijective, they are injective and surjective, so g \circ f is injective by (a) and surjective by (b), that is, bijective. Part (a) is short enough to see whole at level 0 of Logic and Proof, Chapter 5 (Logic and Proof, Section 5.3), a full derivation. Here is its derivation, with the quantifiers bounded and handled by the bounded rules (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-rules), and (g \circ f)(u) already unwound to g(f(u)) by @def-composition. Premises 1 and 2 are the injectivity of f and of g; premise 3 says that f maps X into Y, which the prose used in the clause “the points f(x_1) and f(x_2) lie in Y”. Compare it with the prose of (a). “Let x_1, x_2 \in X” opens the two flagged boxes of lines 4 and 5, and “with g(f(x_1)) = g(f(x_2))” is the assumption of line 6. The first tagged sentence is lines 7–11, and the second is lines 12–14. The closing “so g \circ f is injective” stands for lines 15–17, the closing lines of ulename{{	o}I} and of the two ulename{ orall I}’s; by the convention of Logic and Proof, Chapter 5 on silent steps, the prose may state their result without naming them. The two tags in the prose mark the only steps where a hypothesis is used, and that is what the proof is about. Each hypothesis is needed. In (a), dropping the injectivity of g breaks the conclusion: with f = \id_{
R} and g = q_1, squaring on

R}, gives the same composite. In (b), with f = \id_{

An injective composite g \circ f forces f to be injective and says nothing of the kind about g (exit check C1). A surjective composite forces g to be surjective, and f may miss points (B2). Section 1.5 builds on these facts: a function f with a function g such that g \circ f = \id_X is forced to be injective. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. [B2: Put the proof in order] Let f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon Y 	o Z be functions. The following lines contain a proof that if g \circ f is surjective, then g is surjective, shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the six correct lines in an order that makes a proof, and say why each of the other two lines fails. (i) Then g(y) = g(f(x)) = (g \circ f)(x) = z, by @def-composition. (ii) Let y \in Y. The distractor (vi) uses a hypothesis the statement does not have: nothing says f is surjective, and the claim holds without it. title: 1.5 Left, Right and Two-Sided Inverses
content:
Left, Right and Two-Sided Inverses Section 1.4 sorted functions by two questions. Does f ever send two different inputs to the same output? Does f reach every point of its codomain? The answers were the words injective and surjective (@def-injective, @def-surjective). This section asks a question that sounds different: can the work of f be undone? It turns out that it asks the same two questions again, one for each side of f. Undoing f after it has acted forces f to be injective, and when X is non-empty injectivity is also enough. Undoing it before, so that f finishes the job, forces f to be surjective. The one new idea in the section is an inverse on one side; an inverse on both sides, written f^{-1}, is simply a map that is both. Throughout, f \colon X 	o Y is a function in the sense of @def-function, and composites are formed as in @def-composition: g \circ f is defined when the codomain of f is the domain of g, and (g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)). Undoing a function Start with a function we can compute in our heads. Let d \colon 
N 	o 
N be the doubling map, d(n) = 2n. Suppose someone applies d to a secret number and tells us the result, say 14. We recover the secret by halving: it was 7. Halving undoes doubling. But halving is not quite a function from 
N to 
N: 7 has no half in 
N. If we want a function h \colon 
N 	o 
N that undoes d, we must give h a value at every odd number as well. Those values do not matter for the undoing, because d never produces an odd number. Any choice will do. So one answer is h(m) \coloneqq  egin{cases} m/2 & 	ext{if } m 	ext{ is even}, \ 1 & 	ext{if } m 	ext{ is odd}, \end{cases} and another is h'(m) \coloneqq m/2 for even m and h'(m) \coloneqq m for odd m. Both are functions 
N 	o 
N: every m \in 
N is even or odd and not both, and an even m is 2k for exactly one k \in 
N, which is m/2. Both undo d: for every n \in 
N, the number 2n is even, so h(d(n)) = h(2n) =  rac{2n}{2} = n, and the same computation holds for h'. In the language of composition, h \circ d = \id_{
N} and h' \circ d = \id_{
N}. Now try to undo in the other order. Is there a function k \colon 
N 	o 
N with d \circ k = \id_{
N}, so that d undoes k? Such a k would give d(k(1)) = 1, that is 2k(1) = 1, and 1 is odd, not twice a natural number. So there is no such k. The obstacle is visible: 1 is not in the range of d, so no input to d, however chosen, comes out as 1. Two things happened here, and they are the whole section in miniature. Undoing d afterwards was possible, in more than one way, and the reason is that d loses no information: different inputs give different outputs. Undoing it beforehand was impossible, and the reason is that d misses a point of its codomain. The two sides behave differently, so they get two names. Left and right inverses A left inverse undoes f after it acts; a right inverse is undone by f. Left and Right Inverses Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function, and let g \colon Y 	o X be a function in the opposite direction. 1. g is a left inverse of f if g \circ f = \id_X, that is, g(f(x)) = x for every x \in X. 2. g is a right inverse of f if f \circ g = \id_Y, that is, f(g(y)) = y for every y \in Y. In words: a left inverse is written on the left of f in the composite, and the composite g \circ f does nothing to points of X. A right inverse is written on the right, and f \circ g does nothing to points of Y. The two phrasings in each clause say the same thing. Two functions X 	o X are equal exactly when they agree at every point (@prp-function-equality), and g \circ f and \id_X have the same domain and codomain X; so g \circ f = \id_X means (g \circ f)(x) = \id_X(x) for every x \in X, which is g(f(x)) = x. The phrase “g is a left inverse of f” and the phrase “f is a right inverse of g” say the same thing: both say g \circ f = \id_X. Which word applies depends on which function we are talking about. Check the definition against the doubling map. With d(n) = 2n on 
N, the functions h and h' above are left inverses of d: the composite h \circ d sends every n back to n. And d has no right inverse, because clause (b) fails at the single point y = 1. For a right inverse the “for every y \in Y” is the demanding part: one bad y is enough to rule it out. [Left inverses on small sets] Let X = \{1, 2\}, Y = \{1, 2, 3\}, and e \colon X 	o Y, e(1) = 1, e(2) = 2: the inclusion of X into Y. 1. Show that g \colon Y 	o X with g(1) = 1, g(2) = 2, g(3) = 2 is a left inverse of e, and that e is a right inverse of g. 2. Is g a right inverse of e? 3. Let c \colon X 	o Y be constant, c(1) = c(2) = 3. Does c have a left inverse? (a) Clause (a) of @def-left-right-inverse asks for g(e(x)) = x at each of the two points of X: g(e(1)) = g(1) = 1 and g(e(2)) = g(2) = 2. So g \circ e = \id_X, and g is a left inverse of e. Read with the roles exchanged, the same equation g \circ e = \id_X is clause (b) for g \colon Y 	o X and e \colon X 	o Y: e is a right inverse of g. (b) No. Clause (b) would need e(g(y)) = y for every y \in Y, and at y = 3 we get e(g(3)) = e(2) = 2 
e 3. The equation e \circ g = \id_Y fails at one point, which is enough. (c) No. A left inverse g would need g(c(1)) = 1 and g(c(2)) = 2, that is g(3) = 1 and g(3) = 2. A function has one value at 3, and 1 
e 2. The information “which input was it” is gone once both inputs land on 3, and nothing applied afterwards can bring it back. Part (c) is the degenerate case of the example, and it is the one to remember. A left inverse must recover x from f(x), so it cannot exist when two inputs share an output. Part (b) shows the other side: g undoes e, but e does not undo g, because e never produces 3. A left inverse need not be a right inverse. For the doubling map d(n) = 2n on 
N and its left inverse h above, h(d(n)) = n for every n, but d(h(1)) = d(1) = 2 
e 1. The equation h \circ d = \id_{
