The candidate f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} \colon Z 	o X is defined, since g^{-1} \colon Z 	o Y and f^{-1} \colon Y 	o X exist by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. We check the two equations of @def-inverse-function, using @prp-composition-associative to regroup and for its identity laws k \circ \id = k = \id \circ k:  egin{aligned} (f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}) \circ (g \circ f) &= f^{-1} \circ (g^{-1} \circ g) \circ f = f^{-1} \circ \id_Y \circ f = f^{-1} \circ f = \id_X , \ (g \circ f) \circ (f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}) &= g \circ (f \circ f^{-1}) \circ g^{-1} = g \circ \id_Y \circ g^{-1} = g \circ g^{-1} = \id_Z . \end{aligned} So f^{-1} \circ g^{-1} is a two-sided inverse of g \circ f. By the uniqueness of inverses (@prp-inverse-unique, as in @def-inverse-function), it is the inverse: (g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}. Notice the order: to undo “first f, then g”, undo g first. [B3: A bijection between an interval and the line] Let h \colon (-1, 1) 	o 
R, h(x) = x/(1 - \abs{x}), and k \colon 
R 	o (-1, 1), k(y) = y/(1 + \abs{y}). Show that h and k are well defined (each denominator is non-zero, and k takes values in (-1, 1)), and that k is the inverse of h, by checking both composites by cases on the sign. Hence h is a bijection. Well defined. For x \in (-1, 1), \abs{x} < 1, so 1 - \abs{x} > 0. For y \in 
R, 1 + \abs{y} \ge 1 > 0, and \abs{k(y)} = \abs{y}/(1 + \abs{y}) < 1 because \abs{y} < 1 + \abs{y}; so k(y) \in (-1, 1). First check, k(h(x)) = x for x \in (-1, 1). If 0 \le x < 1, then h(x) = x/(1 - x) \ge 0, so k(h(x)) =  rac{x/(1 - x)}{1 + x/(1 - x)} =  rac{x/(1 - x)}{1/(1 - x)} = x . If -1 < x < 0, then \abs{x} = -x and h(x) = x/(1 + x) < 0, so \abs{h(x)} = -x/(1 + x) and k(h(x)) =  rac{x/(1 + x)}{1 - x/(1 + x)} =  rac{x/(1 + x)}{1/(1 + x)} = x . Second check, h(k(y)) = y for y \in 
R. If y \ge 0, then k(y) = y/(1 + y) \in [0, 1), so h(k(y)) =  rac{y/(1 + y)}{1 - y/(1 + y)} =  rac{y/(1 + y)}{1/(1 + y)} = y . If y < 0, then k(y) = y/(1 - y) \in (-1, 0), so \abs{k(y)} = -y/(1 - y) and h(k(y)) =  rac{y/(1 - y)}{1 + y/(1 - y)} =  rac{y/(1 - y)}{1/(1 - y)} = y . Both composites are identities, so k = h^{-1}, and h is a bijection by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. C. Going deeper [C1: One composite equal to the identity] Let f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon Y 	o X be functions with g \circ f = \id_X. 1. Prove that f is injective and g is surjective. 2. Show by an example that neither f nor g need be bijective. 3. Prove that if, in addition, f is surjective, then g = f^{-1}. [Hint 1] Read the equation g \circ f = \id_X twice: once as a statement about f, once as a statement about g. [Hint 2] For g: let x \in X; you need a point of Y that g sends to x. (a) The equation says that g is a left inverse of f, so f is injective by @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (a). The same equation says that f is a right inverse of g, so g is surjective by @prp-right-inverse-surjective. (Directly: for x \in X, the point f(x) \in Y satisfies g(f(x)) = x.) (b) Let f \colon \{1\} 	o \{1, 2\}, f(1) = 1, and g \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{1\}, g(1) = g(2) = 1. Then g(f(1)) = 1, so g \circ f = \id_{\{1\}}. But f is not surjective (2 has no preimage) and g is not injective (g(1) = g(2) with 1 
e 2), so neither is bijective. (c) If f is also surjective, it is bijective by (a), so f^{-1} exists by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, and it is in particular a right inverse of f. Also g is a left inverse of f. By @prp-inverse-unique, g = f^{-1}. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: f injective, from the left-inverse equation (citing @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (a) or arguing directly from f(x_1) = f(x_2)). - 2: g surjective, either by citing @prp-right-inverse-surjective (f is a right inverse of g) or directly, naming the witness f(x) for a given x \in X. - 3: an example with explicit sets and both failures checked (a point missed by f, two points identified by g). - 3: (c) obtains a right inverse of f (from bijectivity) and applies uniqueness of one-sided inverses, or checks f \circ g = \id_Y directly (for y = f(x), f(g(y)) = f(g(f(x))) = f(x) = y, using surjectivity to write y = f(x)). Fatal errors (0 for the step): assuming f \circ g = \id_Y in (a) or (c) without proof; in (c), writing f^{-1} before showing f bijective. [C2: When is a left inverse unique?] Let f \colon X 	o Y be injective, with X 
e \emptyset. 1. Prove that if f is surjective, or X has exactly one element, then f has exactly one left inverse. 2. Prove that if some y_1 \in Y is not in f(X), and X has two different elements x_0 
e x_1, then f has at least two different left inverses. 3. Let f \colon \{1, 2\} 	o \{1, 2, 3, 4\}, f(k) = 2k. List all left inverses of f, and explain in one sentence why there are 2^2 = 4 of them. [Hint 1] For (a), a left inverse exists by @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (b); only “at most one” needs proof. For (b), run the construction of that proof twice. [Hint 2] For (a), let g and g' be left inverses of f. If f is surjective, write a given y \in Y as y = f(x) and compare g(y) with g'(y). (a) A left inverse exists by @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (b). For “at most one”, let g and g' be left inverses of f. Case 1: f is surjective. Then f is bijective (@def-bijective), so it has the inverse f^{-1} (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse), which is in particular a right inverse of f. By @prp-inverse-unique, g = f^{-1} and g' = f^{-1}, so g = g'. Case 2: X has exactly one element x_0. For every y \in Y, both g(y) and g'(y) are elements of X, so g(y) = x_0 = g'(y); hence g = g' by @prp-function-equality. In either case any two left inverses are equal, so f has exactly one. (b) Run the proof of @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (b) once with the fixed point x_0 and once with x_1; call the resulting left inverses g_0 and g_1. The point y_1 is outside the range, so the second alternative in the definition of G applies to it: g_0(y_1) = x_0 and g_1(y_1) = x_1. Since x_0 
e x_1, the functions g_0 and g_1 differ at y_1, so g_0 
e g_1. (c) The range is \{2, 4\}. A left inverse g \colon \{1, 2, 3, 4\} 	o \{1, 2\} must satisfy g(f(1)) = 1 and g(f(2)) = 2, that is g(2) = 1 and g(4) = 2. The values g(1) and g(3) are free, each in \{1, 2\}, and every choice gives a left inverse. The four are (g(1), g(2), g(3), g(4)) = (1, 1, 1, 2),\ (1, 1, 2, 2),\ (2, 1, 1, 2),\ (2, 1, 2, 2). The values on the range are forced, and each of the two points 1, 3 outside the range may go to either of the two points of the domain, independently: 2 \cdot 2 = 4 choices. This is the situation of (b): f is not surjective and its domain has two elements. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 1: (a) existence of a left inverse, citing @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (b). - 2: (a) surjective case: an inverse exists, and uniqueness of one-sided inverses (@prp-inverse-unique) forces every left inverse to equal it (or a direct argument: for y = f(x), g(y) = x = g'(y)). - 2: (a) one-element case: any two functions into a one-element set agree at every point, so they are equal. - 3: (b) two left inverses that take the values x_0 and x_1 at y_1 (by the construction or defined directly), each checked to be a left inverse, and shown to differ at y_1. - 2: (c) the forced values g(2) = 1, g(4) = 2, the four left inverses, and the count 2 \cdot 2. Fatal errors (0 for the step): in (a), writing f^{-1} before showing f bijective; in (b), concluding g_0 
e g_1 without exhibiting a point where they differ.

title: 1.6 Images and Preimages
content:
Images and Preimages A function f \colon X 	o Y sends points to points. Much of analysis asks what it does to sets of points. Where does f send an interval? Which inputs land in a given set of outputs? The first question is answered by the image f(A), the second by the preimage f^{-1}(B), and the two are the subject of this section. They look like mirror images of each other, and they are not: preimages respect every set operation of Section 1.2, while images respect only unions. The reason is one quantifier, and by the end of the section we will be able to point at it. Throughout, f \colon X 	o Y is a function (@def-function), and the unions and intersections of families are those of @def-family-union-intersection. An intersection of a family of subsets of Y is taken inside Y; of subsets of X, inside X. A question about squares Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = x^2, and take the two intervals A = [-1, 0] and B = [0, 1]. Squaring A gives every number from 0 to 1, and so does squaring B. So the set of squares of points of A and the set of squares of points of B are both [0, 1], and the points they share make up [0, 1]. Now intersect first. The intervals A and B share only the point 0, so A \cap B = \{0\}, and its only square is 0. Squaring the intersection gives \{0\}; intersecting the squares gives [0, 1]. The order of the two operations matters. Try the same thing backwards. Instead of pushing sets forwards through f, pull them back: for a set C of outputs, collect the inputs whose squares lie in C. Take C = [0, 1] and D = [1, 4]. The inputs with square in C form [-1, 1], those with square in D form [-2, -1] \cup [1, 2], and the inputs common to both are -1 and 1. Intersecting first gives C \cap D = \{1\}, whose inputs are again -1 and 1. This time the order does not matter. Is that an accident of these intervals? No. Pulling back will turn out to respect intersections for every function and all sets, while pushing forwards respects them exactly for the injective functions. To see why, we first need names for the two operations. Images and preimages The two sets in the question above keep recurring: “all the values f(a) for a in A” and “all the inputs x with f(x) in B”. The first was already used in Section 1.4 for A = X, where it is the range of f. An image hides a “there exists”; a preimage hides nothing. [Image] Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function and A \subseteq X. The image of A under f is the set f(A) \coloneqq \{ y \in Y : 	ext{there exists } a \in A 	ext{ with } f(a) = y \}. We also write it \{ f(a) : a \in A \}. In symbols, for every y, y \in f(A) \iff y \in Y \wedge \exists a \in A\ \, f(a) = y . [Preimage] Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function and B \subseteq Y. The preimage of B under f, also called its inverse image, is the set f^{-1}(B) \coloneqq \{ x \in X : f(x) \in B \}. In symbols, for every x, x \in f^{-1}(B) \iff x \in X \wedge f(x) \in B. The preimage is defined for every function f, whether or not f has an inverse. In Section 1.4 a point x with f(x) = y was called a preimage of y; that is, x \in f^{-1}(\{y\}). So the preimages of a point y are the elements of the preimage of the set \{y\}. Read the two definitions clause by clause. - The ambient sets. Both are sets by specification (@def-set-builder): f(A) is carved out of the codomain Y, and f^{-1}(B) out of the domain X. So f(A) \subseteq Y and f^{-1}(B) \subseteq X always. The shorthand \{ f(a) : a \in A \} names the same subset of Y; it is a way of writing, not a new rule of set formation. - The image. “y \in f(A)” says that y is hit by some point of A. The words “there exists” are part of the definition. To use a line y \in f(A), we must name a witness: “let a \in A with f(a) = y”. That is the rule \existsE of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 (Logic and Proof, Section 4.6), and the name must be fresh. To prove y \in f(A), we exhibit a witness, by \existsI (Logic and Proof, Chapter 4, Logic and Proof, Section 4.5). - The preimage. “x \in f^{-1}(B)” says that x is sent into B. There is no quantifier. For x \in X, a line x \in f^{-1}(B) is used and proved by one substitution: it is exchanged for f(x) \in B, and back. - The symbol f^{-1}. In f^{-1}(B), the symbol f^{-1} is not a function that is applied to B. The whole expression f^{-1}(B) is the name of a set built from f and B. Section 1.5 used f^{-1} for the inverse function of a bijection; the remark at the end of this section reconciles the two readings. The notation f(A) puts a set where f(x) puts a point. When the letter in the brackets has been declared a subset of X, the expression is an image; when it has been declared a point, it is a value. As with the pair and the interval of Section 1.3, the declaration decides. Start with the smallest possible example, where everything can be listed. [Images and preimages by listing] Let X = \{1, 2, 3, 4\}, Y = \{0, 1, 2, 5\}, and let f \colon X 	o Y be given by f(1) = 1, \quad f(2) = 2, \quad f(3) = 0, \quad f(4) = 1 . Find f(\{1, 4\}), f(\{2, 3\}), f(X), and f(\emptyset); then f^{-1}(\{1\}), f^{-1}(\{0, 2\}), f^{-1}(\{5\}), f^{-1}(\emptyset), and f^{-1}(Y). Images. A point y lies in f(A) when some a \in A has f(a) = y, so we apply f to each point of A and collect the results. f(\{1, 4\}) = \{1\}: both points go to 1, and a set lists 1 once. f(\{2, 3\}) = \{0, 2\}. f(X) = \{0, 1, 2\}, the range; 5 is not in it. f(\emptyset) = \emptyset: a point y in it would need some a \in \emptyset, and there is none. Preimages. A point x \in X lies in f^{-1}(B) when f(x) \in B, so we test each of the four points of X. f^{-1}(\{1\}) = \{1, 4\}. f^{-1}(\{0, 2\}) = \{2, 3\}. f^{-1}(\{5\}) = \emptyset: no point of X is sent to 5. f^{-1}(\emptyset) = \emptyset, since f(x) \in \emptyset never holds. f^{-1}(Y) = X, since f(x) \in Y holds for every x \in X. The two computations differ in shape. For the image we ran through the points of A and produced outputs. For the preimage we ran through the points of X and tested each one. That is the “there exists” of the image and the plain condition of the preimage, seen on a four-point set. The example also contains a non-example by minimal change. The sets \{1\} and \{5\} are both one-point subsets of Y. The first has a two-point preimage; change 1 to 5 and the preimage becomes empty, because 5 lies outside the range. The preimage of a non-empty set can be empty. What fails is the existence of a point of X sent into the set. Why is the preimage defined for every function, when f^{-1} as a function exists only for bijections? Because the question “which inputs land in B?” makes sense for any f: its answer may be empty, or contain many points, and neither is a problem for a set. The function f^{-1} of Section 1.5 asks for more: exactly one input for each output. This is why analysis states its definitions with preimages. “The preimage of every open set is open” makes sense for every function; Metric and Topological Spaces, Chapter 1 uses it to characterize continuity. The preimage f^{-1}(B) does not presuppose that f is invertible. For the squaring map on 
R, which has no inverse function, f^{-1}(\{4\}) = \{-2, 2\} is a perfectly good set. What the symbol does not give is a value “f^{-1}(4)”: that would be a point, and there are two candidates. Computing images and preimages With an infinite set, listing is impossible, and the definitions are used as they stand. The image asks us to name witnesses; the preimage asks us to solve an inequality. [Images and preimages of intervals under squaring] Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R, f(x) = x^2. Prove that 1. f([-1, 2]) = [0, 4]; 2. f^{-1}([1, 4]) = [-2, -1] \cup [1, 2]; 3. f^{-1}(\{-1\}) = \emptyset; 4. f^{-1}(f([0, 1])) = [-1, 1]. We use school facts about real numbers, x^2 \ge 0 and every y \ge 0 has a square root \sqrt y \ge 0, and, by @fd1:thm-squares-order, for s, t \ge 0, s \le t holds exactly when s^2 \le t^2. (a) Idea. An image is proved equal to a set by two inclusions. The inclusion \subseteq uses y \in f([-1, 2]), so it names a witness. The inclusion \supseteq proves y \in f([-1, 2]), so it exhibits one. (\subseteq) Let y \in f([-1, 2]). Then y = a^2 for some a \in [-1, 2]; name it a. Certainly y = a^2 \ge 0. If a \ge 0, then 0 \le a \le 2, so a^2 \le 4. If a < 0, then 0 < -a \le 1, so a^2 = (-a)^2 \le 1 \le 4. In either case 0 \le y \le 4, that is, y \in [0, 4]. (\supseteq) Let y \in [0, 4]. Take a \coloneqq \sqrt y. Then 0 \le a \le \sqrt 4 = 2, so a \in [-1, 2], and f(a) = y. Hence y \in f([-1, 2]). The witness in (\supseteq) could have been -\sqrt y for y \le 1, but not for y > 1, where -\sqrt y < -1. One witness per y is all we need, so we choose the one that always works. (b) Idea. A preimage is a set of solutions of a condition on x. No witness is needed: each line is an equivalence. For every x \in 
R,  egin{aligned} x \in f^{-1}([1, 4]) &\iff 1 \le x^2 \le 4 \iff 1 \le \abs{x} \le 2 \ &\iff x \in [-2, -1] \cup [1, 2] . \end{aligned} The first step is @def-preimage. The second uses x^2 = \abs{x}^2 and @fd1:thm-squares-order with s, t among 1, \abs{x}, 2. The third splits by the sign of x: for x \ge 0, \abs{x} = x, and for x < 0, \abs{x} = -x. So the two sets have the same elements. (c) For every x \in 
R, f(x) = x^2 \ge 0 > -1, so f(x) \in \{-1\} never holds. The preimage is empty, although \{-1\} is not. (d) First f([0, 1]) = [0, 1], by the argument of (a): a square of a number in [0, 1] lies in [0, 1], and each y \in [0, 1] is (\sqrt y)^2 with \sqrt y \in [0, 1]. Then, as in (b), for every x \in 
R, x \in f^{-1}([0, 1]) \iff 0 \le x^2 \le 1 \iff \abs{x} \le 1 \iff x \in [-1, 1]. Part (d) is worth a second look. We started with [0, 1], pushed it forwards and pulled it back, and got the bigger set [-1, 1]. The negative numbers came in because they have the same squares as the positive ones. That is a failure of injectivity, and the subsection “There and back” later in this section proves that it is the only way the round trip can grow a set. For f(x) = x^2 on 
R, find f^{-1}(\{4\}), f^{-1}([-4, -1]), and f(f^{-1}([-1, 1])). f^{-1}(\{4\}) = \{-2, 2\}, the solutions of x^2 = 4. f^{-1}([-4, -1]) = \emptyset, since x^2 \ge 0 > -1. For the last, f^{-1}([-1, 1]) = \{ x \in 
R : -1 \le x^2 \le 1 \} = [-1, 1], and then f([-1, 1]) = [0, 1], by the argument of @exm-images-of-square (a). So f(f^{-1}([-1, 1])) = [0, 1], which is smaller than [-1, 1]: the negative numbers are not squares. Sets of numbers as images Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 works with three ways of making new sets of real numbers from old ones: for A, B \subseteq 
R and c \in 
R, -A \coloneqq \{ -a : a \in A \}, \quad cA \coloneqq \{ ca : a \in A \}, \quad A + B \coloneqq \{ a + b : a \in A,\ b \in B \}. The first two are images in the sense of @def-image. In the third, two letters vary, and the notation means, as for @def-cartesian-product, A + B = \{ y \in 
R : \exists a \in A\ \exists b \in B\ \, y = a + b \}. Each is an image, and seeing them as images tells us how to prove things about them: an element of A + B is used by naming two witnesses. [Reflections, scalings and sums as images] Let A, B \subseteq 
R and c \in 
R. 1. Let n \colon 
R 	o 
R, n(x) = -x, and m_c \colon 
R 	o 
R, m_c(x) = cx. Show that -A = n(A) and cA = m_c(A). 2. Let s \colon 
R 	imes 
R 	o 
R, s(a, b) = a + b. Show that A + B = s(A 	imes B). 3. Compute -[0, 1], \{1, 2\} + \{10, 20\}, and \{1, 2\} + \{1, 2\}. (a) By the shorthand of @def-image, n(A) = \{ n(a) : a \in A \} = \{ -a : a \in A \}, which is -A as written above. In the same way, m_c(A) = \{ ca : a \in A \} = cA. Nothing more is needed: the set-builder \{ -a : a \in A \} is the image, written in the form of @def-image. (b) Here the domain is the product 
R 	imes 
R of Section 1.3, and A 	imes B \subseteq 
R 	imes 
R. An element p of A 	imes B is a pair (a, b) with a \in A and b \in B (@def-cartesian-product). (\subseteq) Let y \in A + B. Then y = a + b for some a \in A and b \in B; name them. The pair p \coloneqq (a, b) lies in A 	imes B, and s(p) = a + b = y. So y \in s(A 	imes B), with witness p. (\supseteq) Let y \in s(A 	imes B). Then y = s(p) for some p \in A 	imes B; name it p. Since p \in A 	imes B, p = (a, b) for some a \in A and b \in B; name them. Then y = s(a, b) = a + b, so y \in A + B. Unwinding y \in s(A 	imes B) took two layers of witnesses: first the pair p from the image, then its coordinates a, b from the product. (c) -[0, 1] = [-1, 0]: if y = -a with 0 \le a \le 1, then -1 \le y \le 0; and if -1 \le y \le 0, then a \coloneqq -y \in [0, 1] and y = -a. Next, \{1, 2\} + \{10, 20\} is the image of the four pairs (1, 10), (1, 20), (2, 10), (2, 20), so it is \{11, 21, 12, 22\}, with 4 elements. Finally, \{1, 2\} + \{1, 2\} is the image of (1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 2), which is \{2, 3, 4\}, with only 3 elements: the pairs (1, 2) and (2, 1) have the same image 3, because s is not injective. This pays a debt. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 introduces these sets by set-builder, and part (b) shows that even the two-variable form is an image, of A 	imes B under s, so @def-image is what all three rest on: an element of A + B is used by naming two witnesses, as in part (b). Preimages respect every operation Now the promised theorem. The preimage of a union is the union of the preimages, and the same holds for intersections, complements, and differences. No hypothesis on f is needed. [Preimages of Set Operations] Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function. 1. For every family (B_i)_{i \in I} of subsets of Y, \displaystyle f^{-1}\Bigl( igcup_{i \in I} B_i\Bigr) =  igcup_{i \in I} f^{-1}(B_i). 2. For every family (B_i)_{i \in I} of subsets of Y, \displaystyle f^{-1}\Bigl( igcap_{i \in I} B_i\Bigr) =  igcap_{i \in I} f^{-1}(B_i), the intersection on the left taken in Y and on the right in X. 3. For every B \subseteq Y, f^{-1}(Y \setminus B) = X \setminus f^{-1}(B). 4. For all B, C \subseteq Y, f^{-1}(B \setminus C) = f^{-1}(B) \setminus f^{-1}(C). Unwind each side at a point x \in X. A preimage turns “x is in the preimage of something” into “f(x) is in that something”. The set operation is then applied to one point, f(x), and on the other side it is applied to one point, x, whose membership in each f^{-1}(B_i) is again a statement about f(x). The two sides say the same thing about the same point. No point is ever named as a witness for an image. The only “there exists” is over the index i in (a), and its witness is handed straight from \existsE to \existsI, so no witness can go wrong, and nothing is asked of f. Every set in the four laws is a subset of X: a preimage is one by @def-preimage, a union of subsets of X is one because each of its elements lies in some f^{-1}(B_i) \subseteq X, an intersection in X and a difference X \setminus \cdot are subsets of X by @def-family-union-intersection and @def-set-operations, and f^{-1}(B) \setminus f^{-1}(C) \subseteq f^{-1}(B). For two subsets S, T of X, a point outside X lies in neither, so by @def-set-equality, S = T holds as soon as x \in S \iff x \in T for every x \in X. Let x \in X. In each chain below, the steps labeled (P) are @def-preimage, which applies because x \in X; the others are named. (a)  egin{aligned} x \in f^{-1}\Bigl( igcup_{i \in I} B_i\Bigr) &\iff f(x) \in  igcup_{i \in I} B_i && 	ext{(P)} \ &\iff \exists i \in I,\ f(x) \in B_i && 	ext{(union)} \ &\iff \exists i \in I,\ x \in f^{-1}(B_i) && 	ext{(P)} \ &\iff x \in  igcup_{i \in I} f^{-1}(B_i) && 	ext{(union).} \end{aligned} The steps marked “union” are @def-family-union-intersection. In the third step, for each fixed i \in I the statements f(x) \in B_i and x \in f^{-1}(B_i) are equivalent, so one holds for some i exactly when the other does: a witness i for one is a witness for the other. R. Review [R1] Here is a derivation of “if A \subseteq B, then \powerset{A} \subseteq \powerset{B}”. The steps “by def.” unwind or rewind @def-subset and @def-power-set. Write the proof as plain prose, the way a mathematician would. Then say which sentence of your proof carries each of the five boxes. Proof. Suppose A \subseteq B. title: Equivalence Relations, Orders, and Induction
content:
Equivalence Relations, Orders, and Induction Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 took one fact about the natural numbers on trust: induction. Everything else we have used about them came from school: that 7 - 3 is a natural number, that none lies strictly between 3 and 4, that every non-empty set of them has a least member, that every integer is even or odd and not both. This chapter derives all of these from induction, extends them to the integers, and proves that the least-member property, well-ordering, is induction in another form. It then turns induction from a principle into a craft: which form fits a claim, where to start, when to argue from a smallest counterexample, when to prove more than was asked, and how a flawed induction fails at exactly one step. It also proves that a starting value and a rule for the next value really do define a sequence, which is what makes \sum, \prod, n! and powers definitions rather than abbreviations. The first motivating problem comes from Logic and Proof, Chapter 2, which reduced a fraction by halving numerator and denominator for as long as both were even: what stops the halving from going on for ever? The second half of the chapter is about relations. When is “the same” a legitimate way to identify different things, as a clock identifies 2 with 14, or a function identifies two points with the same value? And what does “larger” mean when not everything can be compared, as with sets under inclusion or natural numbers under divisibility? The second motivating problem: in what sense is “9 + 5 = 2 on a clock” a true statement? The answer is an equivalence relation, the partition it cuts its set into, and a check that arithmetic on the pieces does not depend on which integer names a piece. For orders the answer is that “largest” splits into two notions, greatest and maximal, which agree only when every two elements are comparable. The last section reaches least upper bounds in a general partially ordered set (Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1’s supremum is the case of \le on 
R, and its axiom says that such suprema exist) and closes with well-ordered sets, the order-theoretic name for what Section 2.1 proved about 
N. What you need. Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–5, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapter 1. From Logic and Proof, Chapters 1 and 2: the ulename{{	o}I} box (@fd1:def-rules-implication), proof by contradiction (@fd1:def-rule-raa), and the two results whose school facts this chapter proves, the irrationality of \sqrt 2 (@fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational) and @fd1:thm-square-even-implies-even. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 3: the principle of induction (@fd1:ax-induction) and strong induction (@fd1:thm-strong-induction), with the worked examples that introduced them (@fd1:exm-sum-consecutive-products, @fd1:exm-power-inequality, @fd1:exm-threes-and-fives), and structural recursion and induction (@fd1:thm-structural-recursion, @fd1:thm-structural-induction), which appear here as pointers back and in one review exercise. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 4: the rules for “for every” and “there exists” (@fd1:def-rules-universal, @fd1:def-rules-existential), the rules for equality (@fd1:def-rules-equality, @fd1:prp-equality-symmetric-transitive), bounded quantifiers (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-rules), and negating quantifiers and implications (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, @fd1:prp-negated-implication). From Logic and Proof, Chapter 5: how an induction is written in prose (@fd1:exm-rhetoric-induction) and the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue). From Chapter 1: sets cut out by a property (@def-set-builder), power sets (@def-power-set), unions of families (@def-family-union-intersection), relations as sets of pairs (@def-relation), functions and when two are equal (@def-function, @prp-function-equality), and preimages (@def-preimage). The arithmetic and order of 
R are school facts, as in the earlier chapters; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 states them as axioms. Time. About 30 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 45 hours for everything. Roadmap - The natural numbers and well-ordering. From induction alone, the arithmetic of 
N and 
Z, the proof that every non-empty set of natural numbers has a least element, and the theorem that induction and well-ordering are equivalent, with a witness for each hypothesis it needs. - Induction, strong induction and the smallest counterexample. Induction and strong induction from any integer, the smallest counterexample as a method, the division algorithm, lowest terms and prime factors as its first uses, and the ways an induction proof goes wrong, each located at one step. - Definition by recursion. The theorem that a starting value and a rule define exactly one sequence, its variants from another base and with two previous values, sums, products and powers defined by it, and inductions that follow a definition’s clauses or prove more than was asked. - Properties of relations. Reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive, each failure proved by a witness, divisibility as the relation whose antisymmetry depends on the set, and a table of eight relations checked against the four properties. - Equivalence relations and partitions. Relations that behave like equality, the proof that their classes partition the set and that every partition arises from exactly one of them, the integers modulo n, and why arithmetic on classes must be checked to be well defined. - Partial orders, maximal and greatest elements. Relations that behave like \le, greatest elements against maximal ones and when the two agree, least upper bounds in a partially ordered set, and well-ordered sets. Named moves - Smallest counterexample. Suppose the claim fails; well-ordering gives a least failure m; below m the claim holds, and from that produce a failure smaller than m, or the claim at m itself. - Prove more (strengthen the hypothesis). When the inductive step will not go through, ask what the induction hypothesis would need to say, and prove that stronger statement instead. - Recursion, then induction. Define an object by a recursion, and prove facts about it by an induction that follows the same clauses: the base case uses the starting value, and the step uses the rule. - Classes from a relation, a relation from classes. Pass between an equivalence relation and its partition, whichever description makes the next step easier.

title: 2.1 The Natural Numbers and Well-Ordering
content:
The Natural Numbers and Well-Ordering Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 took one fact about the natural numbers on trust: the principle of induction (@fd1:ax-induction), which says that a property holding at 0 and passing from each n to n + 1 holds for every n \in 
N. From it, Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 proved strong induction (@fd1:thm-strong-induction), whose step may use the property at every smaller number. Everything else we have said about 
N was school knowledge: that 7 - 3 is a natural number, that none lies strictly between 3 and 4, that every non-empty set of natural numbers has a least member. This section derives those facts from induction, extends them to the integers, and then proves that the least-member property, well-ordering, is induction in another form. What we assume about the natural numbers The principle of induction is usually used with a property written as a sentence. It has an equivalent form about sets, which is the one Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 uses. Let S \subseteq 
N contain 0, and suppose n + 1 \in S whenever n \in S. Apply @fd1:ax-induction to the property “n \in S”: its base case is 0 \in S, and its step is the closure of S. So every n \in 
N lies in S, that is, 
N \subseteq S, and with S \subseteq 
N this gives S = 
N (@prp-subset-antisymmetric). In words: the only subset of 
N that contains 0 and is closed under n \mapsto n + 1 is 
N itself. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 states this as “
N is contained in every inductive set”, where an inductive set contains 0, as here. Here is everything the section assumes about 
N. The natural numbers form a subset 
N \subseteq 
R of the familiar real numbers such that - (( )0) 0 \in 
N; - (
NS) for every n \in 
N, also n + 1 \in 
N; and @fd1:ax-induction holds. The arithmetic and the order of the real numbers (the laws of +, -, \cdot and \le, trichotomy, multiplying an inequality by a positive number) are school facts in Part 0; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 states them as axioms of an ordered field. These three items are a description of 
N, not new axioms: Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 already used all of them. The rule for this section. From here to the end of the section, a fact about 
N is used only if it is (( )0), (
NS), @fd1:ax-induction, a statement proved earlier in the section, or @fd1:thm-strong-induction once the paragraph after @lem-naturals-arithmetic has shown that its Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 proof rests only on these. The real-number arithmetic is used freely. In particular “n \ge 0” for a natural number n, which looks too obvious to mention, is not available until it is proved below, in @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a). The integers and the rationals are then defined from 
N, as subsets of 
R:  egin{aligned} 
Z &\coloneqq 
N \cup \{ -n : n \in 
N \} , \ 
Z_{>0} &\coloneqq \{ n \in 
N : n 
e 0 \} , \

Z, \ n \in 
Z_{>0} \} . \end{aligned} In words: an integer is a natural number or the negative of one; a positive integer is a natural number other than 0; a rational number is a quotient of an integer by a positive integer. These are word for word the definitions of Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1’s Analysis on the Real Line, Section 1.5, so the two chapters speak of the same sets. Examples: -3 \in 
Z because 3 \in 
N; 0 lies in 
Z twice over, as 0 \in 
N and as -0, which a union does not mind; -	frac12 = (-1)/2 \in 
Q. The definitions do not yet tell us that 	frac12 
otin 
Z, or that 
Z_{>0} is the set of natural numbers \ge 1. Both need the lemma below. Two pieces of notation will save words later. For n \in 
N, \{1, \dots, n\} \coloneqq \{ k \in 
N : 1 \le k \le n \} , \qquad \{0, \dots, n\} \coloneqq \{ k \in 
N : k \le n \} . So \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset, since no k has 1 \le k \le 0. We do not write [n] for these sets: square brackets will mean an equivalence class in Section 2.5. The arithmetic of the natural numbers The facts below are the ones Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 used without proof. Each of (a)–(d) is one ordinary induction, and the only work is to choose the property to induct on; (e) follows from (a) and (d). [Arithmetic of the Natural Numbers] For all m, n \in 
N: 1. n \ge 0; and if n 
e 0, then n \ge 1; 2. m + n \in 
N and mn \in 
N; 3. if n 
e 0 (equivalently, by (a), n \ge 1), then n - 1 \in 
N; 4. if m \le n, then n - m \in 
N; 5. there is no k \in 
N with n < k < n + 1; equivalently, if m < n, then m + 1 \le n. In words: (a) says that 0 is the smallest natural number and that nothing in 
N lies between 0 and 1. (b) says 
N is closed under sums and products, (c) that every natural number except 0 has a predecessor in 
N, and (d) that a difference “larger minus smaller” stays in 
N. (e) says the natural numbers come one unit apart, with no gaps to hide in. Each induction needs a property that is true at 0 and survives the step, and the statement as written does not always qualify. “If n 
e 0, then n \ge 1” says nothing useful at 0, so for (a) we induct on the disjunction “n = 0 or n \ge 1”. For (b) we fix one of the two numbers and induct on the other. For (d) we induct on m. The step from m to m + 1 uses the hypothesis only at the same n, with the weaker bound m \le n, and then subtracts 1 using (c). So n could be fixed first, as m is in (b); the proof below puts “for every n” inside the property instead, which is harmless. (a) Let P(n) be “n = 0 or n \ge 1”. Base case: P(0) holds by its first disjunct. Step: let n \in

N satisfies n = 0 or n \ge 1. In both cases n \ge 0; and if n 
e 0, the first disjunct is excluded, so n \ge 1. (b) Fix m \in 
N. Sums: let P(n) be “m + n \in 
N”. Then P(0) holds, since m + 0 = m \in 
N. If m + n \in 
N, then m + (n + 1) = (m + n) + 1 \in 
N by (
NS). By @fd1:ax-induction, m + n \in 
N for every n \in 
N; as m was arbitrary, this holds for all m, n \in
