Line (vii) reads leastness backwards: “m is least in X \setminus S” says that nothing below m lies in X \setminus S, so a smaller number of X is in S, not outside it. [B3] Prove the second half of @cor-well-ordering-integers directly from @thm-well-ordering, without using the first half: if S \subseteq 
Z is non-empty and b \in 
Z is an upper bound of S, then S has a greatest element. Hint: shift by s \mapsto b - s. Let T \coloneqq \{ b - s : s \in S \}. For s \in S, b - s is an integer by @prp-integers-closed (a), and b - s \ge 0 because s \le b; so b - s \in 
N by @prp-integers-closed (b). Thus T is a non-empty subset of 
N, and by @thm-well-ordering it has a least element, of the form b - s_0 with s_0 \in S. For every s \in S, b - s_0 \le b - s, so s \le s_0. Hence s_0 is a greatest element of S. C. Going deeper [C1: A greatest element from a least upper bound] Let S \subseteq 
N be non-empty, and suppose some M \in 
N satisfies s \le M for every s \in S. 1. Prove that S has a greatest element by applying @thm-well-ordering to the set U of upper bounds of S that lie in 
N, not by citing @cor-well-ordering-integers: show that the least element of U lies in S. 2. Show that the hypothesis “some M \in 
N bounds S above” cannot be dropped. [Hint 1] Consider U \coloneqq \{ u \in 
N : s \le u 	ext{ for every } s \in S \}. [Hint 2] U is non-empty because M \in U; let u be its least element, which exists by @thm-well-ordering. (a) Let U \coloneqq \{ u \in 
N : s \le u 	ext{ for every } s \in S \}. Then M \in U, so U is a non-empty subset of 
N, and @thm-well-ordering gives a least element u of U. We show u \in S. Suppose u 
otin S. Then every s \in S satisfies s \le u and s 
e u, so s < u, and s + 1 \le u by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (e); that is, s \le u - 1. Since S is non-empty, it has an element s_0, and 0 \le s_0 < u by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a), so u 
e 0. By @lem-naturals-arithmetic (c), u - 1 \in 
N. So u - 1 is an upper bound of S in 
N, that is, u - 1 \in U, and u - 1 < u, which contradicts the choice of u. Hence u \in S. Since u \in S and s \le u for every s \in S, u is a greatest element of S. (b) S = 
N is non-empty and has no greatest element: for every n \in 
N, also n + 1 \in 
N by (
NS), and n + 1 > n. In the proof, U is then empty, and @thm-well-ordering has nothing to apply to. The number u of (a) is the least upper bound of S among natural numbers, and the proof shows that it lies in S. Section 2.6 defines least upper bounds in any partially ordered set, and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 is about sets of real numbers whose least upper bound, when it exists, need not lie in the set. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: defines the set of upper bounds in 
N, shows it is non-empty, and takes its least element by @thm-well-ordering. - 2: handles u = 0 separately, or shows u 
e 0 using that S is non-empty, before using u - 1 \in 
N (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (c)). - 3: uses the minimality of u: either shows directly that u - 1 
otin U, so some s \in S has s > u - 1, or, supposing u 
otin S, derives u - 1 \in U and contradicts minimality. - 1: uses discreteness (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e)) to show that an element of S greater than u - 1 equals u, or to get s \le u - 1 in the contradiction route, and concludes that u \in S is a greatest element. - 2: (b) the witness S = 
N, with the reason it has no greatest element. Fatal errors (0 for the step): using u - 1 \in 
N without checking u 
e 0; taking a least element of U without showing U non-empty. A second route, through the least element M - s_0 of \{ M - s : s \in S \} \subseteq 
N (as in @exr-naturals-and-well-ordering-b3), proves the conclusion of (a) but not by the method the task names, so it earns at most 4 points for (a): 2 for showing that this set is a non-empty subset of 
N and taking its least element, and 2 for deducing s \le s_0 for every s \in S from M - s_0 \le M - s, with s_0 \in S; and (b) as above. [C2: A well-ordered set with gaps] Let X \coloneqq 
N \cup \{ n + 	frac12 : n \in 
N \}. Prove that every non-empty subset of X has a least element. Let T \subseteq X be non-empty, and put A \coloneqq T \cap 
N , \qquad B \coloneqq \{ t - 	frac12 : t \in T \setminus 
N \} . Every t \in T \setminus 
N is n + 	frac12 for some n \in 
N, since t \in X; so t - 	frac12 = n \in 
N, and B \subseteq 
N. Since T = A \cup (T \setminus 
N) is non-empty, A or B is non-empty. By @thm-well-ordering, A, if non-empty, has a least element a, and B, if non-empty, has a least element b. Define c \coloneqq  egin{cases} a & 	ext{if } B = \emptyset , \ b + 	frac12 & 	ext{if } A = \emptyset , \ \min\{ a, \, b + 	frac12 \} & 	ext{otherwise.} \end{cases} In each case c \in T: a \in A \subseteq T, and b = t - 	frac12 for some t \in T \setminus 
N, so b + 	frac12 = t \in T. Let t \in T. If t \in 
N, then t \in A, so A 
e \emptyset and t \ge a \ge c. If t 
otin 
N, then t - 	frac12 \in B, so B 
e \emptyset and t - 	frac12 \ge b, that is, t \ge b + 	frac12 \ge c. (In both chains, the last inequality holds in every case of the definition of c that can occur.) So c is a least element of T. The set X has the least-element property, contains 0 and is closed under n \mapsto n + 1, but it does not have the induction property (
N \subseteq X contains 0 and is closed, and 
N 
e X). That is the first witness after @thm-induction-iff-well-ordering: without the predecessor property, well-ordering does not give induction. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: splits T into its natural-number part and its half part, and shows the shifted half part lies in 
N. - 2: applies @thm-well-ordering to each non-empty part, saying that at least one part is non-empty. - 2: defines the candidate in all cases, including those where one part is empty, and checks it lies in T. - 3: checks the candidate is \le t for every t \in T, by cases on t \in 
N or not. - 1: concludes, with the quantifiers right: one least element for the given T. Fatal errors (0 for the step): applying @thm-well-ordering to T itself (it need not be a subset of 
N); taking a least element of an empty part. A second route, through the least element of \{ 2t : t \in T \} \subseteq 
N, earns the same points. It earns 4 for showing that this set lies in 
N, checking both 2n and 2n + 1 by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (b), and that it is non-empty, and for taking its least element 2t_0 with t_0 \in T by @thm-well-ordering. It earns 4 for deducing t_0 \le t from 2t_0 \le 2t for every t \in T, and 2 for the conclusion. The same fatal errors apply.

title: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content:
Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 gave the principle of induction (@fd1:ax-induction), its strong form (@fd1:thm-strong-induction), and the first worked proofs: a sum (@fd1:exm-sum-consecutive-products), an inequality (@fd1:exm-power-inequality), and a strong induction with three base cases (@fd1:exm-threes-and-fives). Logic and Proof, Chapter 5 showed how an induction is written in prose and which rule each phrase stands for (@fd1:exm-rhetoric-induction). This section is about the craft: which form of induction fits a claim, where it starts, how a smallest counterexample becomes a proof, and how an induction goes wrong, each failure located at one step. On the way it proves facts that Logic and Proof, Chapters 1, 2 and 5 took from school: every integer is even or odd and not both, a fraction can be reduced until numerator and denominator are not both even, and every integer n \ge 2 has a prime factor. Induction from any integer Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 already started inductions at numbers other than 0 (Logic and Proof, Section 3.2, “Starting from another number”), for a starting point b \in 
N. With 
Z and @prp-integers-closed in hand, the starting point may be any integer, negative ones included. To prove a statement for every integer from n_0 on, prove it at n_0 and show that it passes from each integer to the next. [Induction from a Base] Let n_0 be an integer, and for each integer n \ge n_0 let P(n) be a statement. Suppose 1. (base case) P(n_0) is true, and 2. (inductive step) for every integer n \ge n_0, if P(n) is true then P(n + 1) is true. Then P(n) is true for every integer n \ge n_0. Count from the base. The integers n \ge n_0 are exactly n_0 + k with k \in 
N, and moving from n to n + 1 moves k to k + 1. So the statement “P(n_0 + k)” about k \in 
N is ready for @fd1:ax-induction, and its base case is P(n_0). For k \in 
N, let Q(k) be the statement P(n_0 + k). This makes sense: n_0 + k is an integer by @prp-integers-closed (a), and n_0 + k \ge n_0 since k \ge 0 by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a). Base case. Q(0) is P(n_0), which holds by (i). Inductive step. Let k \in 
N, and suppose Q(k), that is, P(n_0 + k). The integer n \coloneqq n_0 + k satisfies n \ge n_0, so (ii) gives P(n + 1). Since n + 1 = n_0 + (k + 1), this is Q(k + 1). By @fd1:ax-induction, Q(k) holds for every k \in 
N. Now let n be an integer with n \ge n_0. Then k \coloneqq n - n_0 is an integer by @prp-integers-closed (a), and k \ge 0, so k \in 
N by @prp-integers-closed (b). Hence Q(k) holds, and Q(k) is P(n_0 + k) = P(n). This proves the theorem. For n_0 = 0 the theorem is @fd1:ax-induction itself, and for n_0 \in 
N it is Logic and Proof, Chapter 3’s induction started at n_0. In the inductive step, “P(n) is true” is the induction hypothesis: one implication, proved once, inside a ulename{{	o}I} box whose assumption is P(n) for one fixed but arbitrary integer n \ge n_0. The strong form moves to a base in the same way. [Strong Induction from a Base] Let n_0 be an integer, and for each integer n \ge n_0 let P(n) be a statement. Suppose that, for every integer n \ge n_0: if P(k) is true for every integer k with n_0 \le k < n, then P(n) is true. Then P(n) is true for every integer n \ge n_0. For j \in 
N, let Q(j) be P(n_0 + j), as in the proof of @thm-induction. We check the hypothesis of @fd1:thm-strong-induction for Q. Let j \in 
N, and suppose Q(i) holds for every i \in 
N with i < j. Put n \coloneqq n_0 + j, an integer with n \ge n_0. Let k be an integer with n_0 \le k < n. Then i \coloneqq k - n_0 is an integer with i \ge 0, so i \in 
N by @prp-integers-closed (b), and i < n - n_0 = j; so Q(i), which is P(k), holds. The hypothesis of the theorem at n now gives P(n), that is, Q(j). By @fd1:thm-strong-induction, Q(j) holds for every j \in 
N, and every integer n \ge n_0 is n_0 + j with j = n - n_0 \in 
N, as in the proof of @thm-induction. This proves the theorem. So @thm-strong-induction-from-base is a corollary of @fd1:thm-strong-induction, by the same shift. When n_0 \in 
N, it says what @fd1:exm-threes-and-fives achieved with a guard: there the property was “if n \ge 8, then …”, stated for every n \in 
N and vacuous below 8. Here the property is stated only for n \ge n_0, and the hypothesis speaks only about k \ge n_0. The two are the same argument in two notations, and the base cases sit in the same place: they are the n for which the step reaches below n_0. Every integer n \ge 24 is 5a + 7b for some integers a, b \ge 0. A proof by @thm-strong-induction-from-base writes n = (n - 5) + 5 in its step. How many base cases does it need, and which? Can the base 24 be lowered? The step uses P(n - 5), which the hypothesis supplies only when n - 5 \ge 24, that is, n \ge 29. So n = 24, 25, 26, 27, 28 are base cases, five of them, checked directly:  egin{aligned} 24 &= 5 \cdot 2 + 7 \cdot 2 , & 25 &= 5 \cdot 5 , & 26 &= 5 \cdot 1 + 7 \cdot 3 , \ 27 &= 5 \cdot 4 + 7 \cdot 1 , & 28 &= 7 \cdot 4 . \end{aligned} The base cannot be lowered: 23 is not of the form. With b = 0, 1, 2, 3 the remainder 23 - 7b is 23, 16, 9, 2, none a multiple of 5, and b \ge 4 gives 23 - 7b < 0. The smallest counterexample Well-ordering gives the same power as strong induction, in a form that often reads more naturally. To prove a claim about every integer from n_0 on, suppose it fails somewhere. The failures form a non-empty set of integers with the integer lower bound n_0, so @cor-well-ordering-integers gives a least one. Below it the claim holds. If that is enough to produce a failure that is smaller still, or to show the claim at the least failure after all, we have a contradiction. To prove “P(n) for every integer n \ge n_0” by a smallest counterexample: - Suppose it fails: some integer n \ge n_0 has P(n) false. - Take the least failure: the set F of integers n \ge n_0 with P(n) false is non-empty and has the integer lower bound n_0, so it has a least element m (@cor-well-ordering-integers; @thm-well-ordering when n_0 = 0). - Use the claim below m: P(k) holds for every integer k with n_0 \le k < m, since such a k is not in F. - Produce a contradiction: a failure k < m, or P(m) itself. Then F is empty, and P(n) holds for every integer n \ge n_0. The method is strong induction with an ulename{RAA} box drawn around it. The work done inside the box, “if P(k) for every k with n_0 \le k < m, then P(m)”, is exactly the hypothesis of @thm-strong-induction-from-base at m; so any smallest-counterexample proof can be rewritten as a strong induction, and the reverse rewriting works too. Which one to write is a matter of which reads better. A smallest counterexample suits claims whose failure has a natural “smaller failure”, like a fraction that can be reduced, or a number with a factor. Divisibility and the division algorithm The first uses of the method are about divisibility, and here is the vocabulary. [Divisibility] Let a, b \in 
Z. We say that a divides b, written a \mid b, if there exists k \in 
Z with b = ka. Then a is a divisor of b, and b is a multiple of a. So 3 \mid 12, with k = 4, and -3 \mid 12, with k = -4. Every integer a divides 0, with k = 0; this is the degenerate case, and it shows that “a \mid b” is a statement, not the number b/a: 0 \mid 0 is true, while 0/0 is not defined. Also 1 \mid b and b \mid b for every integer b, and “n is even” is “2 \mid n”. If a \mid b and b \mid c, then a \mid c: from b = ka and c = lb we get c = (lk)a, with lk \in 
Z by @prp-integers-closed (a). Change 12 to 14: 3 
mid 14. The witness k would have to be 14/3, and 4 < 14/3 < 5, so 14/3 is not an integer, by the discreteness clause of @prp-integers-closed. The clause that fails is “k \in 
Z”: the equation 14 = k \cdot 3 has a real solution, just not an integer one. Divisibility claims about powers are a staple of induction, because the step usually factors out one copy. For instance, 3 \mid 4^n - 1 for every n \in 
N, with 4^n in its school meaning (4^0 = 1, 4^{n+1} = 4^n \cdot 4; Section 2.3 makes this a definition). Base case: 4^0 - 1 = 0 = 3 \cdot 0. Step: if 4^n - 1 = 3k with k \in 
Z, then 4^{n+1} - 1 = 4(4^n - 1) + 3 = 3(4k + 1) , and 4k + 1 \in 
Z. By @fd1:ax-induction, the claim holds for every n \in 
N. [Prime Number] An integer p is prime if p \ge 2 and the only positive divisors of p are 1 and p. A prime factor of an integer n is a prime p with p \mid n. For example, 2 is prime. Let d > 0 divide 2, say 2 = kd with k \in 
Z. Then k > 0, so k \ge 1 by @prp-integers-closed (b), and d \le kd = 2; by discreteness d \in \{1, 2\}. The same argument shows that 3 and 7 are prime, once the candidates d = 2 (and d = 2, \dots, 6 for 7) are ruled out as 3 
mid 14 was. Non-examples: 9 is not prime, since 9 = 3 \cdot 3 gives the positive divisor 3 
otin \{1, 9\}; and 1 is not prime, though its only positive divisor is 1, because the definition demands p \ge 2. The clause p \ge 2 keeps 1 out so that factorizations into primes can be unique, a fact this chapter does not prove or use: Exercise B2 below is about existence only. Every integer, divided by a positive integer n, leaves a remainder between 0 and n - 1. This is school arithmetic, and it is the tool behind “even or odd”. [Division Algorithm] Let a \in 
Z and n \in 
Z_{>0}. Then there are unique integers q and r with a = qn + r \quad 	ext{and} \quad 0 \le r < n . The hypothesis n > 0 matters: for n = 0 no r satisfies 0 \le r < 0. Try it first (ten minutes): which set of non-negative integers should have a least element, and why is that least element the remainder? The obvious attempt subtracts n from a again and again until what is left lies in [0, n), adding n instead when a is negative. “Again and again until” is a process, not yet a proof: why does it stop, and why at a number below n? Well-ordering replaces the process by its outcome. Among all the non-negative integers a - qn, take the least. If it were n or more, subtracting one more n would leave a smaller non-negative one. For uniqueness: two remainders differ by a multiple of n, yet lie less than n apart, so the multiple is 0. Existence. Let R \coloneqq \{ a - qn : q \in 
Z \} \cap \{ x \in 
Z : x \ge 0 \} , the set of non-negative integers of the form a - qn (each a - qn is an integer by @prp-integers-closed (a)). The set R is non-empty. If a \ge 0, take q = 0: then a - 0 \cdot n = a \in R. If a < 0, take q = a: then a - an = a(1 - n) \ge 0, since a < 0 and 1 - n \le 0 (as n \ge 1 by @prp-integers-closed (b)). The set R is a non-empty set of integers with the integer lower bound 0, so by @cor-well-ordering-integers it has a least element r; write r = a - qn with q \in 
Z. Then a = qn + r and r \ge 0. Suppose r \ge n. Then r - n = a - (q + 1)n is an integer of the required form with r - n \ge 0, so r - n \in R; and r - n < r, since n > 0. This contradicts the choice of r. Hence r < n. Uniqueness. Let a = qn + r = q'n + r' with q, q', r, r' \in 
Z, 0 \le r < n and 0 \le r' < n. Suppose r 
e r'. By symmetry (exchanging (q, r) and (q', r') changes neither the hypotheses nor the goal) we may suppose r' < r. Then r - r' = (q' - q)n, and k \coloneqq q' - q is an integer with kn = r - r' > 0. Since n > 0, also k > 0, so k \ge 1 by @prp-integers-closed (b), and r - r' = kn \ge n . But r - r' \le r < n, since r' \ge 0. This contradiction shows r = r'. Then qn = q'n, and since n 
e 0, q = q'. This proves the theorem. The integers q and r are the quotient and the remainder of a on division by n. For negative a the remainder is still non-negative: -7 = 3 \cdot (-3) + 2, with remainder 2, not -1. Existence and uniqueness do separate jobs, and the case n = 2 shows both: - Existence says that every integer a is 2q or 2q + 1: every integer is even or odd. - Uniqueness says that no integer is both. If a = 2q = 2q' + 1, then a would have remainders 0 and 1. This is the school fact that Logic and Proof, Chapter 1 used in Argument A and Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 used in the proof of @fd1:thm-square-even-implies-even, now proved. The same uniqueness shows that no integer m has 2m = 1, since 1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1 has remainder 1 and 2m = 2m + 0 has remainder 0; this is the fact Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 uses to show that 
Z is not a field. An integer 4k + 1 = 2(2k) + 1 or 4k + 3 = 2(2k + 1) + 1 is odd. With n = 3, every integer is 3k, 3k + 1 or 3k + 2, for exactly one of the three forms. “The remainder” is the r of the theorem, with 0 \le r < n. The equations 17 = 5 \cdot 4 - 3 and 17 = 5 \cdot 2 + 7 are true, but -3 and 7 are not remainders, and allowing them destroys uniqueness: 17 would have the three “remainders” -3, 2 and 7. Every argument above that concludes from “remainder 1” that a number is not a multiple of 2 uses the range 0 \le r < n, through uniqueness. Lowest terms and prime factors Logic and Proof, Chapter 2 needed one more fact about fractions, the fact (L) in the proof of @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational: every rational number can be written with numerator and denominator not both even. The reason given there was that halving cannot go on for ever. Here is that reason as a proof, written in the steps of the smallest-counterexample method, each step named. [Lowest Terms, Up to Factors of Two] Every rational number can be written as p/q with p \in 
Z, q \in 
Z_{>0}, and p and q not both even. A representation with both entries even can be halved. Halving makes the denominator smaller, so a least denominator cannot belong to a representation that can be halved. Well-ordering supplies the least denominator. Suppose it fails. Fix r \in 
Q, and suppose that r has no representation p/q with p \in 
Z, q \in 
Z_{>0}, and p and q not both even. Let F \coloneqq \{ q \in 
Z_{>0} : r = p/q 	ext{ for some } p \in 
Z \} . Under the supposition, every q \in F is the denominator of a failing representation. Take the least failure. By the definition of 
Q, r = p/q for some p \in 
Z and q \in 
Z_{>0}, so F is non-empty; and F \subseteq 
Z_{>0} \subseteq 
N. By @thm-well-ordering, F has a least element m. Write r = p/m with p \in 
Z. Use the supposition at m. The representation r = p/m fails, so p and m are both even: p = 2p' and m = 2m' with p', m' \in 
Z. Produce a smaller failure. Since m > 0, m' = m/2 > 0, so m' \in 
Z_{>0} by @prp-integers-closed (b). Moreover r = 2p'/(2m') = p'/m', so m' \in F; and m' < m' + m' = m. So m' is an element of F smaller than its least element m, a contradiction. Hence r has a representation of the required kind. As r \in 
Q was arbitrary, this proves the lemma. This is (L), with more: the denominator can be taken positive, not merely non-zero. The proof of @fd1:thm-sqrt2-irrational now rests on a proved lemma. The same argument with “not both even” replaced by “no common divisor d \ge 2” puts every fraction in lowest terms in the full sense; that is Exercise C2. Two of the proof’s steps adapt those of the smallest-counterexample method above: the failures are the denominators in F, and the supposition makes every element of F one, so the third step needs only the supposition at m, not the claim below m, and the contradiction of the fourth step is the smaller failure m'. This proof is written out in full; two later exercises use the same move with less given: Exercise B2 below leaves its last step blank, and Exercise C1 of Section 2.3 leaves the last half blank. The next result is the prime-factor fact that Logic and Proof, Chapter 5 used. Its proof is a strong induction from base 2; the same argument inside an ulename{RAA} box is a smallest-counterexample proof, in which the least failure m gets a prime factor from its divisor a, contradicting the choice of m (compare Exercise B2). [Every Integer at Least Two Has a Prime Factor] Every integer n \ge 2 has a prime factor. A prime is its own prime factor. A number that is not prime has a divisor strictly between 1 and itself; that divisor is smaller, so it has a prime factor by the strong hypothesis, and divisibility passes it on. We use @thm-strong-induction-from-base with n_0 = 2. Let n \ge 2 be an integer, and suppose every integer k with 2 \le k < n has a prime factor. If n is prime, then n is a prime factor of itself, since n = 1 \cdot n. If n is not prime, then, as n \ge 2, it has a positive divisor a 
otin \{1, n\} (@def-prime). Write n = ka with k \in 
Z. Since n > 0 and a > 0, also k > 0, so k \ge 1 and a \ge 1 by @prp-integers-closed (b). Hence a \le ka = n. With a 
e 1 and a 
e n this gives 1 < a < n, and so 2 \le a < n by the discreteness clause of @prp-integers-closed. By the hypothesis, a has a prime factor p, say a = lp with l \in 
Z. Then n = ka = (kl)p, with kl \in 
Z by @prp-integers-closed (a), so p \mid n. In both cases n has a prime factor. By @thm-strong-induction-from-base, every integer n \ge 2 has one. This proves the theorem. The hypothesis was used at a, which can be far below n - 1: for n = 91 = 7 \cdot 13 it is used at 7 or at 13. Ordinary induction, which offers only n - 1, would have nothing to say about 91 from 90. How induction proofs go wrong An induction proof has few moving parts: a property, a base case, a step, and a citation of the right principle. Each can fail, and each failure has a place in the proof where it can be pointed at. Two questions are kept apart throughout: is the conclusion true, and does the argument prove it? [All Numbers Are Equal] Here is a “theorem” and a “proof”. Find the line that fails. “Theorem.” For every integer n \ge 1 and all real numbers x_1, \dots, x_n, we have x_1 = x_2 = \dots = x_n. “Proof.” For an integer n \ge 1, let P(n) be the statement “for all real numbers x_1, \dots, x_n, all the entries of the list x_1, \dots, x_n are equal”. We use @thm-induction with n_0 = 1. 1. Base case. A list x_1 of one number has only one entry, so all its entries are equal: P(1) holds. 2. Step. Let n \ge 1 be an integer, suppose P(n), and let x_1, \dots, x_{n+1} be real numbers. 3. The list x_1, \dots, x_n has n entries, so by P(n) its entries are all equal. 4. The list x_2, \dots, x_{n+1} has n entries, so by P(n) its entries are all equal. 5. The entry x_2 lies in both lists, so every entry of either list equals x_2. 6. Hence x_1 = x_2 = \dots = x_{n+1}, which is P(n + 1). By @thm-induction, P(n) holds for every n \ge 1. Is the conclusion true? No: the list x_1 = 0, x_2 = 1 has unequal entries, so P(2) is false. Does the argument prove it? No, and the failing line is (5) at n = 1. Then the two lists of lines (3) and (4) are x_1 and x_2, one entry each, and x_2 is not in the first. They share an entry exactly when the first list, x_1, \dots, x_n, contains x_2, that is, when n \ge 2. In the terms of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, line (5) cites a “fact” that is false in the case at hand: entry (N9). Everything else is correct. The base case (1) is true. For every n \ge 2 the step (2)–(6) is valid: if all lists of n reals had equal entries, so would all lists of n + 1. So the induction fails at exactly one transition, from 1 to 2, and the valid transitions from 2 on carry nothing, because P(2) is false and every later P(n) with it. A counterexample to the illegal step, as opposed to the conclusion: n = 1, x_1 = 0, x_2 = 1, where lines (3) and (4) hold and (5) does not. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- statement true? proved by the argument? --------------------------------------- ----------------------- ------------------------- P(1) yes yes, line (1) P(1) \Rightarrow P(2) no no: line (5) fails P(n) \Rightarrow P(n + 1) for n \ge 2 yes yes, lines (2)–(6) P(n) for every n \ge 1 no no ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- This is the failure that Logic and Proof, Chapter 3’s warning about 2^n \ge n^2 foreshadowed: a step that holds only from some point on, with a gap at the first transition. A step must be proved for every n \ge n_0, and the place to look for a gap is the smallest n, where the objects the step talks about are smallest. The other failures are quicker to state. The missing base case. “n = n + 1 for every n \in 
N.” The step is valid: if n = n + 1, adding 1 to both sides gives n + 1 = n + 2. But P(0), “0 = 1”, is false, and so is every P(n). The step is a true implication between false statements, and an induction with no true base proves nothing. The hypothesis used out of range. A strong induction from a base n_0 may use P(k) only for n_0 \le k < n. A step that writes n in terms of n - 3 needs n - 3 \ge n_0, and for the first few n that fails. @fd1:exm-threes-and-fives handled this correctly, with three base cases; the exit check C1 below is a proof that did not. The claim too weak to carry its own step. Sometimes the statement is true and the base case holds, but the inductive step cannot be completed, because the hypothesis gives too little. The repair is to prove more. Section 2.3 shows a sum bounded by 2 whose own step will not go through, and which a stronger bound carries. The induction hypothesis is “P(n)” for one fixed but arbitrary n: the assumption of the ulename{{	o}I} box inside the ulename{ orall I} box of the step (@fd1:def-rules-universal). A step that begins “assume that P(n) holds for every n” assumes the conclusion of the theorem, and whatever follows is circular: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. The witness is a “for every n” in the assumption that binds the induction variable n itself; it should not be there. A quantifier over another variable is part of the statement and may stay: “for every k with n_0 \le k < n” in strong induction, or the “for every n” inside P(m) in the proof of @lem-naturals-arithmetic (d), where the induction is on m. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. For each claim, name the form of proof that fits it most naturally (ordinary induction from 0, induction from another base, strong induction from a base with several base cases, or a smallest counterexample), and say in one clause why. Do not prove the claims. (i) 6 \mid 7^n - 1 for every n \in 
N. (ii) 2^n > n^2 for every integer n \ge 5. (iii) Every integer n \ge 12 is 3a + 7b for some integers a, b \ge 0. (iv) There are no m, n \in 
Z_{>0} with n^2 = 2m^2. 2. Negate “every integer n \ge 2 has a prime factor”, and say what a smallest counterexample to it would be. 3. In @exm-all-equal-induction, what is the smallest n for which the two lists x_1, \dots, x_n and x_2, \dots, x_{n+1} of lines (3) and (4) share an entry? 4. Find the error. Here is a “proof” that a^n = 1 for every real a 
e 0 and every n \in 
N; the powers a^n, a^0 = 1 and a^{-1} = 1/a have their school meaning (Section 2.3 defines a^n for n \in 
N only, so negative exponents lie outside that definition). “Fix a 
e 0. Base: a^0 = 1. Step: let n \in 
N and suppose a^k = 1 for every k \in 
N with k \le n. Then a^{n+1} = a^n \cdot a^n / a^{n-1} = 1 \cdot 1 / 1 = 1.” The conclusion is false (take a = 2, n = 1). Which transition fails, and why? (a) (i) Ordinary induction from 0: the step factors out one copy of 7, as in the example 3 \mid 4^n - 1 after @def-divides. (ii) Induction from base 5 (@thm-induction): the claim fails at n = 2, 3, 4, so it cannot start at 0, and the step 2^{n+1} = 2 \cdot 2^n > 2n^2 \ge (n + 1)^2 works for n \ge 5. (iii) Strong induction from base 12 with three base cases 12 = 3 \cdot 4, 13 = 3 \cdot 2 + 7, 14 = 7 \cdot 2: the step reaches back three, from n to n - 3. (iv) A smallest counterexample: in a solution (m, n) with least n, n^2 is even, so n = 2n' is even (@fd1:thm-square-even-implies-even), and then m^2 = 2n'^2, so (n', m) is a solution whose second entry m is smaller than n, since n^2 = 2m^2 > m^2. (Strong induction would also do; the forms are interchangeable, and the answers above name the natural fit.) (b) The negation is: there is an integer n \ge 2 with no prime factor. A smallest counterexample would be an integer m \ge 2 with no prime factor such that every integer k with 2 \le k < m has one. (c) n = 2. For n = 1 the lists are x_1 and x_2; for n \ge 2 both contain x_2. (d) The transition from 0 to 1 fails. At n = 0 the step writes a^1 = a^0 \cdot a^0 / a^{-1} and uses a^{-1} = 1, which is “P(-1)”; but the hypothesis covers only k \in 
N with k \le 0, that is, k = 0, and -1 
otin 
N. In fact a^{-1} = 1/a 
e 1 unless a = 1. The base case a^0 = 1 is true, and every transition from n \ge 1 on is valid, since then n - 1 \in 
N and n - 1 \le n, and a^n a^n / a^{n-1} = a^{n+1} for n \ge 1. As in @exm-all-equal-induction, the valid transitions carry nothing, because P(1) is already false. B. Practice [B1] Prove that 5 \mid 6^n - 1 for every n \in 
N, without adding up the powers of 6. Here 6^n has its school meaning: 6^0 = 1, 6^{n+1} = 6^n \cdot 6, and 6^n is an integer; Section 2.3 makes these official. For n \in 
N, let P(n) be “there is k \in 
Z with 6^n - 1 = 5k”. Base case: 6^0 - 1 = 0 = 5 \cdot 0. Step: let n \in 
N and suppose 6^n - 1 = 5k with k \in 
Z. Then 6^{n+1} - 1 = 6 \cdot 6^n - 1 = 6(6^n - 1) + 5 = 5(6k + 1) , and 6k + 1 \in 
Z by @prp-integers-closed (a). So P(n + 1) holds. By @fd1:ax-induction, 5 \mid 6^n - 1 for every n \in 
N. [B2: Products of primes] An integer is a product of primes if it equals p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k for some k \ge 1 and primes p_1, \dots, p_k (a single prime counts, with k = 1). Here p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k has its school meaning, and multiplying two such products gives the product of the joined list; Section 2.3 defines finite products (@def-sum-product). Here is a proof that every integer n \ge 2 is a product of primes, with its last step blank. Name the move, then complete it. Suppose not. Then the set F of integers n \ge 2 that are not products of primes is non-empty and has the integer lower bound 2, so it has a least element m by @cor-well-ordering-integers. Since a prime is a product of primes, m is not prime; as m \ge 2, it has a positive divisor a 
otin \{1, m\}, and m = ab with b \in 
Z. As in the proof of @thm-prime-factor, b > 0 and 2 \le a < m. Since a < m = ab and a > 0, we get b > 1, so b \ge 2 by discreteness; and since a \ge 2, b < 2b \le ab = m. So 2 \le a < m and 2 \le b < m, and as m is the least element of F, neither a nor b lies in F: both are products of primes. \dots The move is the smallest counterexample, and the blank is its last step, produce a contradiction. Write a = p_1 \cdots p_k and b = p'_1 \cdots p'_l with primes p_i, p'_j. Then m = ab = p_1 \cdots p_k \, p'_1 \cdots p'_l is a product of primes, which contradicts m \in F. Hence F is empty, and every integer n \ge 2 is a product of primes. [B3] 1. Find the quotient and remainder of @thm-division-algorithm for a = 17, n = 5, and for a = -17, n = 5. 2. Prove that the square of an odd integer leaves remainder 1 on division by 8. 3. Prove that if 2 \mid n and 3 \mid n, then 6 \mid n, for every integer n. Hint for (c): @thm-division-algorithm, dividing by 3. (a) 17 = 5 \cdot 3 + 2, so q = 3, r = 2. And -17 = 5 \cdot (-4) + 3, so q = -4, r = 3; in both cases 0 \le r < 5, so by uniqueness these are the quotient and remainder. (Not -17 = 5 \cdot (-3) - 2: a remainder is never negative.) (b) Let x = 2k + 1 with k \in 
Z. Then x^2 = 4k^2 + 4k + 1 = 4k(k + 1) + 1. By @thm-division-algorithm with n = 2, k = 2j or k = 2j + 1 with j \in 
Z. In the first case k(k + 1) = 2 \cdot j(2j + 1); in the second, k(k + 1) = (2j + 1)(2j + 2) = 2(2j + 1)(j + 1). Either way k(k + 1) = 2t with t \in 
Z, so x^2 = 8t + 1. Since 0 \le 1 < 8, the uniqueness in @thm-division-algorithm says that the remainder of x^2 on division by 8 is 1. (c) Let n = 2a with a \in 
Z, and divide a by 3: a = 3q + r with q, r \in 
Z and 0 \le r < 3, so r \in \{0, 1, 2\} by discreteness. Then n = 6q + 2r. Since 3 \mid n, say n = 3s with s \in 
Z, we get 2r = 3(s - 2q), so 3 \mid 2r, where 2r \in \{0, 2, 4\}. But 2 = 3 \cdot 0 + 2 and 4 = 3 \cdot 1 + 1 have non-zero remainders on division by 3, while a multiple 3t = 3t + 0 has remainder 0; by uniqueness, neither 2 nor 4 is a multiple of 3. So 2r = 0, r = 0, and n = 6q: 6 \mid n. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: a flawed induction] Here is a claim and a “proof”. Claim. Every integer n \ge 18 is 4a + 7b for some integers a, b \ge 0. 1. For an integer n \ge 18, let P(n) be “n = 4a + 7b for some integers a, b \ge 0”. We use strong induction from base 18 (@thm-strong-induction-from-base). 2. Base case. 18 = 4 \cdot 1 + 7 \cdot 2, so P(18) holds. 3. Step. Let n \ge 18 be an integer, and suppose P(k) holds for every integer k with 18 \le k \le n. 4. Write n + 1 = (n - 3) + 4. 5. Since n - 3 < n, the induction hypothesis gives n - 3 = 4a + 7b with integers a, b \ge 0. 6. Then n + 1 = 4(a + 1) + 7b, with a + 1 \ge 0 and b \ge 0, so P(n + 1) holds. 7. By @thm-strong-induction-from-base, P(n) holds for every integer n \ge 18. Answer each question. (i) Is the claim true? (ii) Does the argument prove it? (iii) Which line fails, and for which n? (iv) Which rule does that line break? (v) Give a counterexample to the failing step, not merely to some conclusion. (vi) Repair the proof. (i) The claim is true. Directly, 18 = 4 \cdot 1 + 7 \cdot 2 , \quad 19 = 4 \cdot 3 + 7 , \quad 20 = 4 \cdot 5 , \quad 21 = 7 \cdot 3 , and from these four the repaired induction in (vi) reaches every larger integer. (ii) The argument does not prove it, although its conclusion is true. (iii) Line (5) fails for n = 18, 19 and 20. There n - 3 is 15, 16, 17, all below 18, and the induction hypothesis says nothing about them. For n \ge 21, 18 \le n - 3 < n, and line (5) is correct. Lines (1)–(4), (6) and (7) are correct. Line (7) needs one remark, because the step is written from n to n + 1 and not in the theorem’s own form. At N = 18 the theorem’s hypothesis has a vacuous “if” part, so it asks for P(18) outright, which is line (2). At an integer N \ge 19, put n = N - 1 \ge 18. By the discreteness clause of @prp-integers-closed, the integers k with 18 \le k < N are exactly those with 18 \le k \le n, so lines (3)–(6), were they valid for every n \ge 18, would prove the hypothesis at N. (iv) Line (5) applies ulename{ orall E} to the hypothesis “for every integer k with 18 \le k \le n, P(k)” at k = n - 3. That is a bounded quantifier, and its elimination needs the line “18 \le n - 3” (@fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-rules); for n \le 20 that line is false. The proof checked only half of the bound, n - 3 < n. (v) Run the same argument with base 14 = 7 \cdot 2: it “proves” that every integer n \ge 14 is 4a + 7b. That conclusion is false at 17: with b = 0, 1, 2 the remainder 17 - 7b is 17, 10, 3, none a multiple of 4, and b \ge 3 makes it negative. The step that breaks is line (5) at n = 16: it takes P(13) from the hypothesis, but 13 < 14 is outside it, and 13 is not of the form (13 and 6 are not multiples of 4). At n = 16 the induction hypothesis is true (14 = 7 \cdot 2, 15 = 4 \cdot 2 + 7, 16 = 4 \cdot 4), and the step concludes the false P(17). So line (5) is an illegal step, not merely an unlucky one. (vi) Take four base cases, 18, 19, 20, 21, as in (i), and run the step only for n \ge 21, where n - 3 \ge 18. In the form of @thm-strong-induction-from-base: for n \in \{18, 19, 20, 21\}, P(n) holds directly; for n \ge 22, n - 4 \ge 18 and n - 4 < n, so the hypothesis gives n - 4 = 4a + 7b and n = 4(a + 1) + 7b. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: judges the conclusion true, with the small cases 18, 19, 20, 21 written as 4a + 7b. - 3: identifies the failing line exactly: the appeal to the hypothesis for n - 3, for n = 18, 19, 20. - 2: states the reason as a hypothesis used outside its range (ulename{ orall E} at a k with k < 18). - 2: gives a counterexample to the step: the same step carrying a true statement to a false one (for example, base 14 and the failure at 17), not merely a false conclusion. - 1: gives a correct repair (four base cases, or any equivalent). Fatal errors (0 for the item): calling the conclusion false; blaming the base case. [C2: Lowest terms] Prove that every rational number can be written as p/q with p \in 
Z, q \in 
Z_{>0}, and no common divisor d \ge 2 of p and q: there is no integer d \ge 2 with d \mid p and d \mid q. [Hint 1] Follow the proof of @lem-lowest-terms, step by step. [Hint 2] Suppose r \in 
Q has no such representation, and let m be the least element of F \coloneqq \{ q \in 
Z_{>0} : r = p/q 	ext{ for some } p \in 
Z \}. Fix r \in 
Q, and suppose that r has no representation of the required kind. Let F be as in Hint 2. By the definition of 
Q, F is non-empty, and F \subseteq 
Z_{>0} \subseteq 
N, so by @thm-well-ordering it has a least element m. Write r = p/m with p \in 
Z. By the supposition, this representation fails: there is an integer d \ge 2 with d \mid p and d \mid m, say p = dp' and m = dm' with p', m' \in 
Z. Since m > 0 and d > 0, m' = m/d > 0, so m' \in 
Z_{>0} by @prp-integers-closed (b). Then r = dp'/(dm') = p'/m', so m' \in F. And m = dm' \ge 2m' > m', since d \ge 2 and m' > 0. So m' is an element of F smaller than its least element, a contradiction. Hence r has a representation p/q with no common divisor d \ge 2. The statement contains @lem-lowest-terms, since d = 2 is one of the excluded common divisors. The only change in the proof is the size of the step down: m' = m/d instead of m/2, and d \ge 2 is what makes it a step down. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: sets up the smallest counterexample: fixes r, supposes no good representation, and defines the set of denominators. - 2: shows that set is a non-empty subset of 
N and takes its least element by @thm-well-ordering. - 3: extracts the common divisor d \ge 2 and writes the reduced representation p'/m', checking m' \in 
Z_{>0}. - 2: shows m' < m, using d \ge 2 and m' > 0. - 1: concludes, with the contradiction to the choice of m. A strong induction on the denominator earns the same points step for step. Fatal errors (0 for the step): taking a least element of a set not shown to lie in 
N; dividing by d without d 
e 0. [C3: Smallest, not largest] 1. Prove that a set A \subseteq 
R has at most one least element. 2. Deduce that a claim “P(n) for every n \in 
N” that is false has exactly one smallest counterexample. 3. Show that a false claim about 
N need not have a largest counterexample, by examining the claim “n < 5 for every n \in 
N”. (a) Let m and m' be least elements of A. Since m' \in A and m is least, m \le m'; since m \in A and m' is least, m' \le m. Hence m = m'. (b) The smallest counterexamples are the least elements of the set F \coloneqq \{ n \in 
N : P(n) 	ext{ is false} \}. The claim is false, so F is non-empty, and @thm-well-ordering gives a least element. By (a), there is only one. (c) The claim is false, and its counterexamples form F = \{ n \in 
N : n \ge 5 \}, which is non-empty. It has no greatest element: for every n \in F, also n + 1 \in 
N by (
NS), and n + 1 \ge 5, so n + 1 \in F and n + 1 > n. So the claim has a smallest counterexample, 5, and no largest one. Well-ordering has no upward twin in 
N: a non-empty subset of 
N has a greatest element when it is bounded above (@exr-naturals-and-well-ordering-c1), and not in general.

title: 2.3 Definition by Recursion
content:
Definition by Recursion Since school we have defined powers by two clauses: u^0 = 1, and u^{n+1} = u^n u. Sums a_1 + \dots + a_n, factorials and many sequences are defined the same way: a starting value, and a rule that produces the next value from the last. Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 used induction to prove facts about such objects, such as 3^n \ge 2n + 1 in @fd1:exm-power-inequality. But induction proves facts about a function that already exists, and here the function is what we want to obtain. This section proves that two such clauses always define exactly one function on 
N, and then uses the theorem to define sums, products and powers properly and to prove their first laws. Definitions that define something Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 met the same question for formulas. A recursive definition on formulas gives a value for each atom and a rule for each way of building a compound formula, and @fd1:thm-structural-recursion showed that such clauses define exactly one function, because unique readability leaves no choice of clause. On 
N the clauses are simpler: one starting value at 0, and one rule for passing from n to n + 1. What we want to prove is this. A starting value and a rule for the next value determine exactly one sequence. [Recursion Theorem] Let X be a set, let a \in X, and let g \colon 
N 	imes X 	o X be a function. Then there is exactly one function f \colon 
N 	o X such that f(0) = a \quad 	ext{and} \quad f(n + 1) = g igl(n, f(n) igr) \ 	ext{ for every } n \in 
N . In words: a is the starting value, and g is the rule that turns the stage n and the current value f(n) into the next value. The rule may look at n as well as at f(n): the factorial needs this, since (n + 1)! = (n + 1) \cdot n! is g(n, x) = (n + 1)x at x = n!. The hypothesis that g maps into X is what lets the rule be applied again at the next stage. The conclusion has two halves: existence (some f obeys the two equations) and uniqueness (no two different functions do). Uniqueness is an ordinary induction: two solutions agree at 0, and if they agree at n, the second equation makes them agree at n + 1. Existence is harder, because induction cannot produce f; it can only prove statements. So we prove by induction a statement about finite pieces of f. The roadmap: ① Uniqueness, by induction on n. ② Claim: for every n \in 
N there is exactly one function on \{0, \dots, n\} obeying the two equations wherever they make sense (a partial solution). Its graph is the graph of the previous one with one pair added. ③ Glue: collect the graphs of all partial solutions in one set \sS and take the union. The partial solutions agree where they overlap, so the union is the graph of a function on all of 
N, and that function obeys the equations. Before reading on: self-explain the Claim’s inductive step. For n \in 
N, the set \{0, \dots, n\} = \{ k \in 
N : k \le n \} of Section 2.1 contains 0, since 0 \le n by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a). Call a function h \colon \{0, \dots, n\} 	o X a partial solution up to n if h(0) = a and h(k + 1) = g(k, h(k)) for every k \in 
N with k + 1 \le n. (For such k, both k and k + 1 lie in \{0, \dots, n\}, so the equation makes sense.) Step 1 (uniqueness). Let f, f' \colon 
N 	o X both satisfy the two equations, and let P(n) be “f(n) = f'(n)”. P(0) holds, since f(0) = a = f'(0). If P(n) holds, then f(n + 1) = g igl(n, f(n) igr) = g igl(n, f'(n) igr) = f'(n + 1) , so P(n + 1) holds. By @fd1:ax-induction, f(n) = f'(n) for every n \in 
N. The two functions have the same domain and the same codomain, so f = f' by @prp-function-equality. Step 2. For every n \in 
N there is exactly one partial solution up to n. We use @fd1:ax-induction on n. Base case. By @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a), every k \in 
N has k \ge 0, so k \le 0 holds only for k = 0, and \{0, \dots, 0\} = \{0\}. The graph \{(0, a)\} with codomain X is a function on \{0\}, since a \in X: the input 0 has the one output a. It is a partial solution up to 0: its value at 0 is a, and the second condition is vacuous, because k + 1 \ge 1 > 0 for every k \in 
N. Any partial solution up to 0 has value a at 0, so it equals this one by @prp-function-equality. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N, and suppose there is exactly one partial solution up to n; call it f_n, with graph G_n. Let G_{n+1} \coloneqq G_n \cup  igl\{  igl(n + 1, \ g(n, f_n(n)) igr)  igr\} . First, \{0, \dots, n + 1\} = \{0, \dots, n\} \cup \{n + 1\}: a natural number k \le n + 1 is either n + 1 or less than n + 1, and then k \le n, since no natural number lies strictly between n and n + 1 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e)). Also n + 1 
otin \{0, \dots, n\}, since n + 1 > n. We check the clauses of @def-function for G_{n+1} on \{0, \dots, n + 1\} with codomain X. Every pair of G_{n+1} lies in \{0, \dots, n + 1\} 	imes X, because g takes values in X. (Fn1): an input k \le n has the output f_n(k) in G_n, and the input n + 1 has the output g(n, f_n(n)). (Fn2): the pairs with first coordinate k \le n all lie in G_n, since the added pair has first coordinate n + 1 
e k, and G_n satisfies (Fn2); the only pair with first coordinate n + 1 is the added one, since the first coordinates in G_n are at most n. So f_{n+1} \coloneqq (G_{n+1}, X) is a function on \{0, \dots, n + 1\}, and it agrees with f_n on \{0, \dots, n\}. It is a partial solution up to n + 1. Its value at 0 is f_n(0) = a. Let k \in 
N with k + 1 \le n + 1, so k \le n. If k < n, then k + 1 \le n by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (e), and f_{n+1}(k + 1) = f_n(k + 1) = g(k, f_n(k)) = g(k, f_{n+1}(k)), because f_n is a partial solution. If k = n, then f_{n+1}(n + 1) = g(n, f_n(n)) = g(n, f_{n+1}(n)) by the choice of the added pair. It is the only one. Let h be a partial solution up to n + 1. Its restriction h|_{\{0, \dots, n\}} (Section 1.4) is a partial solution up to n, because the conditions on it are among the conditions on h. By the induction hypothesis it is f_n. So h(k) = f_n(k) = f_{n+1}(k) for k \le n, and h(n + 1) = g igl(n, h(n) igr) = g igl(n, f_n(n) igr) = f_{n+1}(n + 1) . By @prp-function-equality, h = f_{n+1}. This proves the claim. For each n \in 
N, let f_n be the partial solution up to n, and G_n its graph. If m \le n, then \{0, \dots, m\} \subseteq \{0, \dots, n\}, and the restriction of f_n to \{0, \dots, m\} is a partial solution up to m, so by the claim it is f_m. In terms of graphs, G_m = G_n \cap  igl(\{0, \dots, m\} 	imes X igr) \subseteq G_n \qquad (m \le n) . Step 3 (existence). Let \sS \coloneqq  igl\{ G \in \powerset{
N 	imes X} : G 	ext{ is the graph of a partial solution up to some } n \in 
N  igr\} , a set by @def-set-builder and @def-power-set. By the claim, the elements of \sS are exactly the graphs G_n. Let F \coloneqq  igcup \sS (@def-family-union-intersection), so a pair lies in F if and only if it lies in some G_n; in particular F \subseteq 
N 	imes X. We check the clauses of @def-function for F. (Fn1): for n \in 
N, the pair (n, f_n(n)) lies in G_n \in \sS, hence in F. (Fn2): let (k, y) \in F and (k, y') \in F, say (k, y) \in G_m and (k, y') \in G_n. [Finite Sets Have a Maximum] For every integer n \ge 1 and all reals x_1, \dots, x_n, the set \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} has a maximum and a minimum. Add the elements one at a time. The maximum of the longer list is the old maximum or the new element, whichever is larger, and comparing the two is all the step needs. Let P(n) be “for all reals x_1, \dots, x_n, the set \{x_1, \dots, x_n\} has a maximum”. We prove P(n) for every n \ge 1 by @thm-induction with base 1. Base case. \{x_1\} has the maximum x_1. Inductive step. Let n \ge 1, suppose P(n), and let x_1, \dots, x_{n+1} be reals. Since \{1, \dots, n + 1\} = \{1, \dots, n\} \cup \{n + 1\} (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e), as in the proof of @thm-recursion), the set B \coloneqq \{x_1, \dots, x_{n+1}\} is A \cup \{x_{n+1}\}, where A \coloneqq \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}. By P(n), applied to the list x_1, \dots, x_n, the set A has a maximum M. By trichotomy, x_{n+1} \le M or M < x_{n+1}. Case 1: x_{n+1} \le M. Then M \in A \subseteq B, and every element of B is an element a \in A, with a \le M, or is x_{n+1} \le M. So M is a maximum of B. Case 2: M < x_{n+1}. Then x_{n+1} \in B, and every a \in A satisfies a \le M < x_{n+1}. So x_{n+1} is a maximum of B. In both cases P(n + 1) holds. By @thm-induction, P(n) holds for every n \ge 1. For the minimum, apply the result to -x_1, \dots, -x_n: if -x_j is a maximum of \{-x_1, \dots, -x_n\}, then -x_k \le -x_j, that is x_j \le x_k, for every k, so x_j is a minimum of \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}. The base is 1, not 0: for n = 0 the set is \emptyset, which has neither a maximum nor a minimum, since both must be elements. The proof used only order properties of \le: any two elements are comparable (trichotomy), \le is reflexive and transitive, and x \mapsto -x reverses \le. All of these hold in any ordered field, so the proof works word for word there; that is the setting in which Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 uses it. Passing from a finite set to a list x_1, \dots, x_n that enumerates it is what “finite” will mean in Chapter 3. It implies the claim, since 2 -  rac1n < 2. Base case. S_1 = 1 = 2 -  rac11. Inductive step. Let n \ge 1 and suppose S_n \le 2 -  rac1n. Then S_{n+1} = S_n +  rac{1}{(n + 1)^2} \le 2 -  rac1n +  rac{1}{(n + 1)^2} . It remains to show - rac1n +  rac{1}{(n + 1)^2} \le - rac{1}{n + 1}, that is,  rac{1}{(n + 1)^2} \le  rac1n -  rac{1}{n + 1} =  rac{1}{n(n + 1)}. Both denominators are positive, and n(n + 1) \le (n + 1)^2 because n \le n + 1 and n + 1 > 0; so the inequality holds. Hence S_{n+1} \le 2 -  rac{1}{n + 1}, which is P(n + 1). By @thm-induction, S_n \le 2 -  rac1n < 2 for every n \ge 1. The stronger statement carries its own step because its hypothesis says how far below 2 the sum is, and that margin pays for the next term. When a step fails, ask what the hypothesis would need to say, and prove that instead. Exercise C3 below uses it twice over, proving two identities together because neither carries its own one-step induction. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These questions are about the proof of @thm-recursion. 1. Why does uniqueness need only an induction, while existence needs the claim about partial solutions? 2. In Step 3, which property of the graphs G_n makes  igcup \sS satisfy (Fn2), and which part of the proof supplies it? 3. Run the construction for X = 
R, a = 1 and g(n, x) = (n + 1)x: write the graphs G_0, G_1, G_2. Which familiar function is f? 4. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. 5. Write \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k and n! as instances of @thm-recursion: name X, a and g for each. (a) Uniqueness is a statement about two functions that are given: it compares their values, and comparing values at n + 1 through the values at n is an induction. Existence asks for a function that is not given. Induction proves statements and does not build objects, so the proof proves a statement (the claim) whose content is that the finite pieces exist and are unique, and then builds f from them as a union. (b) The graphs agree where they overlap: G_m \subseteq G_n for m \le n, more precisely G_m = G_n \cap (\{0, \dots, m\} 	imes X). This comes from the uniqueness half of the claim: the restriction of f_n to \{0, \dots, m\} is a partial solution up to m, so it is f_m. With it, two pairs (k, y) \in G_m and (k, y') \in G_n lie in the larger graph, whose (Fn2) gives y = y'. So it verifies (Fn2) of @def-function for  igcup \sS. (c) G_0 = \{(0, 1)\}. Then g(0, 1) = 1 \cdot 1 = 1, so G_1 = \{(0, 1), (1, 1)\}. Then g(1, 1) = 2 \cdot 1 = 2, so G_2 = \{(0, 1), (1, 1), (2, 2)\}. The function f is n \mapsto n!: by @def-sum-product, 0! = 1 and (n + 1)! = n! \, (n + 1) = g(n, n!), so n \mapsto n! satisfies both equations, and by the uniqueness in @thm-recursion it is f. (d) For each n, induction shows that there is exactly one function on \{0, \dots, n\} obeying the equations, and these pieces extend one another. Their union is the required function, and an induction on n shows there is no other. (e) The sum: X = 
R, a = 0, g(n, x) = x + a_{n+1}. The factorial: X = 
R (or 
N), a = 1, g(n, x) = (n + 1)x, as in (c). B. Practice [B1: Sum of cubes] Prove that \sum_{k=1}^{n} k^3 = \Bigl( rac{n(n + 1)}{2}\Bigr)^2 for every n \in 
N. For n = 0, both sides are 0 (the empty sum, and 0^2 = 0). Suppose the formula holds for n. By @def-sum-product and the induction hypothesis,  egin{aligned} \sum_{k=1}^{n+1} k^3 &=  rac{n^2 (n + 1)^2}{4} + (n + 1)^3 = (n + 1)^2 \,  rac{n^2 + 4n + 4}{4} \ &=  rac{(n + 1)^2 (n + 2)^2}{4} = \Bigl( rac{(n + 1)(n + 2)}{2}\Bigr)^2 , \end{aligned} which is the formula for n + 1. By @fd1:ax-induction the formula holds for every n \in 
N. (Compare @prp-sum-first-n: the sum of the first n cubes is the square of the sum of the first n numbers.) [B2: Starting at the right place] Logic and Proof, Chapter 3 observed, in the warning after @fd1:exm-power-inequality, that “2^n \ge n^2” fails at n = 3 and holds again from n = 4 on. Prove that 2^n \ge n^2 for every integer n \ge 4, using @thm-induction. Say why the base must be 4 and not 3. Let P(n) be “2^n \ge n^2”; we use @thm-induction with n_0 = 4. Base case. 2^4 = 16 \ge 16 = 4^2. Inductive step. Let n \ge 4 and suppose 2^n \ge n^2. Then 2^{n+1} = 2 \cdot 2^n \ge 2n^2 by @def-power and the hypothesis. Moreover 2n^2 \ge (n + 1)^2, because 2n^2 - (n + 1)^2 = n^2 - 2n - 1 = (n - 1)^2 - 2, and (n - 1)^2 \ge 9 > 2 for n \ge 4. Hence 2^{n+1} \ge (n + 1)^2. By @thm-induction, 2^n \ge n^2 for every n \ge 4. The base cannot be 3, because P(3) is false: 2^3 = 8 < 9 = 3^2. The step is valid from n = 3 on, since (n - 1)^2 - 2 \ge 2 for n \ge 3, but it is useless at 3, where its hypothesis is false. At n = 2 the step fails ((2 - 1)^2 - 2 = -1), which is why the true P(2) does not lead to P(3). [B3: A closed form] The sequence a_0 \coloneqq 0, a_{n+1} \coloneqq 2a_n + 1 is defined by @thm-recursion. Compute its first five values, guess a formula for a_n, and prove it. The values are 0, 1, 3, 7, 15: one less than 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. We prove a_n = 2^n - 1 for every n \in 
N. For n = 0: a_0 = 0 = 2^0 - 1. If a_n = 2^n - 1, then a_{n+1} = 2(2^n - 1) + 1 = 2^{n+1} - 1 , using 2 \cdot 2^n = 2^{n+1} (@def-power). By @fd1:ax-induction, a_n = 2^n - 1 for every n \in 
N. The induction follows the two clauses of the definition: the base case is the starting value, the step is the rule. C. Going deeper [C1: Powers of two] Prove that every n \in 
Z_{>0} can be written as 2^k q with k \in 
N and q odd (that is, q = 2j + 1 for an integer j). Below, the proof is started; the second half is blank. Name the move, then complete it. Suppose not. Then the set F of n \in 
Z_{>0} that cannot be written in this form is non-empty, and F \subseteq 
N; let m be its least element. Then m \ge 1, and m is not odd, since otherwise m = 2^0 m would be of the required form. \underline{\hspace{8em}} Why is the statement made for n \ge 1 only? The move is the smallest counterexample of Section 2.2: suppose the claim fails, take the least failure by well-ordering (@thm-well-ordering), and produce a smaller failure. Completion. By @thm-division-algorithm with divisor 2, every integer is even or odd; m is not odd, so m = 2m' for an integer m'. Since m > 0, m' = m/2 > 0, so m' \in 
Z_{>0} (@prp-integers-closed (b)), and m' < 2m' = m. As m is the least element of F, m' 
otin F, so m' = 2^k q with k \in 
N and q odd. Then m = 2 \cdot 2^k q = 2^{k+1} q by @def-power, and k + 1 \in 
N by (
NS). So m has the required form, contradicting m \in F. Hence F = \emptyset, and every n \in 
Z_{>0} is 2^k q with q odd. The restriction to n \ge 1 is needed: 0 = 2^k q forces q = 0, since 2^k > 0 (@prp-power-laws (e)), and 0 = 2 \cdot 0 is even, not odd (@thm-division-algorithm: not both). So 0 is a genuine counterexample, and in the proof it is excluded by taking m \in 
Z_{>0}, which is what makes m' > 0. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: names the move (smallest counterexample) and says that the least element m exists by well-ordering (@thm-well-ordering). - 2: from “m is not odd” concludes m = 2m' with m' \in 
Z, citing even-or-odd. - 3: shows m' \in 
Z_{>0} and m' < m, so m' 
otin F. - 2: writes m = 2^{k+1} q with k + 1 \in 
N and reaches the contradiction. - 1: explains why n = 0 is excluded. Fatal errors (0 for the step): concluding m' 
otin F (or applying the induction hypothesis to m') without having shown both m' < m and m' \ge 1; missing either one is fatal. A reader who restarts by @thm-strong-induction-from-base with base 1 earns the points for the other steps (the induction hypothesis at m' replaces “m' 
otin F”), but not the 2 points for naming the move. [C2: Bernoulli beyond its hypothesis] 1. Show that (1 + x)^n \ge 1 + nx holds for x = -2 and every n \in 
N. 2. Say which line of the proof of @thm-bernoulli fails at x = -2, and why the statement survives anyway. 3. At x = -4, find the first n where the inequality fails, and the first n where the step “P(n) \Rightarrow P(n + 1)” fails. (a) At x = -2 the claim is (-1)^n \ge 1 - 2n. By the remark after @prp-power-laws, (-1)^n is 1 or -1. For n = 0 the claim reads 1 \ge 1. For n \ge 1, 1 - 2n \le -1 \le (-1)^n. (b) The line “multiplying the induction hypothesis by 1 + x” fails. At x = -2 the multiplier is 1 + x = -1 < 0, and multiplying (1 + x)^n \ge 1 + nx by a negative number reverses it: we get (1 + x)^{n+1} \le (1 + nx)(1 + x), the wrong direction. The rest of the proof (nx^2 \ge 0) still holds. The statement survives because (a) proves it by a different argument, which uses the special values (-1)^n = \pm 1. A proof that fails does not make its conclusion false. (c) At x = -4: n = 0 gives 1 \ge 1; n = 1 gives -3 \ge -3; n = 2 gives 9 \ge -7; n = 3 gives -27 \ge -11, false. So the first failure is n = 3. The step P(n) \Rightarrow P(n + 1) holds for n = 0 and n = 1 (both sides are true) and fails at n = 2, where P(2) is true and P(3) false. [C3: Two identities at once] Use @cor-two-step-recursion to define the sequence F_0 \coloneqq 0, F_1 \coloneqq 1, F_{n+2} \coloneqq F_{n+1} + F_n; name X, a, b and h. Then prove, for every n \in 
N, the statement P(n): F_{2n+1} = F_n^2 + F_{n+1}^2 \quad 	ext{and} \quad F_{2n+2} = F_{n+1} igl(F_n + F_{n+2} igr) . Check P(0), P(1) and P(2) numerically first. [Hint 1] Neither identity carries its own one-step inductive step: passing from F_{2n+1} to F_{2n+3} needs F_{2n+2}, which is the other identity. Prove both together, and use F_n + F_{n+1} = F_{n+2} to merge terms. [Hint 2] In the step, start with F_{2n+3} = F_{2n+2} + F_{2n+1} and substitute both halves of P(n). The definition. @cor-two-step-recursion with X = 
R, a = 0, b = 1 and h(n, x, y) = x + y gives exactly one sequence with F_0 = 0, F_1 = 1 and F_{n+2} = F_n + F_{n+1}. Its first values are 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8. Small cases. P(0): F_1 = 1 = 0^2 + 1^2 and F_2 = 1 = 1 \cdot (0 + 1). P(1): F_3 = 2 = 1^2 + 1^2 and F_4 = 3 = 1 \cdot (1 + 2). P(2): F_5 = 5 = 1^2 + 2^2 and F_6 = 8 = 2 \cdot (1 + 3). Proof. We use @fd1:ax-induction. P(0) was checked. Suppose P(n). Using the recursion and then both halves of P(n),  egin{aligned} F_{2n+3} &= F_{2n+2} + F_{2n+1} \ &= F_{n+1} F_n + F_{n+1} F_{n+2} + F_n^2 + F_{n+1}^2 \ &= F_n (F_n + F_{n+1}) + F_{n+1} F_{n+2} + F_{n+1}^2 \ &= F_{n+2} (F_n + F_{n+1}) + F_{n+1}^2 = F_{n+2}^2 + F_{n+1}^2 , \end{aligned} where the last two lines use F_n + F_{n+1} = F_{n+2} twice. This is the first half of P(n + 1). For the second half,  egin{aligned} F_{2n+4} &= F_{2n+3} + F_{2n+2} \ &= F_{n+1}^2 + F_{n+2}^2 + F_{n+1} F_n + F_{n+1} F_{n+2} \ &= F_{n+1} (F_{n+1} + F_n) + F_{n+2}^2 + F_{n+1} F_{n+2} \ &= F_{n+2}  igl(2F_{n+1} + F_{n+2} igr) = F_{n+2}  igl(F_{n+1} + F_{n+3} igr) , \end{aligned} using the first half of P(n + 1) just proved, the second half of P(n), F_{n+1} + F_n = F_{n+2}, and finally F_{n+1} + F_{n+2} = F_{n+3}. So P(n + 1) holds, and by @fd1:ax-induction P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. The second identity is written with F_{n+2} rather than in the form F_{2n} = F_n (F_{n-1} + F_{n+1}), so that both identities make sense on all of 
N and no F_{-1} is needed. The two identities hold together, and together they carry a one-step induction that neither carries alone: this is “prove more” (@exm-strengthen-hypothesis) in the form of a pair, as in the two-step example after @def-power. (A two-step induction can prove the first identity alone; see the marking scheme.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: defines the sequence by @cor-two-step-recursion, naming X, a, b and h. - 1: checks the base case P(0), both halves. - 3: proves the first identity at n + 1 (or for all n): F_{2n+3} = F_{n+1}^2 + F_{n+2}^2. - 3: proves the second identity at n + 1 (or for all n): F_{2n+4} = F_{n+2}(F_{n+1} + F_{n+3}). - 1: concludes by induction (one-step or two-step), with a hypothesis that covers every value the step uses. Alternative route: 3 for proving F_{2n+1} = F_n^2 + F_{n+1}^2 alone by a two-step induction (via F_{k+2} = 3F_k - F_{k-2} for k \ge 2 and the matching recursion for F_n^2 + F_{n+1}^2, with both bases n = 0, 1 checked), and 3 for deriving the second identity as F_{2n+2} = F_{2n+3} - F_{2n+1} = F_{n+2}^2 - F_n^2 = F_{n+1}(F_n + F_{n+2}). Fatal errors (0 for the step): inducting on one identity alone while using the other at n unproved; using the identities at n + 1 to prove themselves.

title: 2.4 Properties of Relations
content:
Properties of Relations Chapter 1 made relations into sets: a relation on a set X is a subset R \subseteq X 	imes X, and x \mathrel{R} y means (x, y) \in R (@def-relation). It named the properties that make a relation an order or an equivalence and left them to this chapter. Equality, \le, inclusion \subseteq, divisibility \mid, and “leaves the same remainder on division by 3” are all relations, and they behave alike in some ways and differently in others. This section names four properties that sort them, proves the ones that divisibility has, and collects witnesses for every failure. Sections 2.5 and 2.6 then study the two combinations that matter most. Four properties Start from equality. Every x equals itself; if x = y, then y = x; and if x = y and y = z, then x = z. The relation \le on 
R keeps the first and third of these and loses the second, but it has a substitute: x \le y and y \le x together force x = y. Each of these is a property a relation may or may not have. Each property is one rule for what the relation must contain, given what it already contains. [Properties of a Relation] Let X be a set and R a relation on X. Then R is - reflexive on X if x \mathrel{R} x for every x \in X:  orall x \in X \ \ x \mathrel{R} x ; - symmetric if x \mathrel{R} y implies y \mathrel{R} x, for all x, y \in X:  orall x \in X \  orall y \in X \ \  igl( x \mathrel{R} y 	o y \mathrel{R} x  igr) ; - antisymmetric if x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x together imply x = y, for all x, y \in X:  orall x \in X \  orall y \in X \ \  igl( (x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} x) 	o x = y  igr) ; - transitive if x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} z together imply x \mathrel{R} z, for all x, y, z \in X:  orall x \in X \  orall y \in X \  orall z \in X \ \  igl( (x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} z) 	o x \mathrel{R} z  igr) . In words: reflexive says every element is related to itself. Symmetric says the relation can be read backwards: whenever it relates x to y, it also relates y to x. Antisymmetric says it can be read both ways only between an element and itself. Transitive says two steps can always be replaced by one. Three of the four are implications, so a relation has them unless some related pair (or triple) makes the conclusion false: for symmetry and transitivity a pair is missing from R, and for antisymmetry two different elements are related both ways. Negating with @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation and @fd1:prp-negated-implication turns each failure into a witness:  egin{aligned} 	ext{not reflexive:} \quad & \exists x \in X \ \ 
eg (x \mathrel{R} x) , \ 	ext{not symmetric:} \quad & \exists x \in X \ \exists y \in X \ \  igl( x \mathrel{R} y \wedge 
eg (y \mathrel{R} x)  igr) , \ 	ext{not antisymmetric:} \quad & \exists x \in X \ \exists y \in X \ \  igl( (x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} x) \wedge x 
e y  igr) , \ 	ext{not transitive:} \quad & \exists x \in X \ \exists y \in X \ \exists z \in X \ \  igl( (x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} z) \wedge 
eg (x \mathrel{R} z)  igr) . \end{aligned} So “not symmetric” is shown by one pair related in one direction only, and “not transitive” by one triple. A single witness settles a failure; a success needs an argument for all elements. Reading a relation as a picture. Draw the elements of X as points and an arrow from x to y whenever x \mathrel{R} y. The relation \le on \{1, 2, 3\} is \{ (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3) \}: Reflexive means a loop at every point. Symmetric means every arrow has a return arrow. Antisymmetric means no two different points are joined in both directions. Transitive means every path of two arrows has a direct arrow from its start to its end. In the picture there are loops everywhere, no return arrows, and the two-arrow path 1 	o 2 	o 3 has its shortcut 1 	o 3; so \le on \{1, 2, 3\} is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive, and not symmetric, with witness the pair (1, 2). A path may also return to its start: x 	o y 	o x. Transitivity then demands the loop at x. That case is the source of the warning below. Why “reflexive on X”. The other three properties mention elements only when they are related, so they depend on the set R alone. Reflexivity depends on X too. The relation \{(0, 0)\} is reflexive on \{0\}, and the same set of pairs, viewed as a relation on \{0, 1\}, is not reflexive on \{0, 1\}, with witness 1. That is why the definition names the set. Divisibility Divisibility shows that the same rule can give an antisymmetric relation on one set and not on a larger one, because the larger set brings in more pairs: \mid on 
Z contains both (2, -2) and (-2, 2), which \mid on 
N does not. Recall @def-divides: for integers a, b, a \mid b means b = ka for some k \in 
Z. [Divisibility on the Natural Numbers] The relation \mid is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive on 
N. On 
Z it is reflexive and transitive, and not antisymmetric. Reflexivity and transitivity are one line each from @def-divides. For antisymmetry, b = ka and a = lb give a = lka. If a 
e 0, this forces kl = 1, and for positive integers that means k = l = 1. On 
N the multipliers are positive, so b = a; on 
Z they may both be -1. Reflexive. For every integer a, a = 1 \cdot a, so a \mid a. Transitive. Let a \mid b and b \mid c, say b = ka and c = lb with k, l \in 
Z. Then c = (lk)a, and lk \in 
Z by @prp-integers-closed (a), so a \mid c. These two arguments work for all integers, so on 
N and on 
Z. Antisymmetric on 
N. Let a, b \in 
N with a \mid b and b \mid a, say b = ka and a = lb with k, l \in 
Z. Case 1: a = 0 or b = 0. If a = 0, then b = k \cdot 0 = 0; if b = 0, then a = l \cdot 0 = 0. Either way a = b. Case 2: a 
e 0 and b 
e 0. By @lem-naturals-arithmetic (a), a \ge 1 and b \ge 1, so both are positive. Since ka = b > 0 and a > 0, we have k > 0 (if k \le 0, then ka \le 0); likewise l > 0. By @prp-integers-closed (b), k, l \in 
Z_{>0} = \{ n \in 
N : n \ge 1 \}, so k \ge 1 and l \ge 1. Now a = lb = lka, and a 
e 0, so kl = 1. If k > 1, then multiplying by l > 0 gives kl > l \ge 1, contradicting kl = 1. So k \le 1, hence k = 1, and b = a. Not antisymmetric on 
Z. -2 = (-1) \cdot 2 and 2 = (-1) \cdot (-2), so 2 \mid -2 and -2 \mid 2, but 2 
e -2. The failure on 
Z is a non-example by minimal change: enlarging the set from 
N to 
Z keeps reflexivity and transitivity, and antisymmetry fails exactly because an integer and its negative divide each other. Two facts about (
N, \mid) will matter in Section 2.6: every a \in 
N divides 0, since 0 = 0 \cdot a, and 1 divides every a, since a = a \cdot 1. In the divisibility relation, 0 sits above everything and 1 below everything. A table of examples Here are eight relations checked against the four properties. Each “no” comes with its witness, which is how a failure is proved; each “yes” is a one-line argument given after the table. [Eight relations, four properties] Decide which of the four properties each relation has: =, \le and < on 
R; \subseteq on \powerset{X} for a set X with at least one element; \mid on 
N and on 
Z; “x - y \in 
Z” on 
R; and the empty relation \emptyset on a set X with at least one element. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Relation reflexive symmetric antisymmetric transitive --------------------------- -------------- ------------------ --------------- -------------- = on 
R yes yes yes yes \le on 
R yes no: 0, 1 yes yes < on 
R no: 0 no: 0, 1 yes yes \subseteq on \powerset{X} yes no: \emptyset, X yes yes \mid on 
N yes no: 1, 2 yes yes \mid on 
Z yes no: 1, 2 no: 2, -2 yes x - y \in 
Z on 
R yes yes no: 0, 1 yes \emptyset on X no: any x yes yes yes -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The witnesses. 0 \le 1 and not 1 \le 0; 0 < 1 and not 1 < 0; not 0 < 0. \emptyset \subseteq X, since the empty set is a subset of every set (Section 1.1, after @prp-empty-set-unique), and X 
ot\subseteq \emptyset, since X has an element and \emptyset has none. 1 \mid 2, and 2 
mid 1: 1 = 2k would give 0 < k < 1, and no integer lies there (@prp-integers-closed (c)). The pair 2, -2 is from @prp-divides-partial-order. For x - y \in 
Z: 0 - 1 = -1 and 1 - 0 = 1 are integers, and 0 
e 1. For \emptyset: no x has (x, x) \in \emptyset. The “yes” entries. Equality is reflexive by ulename{{=}I} (@fd1:def-rules-equality), symmetric and transitive by @fd1:prp-equality-symmetric-transitive, and antisymmetric because its conclusion x = y is one of its hypotheses. For \le and <, antisymmetry and transitivity are order facts about 
R, and \le is reflexive because x = x gives x \le x; for <, antisymmetry holds vacuously, since x < y and y < x never hold together. For \subseteq, reflexivity is immediate from @def-subset, transitivity is @prp-subset-transitive, and antisymmetry is @prp-subset-antisymmetric. For \mid, see @prp-divides-partial-order. For x - y \in 
Z: x - x = 0 \in 
Z; y - x = -(x - y); and x - z = (x - y) + (y - z); these are integers by @prp-integers-closed (a). The empty relation is symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive vacuously: each property is an implication whose hypothesis requires a pair in \emptyset. Three degenerate cases are worth a sentence each, because each shows a property holding for a reason other than the one we expect. - The empty relation on a non-empty X has every property except reflexivity, all vacuously. It is the standard witness that the three implication properties do not imply reflexivity. - The full relation X 	imes X relates everything to everything. It is reflexive, symmetric and transitive; it is antisymmetric only if X has at most one element. - If X = \emptyset, then \powerset{X} = \{\emptyset\}, and \subseteq on it is \{(\emptyset, \emptyset)\}: with only one element, it is symmetric. The non-emptiness of X in the table is what the witness \emptyset, X needs. On the set \{2, 3, 4, \dots\} of integers \ge 2, let x \mathrel{C} y mean “x and y have a common prime factor”, that is, some prime p divides both. Which of the four properties does C have? Reflexive: every integer x \ge 2 has a prime factor p (@thm-prime-factor), and p divides x and x. Symmetric: the condition “p \mid x and p \mid y” does not depend on the order of x and y. Not antisymmetric: 2 \mathrel{C} 4 and 4 \mathrel{C} 2 (both divisible by 2), and 2 
e 4. Not transitive: 2 \mathrel{C} 6 (common factor 2) and 6 \mathrel{C} 3 (common factor 3), but 2 and 3 have no common prime factor, since a prime dividing 2 is a positive divisor of 2 that is at least 2, hence is 2 (the example after @def-prime), and 2 
mid 3: 3 = 2k would give 1 < k < 2, and no integer lies there (@prp-integers-closed (c)). Sharing a factor with a middle element does not pass along, because the shared factor may change. A false theorem: “symmetric and transitive imply reflexive.” The “proof”: let x \in X, and take y with x \mathrel{R} y; by symmetry y \mathrel{R} x, and by transitivity x \mathrel{R} x. The conclusion is false: the empty relation on \{1\} is symmetric and transitive (vacuously) and not reflexive, with witness 1. The illegal step, “take y with x \mathrel{R} y”, is an ulename{\exists E} (@fd1:def-rules-existential) on \exists y \in X \ x \mathrel{R} y, which was never derived and need not be true: (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue (Exercise C2 gives the correct version). “Antisymmetric” is not “not symmetric”. Equality is both symmetric and antisymmetric. And \{ (1, 2), (2, 1), (2, 3) \} on \{1, 2, 3\} is neither: it is not symmetric, since 2 \mathrel{R} 3 and not 3 \mathrel{R} 2; and it is not antisymmetric, since 1 \mathrel{R} 2, 2 \mathrel{R} 1 and 1 
e 2. Two combinations of the properties organize the rest of the chapter. A relation that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive behaves like equality; Section 2.5 calls it an equivalence relation and shows that it cuts X into classes. A relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive behaves like \le; Section 2.6 calls it a partial order; inclusion on \powerset{X} and divisibility on 
N are examples that are not comparisons of sizes. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. State in symbols what it means for a relation R on X to be antisymmetric, and write its negation in symbols. 2. True or false, with a witness: every antisymmetric relation fails to be symmetric. 3. Which of the four properties does the relation “\abs{x - y} \le 1” have on 
R? 4. Let X = \{p, q\} with p

Its negation, by @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation and @fd1:prp-negated-implication: \exists x \in X \ \exists y \in X \ ((x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} x) \wedge x 
e y). (b) False. Equality on any set is antisymmetric and symmetric. So is the empty relation (vacuously). (c) Reflexive: \abs{x - x} = 0 \le 1. Symmetric: \abs{y - x} = \abs{x - y}. Not antisymmetric: \abs{0 - 1} \le 1 both ways and 0 
e 1. Not transitive: \abs{0 - 1} \le 1 and \abs{1 - 2} \le 1, but \abs{0 - 2} = 2 > 1. “Close to” does not pass along a chain, because small differences add up. (d) Four. A reflexive relation must contain (p, p) and (q, q). The other two pairs of X 	imes X, (p, q) and (q, p), may each be in or out, independently, which gives 2 \cdot 2 = 4 relations: \{(p, p), (q, q)\} together with one of \emptyset, \{(p, q)\}, \{(q, p)\}, \{(p, q), (q, p)\}. Transitive: from a + d = b + c and c + f = d + e, adding gives a + d + c + f = b + c + d + e, and canceling c + d gives a + f = b + e. Not antisymmetric: (0, 0) \mathrel{E} (1, 1) both ways, and (0, 0)

e -1. (c) Reflexive: f(x) \le f(x). Transitive: f(x) \le g(x) \le h(x) at each x. Antisymmetric: if f \mathrel{L} g and g \mathrel{L} f, then f(x) = g(x) for every x, and f = g by @prp-function-equality (same domain and codomain). Not symmetric: the constant functions 0 and 1 satisfy 0 \mathrel{L} 1 and not 1 \mathrel{L} 0. In addition, two functions need not be comparable: for f(x) = x and the constant 0, neither f \mathrel{L} 0 (fails at x = 1) nor 0 \mathrel{L} f (fails at x = -1). (d) Symmetric: xy = yx. Transitive: if xy > 0 and yz > 0, then (xy)(yz) = xz \, y^2 > 0, and y^2 > 0 (since y 
e 0, as xy 
e 0), so xz > 0. Not reflexive: 0 \cdot 0 = 0, so 0 is not related to itself. Not antisymmetric: 1 \mathrel{P} 2 and 2 \mathrel{P} 1 (both products are 2 > 0), and 1
