e 2). Not transitive: 0 \mathrel{N} 1 and 1 \mathrel{N} 2, and not 0 \mathrel{N} 2. Antisymmetric, vacuously: x \mathrel{N} y and y \mathrel{N} x would give y = x + 1 and x = y + 1 = x + 2, which is impossible, so no pair satisfies the hypothesis. [B2: Example generation] Give an example of a relation on \{1, 2, 3\} that is reflexive and transitive, but neither symmetric nor antisymmetric. Check each property. Then list the properties that every correct answer must have. One answer: R = \{ (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 3), (2, 3) \} . Reflexive: the three loops are in R. Not symmetric: 1 \mathrel{R} 3 and not 3 \mathrel{R} 1. Not antisymmetric: 1 \mathrel{R} 2, 2 \mathrel{R} 1 and 1 
e 2. Transitive: we check every two-step path x \mathrel{R} y \mathrel{R} z with x 
e y and y 
e z (a step along a loop changes nothing). They are 1 	o 2 	o 1, 1 	o 2 	o 3, 2 	o 1 	o 2 and 2 	o 1 	o 3, and their shortcuts (1, 1), (1, 3), (2, 2), (2, 3) are all in R. Element 3 has no arrow out except its loop, so no other path exists. Every correct answer must: - contain the three pairs (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3); - contain two different elements related both ways (to fail antisymmetry); - contain a pair related one way only (to fail symmetry); - contain the shortcut of every two-arrow path. The second and fourth items together force more: if a \mathrel{R} b, b \mathrel{R} a and b \mathrel{R} c, transitivity puts a \mathrel{R} c in. First, there is only one two-way pair: two of them, say \{a, b\} and \{b, c\}, give a \mathrel{R} c and c \mathrel{R} a by transitivity, so R is the full relation, which is symmetric. Call the two-way pair \{a, b\} and the third element c. Every arrow between a and b is two-way, so a one-way arrow must have c at one end, and one such arrow is never enough: transitivity relates c to the other element of the pair too, in the same direction. For example, \{(1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3), (1, 2), (2, 1), (3, 1)\} fails transitivity, since 3 \mathrel{R} 1 \mathrel{R} 2 and not 3 \mathrel{R} 2. If c \mathrel{R} a, then c \mathrel{R} a \mathrel{R} b gives c \mathrel{R} b, and neither a \mathrel{R} c nor b \mathrel{R} c can hold, since that would make a second two-way pair; so both arrows point out of c. Likewise a \mathrel{R} c forces b \mathrel{R} c, and both arrows point into c. Conversely, each of these six relations is a correct answer. Those with c above the pair are the answer above with the elements renamed. Those with c below are obtained from them by reversing every arrow, which keeps the loops, the two-way pair and the one-way arrows, and keeps transitivity: a path z 	o y 	o x of the reversed relation is the reverse of a path x 	o y 	o z, and the reverse of its shortcut (x, z) is (z, x). So \{1, 2, 3\} carries exactly six correct answers: one for each choice of the two-way pair (three choices) and of whether the third element lies above the pair or below it (two choices); the answer above has 3 above the pair \{1, 2\}. [B3: Intersections and unions] Let R and S be transitive relations on a set X. Prove that R \cap S is transitive. Show by an example on \{1, 2, 3\} that R \cup S need not be transitive. Let x, y, z \in X with (x, y) \in R \cap S and (y, z) \in R \cap S. Then (x, y), (y, z) \in R, so (x, z) \in R because R is transitive; likewise (x, z) \in S. Hence (x, z) \in R \cap S. For the union, let R = \{(1, 2)\} and S = \{(2, 3)\}. Each is transitive, vacuously: in R a two-step path would need a pair starting at 2, and there is none; in S one would need a pair ending at 2. But R \cup S = \{ (1, 2), (2, 3) \} contains (1, 2) and (2, 3) and not (1, 3), so it is not transitive. The intersection keeps both relations’ shortcuts; the union creates paths that neither relation contains, so neither supplies their shortcuts. C. Going deeper [C1: Properties as equations between sets] Let R be a relation on X, let R^{-1} be its inverse relation (@def-relation), and let \Delta_X \coloneqq \{ (x, x) : x \in X \} be the diagonal. 1. Prove that R is symmetric if and only if R = R^{-1}, and that R is antisymmetric if and only if R \cap R^{-1} \subseteq \Delta_X. 2. Deduce that a relation that is both symmetric and antisymmetric satisfies R \subseteq \Delta_X. Is every subset of \Delta_X both symmetric and antisymmetric? Recall that (x, y) \in R^{-1} if and only if (y, x) \in R. (a) Symmetric. (\Rightarrow) Let R be symmetric. If (x, y) \in R, then (y, x) \in R, that is, (x, y) \in R^{-1}; so R \subseteq R^{-1}. If (x, y) \in R^{-1}, then (y, x) \in R, so (x, y) \in R by symmetry; so R^{-1} \subseteq R. By @prp-subset-antisymmetric, R = R^{-1}. (\Leftarrow) If R = R^{-1} and x \mathrel{R} y, then (x, y) \in R^{-1}, so (y, x) \in R. Antisymmetric. A pair (x, y) lies in R \cap R^{-1} exactly when x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x, and it lies in \Delta_X exactly when x = y (by the characteristic property of pairs, @def-ordered-pair). So “R \cap R^{-1} \subseteq \Delta_X” says: for all x, y \in X, if x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x, then x = y. That is antisymmetry, word for word. (b) If R is symmetric and antisymmetric, then by (a), R = R \cap R = R \cap R^{-1} \subseteq \Delta_X. Conversely, every R \subseteq \Delta_X is symmetric (each of its pairs is (x, x), which is its own reverse) and antisymmetric (x \mathrel{R} y already forces x = y). So the relations with both properties are exactly the subsets of the diagonal; equality, \Delta_X itself, is the largest of them, and \emptyset the smallest. [C2: What symmetry and transitivity do give] Let R be a symmetric and transitive relation on X, and let D \coloneqq \{ x \in X : \exists y \in X \ \ x \mathrel{R} y \} be its domain. Prove that R \subseteq D 	imes D and that R, as a relation on D, is reflexive on D, symmetric and transitive. R \subseteq D 	imes D. Let (x, y) \in R. Then x \in D, with witness y. By symmetry y \mathrel{R} x, so y \in D, with witness x. Hence (x, y) \in D 	imes D. Reflexive on D. Let x \in D. By the definition of D there is y \in X with x \mathrel{R} y; fix one (an ulename{\exists E}, legitimate now, because x \in D is exactly the statement \exists y \in X \ x \mathrel{R} y). By symmetry y \mathrel{R} x, and by transitivity, from x \mathrel{R} y and y \mathrel{R} x, x \mathrel{R} x. Symmetric and transitive on D. These are implications about related elements, and every related pair lies in D 	imes D; so they hold on D because they hold on X. This is the correct version of the false theorem in the warning: its argument proves reflexivity exactly on the set of elements for which “take y with x \mathrel{R} y” is available. Elements outside D are related to nothing, and there reflexivity fails. In the language of Section 2.5, R is an equivalence relation on D. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: shows R \subseteq D 	imes D, using symmetry to put the second coordinate in D. - 4: for reflexivity on D, obtains y with x \mathrel{R} y from x \in D, and says why this step is now legitimate. - 2: applies symmetry and then transitivity, in that order, to get x \mathrel{R} x. - 2: explains why symmetry and transitivity restrict to D. Fatal errors (0 for the step): taking y with x \mathrel{R} y for an arbitrary x \in X rather than x \in D (the error of the warning); applying transitivity to x \mathrel{R} y and x \mathrel{R} y.

title: 2.5 Equivalence Relations and Partitions
content:
Equivalence Relations and Partitions Section 2.4 sorted relations by four properties: reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric and transitive (@def-relation-properties). This section studies the relations that have the first, second and fourth. They are the relations that say two things are “the same” in some respect, and each of them cuts its set into disjoint pieces of mutually “same” elements. We prove that the pieces always form a partition, and that every partition arises from exactly one such relation. Then we build the integers modulo n, and meet the check that every definition on pieces needs: that it does not depend on which element names the piece. Section 1.4 promised that check for functions defined on classes; here it is. Arithmetic on a clock On a twelve-hour clock, five hours after nine o’clock it is two o’clock. People say “9 + 5 = 2 on a clock”, and nobody is confused. Read as a statement about integers, it is false: 9 + 5 = 14. So what is it a statement about? The clock does not distinguish 2 from 14, or from 26 or -10: all of them put the hand in the same place. Two integers name the same hour when they differ by a multiple of 12. The sentence “9 + 5 = 2” is then about hours, and an hour is not one integer but a whole collection of them, \{ \dots, -10, 2, 14, 26, \dots \}. The addition adds collections: take any integer from the first, any from the second, add them, and see which collection the sum lands in. Two things have to be checked before this is mathematics. First, “differ by a multiple of 12” must behave like “is the same as”: it must cut the integers into separate collections, and no integer may land in two of them. Second, the answer must not depend on the choice: if we take 21 for “nine” and -7 for “five”, the sum 14 must still name two o’clock. It does, since 21 + (-7) = 14. The first check is the theory of equivalence relations and partitions. The second is called well-definedness, and it comes at the end of the section. Equivalence relations Equality has three properties that every argument with “=” uses silently: x = x; if x = y, then y = x; and if x = y and y = z, then x = z (@fd1:prp-equality-symmetric-transitive). They are exactly what lets us replace a thing by an equal thing, as often as we like, in either direction. “Same hour on the clock”, “same remainder on division by 3” and “same absolute value” all have the same three properties, although none of them is equality. They deserve a common name. An equivalence relation declares things the same in a way that behaves like equality. [Equivalence Relation] Let X be a set. An equivalence relation on X is a relation \sim on X (@def-relation) that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive on X (@def-relation-properties): 1. for every x \in X, x \sim x; 2. for all x, y \in X, if x \sim y, then y \sim x; 3. for all x, y, z \in X, if x \sim y and y \sim z, then x \sim z. When x \sim y, we say that x is equivalent to y (under \sim). In words: (Eq1) says everything is the same as itself. (Eq2) says “the same” has no direction: if x counts as the same as y, then y counts as the same as x. (Eq3) says sameness passes along a chain: two things that are each the same as a third are linked through it. In symbols, (Eq1)–(Eq3) are  orall x \in X \ \, x \sim x , \qquad  orall x, y \in X \ \, (x \sim y 	o y \sim x) ,  orall x, y, z \in X \ \,  igl( (x \sim y \wedge y \sim z) 	o x \sim z  igr) . The symbol \sim is a letter for a relation, like R in Section 2.4; it is written between its arguments because it is read like =. Nothing needs checking for well-definedness: the definition names a property of a set of pairs. [Four equivalence relations] Check (Eq1)–(Eq3) for each relation. 1. Equality on any set X: x \sim y if and only if x = y. 2. The relation X 	imes X on a set X, which relates every x to every y. 3. “Same absolute value” on 
R: x \sim y if and only if \abs{x} = \abs{y}. 4. The empty relation \emptyset on the empty set. (a) (Eq1)–(Eq3) are the three properties of equality recalled above: x = x is ulename{{=}I}, and symmetry and transitivity are @fd1:prp-equality-symmetric-transitive. (b) Every pair (x, y) with x, y \in X lies in X 	imes X, so each of (Eq1)–(Eq3) has a conclusion of the form (u, v) \in X 	imes X with u, v \in X, and that conclusion is true. This is the coarsest sameness: everything is the same as everything. (c) Each of (Eq1)–(Eq3) for \sim is the same property for equality, applied to the numbers \abs{x}, \abs{y}, \abs{z}. For instance, (Eq3): if \abs{x} = \abs{y} and \abs{y} = \abs{z}, then \abs{x} = \abs{z} by transitivity of =. Here 3 \sim -3, and 3 
ot\sim 2. (d) Each of (Eq1)–(Eq3) begins “for every element of X”, and X = \emptyset has none, so all three hold vacuously. The empty relation is an equivalence relation on \emptyset. Part (d) is the degenerate case, and it is worth keeping: it says that the definition makes no demand on an empty set, so the theorems below hold for X = \emptyset without a separate case. On a non-empty set the empty relation is not an equivalence relation: (Eq1) fails at any element x, since (x, x) 
otin \emptyset. The same set of pairs passes on one set and fails on another, because (Eq1) speaks about every element of X. Part (c) is an instance of a pattern that returns later in this section, with the fibers of a function: “x \sim y when some quantity attached to x equals the same quantity attached to y”. Any such relation inherits (Eq1)–(Eq3) from equality. A non-example by minimal change. On 
R, let x \sim y mean x - y \in 
Z, and let x \mathrel{R} y mean x - y \in 
N. The first is an equivalence relation, as an example later in this section checks. The second changes one letter. It is still reflexive, since x - x = 0 \in 
N by (( )0), and still transitive: if x - y \in 
N and y - z \in 
N, then x - z = (x - y) + (y - z) \in 
N by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (b). But it is not symmetric: 1 \mathrel{R} 0, since 1 - 0 = 1 \in 
N, while 0 - 1 = -1, and -1 
otin 
N because every natural number is \ge 0 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (a)). The clause that fails is (Eq2). The relation R is the order y \le x restricted to pairs at integer distance; it has a direction, and sameness has none. Why these three clauses. Each clause has a job, and each failure has a witness. - Drop (Eq1), and an element may be the same as nothing at all. On \{1\}, the empty relation is symmetric and transitive (Section 2.4’s warning), and 1 is related to nothing; it would sit in no piece of the cutting. - Drop (Eq2), and the pieces overlap. The relation \le on \{1, 2\} is reflexive and transitive; the set of elements below 2 is \{1, 2\}, the set below 1 is \{1\}, and the two share 1 without being equal. - Drop (Eq3), and sameness leaks. “\abs{x - y} \le 1” on 
R is reflexive and symmetric, and 0 is related to 1, 1 to 2, 2 to 3, and so on, while 0 is not related to 2. Every integer is linked to every other through a chain of steps of length 1, though few are related directly. The name comes from “equal value”: equivalent elements are equal in whatever respect the relation measures. An equivalence relation is an equivalence relation on a named set. The relation \{ (1, 1), (2, 2) \} is equality on \{1, 2\}, an equivalence relation; on \{1, 2, 3\} it is the same set of pairs and not an equivalence relation, since (3, 3) is missing and (Eq1) fails at 3. Before checking (Eq1), name the set. The payoff is the object the clock was after: the collection of everything that counts as the same as a given element. Equivalence classes An equivalence class is everything that counts as the same as one element. [Equivalence Class] Let \sim be an equivalence relation on a set X, and let a \in X. The equivalence class of a is [a] \coloneqq \{ x \in X : x \sim a \} . When the relation must be named, we write [a]_\sim. Any element of a class is called a representative of it. The class is a subset of X, by specification (@def-set-builder). Its definition fixes the order of the letters as x \sim a; by (Eq2) the order does not matter, and x \in [a] holds exactly when a \sim x. For the four relations of @exm-first-equivalences: under equality, [a] = \{a\}; under X 	imes X, [a] = X for every a \in X; under “same absolute value”, [3] = \{-3, 3\} and [0] = \{0\}; and on the empty set there are no elements and so no classes. On \{1, 2, \dots, 30\}, let x \sim y mean that x and y have the same last digit. List the classes. How many are there, and how many elements has each? The classes are \{1, 11, 21\}, \{2, 12, 22\}, …, \{9, 19, 29\} and \{10, 20, 30\}: ten classes, three elements each. Each class is the class of any of its elements; for instance [11] = [21] = [1]. The quick check shows the features the theorem below proves in general: every class is non-empty, no number is in two classes, and every number is in one. A family of subsets with these three features has a name. [Partition] Let X be a set. A partition of X is a set \sP of subsets of X, called blocks, such that 1. every block is non-empty: P 
e \emptyset for every P \in \sP; 2. the blocks are pairwise disjoint: for all P, Q \in \sP, if P 
e Q, then P \cap Q = \emptyset; 3. the blocks cover X:  igcup \sP = X. Here  igcup \sP is the union of the set of sets \sP (@def-family-union-intersection): the set of points lying in some block. Since every block is a subset of X, the union is always a subset of X, and (P3) says that every x \in X lies in some block. With (P2), it lies in exactly one: if x \in P and x \in Q, then P \cap Q 
e \emptyset, so P = Q. Examples: \{ \{1, 2\}, \{3\} \} is a partition of \{1, 2, 3\}. For a non-empty X, \{X\} is a partition with one block, and \{ \{x\} : x \in X \} is one with a block for each point. The even and the odd integers form a partition of 
Z with two blocks, because every integer is even or odd and not both (@thm-division-algorithm with n = 2). For X = \emptyset, the empty set of blocks \sP = \emptyset is a partition: (P1) and (P2) are vacuous, and  igcup \emptyset = \emptyset. Non-examples by minimal change. \{ \{1, 2\}, \{2, 3\} \} covers \{1, 2, 3\} and its sets are non-empty, but 2 lies in both, so (P2) fails. \{ \{1, 2\}, \{3\}, \emptyset \} satisfies (P2) and (P3), and fails (P1). Without (P1), “the block containing x” would still be unique, but a partition could carry useless empty blocks, and the correspondence with equivalence relations below would break, since no class is empty. A partition is a set of subsets of X. So is the set of all classes of an equivalence relation, and it gets its own name. [Quotient Set] Let \sim be an equivalence relation on a set X. The quotient set of X by \sim is the set of all equivalence classes, X/{\sim} \coloneqq \{ C \in \powerset{X} : C = [a] 	ext{ for some } a \in X \} . The quotient map is q \colon X 	o X/{\sim}, q(a) \coloneqq [a]. The quotient set is a set by specification inside \powerset{X} (@def-set-builder, @def-power-set), and it is often written \{ [a] : a \in X \}. The quotient map is a function by @def-function: each a \in X has the value [a], which lies in X/{\sim}, and only that value. It is surjective: an element of X/{\sim} is [a] for some a \in X, and then it is q(a) (@def-surjective). The quotient map forgets everything about a except which class it lies in, and that is the point of it. Read “X/{\sim}” as “X with equivalent elements identified”. The classes form a partition Here is the theorem the clock needs. It also says exactly when two names give the same class. [Equivalence Classes Partition the Set] Let \sim be an equivalence relation on a set X. 1. For every a \in X, a \in [a]; in particular every class is non-empty. 2. For all a, b \in X, [a] = [b] if and only if a \sim b. 3. For all a, b \in X, if [a] \cap [b] 
e \emptyset, then [a] = [b]. 4. The quotient set X/{\sim} is a partition of X. Each property of \sim does one job. Reflexivity puts a in its own class, which gives (a) and the covering. For (b), a class is determined by any one of its elements: if a \sim b, then anything the same as a is the same as b, by transitivity, and the reverse needs symmetry first. For (c), a common element c of two classes has c \sim a and c \sim b; symmetry turns the first around, transitivity joins the two, and (b) finishes. Then (d) is (a), (c) and the covering, read against the three clauses of @def-partition. Before reading on: which property of \sim does each line use? (a) Let a \in X. By (Eq1), a \sim a, so a \in [a] by @def-equivalence-class. Hence [a] 
e \emptyset. (b) (\Rightarrow) Suppose [a] = [b]. By (a), a \in [a] = [b], so a \sim b. (\Leftarrow) Suppose a \sim b. (\subseteq) Let x \in [a], so x \sim a. With a \sim b, (Eq3) gives x \sim b, so x \in [b]. (\supseteq) Let x \in [b], so x \sim b. By (Eq2) applied to a \sim b, b \sim a; with x \sim b, (Eq3) gives x \sim a, so x \in [a]. If a \equiv a' \pmod{n}, the product clause of @prp-congruence-arithmetic, applied to a \equiv a' twice, gives a \cdot a \equiv a' \cdot a', so [a^2]_n = [a'^2]_n. (b) No. [0]_5 = [5]_5, since 5 - 0 = 5. But [0]_{10} 
e [5]_{10}, since 5 - 0 = 5 is not a multiple of 10 (0 < 5 < 10). The input [0]_5 would get two values. (c) Yes. If a - a' = 10k with k \in 
Z, then a - a' = 5(2k) with 2k \in 
Z (@prp-integers-closed (a)), so [a]_5 = [a']_5. The difference from (b) is the direction: 5 \mid 10, so a multiple of 10 is a multiple of 5, not conversely. C. Going deeper [C1: Exit check: classes partition] Let \sim be an equivalence relation on a set X. Prove that the equivalence classes of \sim form a partition of X, and that for all a, b \in X, [a] = [b] if and only if a \sim b. Write the proof without looking at the text, naming the property of \sim behind each step. Non-empty. For a \in X, reflexivity gives a \sim a, so a \in [a], and [a] 
e \emptyset. Cover. Every class is a subset of X by definition. Every x \in X lies in the class [x], as just shown. So the union of all classes is X. [a] = [b] \iff a \sim b. (\Rightarrow) a \in [a] = [b], so a \sim b. (\Leftarrow) Let a \sim b. If x \in [a], then x \sim a and a \sim b, so x \sim b by transitivity: [a] \subseteq [b]. By symmetry b \sim a; if x \in [b], then x \sim b and b \sim a give x \sim a by transitivity: [b] \subseteq [a]. So [a] = [b]. Disjoint or equal. Let [a] \cap [b] 
e \emptyset, with a common element c. Then c \sim a and c \sim b. By symmetry a \sim c, and by transitivity a \sim b. By the previous paragraph, [a] = [b]. Hence two different classes are disjoint. The three paragraphs on non-emptiness, covering and disjointness are the three clauses of @def-partition, so the set of classes X/{\sim} is a partition of X. (This is @thm-classes-partition.) Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: each class is non-empty, by reflexivity. - 1: every element lies in some class (its own), so the classes cover X. - 4: overlapping classes are equal: a common element c with c \sim a and c \sim b; symmetry to reverse one of them; transitivity to link a and b; both inclusions (or the equivalence [a] = [b] \iff a \sim b) to conclude equality. - 2: [a] = [b] \iff a \sim b, both directions. - 1: the conclusion names the three conditions of a partition. A proof that shows “overlapping classes are equal” by proving [a] \subseteq [c] \subseteq [b] and back directly from the definition earns the 4 points for that step if each use of symmetry and transitivity is named. So does a proof that, from c \sim a and c \sim b, applies the (\Leftarrow) direction of [a] = [b] \iff a \sim b twice to get [a] = [c] = [b], provided that equivalence was proved independently of this step, with symmetry and transitivity named. Fatal errors (0 for the step): applying transitivity to a \sim c and b \sim c without reversing one by symmetry; showing only [a] \subseteq [b] and concluding [a] = [b]. [C2: Find the error] A student proves part of @thm-partition-equivalence. Let \sP be a partition of X, and let x \sim y mean that x and y lie in a common block of \sP. Claim. \sim is transitive. Proof. (1) Let x, y, z \in X with x \sim y and y \sim z. (2) Since x \sim y, there is a block P \in \sP with x \in P and y \in P. (3) Since y \sim z, y and z lie in a common block, and that block is P, so z \in P. (4) Hence x and z both lie in P, and x \sim z. 1. Is the claim true? 2. Which line fails, and which rule does it break? 3. Give a counterexample to the failing step, and repair the proof. (a) The claim is true: it is the transitivity step (Eq3) in the proof of @thm-partition-equivalence (a). (b) Line (3) fails. “y and z lie in a common block” is an existential statement, and to use it the proof must name its witness by ulename{\exists E}, with a new name. Line (3) gives the second witness the name P, already in use for the witness of line (2): this is entry (N4) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, reusing one witness name for two ulename{\exists E}’s (@fd1:def-rules-existential). The tell is that the proof never uses (P2), the disjointness of the blocks; and without (P2) the claim is false, as (c) shows. (c) A counterexample to the step needs blocks that overlap, since for a partition the step’s conclusion happens to be true. Take the cover \{ \{1, 2\}, \{2, 3\} \} of \{1, 2, 3\}, which is not a partition, with x = 1, y = 2, z = 3. Then 1 \sim 2 with P = \{1, 2\}, and 2 \sim 3 through \{2, 3\}; line (3) concludes 3 \in \{1, 2\}, which is false, and the argument “proves” 1 \sim 3, although no set of the cover contains 1 and 3. Repair: replace (3) and (4) by “Since y \sim z, there is a block Q \in \sP with y \in Q and z \in Q. Then y \in P \cap Q, so P \cap Q 
e \emptyset, and P = Q by (P2). Hence x \in P and z \in P, so x \sim z.”

title: 2.6 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content:
Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements Section 2.5 studied the relations that behave like equality. This section studies the ones that behave like \le: reflexive and transitive like an equivalence relation, but antisymmetric instead of symmetric, so that they have a direction. For numbers, “the largest element of a set” is clear. For sets under \subseteq, or for natural numbers under divisibility, two elements can be incomparable, neither below the other, and “largest” splits into two different notions. We separate them, prove what links them, and then take a first look at least upper bounds. That is the vocabulary Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 needs for the supremum. Partial orders Section 2.4 found three relations with the same three properties: \le on 
R, \subseteq on \powerset{X} (@exm-relation-table), and \mid on 
N (@prp-divides-partial-order). Each is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. Each says “below” in its own sense: smaller, contained in, a divisor of. What they share is what “being below” needs, and it deserves a name, so that a fact proved once holds for all three. A partial order says which elements lie below which, without requiring every two to be comparable. [Partial Order] Let X be a set. A partial order on X is a relation \preceq on X that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive on X (@def-relation-properties): 1. for every x \in X, x \preceq x; 2. for all x, y \in X, if x \preceq y and y \preceq x, then x = y; 3. for all x, y, z \in X, if x \preceq y and y \preceq z, then x \preceq z. The pair (X, \preceq) is a partially ordered set. Elements x, y \in X are comparable if x \preceq y or y \preceq x. The partial order is total if every two elements of X are comparable. The strict part of \preceq is the relation \prec on X given by x \prec y \iff x \preceq y \ 	ext{ and } \ x 
e y . We also write y \succeq x for x \preceq y. In words: (PO1) everything is below itself. (PO2) is the clause that gives an order its direction: two elements below each other are the same element, so “below” cannot run both ways between different things. (PO3) lets “below” pass along a chain. “Total” adds that any two elements can be compared; “partial” is the word for not requiring it. The symbol \preceq is a letter for an arbitrary partial order, chosen so that \le keeps its meaning on numbers. The strict part is irreflexive and transitive. No x has x \prec x, since that would need x 
e x. If x \prec y and y \prec z, then x \preceq z by (PO3); and x 
e z, because x = z would give x \preceq y and y \preceq x, hence x = y by (PO2), contradicting x 
e y. So x \prec z. Examples. - (
R, \le) is a partially ordered set, and it is total: for real numbers x \le y or y \le x. Its strict part is <. The same holds for (
N, \le) and (
Z, \le), since restricting a total order to a subset keeps all four properties: each is a statement about all elements, and holds in particular for the elements of the subset. - (
N, \mid) is a partially ordered set by @prp-divides-partial-order, and it is not total: 2 
mid 3 and 3 
mid 2, so 2 and 3 are incomparable. - (\powerset{X}, \subseteq) is a partially ordered set; the example after this list decides when it is total. - Degenerate cases: equality on any set X is a partial order, in which no two different elements are comparable; and the empty relation is a partial order on \emptyset, vacuously. Non-examples by minimal change. Divisibility on 
Z is reflexive and transitive, but not antisymmetric: 2 \mid -2 and -2 \mid 2, and 2 
e -2 (@prp-divides-partial-order). Passing from 
N to 
Z loses exactly (PO2). The relation < on 
R is antisymmetric (vacuously: x < y and y < x never both hold) and transitive, but not reflexive, since 0 < 0 fails. It is the strict part of \le, not a partial order. Why these clauses. Without (PO2), two different elements could each be below the other, and “the largest element” of a set could fail to be unique; the uniqueness proof in the next subsection uses (PO2) and nothing else. A relation that keeps (PO1) and (PO3) and drops (PO2) is often called a preorder; \mid on 
Z is one. Totality is left out because the important examples, \subseteq and \mid, do not have it, and much of the interest lies in what changes without it. [Inclusion is a partial order, rarely total] Let X be a set. Show that \subseteq is a partial order on \powerset{X}, and that it is total if and only if X has at most one element. A partial order. (PO1) A \subseteq A for every set A. (PO2) If A \subseteq B and B \subseteq A, then A = B by @prp-subset-antisymmetric. (PO3) is @prp-subset-transitive. (These are the entries of @exm-relation-table.) Total exactly when X has at most one element. Suppose X has two different elements a 
e b. Then \{a\}, \{b\} \in \powerset{X}, and \{a\} 
ot\subseteq \{b\}, since a \in \{a\} and a 
otin \{b\}; likewise \{b\} 
ot\subseteq \{a\}. So \{a\} and \{b\} are incomparable, and \subseteq is not total. For X = \{1, 2\}, the incomparable pair is \{1\}, \{2\}. Conversely, suppose any two elements of X are equal. Let A \subseteq X. If A 
e \emptyset, take a \in A; then every x \in X equals a, so x \in A, and A = X. So every subset of X is \emptyset or X. Any two of these are comparable, since \emptyset \subseteq X (Section 1.1, after @prp-empty-set-unique) and each is a subset of itself. So \subseteq is total on \powerset{X}. In a partial order, “x \preceq y fails” does not give “y \prec x”. In (\powerset{\{1, 2\}}, \subseteq), \{1\} 
ot\subseteq \{2\}, and \{2\} \subsetneq \{1\} is false too: the two are incomparable. The habit from numbers, “not \le means >”, is the totality of \le on 
R, and it must not be carried into a partial order. Bounds, greatest and maximal elements From now on, (X, \preceq) is a partially ordered set and A \subseteq X. The bounds come first, because both kinds of “largest” are measured against them. [Upper and Lower Bounds] An element u \in X is an upper bound of A if a \preceq u for every a \in A, and a lower bound of A if u \preceq a for every a \in A. The set A is bounded above if it has an upper bound in X, bounded below if it has a lower bound in X, and bounded if both. An upper bound lives in X and need not belong to A: in (
R, \le), 5 is an upper bound of [0, 1]. Every element of X is an upper bound of \emptyset, vacuously. In (
N, \mid), an upper bound of \{4, 6\} is a common multiple of 4 and 6, such as 12, 24 or 0. Now the two notions of “largest”. The first is the familiar one: an element of the set that is above everything in the set. The second asks less: an element with nothing in the set strictly above it. [Greatest and Least Elements] An element g is a greatest element of A if g \in A and a \preceq g for every a \in A. An element l is a least element of A if l \in A and l \preceq a for every a \in A. [Maximal and Minimal Elements] An element m is a maximal element of A if m \in A and there is no a \in A with m \prec a. An element m is a minimal element of A if m \in A and there is no a \in A with a \prec m. In words: a greatest element is an upper bound of A that belongs to A. A maximal element is one that cannot be beaten inside A, which is weaker: an element can be unbeaten simply because it is incomparable with its rivals. In symbols the difference is where the negation sits:  egin{aligned} g 	ext{ greatest:} &\quad g \in A \wedge  orall a \in A \ \, a \preceq g , \ m 	ext{ maximal:} &\quad m \in A \wedge 
eg \exists a \in A \ \, m \prec a . \end{aligned} By @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation (b), 
eg \exists a \in A \ \, m \prec a is  orall a \in A \ \, 
eg (m \prec a), and 
eg (m \prec a) says that m \preceq a implies m = a. So “maximal” reads: everything in A that is above m is m. “Greatest” reads: everything in A is below g. The first only forbids elements above; the second demands that every element be compared. For numbers the two coincide. In (
R, \le), the set \{1, 4, 9\} has greatest element 9, its only maximal element, and least element 1. The interval [0, 1) has least element 0 and neither a greatest nor a maximal element: for each a \in [0, 1), the number (a + 1)/2 lies in [0, 1) and is strictly above a. A one-point set \{x\} has x as greatest, least, maximal and minimal element, and \emptyset has none of the four, since each definition requires an element of A. The first result explains the article in “the greatest element”. [Greatest and Least Elements Are Unique] A subset A of a partially ordered set has at most one greatest element and at most one least element. Let g and g' be greatest elements of A. Since g' \in A and g is greatest, g' \preceq g; since g \in A and g' is greatest, g \preceq g'. By (PO2), g = g'. For least elements the same argument applies with the inequalities reversed. So we may speak of the greatest element and the least element of A when they exist. In (
R, \le), the greatest element of a set is its maximum, \max A, and the least element its minimum, \min A. This settles a point left open in Section 1.4: the least q_0 \in 
Z_{>0} with r q_0 \in 
Z in @exm-not-a-function exists by @thm-well-ordering: the set of such q lies in 
Z_{>0} \subseteq 
N, and it is non-empty, since writing r = p/q with q \in 
Z_{>0} (as the solution of (b) there notes) gives rq = p \in 
Z. It is unique by the least-element half of the proposition, so the rule there names one value. The second result compares the two notions. [Greatest and Maximal Elements] Let (X, \preceq) be a partially ordered set and A \subseteq X. 1. A greatest element of A is a maximal element of A. 2. If \preceq is total, then a maximal element of A is a greatest element of A. The same holds for least and minimal elements. For (a), anything strictly above the greatest element would also be below it, and antisymmetry forbids that. For (b), a maximal element m must be compared with each a \in A, and totality says it can be: either a \preceq m, as wanted, or m \preceq a, and then maximality forces a = m. (a) Let g be a greatest element of A. Then g \in A. Suppose some a \in A has g \prec a, so g \preceq a and g 
e a. Since g is greatest, a \preceq g. By (PO2), a = g, contradicting g 
e a. So no such a exists, and g is maximal. (b) Let \preceq be total and m a maximal element of A, and let a \in A. By totality, a \preceq m or m \preceq a. Case 1: a \preceq m. This is what we want. Case 2: m \preceq a. If m 
e a, then m \prec a with a \in A, which maximality excludes. So m = a, and a \preceq m by (PO1). In either case a \preceq m. Since a \in A was arbitrary and m \in A, m is a greatest element. For least and minimal elements, apply (a) and (b) to the partial order \succeq: its greatest and maximal elements are the least and minimal elements for \preceq, and it is total when \preceq is. (That \succeq satisfies (PO1)–(PO3), and is total when \preceq is, comes from reading those clauses with the two variables exchanged. Its strict part is x \succ y \iff y \prec x, since x 
e y is symmetric in x and y. So “no a \in A with m \succ a” is “no a \in A with a \prec m”, and “a \succeq l for every a \in A” is “l \preceq a for every a \in A”.) Part (b) uses totality once, in the case split of its second sentence, and the case split is where it fails without it. The proof of @prp-finite-max in Section 2.3 compares two elements at a time and keeps the larger. Its maximum half uses nothing about \le on 
R beyond reflexivity, transitivity and the comparability of any two elements, so it works word for word in any totally ordered set. The minimum half passes to -x_1, \dots, -x_n, which needs an ordered field; in a totally ordered set, apply the maximum half to the reverse order \succeq instead, which is total by the last paragraph of the proof above. In particular the whole proposition holds in any ordered field, which is how Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 reads it. Without totality, (b) fails, and maximal elements need not be greatest. [Maximal elements that are not greatest] Find the maximal elements of each set, and decide whether it has a greatest element: (a) A = \{2, 3, 4, 5, 6\} in (
N, \mid); (b) \sB = \{ \{1\}, \{2\} \} in (\powerset{\{1, 2\}}, \subseteq). (a) Within A, the only strict divisibilities are 2 \mid 4, 2 \mid 6 and 3 \mid 6. So 2 \prec 4 and 3 \prec 6, and 2, 3 are not maximal. Nothing in A is strictly above 4, 5 or 6: every element of A is positive, and a positive multiple k n of n \in \{4, 5, 6\} other than n has k > 0 and k 
e 1, so k \ge 2 (@prp-integers-closed (c)), and then k n \ge 2n \ge 8, while every element of A is at most 6. So the maximal elements are 4, 5 and 6. There is no greatest element. By @prp-greatest-maximal (a), a greatest element would be maximal, so it would be 4, 5 or 6. But 5 
mid 4, 4 
mid 5 and 4 
mid 6, so none of the three is above every element of A. (b) \{1\} and \{2\} are incomparable (@exm-subset-order-not-total), so neither is strictly above the other: both are maximal. Neither is greatest, since neither contains the other. In (a), the minimal elements are 2, 3 and 5, and there is no least element either. The example is the minimal change from \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}, which has the least element 1 and still no greatest. “Maximal” is not “greatest”. A set can have many maximal elements and no greatest, as in @exm-maximal-not-greatest; and a set can have no maximal element at all: 
N under \le, where n + 1 \in 
N (by (
NS)) is strictly above n. The answer also depends on the order, not just on the set: under divisibility, 
N has a greatest element, 0, since every a \in 
N divides 0 = 0 \cdot a. In \powerset{\{1, 2, 3\}} \setminus \{ \{1, 2, 3\} \}, ordered by \subseteq, name the maximal elements. Is there a greatest element? The maximal elements are the three two-element sets \{1, 2\}, \{1, 3\}, \{2, 3\}: the only subset of \{1, 2, 3\} strictly containing a two-element set is \{1, 2, 3\}, which was removed, and every set with at most one element lies strictly inside some two-element set. There is no greatest element: it would be maximal (@prp-greatest-maximal (a)), hence a two-element set, and no two-element set contains the other two. Least upper bounds, a first look Here is the notion that the rest of the book is built on. When a set has no greatest element, its upper bounds may still have a least one, and that element plays the part of “the top of the set” from outside. The supremum is the best upper bound: the least element of the set of upper bounds. [Supremum and Infimum] Let (X, \preceq) be a partially ordered set and A \subseteq X. An element s \in X is a least upper bound, or supremum, of A in X if 1. s is an upper bound of A, and 2. s \preceq u for every upper bound u of A. An element i \in X is a greatest lower bound, or infimum, of A in X if i is a lower bound of A and u \preceq i for every lower bound u of A. In other words, a supremum of A is a least element of the set of upper bounds of A, and an infimum a greatest element of the set of lower bounds. By @prp-greatest-unique, applied to those sets, each is unique when it exists, and we write \sup A and \inf A. The words “in X” matter: the upper bounds are taken in X, and enlarging or shrinking X can create or destroy a supremum. The definition also carries no promise that \sup A exists, or that it belongs to A. Two quick consequences. If A has a greatest element g, then g = \sup A: g is an upper bound, and every upper bound u has g \preceq u because g \in A. And a supremum that belongs to A is a greatest element of A, by (S1). So a supremum is a greatest element exactly when it lies in the set; the new cases are the ones where it lies outside. Suprema of sets. In (\powerset{X}, \subseteq), let A, B \subseteq X. Then \sup \{A, B\} = A \cup B. (S1): A \subseteq A \cup B and B \subseteq A \cup B, and A \cup B \in \powerset{X}. (S2): let C \in \powerset{X} be an upper bound, so A \subseteq C and B \subseteq C; every element of A \cup B lies in A or in B, hence in C, so A \cup B \subseteq C. The supremum A \cup B belongs to \{A, B\} only when one of the two sets contains the other; for \{ \{1\}, \{2\} \} it is \{1, 2\}, which is not in the set. Exercise B1 extends this to every family of subsets, and adds the infimum. Suprema under divisibility. In (
N, \mid), an upper bound of \{a, b\} is a common multiple of a and b. The least upper bound turns out to be the least common multiple, and proving that it is least in the divisibility order, not merely the smallest number, is a job for the division algorithm. [The supremum under divisibility is the least common multiple] Let a, b \in 
N. Find \sup \{a, b\} in (
N, \mid). Deduce that an integer divisible by 2 and by 3 is divisible by 6. Case a, b \in 
Z_{>0}. Let M \coloneqq \{ m \in 
Z_{>0} : a \mid m 	ext{ and } b \mid m \}, the positive common multiples. It is non-empty: ab \in 
N by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (b), ab > 0 as a product of positive numbers, so ab \in 
Z_{>0} (@prp-integers-closed (b)), and ab = b \cdot a = a \cdot b is a multiple of both. Since M \subseteq 
Z_{>0} \subseteq 
N, M has a least element L (@thm-well-ordering), the least common multiple of a and b. We show that L divides every integer common multiple c of a and b. By @thm-division-algorithm, c = qL + r with q, r \in 
Z and 0 \le r < L. Write c = as, L = at with s, t \in 
Z; then r = c - qL = a(s - qt) with s - qt \in 
Z (@prp-integers-closed (a)), so a \mid r, and in the same way b \mid r. If r > 0, then r \in 
Z_{>0} (@prp-integers-closed (b)), so r \in M and r < L, contradicting the choice of L. Hence r = 0, and c = qL: L \mid c. The argument never used c \ge 0. Now L = \sup \{a, b\}. (S1): a \mid L and b \mid L, since L \in M. (S2): an upper bound c \in 
N of \{a, b\} is a common multiple, so L \mid c by the previous paragraph. Case a = 0 or b = 0. Say a = 0. An upper bound c has 0 \mid c, that is, c = k \cdot 0 = 0 for some k \in 
Z. And 0 is an upper bound, since n \mid 0 = 0 \cdot n for every n \in 
N. So 0 is the only upper bound, and \sup \{a, b\} = 0, the greatest element of (
N, \mid). The instance. For a = 2, b = 3: 6 \in M, and none of 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 is a multiple of both 2 and 3 (1, 3, 5 are odd, and 2, 4 lie strictly between consecutive multiples of 3). So L = 6, and every integer n with 2 \mid n and 3 \mid n has 6 \mid n, by the second paragraph with c = n. The instance proves the fact that Section 1.2 used as a school fact: an integer divisible by 2 and by 3 is divisible by 6. It also shows the two orders on 
N disagreeing: \sup \{4, 6\} is 12 under divisibility and 6 under \le. A supremum that does not exist. In (
Q, \le), the set \{ x \in 
Q : x > 0, \ x^2 < 2 \} is non-empty and bounded above (by 2, for instance: a rational x > 2 has x^2 > 4). It has no least upper bound in 
Q. We do not prove this here. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves it, and then takes the existence of suprema in 
R as its axiom: the supremum of Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1, defined in an ordered field, is @def-order-supremum for the order \le of that field; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 uses it in 
Q and in 
R. The ambient set decides: the same set has a supremum in (
R, \le), namely \sqrt 2. Well-ordered sets Section 2.1 proved that every non-empty subset of 
N has a least element (@thm-well-ordering). In the language of this section, that is a property of the partially ordered set (
N, \le), and it has a name. [Well-Ordered Set] A partially ordered set (X, \preceq) is well-ordered, and \preceq is a well-order on X, if \preceq is total and every non-empty subset of X has a least element. (
N, \le) is well-ordered: \le is total, and @thm-well-ordering supplies the least elements. (
Z, \le) is not: 
Z itself has no least element, since for every n \in 
Z also n - 1 \in 
Z (@prp-integers-closed (a)) and n - 1 < n. Nor is the set of positive rationals, which has no least element (q/2 < q). The word “non-empty” is needed because \emptyset has no least element in any order. Totality is in fact automatic: any two elements x, y form a non-empty set \{x, y\}, whose least element is below the other one. Upper bounds work too: in (
N, \le) a non-empty set bounded above has a greatest element (@cor-well-ordering-integers). Exercise C1 gives a well-ordered set that does not look like 
N. In a general partially ordered set, one may ask: if every chain (a subset on which \preceq is total) has an upper bound, must there be a maximal element? For a non-empty partially ordered set the answer “yes” is Zorn’s lemma, and it cannot be proved from what we have: it is equivalent to the axiom of choice, which Chapter 3 states. Functional Analysis, Chapter 4 proves Zorn’s lemma from the axiom of choice, and Number Systems: From 
N to 
R, Chapter 1 lists the other statements equivalent to choice, among them the claim that every set has a well-order. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Let (X, \preceq) be a partially ordered set and A \subseteq X. Write “g is a greatest element of A” and “m is a maximal element of A” in symbols, and negate each. 2. True or false, with a witness: every finite non-empty subset of a partially ordered set has a greatest element. 3. Find \sup \{4, 6\} in (
N, \mid) and in (
N, \le). 4. On 
N 	imes

e x_{n+1}, so a \in A; and m \prec x_{n+1} \prec a gives m \prec a, since the strict part of a partial order is transitive. This contradicts the maximality of m in A.
