title: Cardinality: Countable and Uncountable Sets
content:
Cardinality: Countable and Uncountable Sets Are there more rational numbers than natural numbers? The rationals are dense, with a third between any two, while the naturals are spread out one unit apart; and yet the answer is no, because the rationals can be listed. Are there more real numbers than rationals? Yes: no list of real numbers, however cleverly it is made, contains them all. This chapter makes “more” exact, with bijections and injections in place of counting, and proves both answers. It then shows that there is no largest size at all: by Cantor’s theorem, the set of subsets of any set is strictly bigger than the set itself. A second motivating question comes from school: why does 0.999\ldots = 1 need a definition at all? The answer is in Section 3.4, where a decimal expansion is defined with finite sums only, and 0.999\ldots = 1 becomes true by that definition. On the way the chapter meets a principle that the rules of logic and the working rules for sets do not supply: making infinitely many arbitrary choices at once. The obvious proof that a countable union of countable sets is countable needs a list of every set of the family at the same time, and no rule produces one. The chapter states the missing principle as the axiom of choice, marks the line of each proof that uses it, and shows how often a rule (the least element, a formula) makes it unnecessary. The finite sets come first, with the pigeonhole principle and the facts about counting that the earlier chapters took on trust. The last section is Gate 0, the examination on all of Part 0, which a reader should pass before starting Part I. What you need. Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–5, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1–2. Induction (@fd1:ax-induction) from Logic and Proof, Chapter 3. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 4, the rule ulename{\exists E} (@fd1:def-rules-existential): Section 3.3 shows why one use of it names one object and cannot name infinitely many. From Logic and Proof, Chapter 5, the catalogue of what a proof may not do (@fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue). From Chapter 1: sets cut out by a property (@def-set-builder) and Russell’s theorem (@thm-russell); power sets, families and their unions (@def-power-set, @def-indexed-family, @def-family-union-intersection); ordered pairs and products (@def-ordered-pair, @def-cartesian-product); functions, the empty function and equality of functions (@def-function, @prp-empty-function, @prp-function-equality); injective, surjective and bijective maps and their composites (@def-injective, @def-surjective, @thm-composition-injective-surjective); inverses (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse, @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective, @prp-right-inverse-surjective); images and preimages (@def-image, @def-preimage). From Chapter 2: the arithmetic of 
N and 
Z (@lem-naturals-arithmetic, @prp-integers-closed), well-ordering (@thm-well-ordering), induction from any base (@thm-induction), the division algorithm (@thm-division-algorithm), definition by recursion (@thm-recursion), and powers and sums (@def-power, @prp-power-laws, @def-sum-product, @prp-geometric-sum). The arithmetic and order of 
R are school facts in examples, as in the earlier chapters. Section 3.4 states three school facts about decimal expansions, (D1)–(D3), and Sections 3.4–3.5 use them by name without proof; Section 3.3 uses one fact from school algebra, that a non-zero polynomial of degree d has at most d real roots. Gate 0 examines all of Logic and Proof, Chapters 1–5, and Sets, Relations, and Cardinality, Chapters 1–3. Time. About 35 hours on the core track (all of A, one B and one C per section, the exit checks); about 45 hours for everything. Both include Gate 0, about 5 hours: the definition drill, the two-hour examination, and grading it against the marking schemes. Roadmap - Equinumerous sets and finite sets. “The same size” defined by a bijection, finite sets and their number of elements, the pigeonhole principle and the uniqueness of that number, subsets, disjoint unions and the 2^n subsets of an n-element set, and the theorem that no finite set is equinumerous with a proper subset, which Hilbert’s hotel turns into a proof that 
N is infinite. - Countable sets. Countable as listable with repetitions allowed (empty, or the image of 
N), the equivalent forms “an injection into 
N” and “finite or countably infinite”, closure under subsets, images, unions of two sets and finite products, and the countability of 
N 	imes 
N, 
Z and 
Q. - Countable unions and the axiom of choice. The step in the proof for countable unions that no rule justifies, the axiom of choice that licenses it, the constructions that look like choice and are not, right inverses of surjections, countable unions of countable sets, and the countability of the algebraic numbers. - Diagonal arguments: uncountable sets and Cantor’s theorem. The diagonal argument for 0–1 sequences, Cantor’s theorem that no map from a set onto its power set exists, decimal expansions defined with finite sums, the uncountability of 
R, and the existence of transcendental numbers. - Comparing sizes: the Schröder–Bernstein theorem. Comparing sizes by injections, its exchange with surjections at the price of choice, the Schröder–Bernstein theorem proved without choice, and every interval with more than one point equinumerous with 
R. - Infinite sets. Every infinite set contains a countably infinite subset (a stronger use of choice), so 
N is the smallest infinite size, and a set is infinite exactly when it is equinumerous with a proper subset of itself; the review exercises reach back across Part 0. - Gate 0: Part 0 examination. A definition drill and six problems, two hours, closed book, with a marking scheme for each problem; the pass line is 42 of 60 points with no core problem at 0, and a remediation map sends each lost problem back to named sections. Named moves - List it. To show that A is countable, give a surjection 
N 	o A or an injection A 	o 
N, whichever is cheaper to write down and check; repetitions in a list are free. An injection only has to keep different elements apart, as (m, n) \mapsto 2^m 3^n does for 
N 	imes 
N. - The diagonal. Given any list, build an object that differs from the n-th entry at the n-th place. It is not on the list, and since the list was arbitrary, no list contains everything. - Injections both ways. To show \card{A} = \card{B}, find an injection A 	o B and an injection B 	o A, and invoke the Schröder–Bernstein theorem; do not hunt for the bijection. - Name the choice. When a proof picks one object for each of infinitely many indices with no rule that names it, say at that line that the axiom of choice is used. When a rule names the object, such as the least element of a set of natural numbers or a formula, no choice is used.

title: 3.1 Equinumerous Sets and Finite Sets
content:
Equinumerous Sets and Finite Sets Chapter 1 made functions exact and sorted them into injective, surjective and bijective ones. Chapter 2 put the natural numbers on firm ground: their arithmetic, well-ordering, induction from any base and definition by recursion. This chapter asks how large a set is. For a finite set we count. For 
N, 
Q or 
R counting gives no answer, and the question “are there more rational numbers than natural numbers?” needs a meaning before it can have an answer. This section gives “the same size” its meaning, a pairing, and then proves the facts about finite sets on which counting rests, starting with the pigeonhole principle. Same size without counting So far we have compared functions; now we compare sets. The everyday word is “as many as”, and we can check it without knowing any numbers. Put two piles of coins on a table, and take one coin from each pile at a time, setting the two aside as a pair. If both piles run out at the same moment, they had the same number of coins. We know this before counting either pile, and a child who cannot count past ten can do it with piles of a thousand. The pairing is a function from the first pile to the second. Different coins are paired with different coins, so it is injective; every coin of the second pile is used, so it is surjective. Pairing makes sense for any two sets, finite or not, and that is the definition. Same size means there is a pairing. [Equinumerous Sets] Let A and B be sets. We say that A and B are equinumerous, and write \card{A} = \card{B}, if there exists a bijection f \colon A 	o B. In symbols, \card{A} = \card{B} \iff \exists f \in B^A \ \ (f 	ext{ is injective} \wedge f 	ext{ is surjective}) . In words: the definition asks for one bijection, and it does not care which. Injectivity says that no two elements of A are paired with the same element of B; surjectivity says that no element of B is left over. The statement \card{A} = \card{B} is read as a whole, “A and B are equinumerous”. It is a relation between two sets. We do not define an object \card{A}, “the size of A”, standing alone, and a remark below explains why the obvious candidate is not available. For finite sets, the definition of a finite set below gives \card{A} a meaning as a natural number, and the two uses agree. Here are four examples, the degenerate one first. - The empty set. The empty function \emptyset 	o \emptyset of @prp-empty-function (a) is injective and surjective, vacuously: there are no two inputs to compare and no output to reach. So \card{\emptyset} = \card{\emptyset}. Conversely, if \card{A} = \card{\emptyset}, there is a function A 	o \emptyset, so A = \emptyset by @prp-empty-function (b). The empty set is equinumerous with itself and with nothing else. This case is the test case for every statement below about sets “with n elements”, at n = 0. - Three letters and three numbers. Let a, b, c be three different letters. The function \{a, b, c\} 	o \{1, 2, 3\} with a \mapsto 1, b \mapsto 2, c \mapsto 3 sends different letters to different numbers and reaches each of 1, 2, 3. So \card{\{a, b, c\}} = \card{\{1, 2, 3\}}. - Two intervals of different lengths. The function f \colon [0, 1] 	o [0, 2], f(x) = 2x, has the inverse y \mapsto y/2, since y/2 \in [0, 1] for y \in [0, 2], f(y/2) = y and f(x)/2 = x. By @thm-bijection-iff-inverse it is a bijection, so \card{[0, 1]} = \card{[0, 2]}. Length and size are different things. - The natural numbers and the positive integers. The function 
N 	o 
Z_{>0}, n \mapsto n + 1, is a bijection. It is the Quick check near the end of this section, where it shows that 
N is infinite. A non-example by a minimal change. Shrink \{1, 2, 3\} to \{1, 2\}. There is no bijection \{a, b, c\} 	o \{1, 2\}. Let g be any function \{a, b, c\} 	o \{1, 2\}. If g(a) = g(b), then g is not injective. Otherwise g(a) and g(b) are 1 and 2 in some order, and g(c), which is 1 or 2, equals one of them. In every case two different letters share a value. So the clause that fails is injectivity, and it fails for every function, which is what “not equinumerous” requires. Surjectivity can hold: a \mapsto 1, b \mapsto 2, c \mapsto 2 reaches both numbers. To show that two sets are not equinumerous, one map is never enough. The map x \mapsto x from [0, 1] to [0, 2] is not surjective, since 2 is not a value, and yet \card{[0, 1]} = \card{[0, 2]} by the map x \mapsto 2x above. “Not equinumerous” is a statement about all functions,  orall f \in B^A \, 
eg(f 	ext{ bijective}), and a proof of it must deal with an arbitrary f, as the non-example did. Why this definition. To count a set is to pair it with \{1, \dots, n\}: saying “one, two, three” while pointing at the coins is a bijection from \{1, 2, 3\} onto the pile. So the definition does not replace counting; it isolates the part of counting that still makes sense when the set is infinite. Each clause has a job. Without injectivity, the surjection \{1, 2, 3\} 	o \{1\} would make a three-element set as large as a one-element set. Without surjectivity, the inclusion \{1\} 	o \{1, 2, 3\} would do the same in the other direction. The first result says that equinumerosity behaves like an equivalence relation. [Equinumerosity Is Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive] For all sets A, B and C: 1. \card{A} = \card{A}; 2. if \card{A} = \card{B}, then \card{B} = \card{A}; 3. if \card{A} = \card{B} and \card{B} = \card{C}, then \card{A} = \card{C}. (a) The identity \id_A is injective, since \id_A(x) = \id_A(y) says x = y, and surjective, since every x \in A is \id_A(x). (b) Let f \colon A 	o B be a bijection. By @thm-bijection-iff-inverse it has a two-sided inverse f^{-1} \colon B 	o A, with f^{-1} \circ f = \id_A and f \circ f^{-1} = \id_B. Read with the roles exchanged, these two equations say that f is a two-sided inverse of f^{-1} (@def-inverse-function). So f^{-1} is a bijection B 	o A, by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse again. (c) If f \colon A 	o B and g \colon B 	o C are bijections, then g \circ f \colon A 	o C is a bijection by @thm-composition-injective-surjective (c). This proves the proposition. Clauses (a)–(c) have the form of (Eq1)–(Eq3) of @def-equivalence-relation, and yet we do not call equinumerosity an equivalence relation. An equivalence relation in Chapter 2 is a relation on a set X, a subset of X 	imes X. Equinumerosity relates any two sets whatever, and there is no set of all sets for it to live on (@thm-russell). That is also why the book reserves the symbol \sim for equivalence relations and writes \card{A} = \card{B} here. Why not define \card{A} as “the collection of all sets equinumerous with A”? Because that collection is in general not a set. The next paragraph proves this for A = \{0\}. Take A = \{0\}. Every singleton \{x\} is equinumerous with \{0\}, by 0 \mapsto x. If the singletons formed a set \sS, its union  igcup \sS would be a set by (W3) of Section 1.1, and every object x would be an element of it, since x \in \{x\} \in \sS. That is a set of which every set is an element, which @thm-russell rules out. Finite sets Counting is pairing with \{1, \dots, n\}, so “finite” is defined by such a pairing. Recall from Section 2.1 that for n \in 
N, \{1, \dots, n\} \coloneqq \{ k \in 
N : 1 \le k \le n \} , so that \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset, since no k has 1 \le k \le 0. [Finite Set, Number of Elements] Let A be a set and n \in 
N. We say that A has n elements if \card{\{1, \dots, n\}} = \card{A}, that is, if there exists a bijection \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A. The set A is finite if it has n elements for some n \in 
N. In that case we write \card{A} = n. In words: \varphi numbers the elements of A as \varphi(1), \varphi(2), \dots, \varphi(n). Injectivity says that no element gets two numbers; surjectivity says that every element gets one. So a non-empty finite set is A = \{\varphi(1), \dots, \varphi(n)\}, a list without repetitions. By @prp-equinumerous-properties (b), “A has n elements” is the same as \card{A} = \card{\{1, \dots, n\}}, so the notation \card{A} = n is consistent with the relation of @def-equinumerous. There is a gap in the notation \card{A} = n. It presents n as the number of elements, but the definition only says that some n works. Could a set have 3 elements and also 4? It cannot, and a corollary of the pigeonhole principle below proves it. That corollary is the well-definedness step this definition needs. Until it is proved, read \card{A} = n as “A has n elements”. Examples: - The empty set has 0 elements: \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset, and the empty function \emptyset 	o \emptyset is a bijection. Conversely, a set with 0 elements is empty, since a bijection \emptyset 	o A is surjective and has no values. - \{1, \dots, n\} has n elements, by \id_{\{1, \dots, n\}}. - For n \in 
N, \{0, \dots, n\} has n + 1 elements: k \mapsto k - 1 maps \{1, \dots, n + 1\} to \{0, \dots, n\}, because k - 1 \in 
N for k 
e 0 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (c)) and k - 1 \le n. It has the inverse j \mapsto j + 1, so it is a bijection (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse). - The three-letter set \{a, b, c\} has 3 elements, by the inverse of the bijection of the second example after @def-equinumerous. [Infinite Set] A set A is infinite if it is not finite: for every n \in 
N there is no bijection \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A. To prove a set infinite we must rule out every n at once, and for every n every candidate bijection. Nothing so far does that, not even for 
N. The tool is the pigeonhole principle, and the last theorem of this section turns it into a usable test. Shrinking the codomain. One small device is used throughout the chapter. Let f \colon X 	o Y be a function, and let C \subseteq Y contain every value f(x). The graph of f is then a subset of X 	imes C, and with the codomain C it is a function X 	o C with the same values (@def-function). We call it “f with codomain C”. It is injective if and only if f is, since injectivity speaks only of values. In particular, f with codomain f(X) is surjective (@def-image). So an injective f \colon X 	o Y is a bijection X 	o f(X) once its codomain is shrunk, and \card{X} = \card{f(X)}. The pigeonhole principle If more pigeons than holes fly into a dovecote, some hole gets two pigeons. In Chapter 1 we found one function from a three-element set to a two-element set that is not injective (@exm-injective-surjective-first (c)), and observed without proof that none can be. Here is the general fact, for the standard sets \{1, \dots, m\} and \{1, \dots, n\}. [Pigeonhole Principle] Let m, n \in 
N with m > n. Then there is no injection \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}. Induct on the number n of holes. In the step there are n + 1 holes, and we look at the last one. If no pigeon sits in hole n + 1, all the pigeons sit in n holes, and the hypothesis applies at once. If pigeon j sits there, there is only one, by injectivity. Move pigeon j to the hole of pigeon m, and send pigeon m away. That leaves m - 1 pigeons in n holes, still one to a hole, and m - 1 > n. The hypothesis is used at m - 1, not at m, so the property we induct on must say “for every m”. Before reading on: self-explain the construction of the injection g in Case 2: why are its values in \{1, \dots, n\}, and why is it injective? For n \in 
N let P(n) be the statement for every m \in 
N with m > n, there is no injection \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}. We prove P(n) for every n \in 
N by @fd1:ax-induction. Base case P(0). Let m \in 
N with m > 0. Then m \ge 1 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (a)), so 1 \in \{1, \dots, m\} and the domain is non-empty, while \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset. By @prp-empty-function (b) there is no function \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \emptyset at all, so there is no injection. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N and suppose P(n). Let m \in 
N with m > n + 1, and suppose, for a contradiction, that f \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n + 1\} is injective. There are two cases. Case 1: n + 1 is not a value of f. For every i, f(i) \le n + 1 and f(i) 
e n + 1, so f(i) < n + 1, and f(i) \le n by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (e). So f with codomain \{1, \dots, n\} is an injection \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}, with m > n + 1 > n. This contradicts P(n). Case 2: f(j) = n + 1 for some j \in \{1, \dots, m\}. Since m > n + 1 \ge 1, we have m 
e 0, so m - 1 \in 
N by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (c); and m - 1 > n, by subtracting 1 from m > n + 1. Define \sigma \colon \{1, \dots, m - 1\} 	o \{1, \dots, m\} by \sigma(i) \coloneqq  egin{cases} i & 	ext{if } i 
e j , \ m & 	ext{if } i = j . \end{cases} (The second line applies only when j \le m - 1; if j = m, then \sigma(i) = i for every i.) The map \sigma is injective: two different inputs other than j keep their different values, and if one input is j, its value is m, while the other has value i \le m - 1 < m. Moreover \sigma(i) 
e j for every i: either \sigma(i) = i 
e j, or \sigma(i) = m, which happens only when j \le m - 1 < m. Let g \coloneqq f \circ \sigma. It is injective by @thm-composition-injective-surjective (a). For every i, \sigma(i) 
e j, and f is injective with f(j) = n + 1, so g(i) = f(\sigma(i)) 
e n + 1; as in Case 1, g(i) \in \{1, \dots, n\}. So g with codomain \{1, \dots, n\} is an injection \{1, \dots, m - 1\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}, with m - 1 > n. This contradicts P(n), applied to the number m - 1. In both cases the injection f cannot exist, so P(n + 1) holds. By @fd1:ax-induction, P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. This proves the theorem. The theorem is about the standard sets only, but bijections carry it to any finite sets. Part (b) below is its mirror image for surjections. [Pigeonhole for Finite Sets] Let m, n \in 
N, let A have m elements, and let B have n elements. 1. If m > n, there is no injection A 	o B. 2. If m < n, there is no surjection A 	o B. For (a), the bijections of @def-finite turn an injection A 	o B into an injection \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\}, which @thm-pigeonhole forbids. For (b), a surjection g \colon A 	o B has a right inverse h, and h is an injection B 	o A, forbidden by (a). The right inverse is built by a rule: send b to the element of A with the smallest number among those that g sends to b. Let \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o A and \psi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o B be bijections (@def-finite). By @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, \psi has an inverse \psi^{-1} \colon B 	o \{1, \dots, n\}, which is a bijection: the equations \psi^{-1} \circ \psi = \id and \psi \circ \psi^{-1} = \id say that \psi is a two-sided inverse of \psi^{-1} (@def-inverse-function), so @thm-bijection-iff-inverse applies. (a) Suppose m > n and f \colon A 	o B is injective. Then \psi^{-1} \circ f \circ \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\} is injective by @thm-composition-injective-surjective (a), which contradicts @thm-pigeonhole. (b) Suppose m < n and g \colon A 	o B is surjective. For b \in B let S_b \coloneqq \{ i \in \{1, \dots, m\} : g(\varphi(i)) = b \} . It is non-empty: since g is onto, b = g(a) for some a \in A, and a = \varphi(i) for some i, since \varphi is onto. By @thm-well-ordering, S_b has a least element. Define h \colon B 	o A by h(b) \coloneqq \varphi(\min S_b). Then g(h(b)) = b for every b \in B, because \min S_b \in S_b. So g \circ h = \id_B: the function g is a left inverse of h, and h is injective by @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (a). Now h is an injection from the n-element set B to the m-element set A, with n > m, which contradicts (a). This proves the corollary. The function h in (b) is defined by a rule, “the least element”, applied to each b at once, so its existence needs nothing beyond specification. Section 3.3 meets surjections for which no such rule is available, and there the book adds a new principle. Two special cases settle earlier loose ends. With m = n + 1, part (a) says that a set with n elements has no n + 1 different elements: there is no injection \{1, \dots, n + 1\} 	o A. That is the second school fact that @fd1:exr-models-c2 took on trust. With m = 3, n = 2 in (a) and m = 2, n = 3 in (b), the corollary gives the two observations after @exm-injective-surjective-first in general. Here is a typical use of (a). Among any three integers, two have an even sum. Let A be a set of three integers, and let p \colon A 	o \{0, 1\} send each a to its remainder r on division by 2 (@thm-division-algorithm), an integer with 0 \le r < 2; then r \in 
N by @prp-integers-closed (b), and r \le 1 by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (e), so r \in \{0, 1\}. The set \{0, 1\} has 2 elements, so by (a), p is not injective: there are a 
e b in A with the same remainder r. Writing a = 2q + r and b = 2q' + r, a + b = 2(q + q' + r) , which is even, since q + q' + r \in 
Z (@prp-integers-closed (a)). The pigeons are the integers and the holes are the remainders; the whole skill is choosing the holes. The next corollary is the well-definedness promised after @def-finite. [The Number of Elements Is Unique] Let A be a set and m, n \in 
N. If A has m elements and A has n elements, then m = n. Let \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o A and \psi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A be bijections. If m > n, then \psi^{-1} \circ \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\} is injective (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse, @thm-composition-injective-surjective (a)), which contradicts @thm-pigeonhole. Exchanging the roles of \varphi and \psi rules out m < n in the same way. By trichotomy, m = n. So a finite set has exactly one number of elements, and from now on \card{A} = n means “the number of elements of A is n”. Subsets and unions of finite sets Three facts about finite sets are used everywhere below: the sizes of disjoint sets add, a subset is no larger than the whole, and removing one point lowers the size by one. The first uses nothing else from this section, so it comes first. [Disjoint Unions] Let m, n \in 
N, let A have m elements, let B have n elements, and suppose A \cap B = \emptyset. Then A \cup B has m + n elements. Number A with 1, \dots, m and then carry on numbering B with m + 1, \dots, m + n: shift the numbering of B up by m. Let \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o A and \psi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o B be bijections. Note m + n \in 
N by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (b). For k \in \{1, \dots, m + n\} with k > m, we have m + 1 \le k by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (e), so k - m \in 
N with 1 \le k - m \le n (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (d)). So we may define \chi \colon \{1, \dots, m + n\} 	o A \cup B by \chi(k) \coloneqq  egin{cases} \varphi(k) & 	ext{if } k \le m , \ \psi(k - m) & 	ext{if } k > m . \end{cases} Injective. Let \chi(k) = \chi(k'). If k, k' \le m, then \varphi(k) = \varphi(k') gives k = k'. If k, k' > m, then \psi(k - m) = \psi(k' - m) gives k - m = k' - m, so k = k'. If k \le m < k', then \chi(k) \in A and \chi(k') \in B, and A \cap B = \emptyset, so \chi(k) 
e \chi(k'): this case cannot occur, nor can its mirror image. Surjective. Let x \in A \cup B. If x \in A, then x = \varphi(i) with 1 \le i \le m, and \chi(i) = x. If x \in B, then x = \psi(j) with 1 \le j \le n; put k \coloneqq m + j, so m < k \le m + n, and \chi(k) = \psi(j) = x. So \chi is a bijection, and A \cup B has m + n elements. Now subsets. The proof is an induction on the size of the whole set, and it must be set up with care: the step peels off one element, and the obvious way to say “peel off one element” is the corollary after it, on removing a point. But that corollary is proved from this proposition. So the step peels off \varphi(n + 1) by restricting the bijection \varphi directly, and cites nothing proved later. [Subsets of Finite Sets] Let n \in 
N, let A have n elements, and let S \subseteq A. Then S is finite and has k elements for some k \le n. If S 
e A, then k < n. Remove the last element \varphi(n + 1) from A. Either it is outside S, and S sits inside the smaller set; or it is in S, and S is its part in the smaller set plus one point, which @prp-disjoint-union-count counts. For n \in 
N let P(n) be the statement for every set A with n elements and every S \subseteq A, the set S has k elements for some k \le n, and k < n if S 
e A. We prove P(n) for every n by @fd1:ax-induction. Base case P(0). A set A with 0 elements is empty, so S \subseteq \emptyset gives S = \emptyset = A, which has 0 \le 0 elements; the second clause is vacuous. Inductive step. Let n \in 
N and suppose P(n). Let A have n + 1 elements, with a bijection \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, n + 1\} 	o A, and let S \subseteq A. Put A' \coloneqq \varphi(\{1, \dots, n\}) , \qquad a \coloneqq \varphi(n + 1) . The restriction of \varphi to \{1, \dots, n\}, with codomain A', is injective and surjective, so A' has n elements. Every element of A is \varphi(i) with i \le n or i = n + 1 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e)), so A = A' \cup \{a\}. And a 
otin A': if a = \varphi(i) with i \le n, injectivity would give i = n + 1. Case a 
otin S. Then S \subseteq A', and P(n), applied to A' and S, shows that S has k \le n < n + 1 elements. In this case S 
e A, since a \in A \setminus S, and indeed k < n + 1, as required. Case a \in S. Then S = (S \cap A') \cup \{a\}, and the union is disjoint because a 
otin A'. By P(n), applied to A' and S \cap A' \subseteq A', the set S \cap A' has j elements for some j \le n. The set \{a\} has 1 element (by 1 \mapsto a). By @prp-disjoint-union-count, S has j + 1 \le n + 1 elements. If S 
e A, then S \cap A' 
e A', since otherwise S = A' \cup \{a\} = A; so j < n by P(n), and j + 1 < n + 1. In both cases P(n + 1) holds. By @fd1:ax-induction, P(n) holds for every n \in 
N. This proves the proposition. Read contrapositively, with @cor-finite-size-unique: a subset of an n-element set that itself has n elements is the whole set. (If S 
e A, its number of elements is k < n, and by uniqueness it is not n.) That is the first school fact that @fd1:exr-models-c1 took on trust. [Removing a Point] Let n \in 
N, let A have n + 1 elements, and let a \in A. Then A \setminus \{a\} has n elements. Since a \in A, the set A \setminus \{a\} is a proper subset of A, so by @prp-subset-finite it has k elements for some k < n + 1. Now A = (A \setminus \{a\}) \cup \{a\} is a disjoint union, and \{a\} has 1 element, so A has k + 1 elements by @prp-disjoint-union-count. By @cor-finite-size-unique, k + 1 = n + 1, so k = n. Every later induction on the number of elements uses this corollary in the same way: its step starts from an arbitrary set A with n + 1 elements, picks some a \in A (there is one, since n + 1 \ge 1), and applies the hypothesis to A \setminus \{a\}, which has n elements. It never presents the set as “X with one point added” from the outset, which would prove the claim only for sets that come in that form. Here is the first such induction. Chapter 1 promised the count of subsets of a finite set. [Counting Subsets] Let n \in 
N. A set with n elements has 2^n subsets: if \card{A} = n, then \card{\powerset{A}} = 2^n. Fix one element a. Every subset either leaves a out or contains it, and adding a pairs the subsets of the first kind with those of the second. So the count doubles with each new element. We use @fd1:ax-induction on n. Base case. A set with 0 elements is \emptyset, and \powerset{\emptyset} = \{\emptyset\} has 1 = 2^0 element (@def-power). Inductive step. Let n \in 
N, and suppose every set with n elements has 2^n subsets. Let A have n + 1 elements, pick a \in A, and put X \coloneqq A \setminus \{a\}. By @cor-remove-point, X has n elements, so \powerset{X} has 2^n elements by the hypothesis (here 2^n \in 
N by @prp-power-laws (d), so the count makes sense; likewise 2^{n+1} \in 
N). Let T \coloneqq \{ S \cup \{a\} : S \in \powerset{X} \} , the image of \powerset{X} under S \mapsto S \cup \{a\}, a function \powerset{X} 	o \powerset{A}. \powerset{A} is the disjoint union of \powerset{X} and T. Every member of T contains a, and no member of \powerset{X} does, since a 
otin X; so the union is disjoint. Both sets consist of subsets of A. Conversely, let U \subseteq A. If a 
otin U, then U \subseteq X. If a \in U, then U = (U \setminus \{a\}) \cup \{a\} with U \setminus \{a\} \subseteq X, so U \in T. T has 2^n elements. The map S \mapsto S \cup \{a\}, with codomain T, is surjective by the definition of T. It is injective: for S \subseteq X we have a 
otin S, so (S \cup \{a\}) \setminus \{a\} = S, and S can be read back from S \cup \{a\}. So it is a bijection \powerset{X} 	o T, and composing a bijection \{1, \dots, 2^n\} 	o \powerset{X} with it (@thm-composition-injective-surjective (c)) shows that T has 2^n elements. By @prp-disjoint-union-count, \powerset{A} has 2^n + 2^n = 2^n \cdot 2 = 2^{n+1} elements (@def-power). By @fd1:ax-induction, the claim holds for every n \in 
N. For any set Y, the map S \mapsto \ind_S, with inverse f \mapsto \{ y \in Y : f(y) = 1 \}, is a bijection \powerset{Y} 	o \{0, 1\}^Y onto the set of functions Y 	o \{0, 1\} (the correspondence of Section 1.4 between subsets and indicator functions). Taking Y with n elements, a set with n elements also has exactly 2^n functions to \{0, 1\}, and the two counting problems of Chapter 1 are one. Exercise C2 counts all functions between finite sets. No finite set is equinumerous with a proper subset For finite sets, “a proper part is smaller” is a theorem. [A Finite Set Has No Proper Copy] Let A be a finite set and B \subsetneq A. Then A and B are not equinumerous: there is no bijection A 	o B. Let A have n elements, with a bijection \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A. By @prp-subset-finite, B has k elements for some k < n, since B 
e A. Suppose g \colon A 	o B were a bijection. Then g \circ \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o B is a bijection (@thm-composition-injective-surjective (c)), so B also has n elements, and @cor-finite-size-unique gives k = n. This contradicts k < n. Turned around, the theorem is a test for infinity: a set that is equinumerous with a proper subset of itself is infinite. Here is its first use. For the even natural numbers we write 2
N \coloneqq \{ 2n : n \in 
N \} , the image of 
N under n \mapsto 2n. [Hilbert’s Hotel] A hotel has one room for every natural number, and every room is taken. A coach arrives with guests for the odd-numbered rooms: the guest in room n is asked to move to room 2n. Show that this is a bijection 
N 	o 2
N, that 2
N is a proper subset of 
N, and deduce that 
N is infinite. Let d \colon 
N 	o 2
N, d(n) \coloneqq 2n. Its values lie in 2
N by definition, and 2
N \subseteq 
N by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (b). It is injective, since 2n = 2n' gives n = n', and surjective, since every element of 2
N is 2n = d(n) for some n \in 
N. So \card{
N} = \card{2
N}. The inclusion is proper because 1 
otin 2
N: if n = 0, then 2n = 0; if n 
e 0, then n \ge 1 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (a)) and 2n \ge 2. So 2n 
e 1 for every n \in 
N. If 
N were finite, @thm-finite-no-proper-copy would forbid a bijection from 
N onto its proper subset 2
N. So 
N is infinite. Every guest still has a room, and the odd rooms are now free. The finite intuition “a proper part is smaller” fails for 
N, and it fails exactly because 
N is infinite. Section 3.6 proves that it fails for every infinite set. A \subsetneq B does not make A smaller than B when B is infinite: 2
N \subsetneq 
N and \card{2
N} = \card{
N}. Equinumerous is not “one is a subset of the other”, in either direction. “Finite” does not mean “bounded”. The set E \coloneqq \{ 1/n : n \in 
Z_{>0} \} lies in [0, 1], and it is infinite: x \mapsto x/(1 + x) sends 1/n to 1/(n + 1), and it is a bijection from E onto \{ 1/n : n \ge 2 \}, with inverse y \mapsto y/(1 - y). That set is a proper subset of E, since 1 \in E and 1/n \le 1/2 for n \ge 2. Is n \mapsto n + 1 a bijection 
N 	o 
N \setminus \{0\}? What does that show? Yes. Its values lie in 
N \setminus \{0\}, since n + 1 \ge 1. Its inverse is m \mapsto m - 1, which is defined on 
N \setminus \{0\} because m - 1 \in 
N for m 
e 0 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (c)); the two maps undo each other, so it is a bijection by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. So 
N is equinumerous with its proper subset 
N \setminus \{0\} = 
Z_{>0}, and by @thm-finite-no-proper-copy, 
N is infinite, a second time. In the hotel, every guest moves up one room, and room 0 is free. By @def-finite, a non-empty finite set A with n elements is \{x_1, \dots, x_n\}, with x_k \coloneqq \varphi(k). So when its elements are real numbers it has a maximum and a minimum, by @prp-finite-max. Section 2.3 announced this passage from a finite set to a list. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] 1. Define “A is finite”, and write its negation in symbols, with every quantifier shown. 2. True or false, with a reason: a subset of an infinite set is infinite; a set that has an infinite subset is infinite. 3. How many injections \{1, 2, 3\} 	o \{1, 2\} are there? 4. Let f \colon A 	o B, where A and B are finite and A has more elements than B. What does the pigeonhole principle guarantee about f? (a) A is finite if there are n \in 
N and a bijection \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A (@def-finite): \exists n \in 
N \ \exists \varphi \in A^{\{1, \dots, n\}} \ (\varphi 	ext{ injective} \wedge \varphi 	ext{ surjective}). By @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation, applied to each quantifier, and De Morgan, its negation is  orall n \in 
N \  orall \varphi \in A^{\{1, \dots, n\}} \ (\varphi 	ext{ not injective} \vee \varphi 	ext{ not surjective}) , which is @def-infinite. (b) The first is false: \emptyset \subseteq 
N, and \emptyset is finite while 
N is infinite (@exm-hilbert-hotel). The second is true: if B were finite, every subset of B would be finite by @prp-subset-finite; so a set with an infinite subset is not finite. (c) None. By @thm-pigeonhole with m = 3 > 2 = n, there is no injection \{1, 2, 3\} 	o \{1, 2\}. (d) That f is not injective (@cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a)): there are two different elements a 
e a' of A with f(a) = f(a'). It does not say which two, and it says nothing when A has at most as many elements as B. B. Practice [B1: Moving the guests] Give explicit bijections 
N 	o 
N \setminus \{0, 1, 2\}, 
N 	o \{ n \in 
N : n \ge 5 \} and 
N 	o \{ 2n + 1 : n \in 
N \}, and prove that each is a bijection by writing down its inverse. First. For m \in 
N: if m 
otin \{0, 1, 2\}, then m \ge 3. Indeed m 
e 0 gives m \ge 1 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (a)); with m 
e 1, m > 1, so m \ge 2 (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e)); with m 
e 2, m \ge 3 likewise. Conversely every m \ge 3 lies outside \{0, 1, 2\}. So 
N \setminus \{0, 1, 2\} = \{ m \in 
N : m \ge 3 \}. Let f(n) \coloneqq n + 3; then f(n) \in 
N and f(n) \ge 3. Let g(m) \coloneqq m - 3 for m \ge 3; then g(m) \in 
N by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (d). Since g(f(n)) = n and f(g(m)) = m, the map f is a bijection by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. Second. The same with 5 in place of 3: n \mapsto n + 5, with inverse m \mapsto m - 5, which lies in 
N for m \ge 5 by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (d). Third. Let O \coloneqq \{ 2n + 1 : n \in 
N \}, the odd natural numbers, and f(n) \coloneqq 2n + 1, which lies in O by definition. Every m \in O is 2n + 1 for exactly one n \in 
N: one by the definition of O, and only one since 2n + 1 = 2n' + 1 gives n = n'. So g(m) \coloneqq (m - 1)/2 is that n, a natural number. Then g(f(n)) = n and f(g(m)) = m, so f is a bijection 
N 	o O. Each of the three sets is a proper subset of 
N equinumerous with 
N, which shows again that 
N is infinite. [B2: Choosing the holes] 1. Prove that among any 6 different integers, two have the same remainder on division by 5. 2. Prove that among any 5 different elements of \{1, \dots, 8\}, two have sum 9. Hint: in (b), group \{1, \dots, 8\} into pairs. (a) Let A be a set of 6 integers. By @thm-division-algorithm with divisor 5, each a \in A has a unique remainder r(a), an integer with 0 \le r(a) < 5; then r(a) \in 
N by @prp-integers-closed (b), and r(a) \le 4 by discreteness, @prp-integers-closed (c), so r(a) \in \{0, \dots, 4\}. This defines r \colon A 	o \{0, \dots, 4\}. The set \{0, \dots, 4\} has 5 elements (the third example after @def-finite). Since 6 > 5, @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a) shows that r is not injective: there are a 
e a' in A with r(a) = r(a'). (b) Let A \subseteq \{1, \dots, 8\} have 5 elements. The holes are the four pairs \{1, 8\}, \{2, 7\}, \{3, 6\}, \{4, 5\}, each of the form \{x, 9 - x\}. Define p \colon A 	o \{1, 2, 3, 4\} by p(x) \coloneqq \min\{x, 9 - x\}, the smaller element of the pair containing x; for 1 \le x \le 8 this lies in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}, since x \le 4 or 9 - x \le 4. The codomain has 4 elements and 5 > 4, so by @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a) there are x 
e y in A with p(x) = p(y). Then x and y lie in the same pair \{c, 9 - c\}, where c = p(x), and being different they are its two elements, so x + y = 9. Five is the least number that works: \{1, 2, 3, 4\} has 4 elements, and no two of them sum to 9, since their largest sum is 3 + 4 = 7. [B3: Finite unions] Let n \in 
N, and let A_1, \dots, A_n be finite sets, that is, a family (A_i)_{i \in \{1, \dots, n\}} of finite sets. Prove that  igcup_{i \in \{1, \dots, n\}} A_i is finite. For n \in 
N let P(n) be “for every family (A_i)_{i \in \{1, \dots, n\}} of finite sets, the union U_n \coloneqq  igcup_{i \in \{1, \dots, n\}} A_i is finite”. We use @fd1:ax-induction. Base case. For n = 0 the index set is \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset, and the union of the empty family is \emptyset (@def-family-union-intersection: no x lies in some A_i), which has 0 elements. Step. Suppose P(n), and let (A_i)_{i \in \{1, \dots, n + 1\}} be a family of finite sets. Since \{1, \dots, n + 1\} = \{1, \dots, n\} \cup \{n + 1\}, we have U_{n+1} = U_n \cup A_{n+1}, and U_n is finite by P(n), applied to the first n sets; say it has p elements. Write U_{n+1} = U_n \cup (A_{n+1} \setminus U_n) , a disjoint union. The set A_{n+1} \setminus U_n is a subset of the finite set A_{n+1}, so it is finite by @prp-subset-finite; say it has q elements. By @prp-disjoint-union-count, U_{n+1} has p + q elements. By @fd1:ax-induction, P(n) holds for every n. The detour through A_{n+1} \setminus U_n is needed because @prp-disjoint-union-count is about disjoint sets, and U_n and A_{n+1} may overlap. C. Going deeper [C1: Infinite means arbitrarily large finite pieces] Prove that a set A is infinite if and only if for every n \in 
N there is an injection \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A. In the direction (\Rightarrow), say whether your proof makes infinitely many choices at once, and why. [Hint 1] For (\Leftarrow), suppose A has m elements and use the hypothesis at one well-chosen n. For (\Rightarrow), induct on n. [Hint 2] For (\Rightarrow): let P(n) be “there is an injection \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A”; the base case is the empty function. (\Leftarrow) Suppose the condition holds and, for a contradiction, that A has m elements, with a bijection \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o A. Take n \coloneqq m + 1 and an injection f \colon \{1, \dots, m + 1\} 	o A. By @thm-bijection-iff-inverse, \varphi has an inverse \varphi^{-1} \colon A 	o \{1, \dots, m\}, which is a bijection, since \varphi is a two-sided inverse of it (@def-inverse-function, @thm-bijection-iff-inverse). Then \varphi^{-1} \circ f \colon \{1, \dots, m + 1\} 	o \{1, \dots, m\} is injective (@thm-composition-injective-surjective (a)), which contradicts @thm-pigeonhole. So A is infinite. (\Rightarrow) Let A be infinite. For n \in 
N let P(n) be “there is an injection \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A”. We use @fd1:ax-induction. Base case. \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset, and the empty function \emptyset 	o A (@prp-empty-function (a)) is injective, vacuously. Step. Suppose P(n), and let f \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o A be an injection. With its codomain shrunk to its image F \coloneqq f(\{1, \dots, n\}), it is a bijection, so F has n elements. Since A is infinite, F 
e A; and F \subseteq A, so there is some a \in A \setminus F. Define g \colon \{1, \dots, n + 1\} 	o A by g(k) \coloneqq f(k) for k \le n and g(n + 1) \coloneqq a; this is a function because \{1, \dots, n + 1\} = \{1, \dots, n\} \cup \{n + 1\} and n + 1 
otin \{1, \dots, n\} (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (e)). It is injective: two inputs \le n are separated by f, and g(n + 1) = a 
otin F differs from every g(k) with k \le n. So P(n + 1) holds. By @fd1:ax-induction, P(n) holds for every n. No infinitely many choices are made. The step uses two existence statements, P(n) and “A \setminus F 
e \emptyset”, and names one witness for each: one ulename{\exists E} each, inside the proof of the single implication P(n) \Rightarrow P(n + 1). Its conclusion, P(n + 1), is again an existence statement, so the witnesses never leave the step. Induction then gives P(n) for each n separately: for each n some injection exists, and different n may use unrelated ones. Gluing the steps into one injection 
N 	o A, with a new point picked at every stage, would require all the picks at once, with no rule saying which point to pick. That is a different statement; Section 3.6 proves it with the principle of choice of Section 3.3. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (\Leftarrow) supposes A has m elements and uses the hypothesis at n = m + 1 to contradict the pigeonhole principle (@thm-pigeonhole or @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a)). - 1: (\Rightarrow) sets up an induction on n with the base case n = 0 (the empty function); a base n = 1 earns the point only if n = 0 is also covered (by the empty function). - 3: in the step, shows that the image of the given injection has n elements and is therefore not A, and takes a point outside it. - 2: extends the injection by that point and checks injectivity, including the new value against the old ones. - 2: explains that each step makes finitely many choices inside one implication, so no principle of choice is used, and that building one injection on all of 
N would be a different statement. Fatal errors (0 for the step): picking “a new point for every n” to define one function 
N 	o A and calling it induction; taking a point outside the image without showing the image is not all of A. [C2: Counting products and functions] Let m, n \in 
N, let A have m elements, and let B have n elements. 1. Prove that A 	imes B has mn elements. 2. Prove that the set B^A of functions A 	o B has n^m elements. 3. Check your formula in (b) against @prp-empty-function in the cases m = 0 and m \ge 1, n = 0. [Hint 1] Induct on m, with B fixed, and remove one point a from A by @cor-remove-point. [Hint 2] For (b), a function on A is the same as a function on A \setminus \{a\} together with one value at a: consider f \mapsto (f|_{A \setminus \{a\}}, f(a)). (a) Fix B with n elements. For m \in 
N let P(m) be “for every set A with m elements, A 	imes B has mn elements” (mn \in 
N by @lem-naturals-arithmetic (b)). Base case. If A has 0 elements, then A = \emptyset, and A 	imes B = \emptyset, since a pair in it would need a first coordinate in \emptyset. It has 0 = 0 \cdot n elements. Step. Suppose P(m), let A have m + 1 elements, pick a \in A, and put A' \coloneqq A \setminus \{a\}, which has m elements by @cor-remove-point. Then A 	imes B = (A' 	imes B) \cup (\{a\} 	imes B) , and the union is disjoint, since first coordinates in A' differ from a (@def-ordered-pair). The first set has mn elements by P(m). The map B 	o \{a\} 	imes B, b \mapsto (a, b), is injective by @def-ordered-pair and surjective by @def-cartesian-product, so \{a\} 	imes B has n elements. By @prp-disjoint-union-count, A 	imes B has mn + n = (m + 1)n elements. By @fd1:ax-induction, P(m) holds for every m, and B was arbitrary. (b) Fix B with n elements, and let Q(m) be “for every set A with m elements, B^A has n^m elements” (n^m \in 
N by @prp-power-laws (d)). Base case. A = \emptyset, and by @prp-empty-function (a), B^{\emptyset} has exactly one element, the empty function; n^0 = 1 (@def-power), also when n = 0. Step. Suppose Q(m), let A have m + 1 elements, pick a \in A, and let A' \coloneqq A \setminus \{a\}, with m elements. Define R \colon B^A 	o B^{A'} 	imes B , \qquad R(f) \coloneqq (f|_{A'}, f(a)) . Injective: if R(f) = R(f'), then f and f' agree on A' and at a, hence on A = A' \cup \{a\}, and they have the same domain and codomain, so f = f' by @prp-function-equality. Surjective: given (h, b) \in B^{A'} 	imes B, let f have graph G \cup \{(a, b)\}, where G is the graph of h, and codomain B. Each x \in A' has exactly one partner, its h-value, because (a, b) has first coordinate a 
otin A'; and a has exactly one, b, because every pair of G has first coordinate in A'. So f \in B^A, and R(f) = (h, b). Hence R is a bijection. By Q(m), B^{A'} has n^m elements, so by (a), applied to the sets B^{A'} and B, the product B^{A'} 	imes B has n^m \cdot n = n^{m+1} elements (@def-power). Since R is a bijection, \card{B^A} = \card{B^{A'} 	imes B} (@def-equinumerous), and \card{\{1, \dots, n^{m+1}\}} = \card{B^{A'} 	imes B}. By @prp-equinumerous-properties (b) and (c), \card{\{1, \dots, n^{m+1}\}} = \card{B^A}, that is, B^A has n^{m+1} elements. By @fd1:ax-induction, Q(m) holds for every m. (c) For m = 0: B^{\emptyset} has one element by @prp-empty-function (a), and n^0 = 1, even for n = 0. For m \ge 1 and n = 0: A 
e \emptyset, so there is no function A 	o \emptyset by @prp-empty-function (b), and B^A = \emptyset has 0 elements; and 0^m = 0^{m-1} \cdot 0 = 0. Both agree with (b). With B = \{0, 1\}, (b) recovers the count 2^m of the paragraph after @prp-power-set-count. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: sets up each induction on m with B fixed, and handles m = 0 (the empty product; the empty function). - 2: in each step, takes an arbitrary A with m + 1 elements, removes one point by @cor-remove-point, and applies the hypothesis to the rest. - 2: (a) splits A 	imes B into two disjoint pieces and counts \{a\} 	imes B by a bijection with B. - 3: (b) gives a bijection between B^A and B^{A'} 	imes B, checking injectivity (equality of functions) and surjectivity (the extended graph is a function). - 1: (c) checks both degenerate cases against @prp-empty-function. - Direct route for (a): composing the given bijections with a bijection \{1, \dots, m\} 	imes \{1, \dots, n\} 	o \{1, \dots, mn\}, e.g. (i, j) \mapsto (i - 1)n + j, with injectivity and surjectivity checked (for example by @thm-division-algorithm) and the case m = 0 or n = 0 handled, earns the 2 points of the (a) line and the (a) halves (1 point each) of the two induction lines. Fatal errors (0 for the step): “each of the m elements has n possible values, so n^m” with no bijection or induction; a step that applies the hypothesis to a set not shown to have m elements.

title: 3.2 Countable Sets
content:
Countable Sets Section 3.1 made “the same size” exact and settled the finite sets. It also showed that 
N is infinite, because it is equinumerous with its proper subset 2
N (@exm-hilbert-hotel). The next question is which sets can be put into a list indexed by 
N. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 already uses the word for these sets, countable, in its proof that the real numbers cannot be listed. This section defines it, proves three equivalent forms of it, shows that countable sets are closed under subsets, images, unions of two sets and finite products, and lists the integers and the rationals. Lists Can we list the rational numbers as q_0, q_1, q_2, \dots so that every rational number appears somewhere? Density makes it look impossible. Between any two rationals p < q lies a third, (p + q)/2, so no rational has a next one, and a list in increasing order cannot even get from q_0 to q_1. And yet a list need not be in increasing order. It only has to reach every element at some finite position. The rationals can be listed in that sense, and so can many sets that look larger than 
N. A list indexed by 
N is a function on 
N, its n-th entry being the value at n. Reaching every element is surjectivity. Countable means listable, repetitions allowed. [Countable Set] A set A is countable if A = \emptyset or there exists a surjection f \colon 
N 	o A. In the second case A = f(
N) = \{ f(0), f(1), f(2), \dots \} , that is, the elements of A can be listed as x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots, with x_n \coloneqq f(n), repetitions allowed. A set that is not countable is uncountable. In symbols, A is countable if and only if A = \emptyset \ \vee \ \exists f \in A^{
N} \ \  orall a \in A \ \ \exists n \in 
N \ \ f(n) = a . In words: a non-empty set is countable when some list x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots reaches every one of its elements, each at a finite position n \in 
N. The list may repeat an element as often as it likes, and it need not follow any order. The first clause is there because there is no function at all from 
N to \emptyset (@prp-empty-function (b)), so the second clause can never hold for the empty set; without the first clause, \emptyset would be uncountable. For a non-empty set the definition says that it is the image of some function from 
N, which is how Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 states it. Examples, starting from the smallest: - \emptyset is countable, by the first clause. - A non-empty finite set is countable. For three different objects a, b, c, the list a, b, c, c, c, \dots, that is f(0) \coloneqq a, f(1) \coloneqq b and f(n) \coloneqq c for n \ge 2, is a surjection 
N 	o \{a, b, c\}. Repetitions pad a short list out to the length of 
N. - 
N is countable: \id_{
N} is a surjection. - The set of squares \{ n^2 : n \in 
N \} is countable: it is the image of 
N under n \mapsto n^2, and a function is a surjection onto its image (Section 3.1, “Shrinking the codomain”). In the same way 2
N is countable. A non-example by a minimal change. The list n \mapsto 2n is a list of 2
N. Read it as a list of 
N, keeping the rule and changing only the target set, and it fails: the clause “for every a \in 
N there is an n with 2n = a” fails at a = 1. This shows that this list misses 1, not that 
N is uncountable; one map proves nothing about all maps (the warning after the non-example in Section 3.1). Sets that are genuinely uncountable appear in Section 3.4. Why repetitions are allowed. Two reasons. First, finite sets are then countable with no special case: pad the list by repeating an element, as above. Second, the closure proofs below become short. A function applied to a list gives a list of the image, which may have repetitions even if the first list had none; interleaving lists of two overlapping sets repeats their common elements. If repetitions were forbidden, every such proof would need a step that deletes them. The definition puts that work in one place, the theorem on three ways to say countable below, and does it once. Sometimes we need the stronger statement that a set has exactly the size of 
N. [Countably Infinite Set] A set A is countably infinite if \card{A} = \card{
N}, that is, if there is a bijection A 	o 
N (equivalently, by @prp-equinumerous-properties (b), a bijection 
N 	o A). So 
N, 2
N and 
Z_{>0} are countably infinite (Section 3.1), and a countably infinite set is countable, since a bijection is a surjection. In this book “countable” includes the finite sets and \emptyset. Some books use “countable” to mean “countably infinite” and say “at most countable” for our “countable”. Before quoting a theorem about countable sets from elsewhere, check which convention it uses. Here, \{0, 1\} is countable and is not countably infinite. Subsets of the natural numbers Every countable set will turn out to be finite or countably infinite, with nothing in between. The heart of that is a fact about subsets of 
N: an infinite one can be listed in increasing order without gaps. Subsets of the Natural Numbers Every subset S \subseteq 
N is finite or countably infinite. If S is infinite, list it in increasing order: s_0 is the least element of S, and s_{n+1} is the least element of S above s_n. Well-ordering supplies each least element, provided the set is non-empty, and it is non-empty because S has elements beyond any bound, being infinite. Recursion turns the rule into a function. The list misses nothing: if t \in S were skipped, it would lie strictly between two consecutive entries s_{n-1} < t < s_n, and then s_n would not be the least element of S above s_{n-1}. If S is finite there is nothing to prove, so let S be infinite. In particular S 
e \emptyset. Every x \in 
N has an element of S above it. Let x \in 
N, and suppose that no s \in S has s > x. Then S \subseteq \{0, \dots, x\}, a set with x + 1 elements (the third example after @def-finite), so S is finite by @prp-subset-finite, a contradiction. Hence T_x \coloneqq \{ s \in S : s > x \} is non-empty, and by @thm-well-ordering it has a least element. The list. Define g \colon 
N 	imes 
N 	o 
N by g(n, x) \coloneqq \min T_x; by the previous paragraph this is defined for every x \in 
N. By @thm-recursion, with X \coloneqq 
N and a \coloneqq \min S (which exists by @thm-well-ordering), there is a function n \mapsto s_n from
