N 	imes \{0, 1\}; - reach every pair (q, 0) and every pair (q, 1), for every q \in 
N, each at a finite position. For instance s'(2q) \coloneqq (q, 1), s'(2q + 1) \coloneqq (q, 0) also qualifies. The rows-first attempt a \mapsto (a, 0), “then” the pairs (q, 1), fails the third property (@exm-rows-first-listing). C. Going deeper [C1: Finite subsets of the natural numbers] Let \sF be the set of all finite subsets of 
N. Prove that \sF is countable, without using any result about unions of infinitely many sets. [Hint 1] Inject \sF into 
N by sending F to S_N(F) \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{N} \ind_F(k) \, 2^k, for any N with F \subseteq \{0, \dots, N\} (the value does not depend on N): the number whose binary digits are the indicator of F. [Hint 2] To prove injectivity, let m be the largest element at which two different sets F 
e G differ (the largest element of (F \setminus G) \cup (G \setminus F), a non-empty finite subset of 
N). The terms above m are the same for F and G. Then use \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} 2^k = 2^m - 1 < 2^m. The set \sF \subseteq \powerset{
N} exists by specification. We build an injection \sigma \colon \sF 	o 
N in four steps. For N \in 
N and F \subseteq \{0, \dots, N\} let S_N(F) \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{N} \ind_F(k) \, 2^k , a finite sum as in @def-sum-product (indexed from 0), where \ind_F \colon 
N 	o \{0, 1\} is the indicator function of F. Each term is 0 or 2^k, and 2^k \in 
N by @prp-power-laws (d). So S_N(F) \in 
N, by induction on N through the recursive clause of @def-sum-product, using @lem-naturals-arithmetic (b) at each step. Step 1: a bound. Each term is at most 2^k, so 0 \le S_N(F) \le \sum_{k=0}^{N} 2^k = 2^{N+1} - 1 , by @prp-geometric-sum with r = 2 (shifting the index by one). Step 2: one more term. Splitting off the last term (Section 2.3), for F \subseteq \{0, \dots, N + 1\}, S_{N+1}(F) = S_N igl(F \cap \{0, \dots, N\} igr) + \ind_F(N + 1) \, 2^{N+1} . In particular, if F \subseteq \{0, \dots, N\}, then S_{N+1}(F) = S_N(F). By induction on N' \ge N, S_{N'}(F) = S_N(F) for every N' \ge N: the value does not depend on which bound N we use. Step 3: injective for a fixed N. We prove by @fd1:ax-induction on N: if F, G \subseteq \{0, \dots, N\} and S_N(F) = S_N(G), then F = G. For N = 0, F and G are \emptyset or \{0\}, with values 0 and 1. For the step, let F, G \subseteq \{0, \dots, N + 1\} with S_{N+1}(F) = S_{N+1}(G), and write F' \coloneqq F \cap \{0, \dots, N\}, G' \coloneqq G \cap \{0, \dots, N\}. If N + 1 \in F and N + 1 
otin G, then Steps 2 and 1 give S_{N+1}(F) \ge 2^{N+1} > 2^{N+1} - 1 \ge S_N(G') = S_{N+1}(G) , a contradiction; the case N + 1 \in G \setminus F is the same with F and G exchanged. So N + 1 lies in both or in neither, the last terms in Step 2 agree, and S_N(F') = S_N(G'). By the hypothesis, F' = G'. Since \{0, \dots, N + 1\} = \{0, \dots, N\} \cup \{N + 1\}, it follows that F = G. Step 4: the injection. Every F \in \sF lies in some \{0, \dots, N\}: if F = \emptyset, take N = 0; otherwise F is a non-empty finite set of real numbers, so it has a maximum M \in F \subseteq 
N (@prp-finite-max, as in the remark at the end of Section 3.1), and F \subseteq \{0, \dots, M\}. Define \sigma(F) \coloneqq S_N(F) for any such N; by Step 2 this does not depend on N. If \sigma(F) = \sigma(G), take N at least as large as a bound for F and a bound for G; then S_N(F) = S_N(G), and Step 3 gives F = G. So \sigma is injective, and \sF is countable by @thm-countable-characterizations, (ii) \Rightarrow (i). For example \sigma(\emptyset) = 0 (the empty set contributes no terms), \sigma(\{0, 2\}) = 1 + 4 = 5 and \sigma(\{1, 3\}) = 2 + 8 = 10: \sigma(F) is the number whose binary numeral has a 1 exactly in the places listed in F. Step 3 is the uniqueness of binary numerals, and Step 4 uses no principle of choice: every value is given by a formula. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: defines a map from the finite subsets to 
N explicitly, including the value at \emptyset, and checks that its values are natural numbers. - 2: makes the map well defined, either by a bound-independent definition (as in Step 2) or by summing over the elements of F listed in increasing order. - 4: proves injectivity, either by comparing the terms at the largest element at which F and G differ, using \sum_{k=0}^{m-1} 2^k < 2^m, or by an induction on the bound as in Step 3, or by an equivalent proved uniqueness argument for binary numerals. - 2: concludes with @thm-countable-characterizations, (ii) \Rightarrow (i). - Route by surjection: an explicit map 
N 	o \sF that reads off binary digits (for example, D(n) is the set of k \le n for which the quotient of n by 2^k in @thm-division-algorithm is odd) earns the same points: 2 for defining the map, 2 for checking that each value is a finite subset of 
N, 4 for a proof that every F \in \sF is a value, and 2 for concluding by @def-countable. Fatal errors (0 for the step): writing \sF as the union over n of the sets of n-element subsets and citing a result on countable unions (the task excludes it); asserting injectivity, or surjectivity on the second route, “by uniqueness of binary expansions” with no proof. [C2: Find the error] Here is a “proof” that every subset of a countable set is countable. Let B be countable and A \subseteq B. (1) If A = \emptyset, then A is countable by definition. (2) Otherwise B 
e \emptyset, so there is a surjection g \colon 
N 	o B. (3) Define h \colon 
N 	o A by h(n) \coloneqq g(n). (4) Let a \in A. Then a \in B, so a = g(n) for some n \in 
N, and h(n) = a. (5) Hence h is a surjection onto A, and A is countable. Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, name the line that fails, the rule it breaks, and give a counterexample to that line. Then repair the proof. The conclusion is true: it is @prp-countable-subset. The argument does not prove it. Line (3) fails. It does not define a function from 
N to A: @def-function requires, for every n \in 
N, exactly one value in A, and when g(n) 
otin A the formula offers no value in A at all. Counterexample to line (3): B = 
N, g = \id_{
N}, A = \{1\}. Then “h(2) = g(2) = 2”, and 2 
otin A, so h is not a function into A. Lines (1), (2) and (4) are correct, and (5) would follow if h were a function 
N 	o A. Repair. In the case A 
e \emptyset, fix one element a_0 \in A (one ulename{\exists E}) and define h(n) \coloneqq  egin{cases} g(n) & 	ext{if } g(n) \in A , \ a_0 & 	ext{if } g(n) 
otin A . \end{cases} Now h is a function 
N 	o A, and line (4) shows that it is onto: for a \in A, some n has g(n) = a \in A, and then h(n) = g(n) = a. The repaired proof uses that A is non-empty, which line (1) had already split off; the flawed line ignored the elements of B \setminus A, and the default value a_0 is where they go. The proof in the text avoids the issue by restricting an injection instead, since a restriction of a function is always a function. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: says the conclusion is true, citing @prp-countable-subset or an equivalent proof. - 3: names line (3) and the broken requirement: a function into A needs a value in A at every n (@def-function). - 2: gives a concrete instance of the failure of line (3), with a specific n whose value leaves A. - 3: repairs the proof with a default value in A (or by restricting an injection), and checks surjectivity. Fatal errors (0 for the step): calling the conclusion false; blaming line (4) or (5); a “counterexample” that shows a subset that is not countable.

title: 3.3 Countable Unions and the Axiom of Choice
content:
Countable Unions and the Axiom of Choice Section 3.2 listed 
N 	imes 
N, 
Z and 
Q, and showed that a union of two countable sets is countable (@prp-union-two-countable). The next question is a union of countably many countable sets. The natural proof is short, and it contains one step that none of the rules met so far can justify. This section isolates that step, adds the principle that licenses it, the axiom of choice, and then shows how to tell a proof that needs the axiom from one that only seems to. A union of countably many lists Let A_0, A_1, A_2, \dots be countable sets, a family (A_n)_{n \in 
N} in the sense of @def-indexed-family. We want to prove that  igcup_{n \in 
N} A_n is countable. Here is the proof most people write first. List each set: A_n = \{ a_{n,0}, a_{n,1}, a_{n,2}, \dots \}. Put a_{n,m} in row n and column m of an infinite grid. Every element of the union stands somewhere in the grid, and the grid is indexed by 
N 	imes 
N, which is countable (@thm-product-countable). So the union is the image of a countable set, and it is countable. Every step but the first, “list each set”, is a result of Section 3.2. Where do the lists come from? The obstacle, rule by rule For a non-empty A_n, “A_n is countable” says that there exists a surjection 
N 	o A_n (@def-countable). To use it we apply ulename{\exists E} (@fd1:def-rules-existential): we name the object and argue inside the box of that name. One ulename{\exists E} names one surjection, for one n. - Finitely many sets. The proof of @prp-union-two-countable used two ulename{\exists E}’s; for A_0, \dots, A_9 we could nest ten boxes. - All n \in 
N at once. The grid needs a list of A_n for every n, assembled into one object: a function that sends each n to a surjection 
N 	o A_n. A proof is a finite object. It cannot contain one ulename{\exists E} for each of infinitely many indices, and no rule of Logic and Proof, Chapter 4 makes infinitely many choices in one step. Two escape routes fail. Recursion (@thm-recursion) defines a function on all of 
N at once, but from a rule g given in advance, each value determined by the previous one. The list of A_{n+1} is not determined by the list of A_n, and a rule producing a list of every A_{n+1} would already be the missing object. Induction on k, with @prp-union-two-countable at each step, proves “for every k, A_0 \cup \dots \cup A_k is countable” (Exercise C3 writes it out), but that is a statement about each k separately; nothing makes the lists for different k fit together. Section 1.5 met the same wall: a right inverse of a surjection must pick a preimage of every point at once, and the rules could do that only for finitely many points, or when a rule names the preimage. The axiom of choice None of the working rules (W1)–(W6) of Section 1.1 forms a set out of infinitely many arbitrary picks. The principle we add is the simplest statement that does. From any family of non-empty sets, one may pick one element from each set, all at once. [Axiom of Choice] Let I be a set, and let (A_i)_{i \in I} be a family of sets such that A_i is non-empty for every i \in I. Then there exists a function c \colon I 	o  igcup_{i \in I} A_i \quad 	ext{with} \quad c(i) \in A_i \ 	ext{ for every } i \in I . Such a function c is called a choice function for the family. In symbols, with Y^X the set of functions of Section 1.4 and U \coloneqq  igcup_{i \in I} A_i:  orall i \in I \ (A_i 
e \emptyset) \ 	o \ \exists c \in U^{I} \ \  orall i \in I \ \ c(i) \in A_i . In words: the hypothesis says that each set of the family has an element; the conclusion says that one function picks an element of every A_i at the same time. The codomain, a set by (W3), only gives c somewhere to take its values. The axiom asserts that c exists and gives no recipe for it. Its status. For finitely many indices the axiom adds nothing (proved below); for infinitely many it is a genuinely new principle. It is independent of the other axioms of set theory: Gödel (1938) showed that adding it creates no contradiction that was not there already, and Cohen (1963) that it cannot be proved from them. A later chapter states its best-known equivalent, Zorn’s lemma; the companion volume on set theory proves it equivalent to the axiom, together with the other equivalents such as the well-ordering theorem, and surveys the independence results. This book uses the axiom openly on the main line, among other places: here, for countable unions and right inverses; in Section 3.6, for infinite subsets that can be listed; in Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1, for sup approximations (the remark below); in Measure and Integration, Chapter 1, for the Vitali set; in Functional Analysis, Chapter 4, through Zorn’s lemma, for the Hahn–Banach theorem; and in Functional Analysis, Chapter 6, for Tychonoff’s theorem. Each use is flagged at its line. A corollary in Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 gives, for each n \ge 1 separately, some a_n \in A with a_n > \sup A -  rac1n: one ulename{\exists E} per n, and no axiom. Forming the sequence (a_n)_{n \ge 1} from these is a choice function for the family  igl( \{ a \in A : a > \sup A - 	frac1n \}  igr)_{n \in 
Z_{>0}}, an instance of @ax-choice with the countable index set I = 
Z_{>0}. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 flags exactly this step. Examples. 1. The empty family. If I = \emptyset, the empty function \emptyset 	o  igcup_{i \in \emptyset} A_i = \emptyset (@prp-empty-function (a)) is a choice function: the condition “for every i \in \emptyset” holds vacuously. No axiom is needed. 2. A family with a rule. Let I = 
Z_{>0} and A_n \coloneqq \{ k \in 
N : n \mid k, \ k 
e 0 \}, the positive multiples of n. Each A_n contains n. The rule c(n) \coloneqq n is a choice function, defined by specification (@def-set-builder); no axiom is needed. 3. A family with no rule in sight. Let I be the set of non-empty subsets of 
R, and A_S \coloneqq S for S \in I. A choice function picks an element of every non-empty set of reals. “The least element” fails, since (0, 1) has none, and no rule that works for every S is known. Here the axiom supplies what the other rules do not. A non-example by minimal change. In Example 2, add the index n = 0. The positive multiples of 0 form the empty set (0 \mid k means k = 0), so A_0 = \emptyset, and no function can have c(0) \in A_0. Only the clause “A_i is non-empty for every i” fails, and without it the conclusion is false. That is why the proofs below remove the empty sets from a family before they choose. (Dropping “all at once” instead would leave nothing beyond the hypothesis.) When choice is not needed Two kinds of construction look like choice and are not; telling them apart from a real use is the skill this section is for. Finitely many sets. For every finite set I and every family (A_i)_{i \in I} of non-empty sets, a choice function exists, with no appeal to the axiom. For I = \{1, 2, 3\}, three applications of ulename{\exists E} name a_i \in A_i, and \{ (1, a_1), (2, a_2), (3, a_3) \} is the graph of a choice function. For a finite set of arbitrary size we induct on its number of elements (@def-finite). Let P(n) be: “for every set I with n elements and every family (A_i)_{i \in I} of non-empty sets, there is a choice function”. Base case P(0): a set with 0 elements is the image of a bijection from \{1, \dots, 0\} = \emptyset, so it is empty, and the empty function is a choice function (Example 1). Inductive step: assume P(n), and let I have n + 1 elements. Then I 
e \emptyset, since a bijection \{1, \dots, n + 1\} 	o I has a value at 1; pick i_0 \in I by ulename{\exists E}. The set I' \coloneqq I \setminus \{i_0\} has n elements (@cor-remove-point), so P(n) gives a choice function c' for (A_i)_{i \in I'}. Since A_{i_0} 
e \emptyset, one more ulename{\exists E} names a_0 \in A_{i_0}. The graph of c' together with the pair (i_0, a_0), with codomain  igcup_{i \in I} A_i, is a function on I' \cup \{i_0\} = I, because i_0 
otin I'; and it is a choice function. So P(n + 1) holds, and @fd1:ax-induction gives P(n) for every n \in 
N. Each step uses two ulename{\exists E}’s and no new principle; the induction says nothing about an infinite I, which has no number of elements. A rule that picks. If one description names an element of each A_i, the choice function is defined by specification (W1), as the set of pairs (i, a) with a the element named for i. Typical rules: the least element of a non-empty set of natural numbers (@thm-well-ordering); the non-negative square root of a positive real; in a bisection, the left half if it has the property in question, and otherwise the right half. The first rule is how @thm-countable-characterizations passed from a surjection 
N 	o A to an injection A 	o 
N with no axiom: the least preimage is named, not chosen. Choice is not “picking an element”. “Let a \in A” is a single ulename{\exists E} and needs no axiom; neither does picking from ten sets. The axiom is needed only for picking one element from each of infinitely many sets, with no rule. A proof that says “choose” need not use it, and one that never says “choose” may: “for each n, let g_n be a list of A_n” is a use, however it is worded. Right inverses The first consequence settles the question Section 1.5 left open. By @prp-right-inverse-surjective, a function with a right inverse is surjective; the converse is where choice enters. [Surjections Have Right Inverses] Let f \colon X 	o Y be a surjective function. Then f has a right inverse: there is a function g \colon Y 	o X with f(g(y)) = y for every y \in Y. A right inverse must name a preimage of every y. The preimages of the points of Y form a family of sets indexed by Y, each non-empty because f is onto. A choice function for that family is exactly a right inverse. For y \in Y, let P_y \coloneqq f^{-1}(\{y\}) = \{ x \in X : f(x) = y \} (@def-preimage). This defines a family (P_y)_{y \in Y} of subsets of X, indexed by Y. Each P_y is non-empty, since f is surjective (@def-surjective). By @ax-choice there is a function c \colon Y 	o  igcup_{y \in Y} P_y with c(y) \in P_y for every y \in Y. The union is a subset of X, so the graph of c is a subset of Y 	imes X, and with codomain X it is a function g \colon Y 	o X with g(y) = c(y) (@def-function). For every y \in Y, g(y) \in P_y, that is, f(g(y)) = y. So f \circ g = \id_Y, and g is a right inverse of f (@def-left-right-inverse (b)). Together with @prp-right-inverse-surjective: a function is surjective if and only if it has a right inverse. The theorem is in fact equivalent to the axiom: a right inverse of the projection (i, a) \mapsto i, from the set of pairs with a \in A_i onto I, is a choice function in disguise. Let f \colon 
Z 	o 
N, f(k) \coloneqq \abs{k}. It is surjective. Does the existence of a right inverse of f need @ax-choice? No. Each n \in 
N has the preimages n and -n, and the rule “take the non-negative one” names one of them: g(n) \coloneqq n. Then f(g(n)) = \abs{n} = n, so g \colon 
N 	o 
Z is a right inverse, defined by a formula. The axiom is needed only when no such rule is available. Countable unions Now the theorem the section opened with. The second form, with any countable index set, is the one used in practice. [Countable Unions of Countable Sets] (a) Let (A_n)_{n \in 
N} be a family of sets such that A_n is countable for every n \in 
N. Then  igcup_{n \in 
N} A_n is countable. (b) Let I be a countable set and (A_i)_{i \in I} a family of sets such that A_i is countable for every i \in I. Then  igcup_{i \in I} A_i is countable. This is the grid of the opening, with the lists supplied by the axiom. ① Throw away the empty sets: the axiom needs non-empty ones, and they add nothing to the union. ② For each remaining n, the surjections 
N 	o A_n form a non-empty set; choose one from each, all at once. ③ The chosen lists turn the grid J 	imes 
N into a surjection onto the union, and the grid is countable by Section 3.2. Part (b) is part (a) after renumbering the index set by a list. Before reading on: which line uses choice, and why can ulename{\exists E} not replace it? (a) Let U \coloneqq  igcup_{n \in 
N} A_n and J \coloneqq \{ n \in 
N : A_n 
e \emptyset \}. If J = \emptyset, every A_n is empty, so U = \emptyset, which is countable by @def-countable. Suppose J 
e \emptyset. For n \in J, let S_n \coloneqq \{ h \in A_n^{
N} : h 	ext{ is surjective} \} , the set of surjections 
N 	o A_n (@def-set-builder, with A_n^{
N} the set of functions of Section 1.4). Since A_n is countable and non-empty, S_n 
e \emptyset (@def-countable). By @ax-choice, applied to the family (S_n)_{n \in J}, there is a function c \colon J 	o  igcup_{n \in J} S_n with c(n) \in S_n for every n \in J. This is the only line of the proof that uses the axiom. Define F \colon J 	imes 
N 	o U by F(n, m) \coloneqq c(n)(m). It takes values in U: c(n) maps into A_n \subseteq U. It is surjective: let x \in U; then x \in A_n for some n \in 
N (@def-family-union-intersection), so A_n 
e \emptyset and n \in J; since c(n) is a surjection onto A_n, there is m \in 
N with c(n)(m) = x, that is, F(n, m) = x. The set J is countable by @prp-countable-subset, as a subset of 
N, which is countable (the identity is a surjection). So J 	imes 
N is countable by @cor-product-countable (a), and it is non-empty, since it contains (n_0, 0) for any n_0 \in J. By @def-countable there is a surjection s \colon 
N 	o J 	imes 
N. Then F \circ s \colon 
N 	o U is surjective (@thm-composition-injective-surjective (b)), and U is countable. (b) Let U \coloneqq  igcup_{i \in I} A_i. If I = \emptyset, then U = \emptyset, which is countable. Otherwise @def-countable gives a surjection s \colon 
N 	o I; fix one. For n \in 
N put B_n \coloneqq A_{s(n)}, a countable set. Then  igcup_{n \in 
N} B_n = U. (\subseteq) An element of B_n lies in A_{s(n)} with s(n) \in I. (\supseteq) If x \in A_i with i \in I, then i = s(n) for some n \in 
N, because s is onto, and x \in B_n. By (a), U is countable. The line in bold is the only use of the axiom. The surjections s of parts (a) and (b) are single objects, each named by one ulename{\exists E}. What needed the axiom was a surjection for every n \in J at once: ulename{\exists E} supplies c(n) only inside the box of a fixed n, and F needs all of them outside every such box. The set J is there because for A_n = \emptyset there is no function 
N 	o A_n at all (@prp-empty-function (b)), so S_n = \emptyset. The theorem completes the closure properties of countable sets: subsets, images, finite products, countable unions. Neither hypothesis can be dropped: Section 3.4 shows that 
R is not countable, and 
R is the union of the single set 
R, and also of the countable sets \{x\}, x \in 
R. The choice is of the lists, not of preimages. A surjection 
N 	o A gives least preimages by a rule (@thm-countable-characterizations), but only once the surjection is in hand. In @thm-countable-union, what is missing is the surjection itself, one for each A_n, and the sets A_n need not be sets of natural numbers, so no “least” is available to name one. Unions without choice Many countable unions met in practice come with their lists, and then no axiom is used. [Unions that come with their lists] (a) Show that 
Q =  igcup_{n \in 
Z_{>0}} Q_n, where Q_n \coloneqq \{ m/n : m \in 
Z \}, and list the union without using @ax-choice. (b) Does the proof in @thm-integers-rationals-countable that 
Q is countable use @ax-choice? (a) By the definition 
Q \coloneqq \{ m/n : m \in 
Z, \ n \in 
Z_{>0} \}, a number is rational exactly when it lies in Q_n for some n \in 
Z_{>0}, so the two sets are equal. Fix the bijection z \colon 
N 	o 
Z of @thm-integers-rationals-countable (z(2k) = k, z(2k + 1) = -(k + 1)). Then k \mapsto z(k)/n lists Q_n, and the whole family of lists is the single function L \colon 
Z_{>0} 	imes 
N 	o 
Q , \qquad L(n, k) \coloneqq z(k)/n , defined by specification. It is onto 
Q: for m/n with m \in 
Z, n \in 
Z_{>0}, take k with z(k) = m. Since 
Z_{>0} 	imes 
N is countable and non-empty (@prp-countable-subset, @cor-product-countable), composing L with a surjection 
N 	o 
Z_{>0} 	imes 
N lists 
Q. The grid is the same as in @thm-countable-union; the difference is that the rows were written down, not chosen. (b) No, and its place before @ax-choice does not settle this, since by the warning in “When choice is not needed” a proof can use the axiom without naming it; we check the lines. The maps z and (m, n) \mapsto m/n are formulas. The results cited name finitely many objects by ulename{\exists E}: one injection in @prp-countable-subset, two in @cor-product-countable (a), one surjection in @prp-countable-image. The passage from a surjection to an injection in @thm-countable-characterizations takes the least preimage, a rule; the return from an injection to a list goes through @lem-subsets-of-naturals, whose list is defined by recursion from least elements (@thm-well-ordering), again a rule. No line picks from infinitely many sets without a rule. The pattern is general: if one formula in n lists every A_n, the family of lists is a single function, and no axiom is used. Choice enters only when each A_n is known to be countable as a bare existence statement. Algebraic numbers The theorem pays off at once. A real number is called algebraic if it is a root of a non-zero polynomial with integer coefficients. To keep this inside what the book has defined, we speak of coefficient tuples. For d \ge 1 and c = (c_0, c_1, \dots, c_d) \in 
Z^{d+1} (a (d + 1)-tuple, entries numbered from 0), let p_c(x) \coloneqq \sum_{k=0}^{d} c_k x^k \qquad (x \in 
R) (@def-sum-product, @def-power), and call c non-zero if c_k 
e 0 for some k. Then x \in 
R is algebraic if p_c(x) = 0 for some d \ge 1 and some non-zero c \in 
Z^{d+1}. Constant polynomials are left out without loss, since a non-zero constant has no roots. For example, \sqrt 2 is algebraic, a root of x^2 - 2 (c = (-2, 0, 1)). Every rational m/n is algebraic, a root of nx - m (c = (-m, n)). So is \sqrt 2 + \sqrt 3, a root of x^4 - 10x^2 + 1. We use one fact from school algebra, not proved here: if c \in

R : p_c(x) = 0 \} is finite. [The Algebraic Numbers Are Countable] The set of algebraic real numbers is countable. Sort the polynomials by degree. For each d, the coefficient tuples form a countable set, and each polynomial contributes finitely many roots: a countable union of finite sets. Then take the union over d. Both unions are instances of @thm-countable-union (b). Let \mathrm{Alg} be the set of algebraic real numbers, and for d \ge 1 let Z_d be the set of non-zero tuples in 
Z^{d+1}. Step 1. Let d \ge 1. The set 
Z is countable (@thm-integers-rationals-countable), and

Step 3. By definition, \mathrm{Alg} =  igcup_{d \in 
Z_{>0}} \mathrm{Alg}_d. The index set 
Z_{>0} \subseteq

N. The pair (3, 2) has m = 2 even, so F(3, 2) = c(3)(2) = 3 + 1 = 4. (Each c(n) is onto \{n, n + 1\}: c(n)(1) = n and c(n)(0) = n + 1.) (d) Choose, with the axiom, a list of each non-empty A_n, all at once. The lists turn the countable grid J 	imes

N, so it is countable by @prp-countable-subset. (Even the proof can run without the axiom: h_A(m) \coloneqq m for m \in A and h_A(m) \coloneqq \min A otherwise (@thm-well-ordering) is a rule that maps

The rule “the least element” fails, since (0, 1) has no least element, and no rule is known that names an element of every non-empty set of reals. A proof that needs such a function uses the axiom, and says so. (d) No. The rule “the positive one” names one root of each y > 0: y \mapsto \sqrt y. Let \mathrm{ZSeq} be defined as \mathrm{Seq} in @exr-countable-unions-and-choice-b2, with

N that is good for r (@thm-well-ordering), and let ho(r) \coloneqq 	ext{the number of elements of } \{ s \in R(\mu(n(r))) : s < r \} , well defined because this set is a subset of the finite set R(\mu(n(r))) (@prp-subset-finite, @cor-finite-size-unique). N, defined by specification. It is injective. Let r, r' \in \mathrm{Alg} with n(r) = n(r') and ho(r) = ho(r'); call this common index n, and suppose r

By @prp-subset-finite, the first has fewer elements: ho(r) < ho(r'), a contradiction. So r = r'. Following it with the injection (m, k) \mapsto 2^m 3^k of @thm-product-countable gives an injection \mathrm{Alg} 	o

e \emptyset; pick i_0 \in I. (b) The induction proves the statement for each finite number n of sets, and

title: 3.4 Diagonal Arguments: Uncountable Sets and Cantor's Theorem
content:
Diagonal Arguments: Uncountable Sets and Cantor’s Theorem Every infinite set met so far has turned out to be countable: 
N, 
Z, 
Q, finite products of countable sets, countable unions of them (@thm-countable-union), and even the algebraic numbers (@thm-algebraic-countable). Is every infinite set countable? This section shows that the answer is no, by one argument used three times. Given any list, it builds an object that the list misses. The argument proves that the set of 0–1 sequences is uncountable, that no set can be mapped onto the set of its subsets (Cantor’s theorem), and, with decimals, that 
R is uncountable. A sequence that is not on the list Recall from Section 1.4 that \{0, 1\}^{
N} is the set of all functions 
N 	o \{0, 1\}: the sequences of zeros and ones, indexed from 0. It is infinite, and it looks no bigger than 
N 	imes 
N, which is countable. To show that it is not countable we must show, by @def-countable, that it is non-empty and that no function f \colon 
N 	o \{0, 1\}^{
N} is onto. So we take an arbitrary list f(0), f(1), f(2), \dots of sequences and look for a sequence that is not on it. Write the list as a table: row n is the sequence f(n), and the entry in row n and column k is the number f(n)(k). Here is the start of one such table, with the entries in places (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3) boxed: The boxed entries run down the diagonal of the table. The bottom row g is the diagonal with every entry flipped: g(n) = 1 - f(n)(n). It cannot be row 0, because it differs from f(0) in place 0; it cannot be row 1, because it differs from f(1) in place 1; and so on down the table. Nothing in this reasoning used the particular entries. [The 0–1 Sequences Are Uncountable] The set \{0, 1\}^{
N} of all sequences of zeros and ones is uncountable. Let f \colon 
N 	o \{0, 1\}^{
N} be any function. Define g \colon 
N 	o \{0, 1\} by g(n) \coloneqq 1 - f(n)(n) \qquad (n \in 
N) ; its values lie in \{0, 1\}, since 1 - 0 = 1 and 1 - 1 = 0. So g \in \{0, 1\}^{
N}. For every n \in 
N, g(n) 
e f(n)(n), since no b \in \{0, 1\} has 1 - b = b. Hence g 
e f(n): if g = f(n), then g(n) = f(n)(n), which is false; the two functions differ at place n [ulename{{=}E}, ulename{
eg I}; @prp-function-equality]. So g is not a value of f, and f is not surjective. Since f was arbitrary, no function 
N 	o \{0, 1\}^{
N} is surjective. The set \{0, 1\}^{
N} is non-empty, since it contains the zero sequence. By @def-countable, \{0, 1\}^{
N} is not countable. This is the move of the section, and it has a name. The diagonal. Given any list, build an object that differs from the n-th entry at the n-th place. The new object is not on the list, because it disagrees with every entry somewhere, and the place of disagreement is chosen by the entry’s own position. Run the proof on the list f(n) \coloneqq \ind_{\{n\}}, the sequence with a 1 in place n and 0 elsewhere. What is g? Is it on the list? Here f(n)(n) = \ind_{\{n\}}(n) = 1 for every n, so g(n) = 1 - 1 = 0 for every n: g is the zero sequence. It is indeed not on the list, since every f(n) has a 1 in place n. The diagonal object depends on the list. “The diagonal sequence” is not one sequence: each list has its own, and a different list may well contain the g built from this one (the list g, f(0), f(1), \dots does). And the conclusion “uncountable” needs the list to be arbitrary. Running the construction on one list, or on a few, shows only that those lists miss something; concluding “so no list works” from them is the error (N1) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. The proof above starts from “let f be any function”, and that is what makes its conclusion universal. Cantor’s theorem The table had a row for each n \in 
N and a column for each place k \in 
N. Nothing about the diagonal needs the rows and the columns to be indexed by 
N: it needs only that they are indexed by the same set. A subset S of a set X is a row with one entry for each x \in X, “in” or “out”, the values of \ind_S. So the argument applies to any set and the set of its subsets. Cantor’s Theorem Let X be a set. Then there is no surjection X 	o \powerset{X}. Try it first (ten minutes): given a function f \colon X 	o \powerset{X}, which subset of X could be missed by f? Try X = \{1, 2, 3\} with a function of your own first. The first attempts look for a subset that is “too big” or “too small” to be a value, such as X itself or \emptyset, and fail: f may well take both values. Size is the wrong idea. A set D differs from f(x) as soon as the two disagree about one element, and the only element we know anything about in connection with f(x) is x itself. So we make D disagree with f(x) at x: put x into D exactly when x 
otin f(x). This is the diagonal of the table, flipped. Before reading on: where is surjectivity used? Let f \colon X 	o \powerset{X} be a function, and let D \coloneqq \{ x \in X : x 
otin f(x) \} , a subset of X by @def-set-builder, so D \in \powerset{X} (@def-power-set). Suppose f is surjective. Then there is d \in X with f(d) = D (@def-surjective). If d \in D, then d 
otin f(d) by the definition of D, that is, d 
otin D, a contradiction. Hence d 
otin D. Then d 
otin f(d), and since d \in X, the definition of D gives d \in D, a contradiction again. So f is not surjective. This proves the theorem. Surjectivity was used once, to obtain d; everything else holds for every function f. Read without the supposition, the proof shows that D 
e f(x) for every x \in X: the two sets disagree about x. Three consequences follow. (i) Russell’s theorem is the same argument. In @thm-russell, the set R_A = \{ x \in A : x 
otin x \} is the set D built from the rule f(x) \coloneqq x: each x \in A is tested against itself. The proof that D differs from every f(x) becomes the proof that R_A differs from every element of A, that is, R_A 
otin A. (The rule x \mapsto x need not map into \powerset{A}, but the argument never used that f(x) \subseteq X, only the test “x \in f(x)”.) (ii) The power set is strictly bigger. The map x \mapsto \{x\} is an injection X 	o \powerset{X}, since \{x\} = \{y\} gives x = y. So \powerset{X} has at least as many elements as X, in the sense that X is in bijection with a subset of it, and by the theorem it is not equinumerous with X, since a bijection would be a surjection. Section 3.5 names this relation: X is strictly smaller than \powerset{X}. (iii) There is no largest size. 
N, \powerset{
N}, \powerset{\powerset{
N}}, …: each set in this sequence is strictly bigger than the one before. [The Subsets of the Naturals] The power set \powerset{
N} is uncountable. The set \powerset{
N} is non-empty, since \emptyset \in \powerset{
N}, and by @thm-cantor with X = 
N there is no surjection 
N 	o \powerset{
N}. By @def-countable, \powerset{
N} is not countable. The two diagonal proofs are one. By the correspondence of Section 1.4, S \mapsto \ind_S is a bijection \powerset{
N} 	o \{0, 1\}^{
N}, with inverse b \mapsto \{ n \in 
N : b(n) = 1 \} (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse). Given f \colon 
N 	o \powerset{
N}, the sequence g(n) = 1 - \ind_{f(n)}(n) of @thm-binary-sequences-uncountable is 1 exactly when n 
otin f(n), so g = \ind_D for the set D of Cantor’s proof. Decimal expansions The real numbers should be next. A real number in [0, 1) is written as a decimal 0.d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots, a sequence of digits, so the diagonal suggests itself: list the numbers, write their decimals as the rows of a table, and change the diagonal digits. Two questions must be answered first. What does it mean that a sequence of digits is the decimal of x? And what is 0.999\ldots? School says it equals 1, and a diagonal that produces 0.4999\ldots when 0.5000\ldots is on the list has produced a number that is on the list. An infinite sum would answer the first question, but this book has not yet defined one. Finite sums are enough. The first n digits of x should pin x down to within 10^{-n}. A digit sequence is a decimal of x when each of its finite truncations is within one unit of its last place below x. [Decimal Expansion] A digit sequence is a function k \mapsto d_k from 
Z_{>0} to \{0, 1, \dots, 9\}. For n \ge 1 let t_n \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{n} d_k 10^{-k} (@def-sum-product), where 10^{-k} \coloneqq (1/10)^k (@def-power). The digit sequence is a decimal expansion of x \in [0, 1] if for every n \ge 1, t_n \le x \le t_n + 10^{-n} . In words: t_n is the number written with the first n digits, 0.d_1 \ldots d_n, and the condition says that x lies in the closed interval of length 10^{-n} starting at t_n, for every n. The digits are indexed from 1, so that d_k is the digit in the k-th place after the point. No infinite sum appears: every t_n is a finite sum. Examples. 1. Zero. The all-zero sequence has t_n = 0, and 0 \le 0 \le 10^{-n}; it is an expansion of 0. 2. One half, twice. The sequence 5, 0, 0, \dots has t_n =  rac12 for every n \ge 1, and  rac12 \le  rac12 \le  rac12 + 10^{-n}. The sequence 4, 9, 9, \dots has t_n =  rac{4}{10} + \sum_{k=2}^{n} 9 \cdot 10^{-k} =  rac12 - 10^{-n}, by @prp-geometric-sum, so t_n \le  rac12 \le t_n + 10^{-n} =  rac12. Both are expansions of  rac12. 3. One. The all-nine sequence has t_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} 9 \cdot 10^{-k} = 1 - 10^{-n} (@prp-geometric-sum), so t_n \le 1 \le t_n + 10^{-n} = 1: it is an expansion of 1. A non-example by minimal change. Keep the sequence 5, 0, 0, \dots and move x from  rac12 to 0.51. The inequalities still hold for n = 1 (0.5 \le 0.51 \le 0.6) and for n = 2 (0.50 \le 0.51 \le 0.51), and they fail at n = 3: 0.51 > 0.500 + 0.001. So 5, 0, 0, \dots is not an expansion of 0.51; the clause “for every n \ge 1” is what fails. Why this definition. Both inequalities are non-strict. With a strict right inequality, x < t_n + 10^{-n}, the all-nine sequence would be an expansion of no number at all: it would need x < 1 together with 1 - 10^{-n} \le x for every n, and no real number satisfies both, by the Archimedean property (a school fact; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves it). The non-strict form is what makes 0.999\ldots = 1 true, and true by the definition: the inequalities for x = 1 are checked in Example 3, and no other number satisfies them, since 1 - 10^{-n} \le x \le 1 for every n forces x = 1, again by the Archimedean property (this is the uniqueness half of (D2) below). Example 2 shows that the price is two expansions for some numbers. What this book does not prove are the facts that make expansions behave as school says. We state them once and use them in this section and the next, always by name. 1. Every x \in [0, 1) has a decimal expansion that does not end in all 9s. 2. Every digit sequence is a decimal expansion of exactly one x \in [0, 1]. 3. If two different digit sequences are expansions of the same x, then one of them ends in all 9s and the other ends in all 0s. Here a digit sequence ends in all 9s if there is N \ge 1 with d_k = 9 for every k \ge N, and likewise for 0s. By the uniqueness in (D2), we may write x = 0.d_1 d_2 d_3 \ldots for “x is the number of which d_1, d_2, d_3, \dots is an expansion”. So 0.4999\ldots = 0.5000\ldots =  rac12, as in (D3). Neither (D1) nor (D2) follows from what Part 0 has. (D3) does, by a finite computation at the first place where the two sequences differ (@thm-well-ordering, @prp-geometric-sum); we state it with the others to quote it by name. The existence half of (D2), that some x satisfies all the inequalities at once, is where the completeness of 
R hides, and Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 takes completeness as an axiom. The uniqueness half of (D2) and the “not ending in all 9s” of (D1) rest on the Archimedean property: two numbers x, x' with \abs{x - x'} \le 10^{-n} for every n must be equal, which Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 also proves. Until then we use them as school facts, and each use names the fact it uses. One consequence is used below. A digit sequence with no digit 0 and no digit 9 is the only expansion of its number. Indeed, by (D3) a second expansion of the same number would force one of the two to end in all 9s and the other in all 0s; the given sequence ends in neither, since it has no 9s and no 0s at all. The real numbers are uncountable With the facts in hand, the diagonal runs on digits. Two precautions are built in. Each number on the list gets its expansion by a rule, so that no choosing is needed. And the new digits avoid 0 and 9, so that the new number has only one expansion. [The Reals Are Uncountable, by Decimals] The interval [0, 1) is uncountable. Hence 
R is uncountable. Take an arbitrary list of numbers in [0, 1), write each as its expansion with no tail of 9s, and change the n-th digit of the n-th number to 4 or 5. The resulting digit sequence is an expansion of some y, by (D2). If y were the n-th number, it would have two different expansions, one with no 0s or 9s, against (D3). Let f \colon 
N 	o [0, 1) be any function. For n \ge 1 let x_n \coloneqq f(n - 1), so that the list x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots has the same values as f. For each n \ge 1, x_n has an expansion not ending in all 9s, by (D1), and only one: by (D3), two different such expansions would include one ending in all 9s. Let (d_{n,k})_{k \ge 1} be this expansion. It is named by a rule, “the expansion of x_n not ending in all 9s”, so no choice is involved. Define a digit sequence by e_n \coloneqq  egin{cases} 5 & 	ext{if } d_{n,n} 
e 5, \ 4 & 	ext{if } d_{n,n} = 5, \end{cases} \qquad (n \ge 1) . Then e_n 
e d_{n,n} for every n \ge 1. By (D2), there is y \in [0, 1] of which (e_k)_{k \ge 1} is an expansion. Its first truncation is t_1 = e_1/10 \in \{0.4, 0.5\}, so 0.4 \le t_1 \le y \le t_1 + 0.1 \le 0.6, and in particular y \in [0, 1). Let n \ge 1, and suppose y = x_n. Then (e_k) and (d_{n,k}) are both expansions of y, and they are different, since they differ in place n. But (e_k) has no digit 0 and no digit 9, so by the consequence of (D3) stated above it is the only expansion of y, a contradiction. So y 
e x_n for every n \ge 1, and y is not a value of f. Since f was arbitrary, no function 
N 	o [0, 1) is surjective; and [0, 1) is non-empty, since it contains 0. By @def-countable, [0, 1) is not countable. Finally, if 
R were countable, its subset [0, 1) would be countable by @prp-countable-subset. So 
R is uncountable. Why the digits 4 and 5. The first rule that comes to mind is e_n \coloneqq 9 - d_{n,n}, which also changes every diagonal digit. Run it on the list x_1 =  rac12, x_n = 0 for n \ge 2 (that is, f(0) =  rac12 and f(n) = 0 for n \ge 1). The expansions are 0.5000\ldots and 0.000\ldots, so d_{1,1} = 5 and d_{n,n} = 0 for n \ge 2. The naive rule produces e_1 = 4 and e_n = 9 for n \ge 2: the sequence 0.4999\ldots, which is an expansion of  rac12 = x_1 by Example 2. The new digit sequence differs from every row, and its number is on the list. The rule with 4 and 5, on the same list, gives 0.4555\ldots =  rac{41}{90}, which is on no row. Avoiding 0 and 9 is exactly what the last paragraph of the proof uses. Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves that 
R is uncountable again, with no decimals at all, directly from its least upper bound axiom; that proof needs none of (D1)–(D3). Transcendental numbers A real number that is not algebraic is called transcendental. Section 3.3 showed that the set \mathrm{Alg} of algebraic numbers is countable (@thm-algebraic-countable). [Transcendental Numbers Exist] The set 
R \setminus \mathrm{Alg} of transcendental numbers is uncountable. In particular, there is a real number that is not algebraic. By excluded middle (@fd1:prp-excluded-middle), every real number is in \mathrm{Alg} or not, so 
R = \mathrm{Alg} \cup (
R \setminus \mathrm{Alg}). Suppose 
R \setminus \mathrm{Alg} is countable. Since \mathrm{Alg} is countable by @thm-algebraic-countable, 
R is countable by @prp-union-two-countable, contradicting @thm-reals-uncountable-decimal. So 
R \setminus \mathrm{Alg} is uncountable. In particular 
R \setminus \mathrm{Alg} 
e \emptyset, since \emptyset is countable (@def-countable). So not every x satisfies x 
otin 
R \setminus \mathrm{Alg}: otherwise 
R \setminus \mathrm{Alg} would be an empty set (@def-empty-set), hence equal to \emptyset (@prp-empty-set-unique). By the classical law @fd1:prp-quantifier-negation (a) and ulename{
eg
eg E}, some x lies in 
R \setminus \mathrm{Alg}; this x is a real number that is not algebraic. This last passage, from “not empty” to “has an element”, is a classical step (Logic and Proof, Section 5.7). The proof names no transcendental number: it shows that the set of them is too large to be countable, hence not empty. Its classical steps are the split of 
R into \mathrm{Alg} and its complement (excluded middle) and the last one, from “not empty” to “has an element”. Compare the classical proof of @fd1:thm-irrational-power-rational in Logic and Proof, Section 5.7, which also names no witness (unlike @fd1:prp-log2-9-irrational, which does). Proving that a particular number, such as \pi, is transcendental is a different and much harder matter. Exercises A. Check your understanding [A1] These parts are about the proof of @thm-cantor. 1. Where in the proof is the surjectivity of f used, and what does it supply? 2. Run the proof on X = \{1, 2, 3\} and f(1) = \{1, 2\}, f(2) = \emptyset, f(3) = \{1, 3\}. What is D? Is D a value of f? 3. State the idea of the proof in two sentences. 4. Why does the same argument not show that there is no surjection X 	o X? (a) It is used once, right after D is defined: surjectivity supplies an element d \in X with f(d) = D. The two cases d \in D and d 
otin D are then both refuted. Everything before that line holds for every function f. (b) Test each x against f(x): 1 \in f(1), so 1 
otin D; 2 
otin f(2) = \emptyset, so 2 \in D; 3 \in f(3), so 3 
otin D. Hence D = \{2\}. It is not a value of f: the values are \{1, 2\}, \emptyset, \{1, 3\}, and D differs from f(x) about x in each case (1 \in f(1) \setminus D, 2 \in D \setminus f(2), 3 \in f(3) \setminus D). (c) Build the set D of those x that are not in their own image f(x). Then D disagrees with every f(x) about the element x, so it is not a value of f. (d) The set D is a subset of X, so it is a candidate value only for a function into \powerset{X}. For f \colon X 	o X, the argument (where the test x \in f(x) makes sense at all) shows that D is not a value of f, but D need not be an element of X, so nothing contradicts surjectivity. Indeed \id_X is a surjection X 	o X; with f = \id_X the argument is Russell’s, and shows only that D = R_X is not an element of X (@thm-russell). B. Practice [B1: A faded diagonal] Let

N is uncountable. Let \sF be the set of finite subsets of

N} would be countable by @prp-union-two-countable, contradicting @cor-powerset-naturals-uncountable. So \sI is uncountable. [B3: Expansions of three numbers] For each of x =  rac13,  rac12, 1, find all decimal expansions of x, checking the inequalities of @def-decimal-expansion for each one you give, and say which of (D1)–(D3) each case illustrates. We use @prp-geometric-sum with r =  rac{1}{10}, after taking the constant factor  rac{1}{10} out of the sum: \sum_{k=1}^{n} 10^{-k} =  rac{1}{10} \sum_{k=1}^{n} ( rac{1}{10})^{k-1} =  rac{1}{10} \cdot  rac{1 - 10^{-n}}{9/10} =  rac19 (1 - 10^{-n}). x =  rac13. The all-three sequence has t_n =  rac39 (1 - 10^{-n}) =  rac13 -  rac13 10^{-n}, so t_n \le  rac13 \le t_n + 10^{-n}. It is an expansion, and it does not end in all 9s, as (D1) promises. It ends in neither 9s nor 0s, so by (D3) no other expansion of  rac13 exists. Answer: 0.333\ldots only. x =  rac12. Example 2 after @def-decimal-expansion checks that 0.5000\ldots and 0.4999\ldots are expansions. There are no others: if three different expansions existed, two of them would both end in all 9s or both not; but by (D3), of two different expansions of one number, one ends in all 9s and the other in all 0s, and a sequence ending in all 0s does not end in all 9s (from some place on, its digits would be both 0 and 9). Answer: exactly these two, which illustrate (D3); the first is the one (D1) promises. x = 1. The all-nine sequence is an expansion (Example 3). Conversely, let (d_k) be an expansion of 1, and suppose d_m \le 8 for some m. Since every digit is at most 9, t_m \le \sum_{k=1}^{m} 9 \cdot 10^{-k} - 10^{-m} = 1 - 2 \cdot 10^{-m}, so t_m + 10^{-m} \le 1 - 10^{-m} < 1, against the definition. So every digit is 9. Answer: 0.999\ldots only. The all-nine sequence is an expansion of 1, an instance of the existence half of (D2). Here (D3) has no second expansion to compare. The case also shows why (D1) is stated for [0, 1) only: the one expansion of 1 ends in all 9s. C. N} is uncountable. Let f \colon X 	o \powerset{X} be a function, and let D \coloneqq \{ x \in X : x

N}, and \pi_b is a bijection by @thm-bijection-iff-inverse. Let B be the set of bijections

title: 3.5 Comparing Sizes: the Schröder–Bernstein Theorem
content:
Comparing Sizes: the Schröder–Bernstein Theorem We have (0, 1) \subseteq [0, 1] \subseteq 
R. Are the three sets the same size? Section 3.1 made “same size” mean “there is a bijection”, and for these sets a bijection is fiddly to write down: [0, 1] has two endpoints that (0, 1) lacks, and 
R is unbounded. An injection, on the other hand, is easy in both directions: the inclusion goes one way, and squeezing [0, 1] into the middle of (0, 1) goes the other. This section turns injections into a way of comparing sizes, and proves the theorem that makes the comparison useful: injections both ways give a bijection. Comparing sizes with injections An injection A 	o B places a copy of A inside B: distinct elements of A go to distinct elements of B, so B has room for all of A. For finite sets this is the pigeonhole principle read the other way round (@cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets). It deserves a name for all sets. A is at most as big as B when A fits into B without collisions. [Comparing Sizes] Let A and B be sets. We write \card{A} \le \card{B}, and say that A is at most as big as B, if there exists an injection A 	o B. We write \card{A} < \card{B}, and say that A is strictly smaller than B, if \card{A} \le \card{B} and not \card{A} = \card{B}: there is an injection A 	o B, and there is no bijection A 	o B. In words: “\le” asks for one injection, of our choosing. “<” asks for an injection and rules out every bijection, which is a statement about all functions A 	o B at once. As with \card{A} = \card{B} in Section 3.1 (@def-equinumerous), the symbols \card{A} \le \card{B} and \card{A} < \card{B} are relations between the sets A and B. No object \card{A} is defined for an infinite set, and nothing here compares two numbers. Examples. - Subsets. If A \subseteq B, the inclusion a \mapsto a is an injection A 	o B, so \card{A} \le \card{B}. In particular \card{(0, 1)} \le \card{[0, 1]} \le \card{
R}. - The degenerate case. For every set B, \card{\emptyset} \le \card{B}: the empty function \emptyset 	o B (@prp-empty-function (a)) is injective, vacuously, since there are no x_1, x_2 \in \emptyset to test. - Finite sets. Let A have m elements and B have n elements (@def-finite). Then \card{A} \le \card{B} exactly when m \le n. If m \le n, take bijections \varphi \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o A and \psi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} 	o B; the inclusion \iota \colon \{1, \dots, m\} 	o \{1, \dots, n\} is injective, so \psi \circ \iota \circ \varphi^{-1} \colon A 	o B is injective by @thm-composition-injective-surjective (a), \varphi^{-1} being a bijection (@thm-bijection-iff-inverse). If m > n, there is no injection A 	o B by @cor-pigeonhole-finite-sets (a). So the relation agrees with the count of elements, which is why it is allowed to borrow the symbol \le. - Countable sets. By @thm-countable-characterizations, (i) \iff (ii), a set A is countable if and only if \card{A} \le \card{
N}. “Countable” means “at most as big as 
N”. - Power sets. For every set X, \card{X} < \card{\powerset{X}}. The map x \mapsto \{x\} is an injection X 	o \powerset{X}, since \{x_1\} = \{x_2\} gives x_1 \in \{x_2\}, so x_1 = x_2. And there is no bijection X 	o \powerset{X}, because by @thm-cantor there is not even a surjection. In particular \card{
N} < \card{\powerset{
N}}. Non-example by minimal change. Replace “injection” by “function” in the definition. Then any set would be “at most as big as” any non-empty set, by a constant map: 
R 	o \{0\} would put 
R below a one-element set. The clause that carries the meaning is “no two elements collide”. \card{A} < \card{B} does not mean “there is an injection A 	o B that is not a bijection”. The map n \mapsto n + 1 is an injection 
N 	o 
N that misses 0, and yet \card{
N} = \card{
N}. For infinite sets one injection that fails to be onto proves nothing about strictness; \card{A} < \card{B} needs every map A 	o B to fail to be a bijection, which is why Cantor’s theorem, a statement about every f \colon X 	o \powerset{X}, is the source of our strict inequalities. The relation behaves like an order in two of the three ways. The third is the content of this section’s theorem. [Comparing Sizes Is Reflexive and Transitive] For all sets A, B, C: 1. \card{A} \le \card{A}; 2. if \card{A} \le \card{B} and \card{B} \le \card{C}, then \card{A} \le \card{C}. (a) The identity \id_A is injective, since \id_A(x_1) = \id_A(x_2) says x_1 = x_2. (b) Let f \colon A 	o B and g \colon B 	o C be injections. Then g \circ f \colon A 	o C is injective by @thm-composition-injective-surjective (a). This proves the proposition. As with equinumerosity (Section 3.1, after @prp-equinumerous-properties), we do not call this a partial order: there is no set of all sets for it to be a relation on (@thm-russell). And antisymmetry, the clause (PO2) of @def-partial-order, would say “if \card{A} \le \card{B} and \card{B} \le \card{A}, then A = B”, which is false: \card{
N} \le \card{2
N} and \card{2
N} \le \card{
N}, while 2
N 
e 
N. The right replacement for “A = B” is “\card{A} = \card{B}”. That is the Schröder–Bernstein Theorem below. Before it, one more way to read \le. A countable set was defined by a surjection from

The Schröder–Bernstein Theorem Here is the replacement for antisymmetry. To show two sets are the same size, it is enough to fit each into the other. [Schröder–Bernstein Theorem] Let A and B be sets. If \card{A} \le \card{B} and \card{B} \le \card{A}, then \card{A} = \card{B}. Let f \colon A 	o B and g \colon B 	o A be the two injections. We want a bijection h \colon A 	o B, and at each a \in A there are two candidates: go forward, h(a) = f(a), or go back along g: let h(a) be the unique b with g(b) = a. Going back is possible only for a \in g(B). So a point of A not hit by g must be sent forward by f. Then the point f(a) \in B is used up, and g(f(a)) must not go back to it, or h would collide; so g(f(a)) must also be sent forward, and then g(f(g(f(a)))), and so on along the chain. Everything reached this way goes forward; everything else goes back. Infinite Sets Section 3.5 compared sizes with injections. Here we ask where 
N sits in that comparison. Every infinite set we have met contains a copy of 
N, and it is tempting to say that this must always happen by picking new elements one at a time; this section makes that picking exact. It turns out to need @ax-choice again, this time applied to a family with one set for each non-empty subset of the given set, and it gives two results: 
N is the smallest infinite size, and a set is infinite exactly when it is the same size as a proper part of itself. Every infinite set contains a copy of the natural numbers The question has a goal theorem: we want to show that an infinite set X has a countably infinite subset, that is, a subset equinumerous with 
N (@def-countably-infinite). Equivalently, we want an injection 
N 	o X: its image is then such a subset. [Infinite Sets Contain a Countably Infinite Subset] Every infinite set X has a countably infinite subset. Equivalently, there is an injection 
N 	o X. The natural attempt picks x_0 \in X, then x_1 \in X \setminus \{x_0\}, then x_2 \in X \setminus \{x_0, x_1\}, and so on. Each pick is possible, because a finite set cannot exhaust the infinite X, and each single pick is one ulename{\exists E}. But “and so on” is a definition by recursion, and @thm-recursion needs a function g that says, once and for all, which new element to take after any finite stage. That function must pick an element from every non-empty set of the form X \setminus F at once, with no rule for doing so when X is arbitrary. So we let @ax-choice supply a choice function c on all non-empty subsets of X first, and then the recursion is an ordinary one, with c as its rule. Let X be infinite. The family (S)_{S \in \powerset{X} \setminus \{\emptyset\}}, indexed by the non-empty subsets of X with each index as its own member, consists of non-empty sets, and its union is X: every index is a subset of X, and each x \in X lies in the index \{x\}. By @ax-choice there is a function c \colon \powerset{X} \setminus \{\emptyset\} 	o X with c(S) \in S \quad 	ext{for every non-empty } S \subseteq X . This is the one line of the proof that uses the axiom. Define g \colon 
N 	imes \powerset{X} 	o \powerset{X} by g(n, F) \coloneqq F \cup \{ c(X \setminus F) \} if F 
e X, and g(n, F) \coloneqq F if F = X. In the first case X \setminus F is non-empty, so c(X \setminus F) is defined; so g is a function. By @thm-recursion, applied with the set \powerset{X}, the starting value \emptyset and this g, there are sets F_n \subseteq X, for n \in 
N, with F_0 = \emptyset and F_{n+1} = g(n, F_n). We show by induction (@fd1:ax-induction) that F_n has exactly n elements, for every n \in 
N. For n = 0, F_0 = \emptyset has 0 elements (@def-finite). Suppose F_n has n elements. Then F_n is finite and X is not, so F_n 
e X, and F_{n+1} = F_n \cup \{ c(X \setminus F_n) \} with c(X \setminus F_n) \in X \setminus F_n. This is a union of disjoint sets with n elements and 1 element, so F_{n+1} has n + 1 elements by @prp-disjoint-union-count. In particular F_n

The proof shows where the axiom enters and why one ulename{\exists E} per step is not enough: ulename{\exists E} names one element for one set, while the recursion needs g as a single function defined on every stage at once. Each F_n is then determined by c; the only arbitrary thing is c itself. A non-example by a minimal change. Run the same construction on the finite set X = \{a, b\}, with a 
e b. The choice function c and the recursion still make sense, since g is defined on every F \subseteq X. But F_1 = \{ c(X) \} has one element, F_2 adds the other, so F_2 = X, and from then on g leaves F_n unchanged. So x_2 = c(X \setminus F_2) = c(\emptyset) is not defined. e X”, exactly where the hypothesis that X is infinite is used. Compare Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1’s proof that the real numbers cannot be listed. There, a given list is used to build nested closed intervals, and each interval is obtained from the previous one by an explicit rule (keep an outer third that misses the next point of the list), so no choice principle is involved. Here X is an arbitrary infinite set, and there is no rule available for picking an element of an arbitrary non-empty subset of it; the choice function is the rule. For a particular X a rule may exist: for X \subseteq

That the theorem cannot be proved in general from the other rules of set formation alone is a result of set theory; we state it without proof, and nothing depends on it. This proves the theorem. Together with Section 3.1, this gives a characterization of “infinite” that never mentions 
N or counting: a set is infinite precisely when some proper part of it is as big as the whole. The finite intuition “a part is smaller than the whole” is exactly the property that separates finite sets from infinite ones.
