N^N is countable by @cor-product-countable, and so is Z_N (compose a surjection 
N 	o 
N^N with the inverse bijection, @prp-countable-image). By @thm-countable-union, Z is countable. (That theorem uses @ax-choice; here it could be avoided, since each Z_N comes with an explicit listing, but the question did not ask for that.) Why the look-alike fails. A diagonal argument, as in @thm-binary-sequences-uncountable, builds from a list f_0, f_1, \dots of eventually zero functions the function g(n) \coloneqq f_n(n) + 1. It differs from every f_n, but g(n) \ge 1 for every n, so g is not eventually zero: it is not in Z, and nothing is contradicted. A diagonal argument proves uncountability only when the diagonal object stays inside the set.

title: 3.7 Gate 0: Part 0 Examination
content:
Gate 0: Part 0 Examination Part 0 ends here. Its eight main-line chapters taught one skill in many forms: reading a mathematical statement exactly, and proving it in sentences that a reader can check line by line. This section is an examination on all of it, and the test of whether Part I will be readable: from Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 on, every proof assumes that negating a quantified statement, naming a witness, running an induction and chasing an element through a preimage are routine. A reader who comes to the book by a reading path that begins at Part I, such as a first course in real analysis, takes this Gate first, as an entry test, and goes back only to the sections that the remediation map at the end names. Grading your own work is a skill too; the front matter’s page on getting feedback without a teacher describes the loop of attempting, writing, grading against the scheme and only then reading the solution. Instructions - Time: 2 hours. Closed book, no notes; paper and pen. Attempt all six problems. The times in brackets are a guide; they add up to 120 minutes. - Write complete proofs in plain prose, at level 3 of @fd1:def-levels-of-proof. Rule tags are allowed where a problem asks for them. - Each problem is worth 10 points, 60 in all. Its solution is folded. Open a solution only after the two hours, and grade before you read it: apply the marking scheme at the end of the solution to your own script, point by point, and only then read the book’s proof. - Pass line: 70% overall (42 of 60 points), and no core problem at 0. The core problems are marked core: P1, P2, P4 and P5. They test what Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 uses from its first page: quantifiers and their negation, turning a derivation into prose, induction and recursion, sets and functions. P3 and P6 are not core. - If you fail, follow the remediation map, then wait a week and retake the whole Gate (the same problems) before starting Part I. The definition drill comes first and is not scored. It is the one retrieval list of Part 0: every major definition of the Part, to be written from memory before the clock starts. A proof that reads well is not thereby correct, and grading your own script is where a reader working alone is most easily fooled. Grade the step, not the impression: a marking-scheme line such as “y given as a function of \delta” is either on your page or it is not. A script that says “choose y close to 1” in Problem P1 has not given y as a function of \delta, however clear the idea, and loses those points. Definition drill State each of the following in symbols, with every quantifier and every bound written out, as the book defines it. Allow about fifteen minutes, before the two hours start. 1. \Gamma \vdash \psi. 2. \Gamma \models \psi, for formulas of propositional logic. 3. \varphi is a tautology. 4. The side conditions of ulename{ orall I} and of ulename{\exists E} on the flagged name x_0. 5. \exists! x\, \varphi. 6. A \subseteq B. 7.  igcap_{i \in I} A_i, for a family (A_i)_{i \in I} of subsets of a set X. 8. A function f \colon X 	o Y. 9. f \colon X 	o Y is injective; f is surjective. 10. The image f(A) and the preimage f^{-1}(B). 11. An equivalence relation on X; a partition of X. 12. A greatest element and a maximal element of A \subseteq X, for a partial order \preceq on X. 13. A least upper bound of A in a partially ordered set (X, \preceq). 14. The principle of induction; the well-ordering of 
N. 15. A is countable. 16. \card{A} = \card{B}; \card{A} \le \card{B}. 17. The axiom of choice. The answers are the definitions as the book states them; the label after each answer is where to look when an answer is wrong. 1. For a list \Gamma = \varphi_1, \dots, \varphi_n (n \ge 0): \Gamma \vdash \psi if there is a derivation whose premises all belong to \Gamma and whose last line is \psi (@fd1:def-derivable). 2. \Gamma \models \psi if for every valuation v: if v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} for every \varphi in \Gamma, then v(\psi) = \mathrm{T} (@fd1:def-valid-argument). 3. v(\varphi) = \mathrm{T} for every valuation v (@fd1:def-tautology). 4. ulename{ orall I}, closing a flagged box with name x_0 and writing  orall x\, \varphi on line k: at line k, x_0 appears in no premise, in no assumption of a box still open at line k, and not in  orall x\, \varphi (@fd1:def-rules-universal). ulename{\exists E}, from \exists x\, \varphi and a flagged box with name x_0 assuming \varphi[x_0/x] and ending in \chi, writing \chi on line k: x_0 does not appear in \chi, in \exists x\, \varphi, in any premise, or in any assumption of a box still open at line k (@fd1:def-rules-existential). “Appears” means written anywhere, after a quantifier symbol included. 5. \exists x\,  igl( \varphi \wedge  orall y\, (\varphi[y/x] 	o y = x)  igr), where y is a variable other than x that does not appear in \varphi (@fd1:def-unique-existence). 6.  orall x\, (x \in A 	o x \in B) (@def-subset). 7.  igcap_{i \in I} A_i \coloneqq \{ x \in X :  orall i \in I\ (x \in A_i) \}; for I = \emptyset it is X (@def-family-union-intersection). 8. A relation G \subseteq X 	imes Y, the graph, with  orall x \in X\ \exists! \, y \in Y\ (x, y) \in G, together with the codomain Y: formally f = (G, Y) (@def-function). 9. Injective:  orall x_1 \in X\  orall x_2 \in X\  igl( f(x_1) = f(x_2) 	o x_1 = x_2  igr) (@def-injective). Surjective:  orall y \in Y\ \exists x \in X\ f(x) = y (@def-surjective). 10. For A \subseteq X: y \in f(A) \iff y \in Y \wedge \exists a \in A\ f(a) = y (@def-image). For B \subseteq Y: x \in f^{-1}(B) \iff x \in X \wedge f(x) \in B (@def-preimage). 11. A relation \sim on X with (Eq1)  orall x \in X\ x \sim x; (Eq2)  orall x, y \in X\ (x \sim y 	o y \sim x); (Eq3)  orall x, y, z \in X\ (x \sim y \wedge y \sim z 	o x \sim z) (@def-equivalence-relation). A set \sP of subsets of X with (P1)  orall P \in \sP\ P 
e \emptyset; (P2)  orall P, Q \in \sP\ (P 
e Q 	o P \cap Q = \emptyset); (P3)  igcup \sP = X (@def-partition). 12. g is a greatest element: g \in A \wedge  orall a \in A\ a \preceq g (@def-greatest-element). m is a maximal element: m \in A \wedge 
eg \exists a \in A\ m \prec a, where m \prec a means m \preceq a \wedge m 
e a (@def-maximal-element). 13. s \in X with (S1)  orall a \in A\ a \preceq s, and (S2)  orall u \in X\  igl( ( orall a \in A\ a \preceq u) 	o s \preceq u  igr) (@def-order-supremum). 14. For every property P of natural numbers: if P(0) and  orall n \in 
N\  igl( P(n) 	o P(n + 1)  igr), then  orall n \in 
N\ P(n) (@fd1:ax-induction). Every non-empty S \subseteq 
N has a least element: S 
e \emptyset 	o \exists m \in S\  orall s \in S\ m \le s (@thm-well-ordering). 15. A = \emptyset, or there is f \colon 
N 	o A with  orall a \in A\ \exists n \in 
N\ f(n) = a (@def-countable). 16. \card{A} = \card{B} if there is a bijection A 	o B (@def-equinumerous); \card{A} \le \card{B} if there is an injection A 	o B (@def-card-le). 17. For every set I and every family (A_i)_{i \in I} of sets with  orall i \in I\ A_i 
e \emptyset, there is c \colon I 	o  igcup_{i \in I} A_i with  orall i \in I\ c(i) \in A_i (@ax-choice). Count an item right only if every quantifier, every bound and the order of the quantifiers match. The commonest slips are a missing “\in X” bound in (Q9), “\exists y” for “\exists! \, y” in (Q8), and, in (Q12), “ orall a \in A\ a \preceq m” for maximal, which is the definition of greatest. The problems [P1: core] (20 minutes.) Say that a function f \colon 
R 	o 
R has property L if for every x \in 
R there is \delta > 0 such that for every y \in 
R with \abs{y - x} < \delta, we have f(y) \ge f(x). 1. Write property L in symbols, with bounded quantifiers. 2. Write its negation with no 
eg in front of a quantifier, a connective or a parenthesis. 3. Prove that f(x) = x^2 does not have property L. 4. Prove that the function f \colon 
R 	o 
R with f(x) = 1 for x > 0 and f(x) = 0 for x \le 0 (the indicator of (0, \infty), with codomain 
R) has property L, and that it does not have the property obtained from L by moving “there is \delta > 0” to the front. (a) Property L is  orall x \in 
R\ \exists \delta > 0\  orall y \in 
R\  igl( \abs{y - x} < \delta 	o f(y) \ge f(x)  igr). (b) Push the negation inward one symbol at a time, as in the procedure of Logic and Proof, Section 4.9 (“Negating a definition, mechanically”): @fd1:prp-bounded-quantifier-negation three times, the bound of each quantifier kept, and @fd1:prp-negated-implication once. Write \alpha for \abs{y - x} < \delta and  eta for f(y) \ge f(x).  egin{aligned} &
eg\,  orall x \in 
R\ \exists \delta > 0\  orall y \in 
R\ (\alpha 	o  eta) \ &\dashv\vdash \exists x \in 
R\  orall \delta > 0\ 
eg\,  orall y \in 
R\ (\alpha 	o  eta) \ &\dashv\vdash \exists x \in 
R\  orall \delta > 0\ \exists y \in 
R\ 
eg (\alpha 	o  eta) \ &\dashv\vdash \exists x \in 
R\  orall \delta > 0\ \exists y \in 
R\ (\alpha \wedge 
eg eta) . \end{aligned} The first step does two moves at once (
eg orall to \exists
eg, then 
eg\exists to  orall
eg). After the chain, 
eg eta, that is 
eg igl(f(y) \ge f(x) igr), is replaced by f(y) < f(x), a fact about the order of 
R and not a law of logic. The negation of L is therefore \exists x \in 
R\  orall \delta > 0\ \exists y \in 
R\  igl( \abs{y - x} < \delta \wedge f(y) < f(x)  igr). Note what stays: the bound \delta > 0 is kept, and only the quantifier in front of it changes; “\exists \delta \le 0” would be the error of negating the bound. The implication becomes a conjunction, never another implication. (c) We prove the negation (b) for f(x) = x^2, with the witness x = 1. Let \delta > 0 be arbitrary, and put y \coloneqq 1 - 	frac12 \min\{\delta, 1\} . Since 0 < \min\{\delta, 1\} \le 1, we have  rac12 \le y < 1. Then \abs{y - 1} =  rac12 \min\{\delta, 1\} \le  rac12 \delta < \delta, and, as 0 < y < 1, y^2 = y \cdot y < y \cdot 1 < 1 = f(1). So \abs{y - 1} < \delta and f(y) < f(1). Since \delta > 0 was arbitrary, the negation of L holds at x = 1, and x^2 does not have property L. The order of the choices is the order of the quantifiers in (b): x is fixed before \delta, and y is a function of \delta. The minimum with 1 is needed: y \coloneqq 1 - \delta/2 fails for large \delta, since \delta = 4 gives y = -1 and y^2 = 1 
ot< 1. (d) Let f \colon 
R 	o 
R be the function of (d): f(x) = 1 for x > 0 and f(x) = 0 for x \le 0. Let x \in 
R. Case 1: x > 0. Take \delta \coloneqq x, which is positive. If \abs{y - x} < x, then y > x - x = 0, so f(y) = 1 = f(x), and f(y) \ge f(x). Case 2: x \le 0. Take \delta \coloneqq 1. For every y, f(y) \in \{0, 1\}, so f(y) \ge 0 = f(x). So f has property L. In Case 1, \delta depends on x: points close to 0 need small \delta. The swapped property is \exists \delta > 0\  orall x \in 
R\  orall y \in 
R\ (\abs{y - x} < \delta 	o f(y) \ge f(x)). We prove its negation,  orall \delta > 0\ \exists x \in 
R\ \exists y \in 
R\ (\abs{y - x} < \delta \wedge f(y) < f(x)). Let \delta > 0, and take x \coloneqq \delta/4 and y \coloneqq -\delta/4. Then \abs{y - x} = \delta/2 < \delta, while f(y) = 0 < 1 = f(x), since y < 0 < x. So no single \delta serves every x. Here x depends on \delta, which is legitimate, because \delta is now fixed first. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 2: (a) correct, with  orall x \in 
R, \exists \delta > 0,  orall y \in 
R in this order and the condition \abs{y - x} < \delta as the hypothesis of an implication (or as a bound  orall y \in 
R with \abs{y - x} < \delta). - 3: (b) correct: the bounds kept ( orall \delta > 0, not \exists \delta \le 0), every quantifier switched, and the implication negated to a conjunction. - 2: (c) a witness x fixed before \delta, and a y given as a function of \delta that works for every \delta > 0 (any correct y, such as 1 -  rac12\min\{\delta, 1\} or 1 - \min\{\delta/2,  rac12\}, earns the points). - 3: (d) 2 for the case split proving L, with a \delta for each x; 1 for refuting the swap, with x and y depending on \delta. Fatal errors (0 for the step): a negation that keeps “	o”; in (c), y chosen before \delta or for one particular \delta; in the first half of (d), a single \delta claimed for all x. [P2: core] (20 minutes.) Here is a derivation of  egin{aligned} & orall z\, \exists y\, G(y, z),\  orall y\, \exists x\, F(x, y), \ & orall x\,  orall y\,  orall z\,  igl( (F(x, y) \wedge G(y, z)) 	o H(x, z)  igr) \vdash  orall z\, \exists x\, H(x, z), \end{aligned} with four justifications left blank, marked (i)–(iv). 1. Fill in the justifications (i)–(iv): the rule and the cited lines. 2. Explain why line 13 sits inside both of the boxes that begin at lines 5 and 7, and why each of these two boxes may close where it does. 3. Read F(x, y) as “f(x) = y”, G(y, z) as “g(y) = z” and H(x, z) as “g(f(x)) = z”, for functions f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon Y 	o Z. Write the plain-prose proof that this derivation encodes, that the composite of two surjections is surjective, with one sentence for each box. (a) (i) ulename{ orall E} 2, with the term y_0 for y. (ii) ulename{\exists I} 12, with the witness x_0 for x in H(x, z_0). (iii) ulename{\exists E} 6, 7–13: the existential of line 6 and the box of x_0. (iv) ulename{ orall I} 4–15: the flagged box of z_0, whose range runs from its first line, line 4, to its last line, line 15 (@fd1:def-rules-universal). (b) Line 12, H(x_0, z_0), contains the witness x_0. A box of ulename{\exists E} may close only on a last line in which its own name does not appear (@fd1:def-rules-existential). So the box of x_0 cannot close on line 12; the ulename{\exists I} of line 13 replaces x_0 by a bound variable first, and it must come before that box closes, that is, inside it, and therefore inside the box of y_0 that contains it. The box of x_0 closes at line 14. Its name x_0 does not appear in the last line \exists x\, H(x, z_0), nor in the existential \exists x\, F(x, y_0) of line 6, nor in the premises 1–3 (where only the bound variable x is written), nor in the one open assumption at line 14, G(y_0, z_0) on line 5. The box of y_0 closes at line 15. Its name y_0 does not appear in \exists x\, H(x, z_0), nor in \exists y\, G(y, z_0) of line 4, nor in the premises; the only box still open at line 15 is the flagged box of z_0, which has no assumption. Of the four clauses, the last-line clause is the one that shapes this derivation: the other three hold for any fresh names, while the last line had to be prepared by line 13. The names x_0 and y_0 may not leave their boxes because each names one witness, about which only its box’s assumption is known; outside, it would be treated as arbitrary, which is error (N3) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue. The name z_0 is different: it may appear in lines 14 and 15, because its box is closed by ulename{ orall I} at line 16, where it no longer appears. (c) Let f \colon X 	o Y and g \colon Y 	o Z be surjective, and let z \in Z be arbitrary (the box of z_0). Since g is surjective, there is y \in Y with g(y) = z; fix one (the box of y_0, lines 5–14, eliminating line 4). Since f is surjective, there is x \in X with f(x) = y; fix one (the box of x_0, lines 7–13, eliminating line 6). Then g(f(x)) = g(y) = z, so z is a value of g \circ f (lines 8–13; premise 3 is the substitution of equals that the equation chain performs). Since z was arbitrary, g \circ f is surjective, which is the surjectivity half of @thm-composition-injective-surjective. The derivation leaves the bounds z \in Z, y \in Y, x \in X implicit; the prose restores them. Marking scheme. (10 points) - 4: (a), one point per blank: the ulename{ orall E} with its line and instance term; the ulename{\exists I} with its line; the inner ulename{\exists E} citing line 6 and the box 7–13; the final ulename{ orall I} citing the box 4–15. - 2: (b) the fresh-name condition of ulename{\exists E} stated with all its clauses, in terms of where the name appears, for each box’s own name; and why x_0 and y_0 may not leave their boxes (so the \existsI must come first). - 4: (c) “let z \in Z”, “choose y with g(y) = z”, “choose x with f(x) = y”, “then g(f(x)) = z”, in this order, each sentence carrying its box. Fatal errors (0 for the step): “let x be arbitrary” for an ulename{\exists E}; prose in which y is chosen before z is fixed. [P3] (20 minutes.) For each argument below, answer three questions. Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, which line fails, which entry of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue does it fall under, and what is a counterexample to the illegal step (not merely to the conclusion)? 1. Claim: n^2 + n is even for every n \in 
N. Proof: 0^2 + 0 = 0 is even. Assume that n^2 + n is even for all n \in 
N. Then (n + 1)^2 + (n + 1) = (n^2 + n) + 2(n + 1) is even. By induction, the claim holds. 2. Claim: if A_n \subseteq 
R is bounded above for every n \in 
N, then  igcup_{n \in 
N} A_n is bounded above. Proof: For each n, let M_n be an upper bound of A_n. Let M be a number larger than every M_n. Then M is an upper bound of the union. (a) The conclusion is true. Let n \in 
N. By @thm-division-algorithm with divisor 2, n = 2q + r with q \in 
Z and r \in \{0, 1\}. If r = 0, then n^2 + n = n(n + 1) = 2 igl(q(n + 1) igr); if r = 1, then n + 1 = 2(q + 1) and n^2 + n = 2 igl(n(q + 1) igr). In both cases the factor in brackets is an integer (@prp-integers-closed), so 2 \mid n^2 + n (@def-divides). The argument does not prove it. The failing line is “Assume that n^2 + n is even for all n \in 
N”. That assumption is the claim itself, so everything after it is circular: entry (N9) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, citing a line that is not available, here the goal. The step of an induction is a ulename{{	o}I} box inside a ulename{ orall I} box: fix one arbitrary n \in 
N, assume that n^2 + n is even for this n, and derive that (n + 1)^2 + (n + 1) is even. With that one line changed, the rest of the argument is correct: the identity holds, since both sides equal n^2 + 3n + 2, and a sum of two even integers is even (2a + 2b = 2(a + b)). A counterexample to the illegal step. The argument infers  orall n\, P(n) from P(0) and from “if P(n) for all n, then P(n + 1) for all n”. Take P(n): “n = 0”. Then P(0) holds, and the second premise holds because its hypothesis “P(n) for all n” is false (P(1) fails), so the implication is vacuously true. Yet  orall n\, P(n) is false. The conclusion of (a) is true, so it has no counterexample; the step has one. (b) The conclusion is false. Take A_n \coloneqq \{n\}. Each A_n is bounded above, by n. The union is 
N, and 
N is not bounded above in 
R: for every real M there is a natural number larger than M (a school fact here; Analysis on the Real Line, Chapter 1 proves it from its axiom). The failing line is “Let M be a number larger than every M_n”. From “for every n there is a number larger than M_n” it passes to “there is a number larger than M_n for every n”: from  orall n\, \exists M to \exists M\,  orall n. This is entry (N2) of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue, a witness that depends on n presented as uniform. It is the converse of @fd1:prp-exists-forall-swap, and the converse is not even valid: @fd1:exm-counter-model-swap gives a counter-model. A counterexample to the step: M_n \coloneqq n. For each n there is a number larger than M_n, namely n + 1, and no real number is larger than every n. The line before it is not the error. Choosing an upper bound M_n for every n at once, with no rule, is a use of the axiom of choice (@ax-choice), and the book allows it, flagged. And for finitely many indices the bad line becomes correct: \max\{M_0, \dots, M_k\} + 1 exists by @prp-finite-max, so a union of finitely many sets bounded above is bounded above. Marking scheme. (10 points) - (a), 5 points. 1: says the conclusion is true, with a reason (a proof or a correct induction). 2: points to the line “assume … for all n”. 1: names the error, circularity, (N9). 1: gives a counterexample to the step, not to the conclusion. - (b), 5 points. 1: says the conclusion is false, with a witness such as A_n = \{n\}. 2: points to the line “let M be larger than every M_n”. 1: names the quantifier swap  orall n\, \exists M to \exists M\,  orall n, or (N2). 1: gives a counterexample to the step, not to the conclusion, such as M_n = n. Fatal errors (0 for the part): in (a), calling the argument correct; in (b), locating the error in the choice of the M_n. [P4: core] (20 minutes.) Let a_0 = 0, a_1 = 1 and a_{n+2} = 3a_{n+1} - 2a_n for n \in 
N. 1. Say which result guarantees that these equations define a sequence. 2. Prove that a_n = 2^n - 1 for every n \in 
N. 3. Suppose instead that a_1 = 2, with a_0 and the rule unchanged. Compute a_2 and a_3, and say exactly which line of your proof in (b) fails. (a) Two-step recursion, @cor-two-step-recursion, with X = 
R, a = 0, b = 1 and h(n, x, y) \coloneqq 3y - 2x: there is exactly one sequence (a_n)_{n \in 
N} of reals with a_0 = 0, a_1 = 1 and a_{n+2} = 3a_{n+1} - 2a_n for every n \in 
N. (b) The rule looks two steps back, so the induction carries two values at once. For n \in 
N let Q(n) be the statement a_n = 2^n - 1 \quad 	ext{and} \quad a_{n+1} = 2^{n+1} - 1 . Base case. Q(0) says a_0 = 2^0 - 1 = 0 and a_1 = 2^1 - 1 = 1, and both hold. Step. Let n \in 
N and suppose Q(n). The second half of Q(n) is the first half of Q(n + 1). For the second half, by the rule and both halves of Q(n),  egin{aligned} a_{n+2} &= 3a_{n+1} - 2a_n = 3(2^{n+1} - 1) - 2(2^n - 1) \ &= 3 \cdot 2^{n+1} - 2^{n+1} - 1 = 2 \cdot 2^{n+1} - 1 = 2^{n+2} - 1 , \end{aligned} where 2 \cdot 2^n = 2^{n+1} and 2 \cdot 2^{n+1} = 2^{n+2} by @def-power. So Q(n + 1) holds. By @fd1:ax-induction, Q(n) holds for every n \in 
N, and in particular a_n = 2^n - 1 for every n \in 
N. This is the pair induction of the two-step example in Section 2.3, after @def-power. Alternatively, by strong induction (@fd1:thm-strong-induction): let n \in 
N and suppose a_k = 2^k - 1 for every k < n. If n = 0 or n = 1, check the value directly. If n \ge 2, then n - 1 and n - 2 are natural numbers (@lem-naturals-arithmetic (c), twice) smaller than n, so the hypothesis applies to both, and the same computation with n - 2 in place of n gives a_n = 2^n - 1. The two values n = 0, 1 are exactly where the hypothesis would be used out of range. (c) Now a_2 = 3 \cdot 2 - 2 \cdot 0 = 6 and a_3 = 3 \cdot 6 - 2 \cdot 2 = 14, while 2^2 - 1 = 3 and 2^3 - 1 = 7. The failing line is the base case at n = 1: in the proof of (b), the half “a_1 = 2^1 - 1” of Q(0), since now a_1 = 2

(The same induction proves a_n = 2^{n+1} - 2 for the new sequence.) Marking scheme. title: Definition 1.1.4 (Empty Set)
content: An empty set is a set with no elements: a set \(E\) such that \(\forall x\, (x \notin E)\) .

title: Definition 1.1.3 (Specification)
content: Let \(A\) be a set and \(P(x)\) a property of objects \(x\) . Then there is a set, written \[ \{ x \in A : P(x) \}, \] whose elements are exactly the elements of \(A\) that have the property \(P\) : for every \(y\) , \[ y \in \{ x \in A : P(x) \} \iff y \in A \text{ and } P(y). \]

title: Definition 1.1.1 (Equality of Sets)
content: Sets \(A\) and \(B\) are equal, \(A = B\) , if and only if they have the same elements: \[ \forall x\, (x \in A \leftrightarrow x \in B). \]

title: Definition 1.1.2 (Subset)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. \(A\) is a subset of \(B\) , written \(A \subseteq B\) , if every element of \(A\) is an element of \(B\) : \[ \forall x\, (x \in A \to x \in B). \] We also say that \(A\) is contained in \(B\) , or that \(B\) contains \(A\) . If \(A \subseteq B\) and \(A \ne B\) , then \(A\) is a proper subset of \(B\) , written \(A \subsetneq B\) .

title: Example (Computing sets given by a property)
content: Show that \(\{ x \in \nZ : x^2 < 5 \} = \{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2\}\) . Show that \(\{ x \in \nR : x^2 < 0 \} = \emptyset\) .

title: Example (Three inclusions)
content: Show that \([1, 2] \subseteq [0, 3]\) . Let \(S\) be the set of integer multiples of \(6\) and \(T\) the set of integer multiples of \(3\) , as above. Show that \(S \subseteq T\) . Here \(d \mid n\) , “ \(d\) divides \(n\) ”, means that \(n = dk\) for some integer \(k\) , so \(S\) consists of the integers \(x\) with \(6 \mid x\) , and \(T\) of those with \(3 \mid x\) . Let \(A\) be any set. Show that \(A \subseteq A\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Negate “ \(A \subseteq B\) ” in symbols, and then in words, with the negation pushed through the quantifier and the implication. True or false: \(\{1\} \in \{\{1\}, 2\}\) ; \(\{1\} \subseteq \{\{1\}, 2\}\) ; \(\emptyset \subseteq \emptyset\) ; \(\{\emptyset\} \subseteq \{1\}\) . Give a reason for each. List the elements of \(\{ n \in \nZ : 0 < n^2 \le 9 \}\) . In an element-chasing proof of \(A \subseteq B\) , the first sentence is “let \(x \in A\) ”. Which rule of logic gives its first clause, and which its second?

title: Exercise (B1: A set given by an equation)
content: Prove that \(\{ x \in \nR : x^2 - 3x + 2 = 0 \} = \{1, 2\}\) , by two inclusions.

title: Exercise (B2: A subset of the empty set)
content: Let \(A\) be a set with \(A \subseteq \emptyset\) . Prove that \(A = \emptyset\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Equal or not?)
content:
For each pair, determine whether the two sets are equal. Justify your answer: prove each equality, and give a witness element for each inequality. \(\{ x \in 
Z : 4 \mid x \}\) and \(\{ x \in 
Z : 2 \mid x \}\) . \(\{ x \in 
R : x^2 = 4 \}\) and \(\{-2, 2\}\) . \(\{\emptyset, \{\emptyset\}\}\) and \(\{\{\emptyset\}, \emptyset, \emptyset\}\) . \(\{ x \in 
Z : x^2 < 2 \}\) and \(\{ x \in 
N : x < 2 \}\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Every set has something outside it)
content: Let \(A\) be a set, and let \(R_A = \{ x \in A : x \notin x \}\) as in @thm-russell . Let \(A^{+}\) be the set whose elements are the elements of \(A\) together with the object \(R_A\) (it exists by (W2) and (W3)). Show that \(A \subsetneq A^{+}\) . Deduce from @thm-russell that no set \(A\) has the property “every subset of \(A\) is an element of \(A\) ”.

title: Exercise (C2: Antisymmetry for sets of sets)
content: Can there be sets \(A\) and \(B\) , whose elements are themselves sets, such that \(A \subseteq B\) , \(B \subseteq A\) , and \(A \ne B\) ? Explain why the answer does not depend on what the elements of \(A\) and \(B\) are.

title: Proposition 1.1.3 (The Empty Set Is Unique)
content: If \(E\) and \(E'\) are empty sets, then \(E = E'\) .

title: Proposition 1.1.1 (Equality Is Two Inclusions)
content: For all sets \(A\) and \(B\) , \(A = B\) if and only if \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq A\) .

title: Proposition 1.1.2 (Inclusion Is Transitive)
content: For all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , and \(C\) , if \(A \subseteq B\) and \(B \subseteq C\) , then \(A \subseteq C\) .

title: Theorem 1.1.4 (Russell’s Theorem)
content: For every set \(A\) , the set \(R_A = \{ x \in A : x \notin x \}\) is not an element of \(A\) . Hence there is no set of which every set is an element.

title: Definition 1.2.4 (Union and Intersection of a Family)
content: Let \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of sets. The union \(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\) is the set whose elements are exactly the objects lying in \(A_i\) for some \(i \in I\) : \[ x \in \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i \iff \exists i \in I\ (x \in A_i). \] If \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) is a family of subsets of a set \(X\) , the intersection is \[ \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i \coloneqq \{ x \in X : \forall i \in I\ (x \in A_i) \} . \] For a set \(\sS\) whose elements are sets, \(\bigcup \sS \coloneqq \bigcup_{A \in \sS} A\) ; and for a non-empty set \(\sS \subseteq \powerset{X}\) , \(\bigcap \sS \coloneqq \bigcap_{A \in \sS} A\) . In both, the family is indexed by \(\sS\) itself, the member with index \(A\) being \(A\) .

title: Definition 1.2.3 (Indexed Family)
content: Let \(I\) be a set. A family of sets indexed by \(I\) , written \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) , assigns to each \(i \in I\) a set \(A_i\) . The set \(I\) is the index set , and \(A_i\) is the member of the family with index \(i\) . If \(X\) is a set with \(A_i \subseteq X\) for every \(i \in I\) , we speak of a family of subsets of \(X\) .

title: Definition 1.2.2 (Power Set)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. The power set of \(X\) is the set \(\powerset{X}\) whose elements are exactly the subsets of \(X\) : \[ S \in \powerset{X} \iff S \subseteq X . \]

title: Definition 1.2.1 (Union, Intersection, Difference)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. The union \(A \cup B\) is the set whose elements are exactly the objects lying in \(A\) or in \(B\) : \(x \in A \cup B \iff (x \in A \vee x \in B)\) . The intersection \(A \cap B\) is the set \(\{ x \in A : x \in B \}\) : so \(x \in A \cap B \iff (x \in A \wedge x \in B)\) . The difference \(A \setminus B\) is the set \(\{ x \in A : x \notin B \}\) : so \(x \in A \setminus B \iff (x \in A \wedge x \notin B)\) . Sets \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint if \(A \cap B = \emptyset\) . If \(A \subseteq X\) , the difference \(X \setminus A\) is called the complement of \(A\) in \(X\) .

title: Example (Unions and intersections of intervals)
content: Show that: \(\bigcup_{t \in (0, 1)} [t, 1] = (0, 1]\) ; \(\bigcap_{t \in (0, \infty)} (-t, t) = \{0\}\) , inside \(X = \nR\) ; \(\bigcap_{t \in (0, \infty)} (0, t) = \emptyset\) , inside \(X = \nR\) .

title: Example (Small power sets)
content: Compute \(\powerset{\emptyset}\) , \(\powerset{\{\emptyset\}}\) , and \(\powerset{\{1, 2\}}\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: These parts are about @thm-de-morgan-families and its proof. Which law of Logic and Proof , Chapter 4 is used in the \((\subseteq)\) half of the second law, and which of its directions is classical? Run the first law on \(X = \nZ\) , \(I = \{2, 3\}\) , and \(A_i\) the set of integer multiples of \(i\) . Describe both sides in words, and name two integers in each side and two outside it. What are the two sides of each law when \(I = \emptyset\) ? Let \(x \in X\) . Translate \(x \notin \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i\) into a statement with \(\exists\) . What is the correct translation if \(x \in X\) is not assumed?

title: Exercise (B1: Intersection and difference)
content: Prove that \(A \cap (B \setminus C) = (A \cap B) \setminus (A \cap C)\) for all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) , and name the propositional equivalence behind it.

title: Exercise (B2: Three families of intervals)
content: For each family, indexed by \(t \in (0, \infty)\) , compute the union and the intersection (inside \(X = \nR\) ), and prove each answer by two inclusions. \(A_t = [t, 1 + t]\) ; \(B_t = (-t, 1/t)\) ; \(C_t = (t, 2t)\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Canceling a union)
content: Give sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) with \(A \cup B = A \cup C\) and \(B \ne C\) . Then list the properties that any correct answer must have, so that a different answer can be checked against them.

title: Exercise (C1: Power sets and operations)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Decide whether \(\powerset{A \setminus B} = \powerset{A} \setminus \powerset{B}\) can hold. Then prove that every non-empty element of \(\powerset{A \setminus B}\) lies in \(\powerset{A} \setminus \powerset{B}\) . Show by an example that \(\powerset{A} \cup \powerset{B} = \powerset{A \cup B}\) can fail. Then prove that it holds if and only if \(A \subseteq B\) or \(B \subseteq A\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: Here is a “proof” that \((A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C) \subseteq A \cup (B \cap C)\) for all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) . Let \(x \in (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)\) . (2) Then \(x \in A \cup B\) and \(x \in A \cup C\) . (3) We consider two cases, according to \(x \in A \cup B\) . (4) Case \(x \in A\) . Then \(x \in A \cup (B \cap C)\) . (5) Case \(x \in B\) . Since \(x \in A \cup C\) , \(x \in C\) . (6) So \(x \in B \cap C\) , and hence \(x \in A \cup (B \cap C)\) . (7) In both cases \(x \in A \cup (B \cap C)\) , which proves the inclusion. Is the conclusion true? Which line fails, which rule does it break, and which entry of the catalogue of Logic and Proof , Chapter 5 does it commit? Give a counterexample to the illegal step itself: sets and an element for which the line’s premise holds and its conclusion fails. Repair the proof.

title: Proposition 1.2.2 (Smallest Closed Set)
content: Let \(X\) be a set with given starting elements and steps, and let \(\sS \subseteq \powerset{X}\) be the set of closed subsets of \(X\) . Then \(\sS\) is non-empty, and \(M \coloneqq \bigcap \sS\) is closed and lies inside every closed set: \(M\) is the smallest closed subset of \(X\) .

title: Theorem 1.2.3 (De Morgan’s Laws for Families)
content: Let \(X\) be a set and \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) a family of subsets of \(X\) , with any index set \(I\) , including \(I = \emptyset\) . Then \[ X \setminus \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcap_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) \quad\text{and}\quad X \setminus \bigcap_{i \in I} A_i = \bigcup_{i \in I} (X \setminus A_i) . \]

title: Theorem 1.2.1 (Algebra of Sets)
content: For all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , and \(C\) : (commutativity) \(A \cup B = B \cup A\) and \(A \cap B = B \cap A\) ; (associativity) \((A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)\) and \((A \cap B) \cap C = A \cap (B \cap C)\) ; (distributivity) \(A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)\) and \(A \cup (B \cap C) = (A \cup B) \cap (A \cup C)\) ; (differences) \(A \setminus (B \cup C) = (A \setminus B) \cap (A \setminus C)\) and \(A \setminus (B \cap C) = (A \setminus B) \cup (A \setminus C)\) .

title: Definition 1.3.2 (Cartesian product)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Their Cartesian product is the set \[ A \times B \coloneqq \{ (a, b) : a \in A, \ b \in B \} \] of all ordered pairs with first coordinate in \(A\) and second coordinate in \(B\) . Written out, an object \(p\) is an element of \(A \times B\) if and only if \[ \exists a \in A \ \exists b \in B \ \ p = (a, b) . \] For a set \(X\) we write \(X^2 \coloneqq X \times X\) , and, for \(n \in \nN\) with \(n \ge 2\) , \(X^n\) is the set of all \(n\) -tuples \((x_1, \dots, x_n)\) with every \(x_k \in X\) .

title: Definition 1.3.1 (Ordered pair)
content: For any objects \(a\) and \(b\) there is an object \((a, b)\) , the ordered pair of \(a\) and \(b\) ; we call \(a\) its first coordinate and \(b\) its second coordinate . Ordered pairs have the characteristic property : for all \(a, b, c, d\) , \[ (a, b) = (c, d) \iff a = c \text{ and } b = d . \]

title: Definition 1.3.3 (Relation)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. A relation from \(A\) to \(B\) is a subset \(R \subseteq A \times B\) . For \(a \in A\) and \(b \in B\) we write \(a \mathrel{R} b\) , read “ \(a\) is \(R\) -related to \(b\) ”, to mean \((a, b) \in R\) . A relation on \(A\) is a relation from \(A\) to \(A\) , that is, a subset of \(A^2\) . The domain of \(R\) is the set of first coordinates that occur, \(\{ a \in A : \exists b \in B \ \ a \mathrel{R} b \}\) , and its range is the set of second coordinates that occur, \(\{ b \in B : \exists a \in A \ \ a \mathrel{R} b \}\) . Turning every pair of \(R\) around gives a relation from \(B\) to \(A\) , the inverse relation \[ R^{-1} \coloneqq \{ (b, a) \in B \times A : (a, b) \in R \} . \]

title: Example (Solving an equation between pairs)
content: Find all real numbers \(x\) and \(y\) with \((x + y, x - y) = (3, 1)\) . Then decide whether \((1, 2) = (2, 1)\) and whether \((1, 1) = (1, 1)\) .

title: Example (Relations as sets of pairs)
content: Write each relation as a set, and find its domain and range. The relation \(<\) on \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) . Divisibility on \(\{1, \dots, 6\}\) : \(a \mathrel{D} b\) when \(a \mid b\) . The unit circle, as a relation on \(\nR\) . The graph of squaring, as a relation on \(\nR\) . The two extreme relations from \(A\) to \(B\) : \(\emptyset\) and \(A \times B\) .

title: Example (Products, small and large)
content: Let \(a, b, c\) be three different objects, none of them a number. List \(\{1, 2\} \times \{a, b, c\}\) and \(\{a, b, c\} \times \{1, 2\}\) . Describe \(\nR^2\) and \([0, 1] \times [0, 1]\) as sets of points of the plane. What is \(\{1, 2\} \times \emptyset\) ?

title: Exercise (A1)
content: Define \(A \times B\) in symbols, with its membership condition written out using quantifiers. Is \(((1, 2), 3) = (1, (2, 3))\) ? Justify your answer. Write the inverse of the relation \(<\) on \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) as a set of pairs. Is \(\emptyset\) a relation on every set \(A\) ? Justify your answer.

title: Exercise (B1: An L-shaped region)
content: Let \(E \coloneqq ([0, 1] \times [0, 2]) \cup ([1, 2] \times [0, 1])\) . Describe \(E\) as a region of the plane. Then use @prp-product-set-laws to write \(E\) as \(([0, 2] \times [0, 1]) \cup (P \times Q)\) for intervals \(P\) and \(Q\) , and prove the equality.

title: Exercise (B2: The intersection law, written with two pairs)
content: Here is a proof of the inclusion \((\supseteq)\) of \(A \times (B \cap C) = (A \times B) \cap (A \times C)\) that works from the definition of the product and the characteristic property directly, without the shortcut \((\ast)\) . Its last sentence is blank. Name the move, then complete it. Let \(p \in (A \times B) \cap (A \times C)\) . Since \(p \in A \times B\) , there are \(a \in A\) and \(b \in B\) with \(p = (a, b)\) . Since \(p \in A \times C\) , there are \(a' \in A\) and \(c \in C\) with \(p = (a', c)\) ; the names \(a'\) and \(c\) are new, because nothing says that this second pair of coordinates is the first one again. Hence \((a, b) = (a', c)\) . \(\underline{\hspace{8em}}\)

title: Exercise (B3: Two products crossed)
content: Prove that \((A \times B) \cap (B \times A) = (A \cap B) \times (A \cap B)\) for all sets \(A\) and \(B\) .

title: Exercise (C1: The square of a union)
content: Determine whether \((A \cup B) \times (A \cup B) = (A \times A) \cup (B \times B)\) for all sets \(A\) and \(B\) . Justify your answer. Prove the inclusion \((A \times A) \cup (B \times B) \subseteq (A \cup B) \times (A \cup B)\) . Prove, from @prp-product-set-laws , that \[ (A \cup B) \times (A \cup B) = (A \times A) \cup (A \times B) \cup (B \times A) \cup (B \times B) . \]

title: Exercise (C2: When one inclusion forces equality)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. Prove that \(A \times B \subseteq B \times A\) if and only if \(A = B\) or \(A = \emptyset\) or \(B = \emptyset\) .

title: Proposition 1.3.1 (Products and Set Operations)
content: For all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) : \[ \begin{aligned} A \times (B \cup C) &= (A \times B) \cup (A \times C), \\ A \times (B \cap C) &= (A \times B) \cap (A \times C), \\ A \times (B \setminus C) &= (A \times B) \setminus (A \times C), \\ A \times \emptyset &= \emptyset, \end{aligned} \] and the mirror-image laws, with the varying factor on the left: \[ \begin{aligned} (B \cup C) \times A &= (B \times A) \cup (C \times A), \\ (B \cap C) \times A &= (B \times A) \cap (C \times A), \\ (B \setminus C) \times A &= (B \times A) \setminus (C \times A), \\ \emptyset \times A &= \emptyset . \end{aligned} \]

title: Definition 1.4.5 (Bijective)
content: A function is bijective (a bijection ) if it is both injective and surjective.

title: Definition 1.4.2 (Composition)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions, the codomain of \(f\) being the domain of \(g\) . Their composite is the function \[ g \circ f \colon X \to Z, \qquad (g \circ f)(x) \coloneqq g(f(x)) , \] read “ \(g\) after \(f\) ”.

title: Definition 1.4.1 (Function)
content: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be sets. A function from \(X\) to \(Y\) , written \(f \colon X \to Y\) , is given by a relation \(G \subseteq X \times Y\) , the graph of \(f\) , such that \[ \text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is exactly one } y \in Y \text{ with } (x, y) \in G , \] together with the set \(Y\) , the codomain of \(f\) . Formally, \(f\) is the pair \((G, Y)\) . The set \(X\) is the domain of \(f\) . For \(x \in X\) , the unique \(y\) with \((x, y) \in G\) is written \(f(x)\) , the value of \(f\) at \(x\) . We write \((x, y) \in f\) for \((x, y) \in G\) , and \(x \mapsto f(x)\) for the whole function when its domain and codomain are clear. In symbols, the condition on the graph is \[ \forall x \in X \ \ \exists! \, y \in Y \ \ (x, y) \in G , \] where, as with the bounded quantifiers of @fd1:def-bounded-quantifier , \(\exists! \, y \in Y \ \psi\) abbreviates \(\exists! \, y \, (y \in Y \wedge \psi)\) .

title: Definition 1.4.3 (Injective)
content: A function \(f \colon X \to Y\) is injective (an injection , or one-to-one ) if, for all \(x_1, x_2 \in X\) , \(f(x_1) = f(x_2)\) implies \(x_1 = x_2\) . In symbols: \[ \forall x_1 \in X \ \ \forall x_2 \in X \ \ \bigl( f(x_1) = f(x_2) \to x_1 = x_2 \bigr) . \]

title: Definition 1.4.4 (Surjective)
content: A function \(f \colon X \to Y\) is surjective (a surjection , or onto ) if, for every \(y \in Y\) , there exists \(x \in X\) with \(f(x) = y\) . In symbols: \[ \forall y \in Y \ \ \exists x \in X \ \ f(x) = y . \]

title: Exercise (B2: Put the proof in order)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions. The following lines contain a proof that if \(g \circ f\) is surjective, then \(g\) is surjective , shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the six correct lines in an order that makes a proof, and say why each of the other two lines fails. Then \(g(y) = g(f(x)) = (g \circ f)(x) = z\) , by @def-composition . Let \(y \in Y\) . Since \(g \circ f\) is surjective, there is \(x \in X\) with \((g \circ f)(x) = z\) . Since \(z\) was arbitrary, \(g\) is surjective. Let \(y \coloneqq f(x)\) , an element of \(Y\) . Since \(f\) is surjective, \(y = f(x)\) for some \(x \in X\) . Let \(z \in Z\) . So \(z\) has a preimage under \(g\) , namely \(y\) .

title: Exercise (B3: Examples on the natural numbers)
content: Give an example of a function \(\nN \to \nN\) that is surjective and not injective, and one that is injective and not surjective. Check each property.

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: composites)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions. Prove that if \(g \circ f\) is injective, then \(f\) is injective. Give an example in which \(g \circ f\) is injective and \(g\) is not injective, and check both claims.

title: Exercise (C2: When the composite is a bijection)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions. Deduce from @exr-functions-c1 and @exr-functions-b2 that if \(g \circ f\) is bijective, then \(f\) is injective and \(g\) is surjective. Give an example in which \(g \circ f\) is bijective and neither \(f\) nor \(g\) is bijective.

title: Proposition 1.4.3 (Composition Is Associative)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) , \(g \colon Y \to Z\) , and \(h \colon Z \to W\) be functions. Then \[ h \circ (g \circ f) = (h \circ g) \circ f , \] and \(f \circ \id_X = f = \id_Y \circ f\) .

title: Proposition 1.4.2 (Functions and the Empty Set)
content: For every set \(Y\) there is exactly one function from \(\emptyset\) to \(Y\) : the pair \((\emptyset, Y)\) , called the empty function . If \(X\) is nonempty (it has an element), there is no function from \(X\) to \(\emptyset\) .

title: Proposition 1.4.1 (Equality of Functions)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon X' \to Y'\) be functions. Then \(f = g\) if and only if \(X = X'\) , \(Y = Y'\) , and \(f(x) = g(x)\) for every \(x \in X\) .

title: Theorem 1.4.4 (Composites of Injections and Surjections)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions. If \(f\) and \(g\) are injective, then \(g \circ f\) is injective. If \(f\) and \(g\) are surjective, then \(g \circ f\) is surjective. If \(f\) and \(g\) are bijective, then \(g \circ f\) is bijective.

title: Definition 1.5.2 (Inverse Function)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. A function \(g \colon Y \to X\) is a two-sided inverse , or an inverse , of \(f\) if it is both a left inverse and a right inverse of \(f\) : \[ g \circ f = \id_X \quad\text{and}\quad f \circ g = \id_Y . \] A function with an inverse is invertible . Its inverse is unique : if \(g\) and \(g'\) are both inverses of \(f\) , then \(g\) is a left inverse and \(g'\) a right inverse, so \(g = g'\) by @prp-inverse-unique . We call it the inverse of \(f\) and write it \(f^{-1} \colon Y \to X\) .

title: Definition 1.5.1 (Left and Right Inverses)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function, and let \(g \colon Y \to X\) be a function in the opposite direction. \(g\) is a left inverse of \(f\) if \(g \circ f = \id_X\) , that is, \(g(f(x)) = x\) for every \(x \in X\) . \(g\) is a right inverse of \(f\) if \(f \circ g = \id_Y\) , that is, \(f(g(y)) = y\) for every \(y \in Y\) .

title: Example (Running the construction)
content: Let \(f \colon \{1, 2\} \to \{a, b, c\}\) be given by \(f(1) = a\) and \(f(2) = c\) , where \(a\) , \(b\) , \(c\) are three different objects. Run the proof of @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective (b) with \(x_0 = 1\) , then with \(x_0 = 2\) . How many left inverses does \(f\) have?

title: Example (Left inverses on small sets)
content: Let \(X = \{1, 2\}\) , \(Y = \{1, 2, 3\}\) , and \(e \colon X \to Y\) , \(e(1) = 1\) , \(e(2) = 2\) : the inclusion of \(X\) into \(Y\) . Show that \(g \colon Y \to X\) with \(g(1) = 1\) , \(g(2) = 2\) , \(g(3) = 2\) is a left inverse of \(e\) , and that \(e\) is a right inverse of \(g\) . Is \(g\) a right inverse of \(e\) ? Let \(c \colon X \to Y\) be constant, \(c(1) = c(2) = 3\) . Does \(c\) have a left inverse?

title: Example (All right inverses of a small surjection)
content: Let \(q \colon \{1, 2, 3, 4\} \to \{0, 1\}\) send each number to \(0\) if it is even and to \(1\) if it is odd: \(q(1) = 1\) , \(q(2) = 0\) , \(q(3) = 1\) , \(q(4) = 0\) . Find all right inverses of \(q\) .

title: Exercise (A1)
content: These parts are about @thm-left-inverse-iff-injective and its proof. At which line of the proof of (b) is \(X \ne \emptyset\) used, and for what? The proof shows that the set \(G\) is a function by proving two things about the case split into \(y \in f(X)\) and \(y \notin f(X)\) . What are they, and which step of the proof uses each? Run the construction on \(f \colon \{1, 2, 3\} \to \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) , \(f(k) = k + 1\) , with \(x_0 = 3\) . Write out the left inverse \(g\) and check \(g \circ f = \id_{\{1, 2, 3\}}\) . Give the idea of the proof of (b) in two sentences. Let \(f \colon \{1, 2\} \to \{1\}\) be the only function between these sets. Which step of the proof of (b) fails for \(f\) , and why?

title: Exercise (B1: Counting one-sided inverses)
content: Find all left inverses of \(f \colon \{1, 2\} \to \{1, 2, 3\}\) , \(f(k) = k\) . Find all right inverses of \(g \colon \{1, 2, 3\} \to \{1, 2\}\) , \(g(1) = g(2) = 1\) , \(g(3) = 2\) .

title: Exercise (B2: The inverse of a composite)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be bijections. Prove that \(g \circ f\) is invertible and that \((g \circ f)^{-1} = f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}\) . Hint: check the two equations of @def-inverse-function for the candidate \(f^{-1} \circ g^{-1}\) .

title: Exercise (B3: A bijection between an interval and the line)
content: Let \(h \colon (-1, 1) \to \nR\) , \(h(x) = x/(1 - \abs{x})\) , and \(k \colon \nR \to (-1, 1)\) , \(k(y) = y/(1 + \abs{y})\) . Show that \(h\) and \(k\) are well defined (each denominator is non-zero, and \(k\) takes values in \((-1, 1)\) ), and that \(k\) is the inverse of \(h\) , by checking both composites by cases on the sign. Hence \(h\) is a bijection.

title: Exercise (C1: One composite equal to the identity)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to X\) be functions with \(g \circ f = \id_X\) . Prove that \(f\) is injective and \(g\) is surjective. Show by an example that neither \(f\) nor \(g\) need be bijective. Prove that if, in addition, \(f\) is surjective, then \(g = f^{-1}\) .

title: Exercise (C2: When is a left inverse unique?)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be injective, with \(X \ne \emptyset\) . Prove that if \(f\) is surjective, or \(X\) has exactly one element, then \(f\) has exactly one left inverse. Prove that if some \(y_1 \in Y\) is not in \(f(X)\) , and \(X\) has two different elements \(x_0 \ne x_1\) , then \(f\) has at least two different left inverses. Let \(f \colon \{1, 2\} \to \{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) , \(f(k) = 2k\) . List all left inverses of \(f\) , and explain in one sentence why there are \(2^2 = 4\) of them.

title: Proposition 1.5.3 (Left and Right Inverses Agree)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. If \(g \colon Y \to X\) is a left inverse of \(f\) and \(h \colon Y \to X\) is a right inverse of \(f\) , then \(g = h\) .

title: Proposition 1.5.2 (Right Inverses Give Surjectivity)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. If \(f\) has a right inverse, then \(f\) is surjective.

title: Theorem 1.5.4 (Bijections Are the Invertible Functions)
content: A function \(f \colon X \to Y\) is bijective if and only if it has a two-sided inverse.

title: Theorem 1.5.1 (Left Inverses and Injectivity)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. If \(f\) has a left inverse, then \(f\) is injective. If \(X \ne \emptyset\) and \(f\) is injective, then \(f\) has a left inverse. Consequently, if \(X \ne \emptyset\) , then \(f\) has a left inverse if and only if \(f\) is injective.

title: Definition 1.6.1 (Image)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function and \(A \subseteq X\) . The image of \(A\) under \(f\) is the set \[ f(A) \coloneqq \{ y \in Y : \text{there exists } a \in A \text{ with } f(a) = y \}. \] We also write it \(\{ f(a) : a \in A \}\) . In symbols, for every \(y\) , \[ y \in f(A) \iff y \in Y \wedge \exists a \in A\ \, f(a) = y . \]

title: Definition 1.6.2 (Preimage)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function and \(B \subseteq Y\) . The preimage of \(B\) under \(f\) , also called its inverse image , is the set \[ f^{-1}(B) \coloneqq \{ x \in X : f(x) \in B \}. \] In symbols, for every \(x\) , \(x \in f^{-1}(B) \iff x \in X \wedge f(x) \in B\) . The preimage is defined for every function \(f\) , whether or not \(f\) has an inverse.

title: Example (Two witnesses under one name)
content: Here is a “proof” that \(f(A) \cap f(B) \subseteq f(A \cap B)\) for every function \(f \colon X \to Y\) and all \(A, B \subseteq X\) . Let \(y \in f(A) \cap f(B)\) . (2) Then \(y \in f(A)\) , so \(y = f(x)\) for some \(x \in A\) . (3) Also \(y \in f(B)\) , so \(y = f(x)\) for some \(x \in B\) . (4) Hence \(x \in A\) and \(x \in B\) , so \(x \in A \cap B\) . (5) Therefore \(y = f(x) \in f(A \cap B)\) . Show that the conclusion is false, and find the line that fails.

title: Exercise (B2: Two laws, element by element)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. Prove each law directly, by two inclusions or by a chain of equivalences at a point, tagging each step that names or exhibits a witness with \([\rulename{\exists E}]\) or \([\rulename{\exists I}]\) . \(f(A \cup B) = f(A) \cup f(B)\) for \(A, B \subseteq X\) . (This is a case of @thm-image-union ; prove it without citing it.) \(f^{-1}(C \setminus D) = f^{-1}(C) \setminus f^{-1}(D)\) for \(C, D \subseteq Y\) . (This is @thm-preimage-operations (d); prove it without citing it.) Which steps, if any, need a tag?

title: Exercise (B3: The two readings of the inverse)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a bijection, with inverse function \(f^{-1} \colon Y \to X\) , and let \(B \subseteq Y\) . Prove that the image of \(B\) under the function \(f^{-1}\) equals the preimage of \(B\) under \(f\) . To keep the readings apart, write \(g \coloneqq f^{-1}\) for the inverse function, and prove \(g(B) = \{ x \in X : f(x) \in B \}\) . The remark in “Two readings of the inverse symbol” gives the argument in brief; write it out as two inclusions, tagging each step that names or exhibits a witness with \([\rulename{\exists E}]\) or \([\rulename{\exists I}]\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Images and differences)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function and \(A, B \subseteq X\) . Here are the first lines of a proof that \(f(A) \setminus f(B) \subseteq f(A \setminus B)\) . Name the move, then complete it. Let \(y \in f(A) \setminus f(B)\) . Then \(y \in f(A)\) , so there is \(a \in A\) with \(f(a) = y\) ; name it \(a\) \([\rulename{\exists E}]\) . Also \(y \notin f(B)\) . Show that the reverse inclusion can fail, with \(f(x) = x^2\) on \(\nR\) , \(A = \{-1, 1\}\) , and \(B = \{1\}\) . Prove that \(f(A \setminus B) = f(A) \setminus f(B)\) holds for all \(A, B \subseteq X\) if and only if \(f\) is injective.

title: Exercise (C2: Find the error)
content: A student proves the following claim: if \(f \colon X \to Y\) is injective and \(A \subseteq X\) , then \(f^{-1}(f(A)) \subseteq A\) . Let \(x \in f^{-1}(f(A))\) . (2) By the definition of preimage, \(x \in X\) and \(f(x) \in f(A)\) . (3) Since \(f(x) \in f(A)\) , we have \(x \in A\) . (4) Since \(x\) was arbitrary, \(f^{-1}(f(A)) \subseteq A\) . Is the claim true? Which line fails, and which rule does it skip? Give a counterexample to the failing step, and repair the proof.

title: Exercise (C3: Exit check: preimages)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function and \((B_i)_{i \in I}\) a family of subsets of \(Y\) . Prove that \(f^{-1}(\bigcap_{i \in I} B_i) = \bigcap_{i \in I} f^{-1}(B_i)\) , the intersections taken in \(Y\) and in \(X\) . Give a function \(f\) and sets \(A, B\) with \(f(A \cap B) \ne f(A) \cap f(B)\) , computing both sides.

title: Exercise (R1)
content: Here is a derivation of “if \(A \subseteq B\) , then \(\powerset{A} \subseteq \powerset{B}\) ”. The steps “by def.” unwind or rewind @def-subset and @def-power-set . Write the proof as plain prose, the way a mathematician would. Then say which sentence of your proof carries each of the five boxes.

title: Exercise (R2)
content: Decide whether \(A \setminus (B \setminus C) = (A \setminus B) \setminus C\) for all sets \(A, B, C\) , by a table of the eight possible memberships of a point \(x\) in \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) . If the two sides can differ, turn a row where they differ into a counterexample.

title: Exercise (R3)
content: Derive \((P \wedge \neg Q) \to R \vdash P \to (Q \vee R)\) . Then read the derivation as a proof that for sets \(A, B, C\) , if \(A \setminus B \subseteq C\) , then \(A \subseteq B \cup C\) . Which step is classical?

title: Exercise (R4)
content: Show that there is no set that contains every singleton \(\{x\}\) as an element.

title: Proposition 1.6.5 (Image and Preimage Round Trips)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. \(A \subseteq f^{-1}(f(A))\) for every \(A \subseteq X\) . Equality holds for all \(A \subseteq X\) if and only if \(f\) is injective. \(f(f^{-1}(B)) = B \cap f(X)\) for every \(B \subseteq Y\) ; in particular \(f(f^{-1}(B)) \subseteq B\) . Equality \(f(f^{-1}(B)) = B\) holds for all \(B \subseteq Y\) if and only if \(f\) is surjective.

title: Proposition 1.6.2 (Preimage under a Composite)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) be functions, and \(C \subseteq Z\) . Then \[ (g \circ f)^{-1}(C) = f^{-1}\bigl(g^{-1}(C)\bigr). \]

title: Theorem 1.6.4 (Image of an Intersection)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. For all \(A, B \subseteq X\) , \(f(A \cap B) \subseteq f(A) \cap f(B)\) . The equality \(f(A \cap B) = f(A) \cap f(B)\) holds for all \(A, B \subseteq X\) if and only if \(f\) is injective.

title: Theorem 1.6.3 (Image of a Union)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function, and let \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of subsets of \(X\) . Then \[ f\Bigl(\bigcup_{i \in I} A_i\Bigr) = \bigcup_{i \in I} f(A_i). \]

title: Theorem 1.6.1 (Preimages of Set Operations)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. For every family \((B_i)_{i \in I}\) of subsets of \(Y\) , \(\displaystyle f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcup_{i \in I} B_i\Bigr) = \bigcup_{i \in I} f^{-1}(B_i)\) . For every family \((B_i)_{i \in I}\) of subsets of \(Y\) , \(\displaystyle f^{-1}\Bigl(\bigcap_{i \in I} B_i\Bigr) = \bigcap_{i \in I} f^{-1}(B_i)\) , the intersection on the left taken in \(Y\) and on the right in \(X\) . For every \(B \subseteq Y\) , \(f^{-1}(Y \setminus B) = X \setminus f^{-1}(B)\) . For all \(B, C \subseteq Y\) , \(f^{-1}(B \setminus C) = f^{-1}(B) \setminus f^{-1}(C)\) .

title: Corollary 2.1.5 (Well-Ordering of Sets of Integers)
content:
Let \(S \subseteq

title: Example (An induction that ignores its hypothesis)
content: Logic and Proof , Chapter 3, after its first worked induction ( @fd1:exm-sum-consecutive-products ), said: “A proof by induction that never uses its induction hypothesis is either not an induction or is hiding a gap.” The proof of @lem-naturals-arithmetic (c) never uses its induction hypothesis. Is it an induction, and is it hiding a gap?

title: Theorem 2.1.4 (Induction Is Equivalent to Well-Ordering)
content: Let \(X \subseteq \nR\) contain \(0\) , be closed under \(n \mapsto n + 1\) , and have the predecessor property. Then \(X\) has the induction property if and only if \(X\) has the least-element property.

title: Theorem 2.1.3 (Well-Ordering of the Natural Numbers)
content: Every non-empty subset of \(\nN\) has a least element.

title: Definition 2.2.1 (Divisibility)
page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content: Let \(a, b \in \nZ\) . We say that \(a\) divides \(b\) , written \(a \mid b\) , if there exists \(k \in \nZ\) with \(b = ka\) . Then \(a\) is a divisor of \(b\) , and \(b\) is a multiple of \(a\) .

title: Definition 2.2.2 (Prime Number)
page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content: An integer \(p\) is prime if \(p \ge 2\) and the only positive divisors of \(p\) are \(1\) and \(p\) . A prime factor of an integer \(n\) is a prime \(p\) with \(p \mid n\) .

title: Example (All Numbers Are Equal)
page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content: Here is a “theorem” and a “proof”. Find the line that fails. “Theorem.” For every integer \(n \ge 1\) and all real numbers \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) , we have \(x_1 = x_2 = \dots = x_n\) . “Proof.” For an integer \(n \ge 1\) , let \(P(n)\) be the statement “for all real numbers \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) , all the entries of the list \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) are equal”. We use @thm-induction with \(n_0 = 1\) . Base case. A list \(x_1\) of one number has only one entry, so all its entries are equal: \(P(1)\) holds. Step. Let \(n \ge 1\) be an integer, suppose \(P(n)\) , and let \(x_1, \dots, x_{n+1}\) be real numbers. The list \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) has \(n\) entries, so by \(P(n)\) its entries are all equal. The list \(x_2, \dots, x_{n+1}\) has \(n\) entries, so by \(P(n)\) its entries are all equal. The entry \(x_2\) lies in both lists, so every entry of either list equals \(x_2\) . Hence \(x_1 = x_2 = \dots = x_{n+1}\) , which is \(P(n + 1)\) . By @thm-induction , \(P(n)\) holds for every \(n \ge 1\) .

title: Exercise (B1)
page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content: Prove that \(5 \mid 6^n - 1\) for every \(n \in \nN\) , without adding up the powers of \(6\) . Here \(6^n\) has its school meaning: \(6^0 = 1\) , \(6^{n+1} = 6^n \cdot 6\) , and \(6^n\) is an integer; Section 2.3 makes these official.

title: Exercise (B2: Products of primes)
page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content: An integer is a product of primes if it equals \(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k\) for some \(k \ge 1\) and primes \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) (a single prime counts, with \(k = 1\) ). Here \(p_1 p_2 \cdots p_k\) has its school meaning, and multiplying two such products gives the product of the joined list; Section 2.3 defines finite products ( @def-sum-product ). Here is a proof that every integer \(n \ge 2\) is a product of primes, with its last step blank. Name the move, then complete it. Suppose not. Then the set \(F\) of integers \(n \ge 2\) that are not products of primes is non-empty and has the integer lower bound \(2\) , so it has a least element \(m\) by @cor-well-ordering-integers . Since a prime is a product of primes, \(m\) is not prime; as \(m \ge 2\) , it has a positive divisor \(a \notin \{1, m\}\) , and \(m = ab\) with \(b \in \nZ\) . As in the proof of @thm-prime-factor , \(b > 0\) and \(2 \le a < m\) . Since \(a < m = ab\) and \(a > 0\) , we get \(b > 1\) , so \(b \ge 2\) by discreteness; and since \(a \ge 2\) , \(b < 2b \le ab = m\) . So \(2 \le a < m\) and \(2 \le b < m\) , and as \(m\) is the least element of \(F\) , neither \(a\) nor \(b\) lies in \(F\) : both are products of primes. \(\dots\)

title: Exercise (B3)
page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content: Find the quotient and remainder of @thm-division-algorithm for \(a = 17\) , \(n = 5\) , and for \(a = -17\) , \(n = 5\) . Prove that the square of an odd integer leaves remainder \(1\) on division by \(8\) . Prove that if \(2 \mid n\) and \(3 \mid n\) , then \(6 \mid n\) , for every integer \(n\) . Hint for (c): @thm-division-algorithm , dividing by \(3\) .

title: Exercise (C1: Exit check: a flawed induction)
page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content: Here is a claim and a “proof”. Claim. Every integer \(n \ge 18\) is \(4a + 7b\) for some integers \(a, b \ge 0\) . For an integer \(n \ge 18\) , let \(P(n)\) be “ \(n = 4a + 7b\) for some integers \(a, b \ge 0\) ”. We use strong induction from base \(18\) ( @thm-strong-induction-from-base ). Base case. \(18 = 4 \cdot 1 + 7 \cdot 2\) , so \(P(18)\) holds. Step. Let \(n \ge 18\) be an integer, and suppose \(P(k)\) holds for every integer \(k\) with \(18 \le k \le n\) . Write \(n + 1 = (n - 3) + 4\) . Since \(n - 3 < n\) , the induction hypothesis gives \(n - 3 = 4a + 7b\) with integers \(a, b \ge 0\) . Then \(n + 1 = 4(a + 1) + 7b\) , with \(a + 1 \ge 0\) and \(b \ge 0\) , so \(P(n + 1)\) holds. By @thm-strong-induction-from-base , \(P(n)\) holds for every integer \(n \ge 18\) . Answer each question. (i) Is the claim true? (ii) Does the argument prove it? (iii) Which line fails, and for which \(n\) ? (iv) Which rule does that line break? (v) Give a counterexample to the failing step, not merely to some conclusion. (vi) Repair the proof.

page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample

title: Lemma 2.2.4 (Lowest Terms, Up to Factors of Two)
page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content: Every rational number can be written as \(p/q\) with \(p \in \nZ\) , \(q \in \nZ_{>0}\) , and \(p\) and \(q\) not both even.

title: Theorem 2.2.3 (Division Algorithm)
page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content: Let \(a \in \nZ\) and \(n \in \nZ_{>0}\) . Then there are unique integers \(q\) and \(r\) with \[ a = qn + r \quad \text{and} \quad 0 \le r < n . \]

title: Theorem 2.2.1 (Induction from a Base)
page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content: Let \(n_0\) be an integer, and for each integer \(n \ge n_0\) let \(P(n)\) be a statement. Suppose ( base case ) \(P(n_0)\) is true, and ( inductive step ) for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) , if \(P(n)\) is true then \(P(n + 1)\) is true. Then \(P(n)\) is true for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) .

title: Theorem 2.2.5 (Every Integer at Least Two Has a Prime Factor)
page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content: Every integer \(n \ge 2\) has a prime factor.

title: Theorem 2.2.2 (Strong Induction from a Base)
page: 2.2 Induction, Strong Induction and the Smallest Counterexample
content: Let \(n_0\) be an integer, and for each integer \(n \ge n_0\) let \(P(n)\) be a statement. Suppose that, for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) : if \(P(k)\) is true for every integer \(k\) with \(n_0 \le k < n\) , then \(P(n)\) is true. Then \(P(n)\) is true for every integer \(n \ge n_0\) .

title: Corollary 2.3.2 (Recursion from a Base)
content: Let \(n_0\) be an integer, \(D \coloneqq \{ n \in \nZ : n \ge n_0 \}\) , \(X\) a set, \(a \in X\) , and \(g \colon D \times X \to X\) a function. Then there is exactly one function \(f \colon D \to X\) with \(f(n_0) = a\) and \(f(n + 1) = g(n, f(n))\) for every \(n \in D\) .

title: Definition 2.3.2 (Powers)
content: Let \(u \in \nR\) . The powers \(u^n\) , for \(n \in \nN\) , are defined by recursion: \[ u^0 \coloneqq 1, \qquad u^{n+1} \coloneqq u^n u . \]

title: Definition 2.3.1 (Finite Sums and Products)
content: Let \((a_k)_{k \ge 1}\) be a sequence of real numbers. The sums \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k\) and products \(\prod_{k=1}^{n} a_k\) , for \(n \in \nN\) , are defined by recursion: \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{k=1}^{0} a_k &\coloneqq 0, & \sum_{k=1}^{n+1} a_k &\coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k + a_{n+1}, \\ \prod_{k=1}^{0} a_k &\coloneqq 1, & \prod_{k=1}^{n+1} a_k &\coloneqq \Bigl(\prod_{k=1}^{n} a_k\Bigr) a_{n+1}. \end{aligned} \] The factorial of \(n \in \nN\) is \(n! \coloneqq \prod_{k=1}^{n} k\) . For integers \(m \le n + 1\) and reals \(a_k\) given for every integer \(k \ge m\) , \[ \sum_{k=m}^{n} a_k \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^{n-m+1} a_{m-1+i}, \qquad \prod_{k=m}^{n} a_k \coloneqq \prod_{i=1}^{n-m+1} a_{m-1+i} . \]

title: Example (Proving more to prove anything)
content: Prove that \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k^2} < 2\) for every integer \(n \ge 1\) .

content: Prove that \(\sum_{k=1}^{n} k^3 = \Bigl(\frac{n(n + 1)}{2}\Bigr)^2\) for every \(n \in \nN\) .

title: Exercise (B2: Starting at the right place)

Prove that \(2^n \ge n^2\) for every integer \(n \ge 4\) , using @thm-induction . Say why the base must be \(4\) and not \(3\) .

title: Exercise (C2: Bernoulli beyond its hypothesis)

At \(x = -4\) , find the first \(n\) where the inequality fails, and the first \(n\) where the step “ \(P(n) \Rightarrow P(n + 1)\) ” fails.

title: Exercise (C3: Two identities at once)

title: Proposition 2.3.8 (Finite Sets Have a Maximum)
content: For every integer \(n \ge 1\) and all reals \(x_1, \dots, x_n\) , the set \(\{x_1, \dots, x_n\}\) has a maximum and a minimum.

title: Definition 2.4.1 (Properties of a Relation)
content: Let \(X\) be a set and \(R\) a relation on \(X\) . Then \(R\) is reflexive on \(X\) if \(x \mathrel{R} x\) for every \(x \in X\) : \[ \forall x \in X \ \ x \mathrel{R} x ; \] symmetric if \(x \mathrel{R} y\) implies \(y \mathrel{R} x\) , for all \(x, y \in X\) : \[ \forall x \in X \ \forall y \in X \ \ \bigl( x \mathrel{R} y \to y \mathrel{R} x \bigr) ; \] antisymmetric if \(x \mathrel{R} y\) and \(y \mathrel{R} x\) together imply \(x = y\) , for all \(x, y \in X\) : \[ \forall x \in X \ \forall y \in X \ \ \bigl( (x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} x) \to x = y \bigr) ; \] transitive if \(x \mathrel{R} y\) and \(y \mathrel{R} z\) together imply \(x \mathrel{R} z\) , for all \(x, y, z \in X\) : \[ \forall x \in X \ \forall y \in X \ \forall z \in X \ \ \bigl( (x \mathrel{R} y \wedge y \mathrel{R} z) \to x \mathrel{R} z \bigr) . \]

title: Proposition 2.4.1 (Divisibility on the Natural Numbers)
content: The relation \(\mid\) is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive on \(\nN\) . On \(\nZ\) it is reflexive and transitive, and not antisymmetric.

title: Definition 2.5.5 (Congruence Modulo n)
content: Let \(n \in \nZ_{>0}\) . Integers \(a\) and \(b\) are congruent modulo \(n\) , written \(a \equiv b \pmod{n}\) , if \(n \mid a - b\) , that is, if \(a - b = kn\) for some \(k \in \nZ\) .

title: Definition 2.5.2 (Equivalence Class)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(X\) , and let \(a \in X\) . The equivalence class of \(a\) is \[ [a] \coloneqq \{ x \in X : x \sim a \} . \] When the relation must be named, we write \([a]_\sim\) . Any element of a class is called a representative of it.

title: Definition 2.5.1 (Equivalence Relation)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. An equivalence relation on \(X\) is a relation \(\sim\) on \(X\) ( @def-relation ) that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive on \(X\) ( @def-relation-properties ): for every \(x \in X\) , \(x \sim x\) ; for all \(x, y \in X\) , if \(x \sim y\) , then \(y \sim x\) ; for all \(x, y, z \in X\) , if \(x \sim y\) and \(y \sim z\) , then \(x \sim z\) . When \(x \sim y\) , we say that \(x\) is equivalent to \(y\) (under \(\sim\) ).

title: Definition 2.5.3 (Partition)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. A partition of \(X\) is a set \(\sP\) of subsets of \(X\) , called blocks , such that every block is non-empty : \(P \ne \emptyset\) for every \(P \in \sP\) ; the blocks are pairwise disjoint : for all \(P, Q \in \sP\) , if \(P \ne Q\) , then \(P \cap Q = \emptyset\) ; the blocks cover \(X\) : \(\bigcup \sP = X\) .

title: Definition 2.5.4 (Quotient Set)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(X\) . The quotient set of \(X\) by \(\sim\) is the set of all equivalence classes, \[ X/{\sim} \coloneqq \{ C \in \powerset{X} : C = [a] \text{ for some } a \in X \} . \] The quotient map is \(q \colon X \to X/{\sim}\) , \(q(a) \coloneqq [a]\) .

title: Example (The fibers of a function)
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function, and for \(x, y \in X\) let \(x \sim_f y\) mean \(f(x) = f(y)\) . Show that \(\sim_f\) is an equivalence relation on \(X\) , and describe its classes. Then show that every equivalence relation \(\sim\) on \(X\) is of this form, for a suitable function.

title: Proposition 2.5.5 (Congruence Respects Sums and Products)
content:
Let \(n \in

Z\) . If \(a \equiv a' \pmod{n}\) and \(b \equiv b' \pmod{n}\) , then \[ a + b \equiv a' + b' \pmod{n} \qquad 	ext{and} \qquad ab \equiv a'b' \pmod{n} . \] Hence the operations \([a] + [b] \coloneqq [a + b]\) and \([a][b] \coloneqq [ab]\) on \(
Z/n\) are well defined .

title: Proposition 2.5.3 (Congruence Is an Equivalence Relation)
content: For every \(n \in \nZ_{>0}\) , congruence modulo \(n\) is an equivalence relation on \(\nZ\) .

title: Proposition 2.5.4 (The Integers Modulo n)
content:
Let \(n \in 
Z_{>0}\) . For every \(a \in 
Z\) there is exactly one \(r \in \{0, \dots, n - 1\}\) with \([a] = [r]\) in \(
Z/n\) , namely the remainder of \(a\) on division by \(n\) . Hence \[ 
Z/n = \{ [0], [1], \dots, [n - 1] \} , \] and the \(n\) classes listed are pairwise different.

title: Theorem 2.5.1 (Equivalence Classes Partition the Set)
content: Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on a set \(X\) . For every \(a \in X\) , \(a \in [a]\) ; in particular every class is non-empty. For all \(a, b \in X\) , \([a] = [b]\) if and only if \(a \sim b\) . For all \(a, b \in X\) , if \([a] \cap [b] \ne \emptyset\) , then \([a] = [b]\) . The quotient set \(X/{\sim}\) is a partition of \(X\) .

title: Theorem 2.5.2 (Partitions and Equivalence Relations Correspond)
content: Let \(X\) be a set. Let \(\sP\) be a partition of \(X\) . For \(x, y \in X\) , let \(x \sim_{\sP} y\) mean that there is a block \(P \in \sP\) with \(x \in P\) and \(y \in P\) . Then \(\sim_{\sP}\) is an equivalence relation on \(X\) , and its classes are the blocks: \(X/{\sim_{\sP}} = \sP\) . Let \(\sim\) be an equivalence relation on \(X\) . Then \(\sim_{X/{\sim}}\) , the relation of (a) for the partition \(X/{\sim}\) , is \(\sim\) itself. Hence every partition of \(X\) is the quotient set of exactly one equivalence relation on \(X\) , namely \(\sim_{\sP}\) .

title: Definition 2.6.3 (Greatest and Least Elements)
page: 2.6 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: An element \(g\) is a greatest element of \(A\) if \(g \in A\) and \(a \preceq g\) for every \(a \in A\) . An element \(l\) is a least element of \(A\) if \(l \in A\) and \(l \preceq a\) for every \(a \in A\) .

title: Definition 2.6.4 (Maximal and Minimal Elements)
page: 2.6 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: An element \(m\) is a maximal element of \(A\) if \(m \in A\) and there is no \(a \in A\) with \(m \prec a\) . An element \(m\) is a minimal element of \(A\) if \(m \in A\) and there is no \(a \in A\) with \(a \prec m\) .

title: Definition 2.6.2 (Upper and Lower Bounds)
page: 2.6 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: An element \(u \in X\) is an upper bound of \(A\) if \(a \preceq u\) for every \(a \in A\) , and a lower bound of \(A\) if \(u \preceq a\) for every \(a \in A\) . The set \(A\) is bounded above if it has an upper bound in \(X\) , bounded below if it has a lower bound in \(X\) , and bounded if both.

title: Definition 2.6.5 (Supremum and Infimum)
page: 2.6 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: Let \((X, \preceq)\) be a partially ordered set and \(A \subseteq X\) . An element \(s \in X\) is a least upper bound , or supremum , of \(A\) in \(X\) if \(s\) is an upper bound of \(A\) , and \(s \preceq u\) for every upper bound \(u\) of \(A\) . An element \(i \in X\) is a greatest lower bound , or infimum , of \(A\) in \(X\) if \(i\) is a lower bound of \(A\) and \(u \preceq i\) for every lower bound \(u\) of \(A\) .

title: Definition 2.6.1 (Partial Order)
page: 2.6 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: Let \(X\) be a set. A partial order on \(X\) is a relation \(\preceq\) on \(X\) that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive on \(X\) ( @def-relation-properties ): for every \(x \in X\) , \(x \preceq x\) ; for all \(x, y \in X\) , if \(x \preceq y\) and \(y \preceq x\) , then \(x = y\) ; for all \(x, y, z \in X\) , if \(x \preceq y\) and \(y \preceq z\) , then \(x \preceq z\) . The pair \((X, \preceq)\) is a partially ordered set . Elements \(x, y \in X\) are comparable if \(x \preceq y\) or \(y \preceq x\) . The partial order is total if every two elements of \(X\) are comparable. The strict part of \(\preceq\) is the relation \(\prec\) on \(X\) given by \[ x \prec y \iff x \preceq y \ \text{ and } \ x \ne y . \] We also write \(y \succeq x\) for \(x \preceq y\) .

title: Definition 2.6.6 (Well-Ordered Set)
page: 2.6 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: A partially ordered set \((X, \preceq)\) is well-ordered , and \(\preceq\) is a well-order on \(X\) , if \(\preceq\) is total and every non-empty subset of \(X\) has a least element.

title: Example (The supremum under divisibility is the least common multiple)
page: 2.6 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: Let \(a, b \in \nN\) . Find \(\sup \{a, b\}\) in \((\nN, \mid)\) . Deduce that an integer divisible by \(2\) and by \(3\) is divisible by \(6\) .

title: Proposition 2.6.2 (Greatest and Maximal Elements)
page: 2.6 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: Let \((X, \preceq)\) be a partially ordered set and \(A \subseteq X\) . A greatest element of \(A\) is a maximal element of \(A\) . If \(\preceq\) is total, then a maximal element of \(A\) is a greatest element of \(A\) . The same holds for least and minimal elements.

title: Proposition 2.6.1 (Greatest and Least Elements Are Unique)
page: 2.6 Partial Orders, Maximal and Greatest Elements
content: A subset \(A\) of a partially ordered set has at most one greatest element and at most one least element.

title: Corollary 3.1.4 (The Number of Elements Is Unique)
content: Let \(A\) be a set and \(m, n \in \nN\) . If \(A\) has \(m\) elements and \(A\) has \(n\) elements, then \(m = n\) .

title: Corollary 3.1.3 (Pigeonhole for Finite Sets)
content: Let \(m, n \in \nN\) , let \(A\) have \(m\) elements, and let \(B\) have \(n\) elements. If \(m > n\) , there is no injection \(A \to B\) . If \(m < n\) , there is no surjection \(A \to B\) .

title: Corollary 3.1.7 (Removing a Point)
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) , let \(A\) have \(n + 1\) elements, and let \(a \in A\) . Then \(A \setminus \{a\}\) has \(n\) elements.

title: Definition 3.1.1 (Equinumerous Sets)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. We say that \(A\) and \(B\) are equinumerous , and write \(\card{A} = \card{B}\) , if there exists a bijection \(f \colon A \to B\) . In symbols, \[ \card{A} = \card{B} \iff \exists f \in B^A \ \ (f \text{ is injective} \wedge f \text{ is surjective}) . \]

title: Definition 3.1.2 (Finite Set, Number of Elements)
content: Let \(A\) be a set and \(n \in \nN\) . We say that \(A\) has \(n\) elements if \(\card{\{1, \dots, n\}} = \card{A}\) , that is, if there exists a bijection \(\varphi \colon \{1, \dots, n\} \to A\) . The set \(A\) is finite if it has \(n\) elements for some \(n \in \nN\) . In that case we write \(\card{A} = n\) .

title: Definition 3.1.3 (Infinite Set)
content: A set \(A\) is infinite if it is not finite: for every \(n \in \nN\) there is no bijection \(\{1, \dots, n\} \to A\) .

title: Proposition 3.1.5 (Disjoint Unions)
content: Let \(m, n \in \nN\) , let \(A\) have \(m\) elements, let \(B\) have \(n\) elements, and suppose \(A \cap B = \emptyset\) . Then \(A \cup B\) has \(m + n\) elements.

title: Proposition 3.1.1 (Equinumerosity Is Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive)
content: For all sets \(A\) , \(B\) and \(C\) : \(\card{A} = \card{A}\) ; if \(\card{A} = \card{B}\) , then \(\card{B} = \card{A}\) ; if \(\card{A} = \card{B}\) and \(\card{B} = \card{C}\) , then \(\card{A} = \card{C}\) .

title: Proposition 3.1.8 (Counting Subsets)
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) . A set with \(n\) elements has \(2^n\) subsets: if \(\card{A} = n\) , then \(\card{\powerset{A}} = 2^n\) .

title: Proposition 3.1.6 (Subsets of Finite Sets)
content: Let \(n \in \nN\) , let \(A\) have \(n\) elements, and let \(S \subseteq A\) . Then \(S\) is finite and has \(k\) elements for some \(k \le n\) . If \(S \ne A\) , then \(k < n\) .

title: Theorem 3.1.9 (A Finite Set Has No Proper Copy)
content: Let \(A\) be a finite set and \(B \subsetneq A\) . Then \(A\) and \(B\) are not equinumerous: there is no bijection \(A \to B\) .

title: Theorem 3.1.2 (Pigeonhole Principle)
content: Let \(m, n \in \nN\) with \(m > n\) . Then there is no injection \(\{1, \dots, m\} \to \{1, \dots, n\}\) .

title: Corollary 3.2.7 (Products of Countable Sets)
content: If \(A\) and \(B\) are countable, then \(A \times B\) is countable. Let \(k \ge 2\) be an integer. If \(A_1, \dots, A_k\) are countable, then \(A_1 \times \dots \times A_k\) is countable.

title: Exercise (B2: Putting a proof in order)
content:
The lines (i)–(ix) below include the seven lines of a proof that \(2^m 3^n = 2^{m'} 3^{n'}\) implies \(m = m'\) and \(n = n'\) , for \(m, n, m', n' \in 
N\) , shuffled, together with two lines that do not belong. Write the seven lines in an order that makes a correct proof, and say why each of the other two lines fails. The left side is even, because \(m - m' \ge 1\) by the supposition; the right side is odd; no natural number is both ( @thm-division-algorithm , uniqueness of the remainder for divisor \(2\) ). This is a contradiction. Suppose \(2^m 3^n = 2^{m'} 3^{n'}\) . The left side is odd and the right side is even, a contradiction. Canceling \(2^m\) gives \(3^n = 3^{n'}\) . Suppose \(m 
e m'\) ; by symmetry, say \(m > m'\) . Since \(k \mapsto 3^k\) is strictly increasing on \(
N\) , \(n = n'\) . Since \(2\) and \(3\) are prime, unique factorization gives \(m = m'\) and \(n = n'\) . Canceling \(2^{m'}\) gives \(2^{m - m'} 3^n = 3^{n'}\) . So \(m = m'\) .
