title: Lemma 3.2.1 (Subsets of the Natural Numbers)
content: Every subset \(S \subseteq \nN\) is finite or countably infinite.

title: Proposition 3.2.4 (Images of Countable Sets)
content: Let \(A\) be countable and \(f \colon A \to B\) a function. Then \(f(A)\) is countable. In particular, if \(f\) is surjective, then \(B\) is countable.

title: Proposition 3.2.3 (Subsets of Countable Sets)
content: Every subset of a countable set is countable.

title: Proposition 3.2.5 (Union of Two Countable Sets)
content: If \(A\) and \(B\) are countable, then \(A \cup B\) is countable.

title: Theorem 3.2.2 (Characterizations of Countable Sets)
content: For every set \(A\) , the following are equivalent. \(A\) is countable. There is an injection \(A \to \nN\) . \(A\) is finite or countably infinite.

title: Axiom 3.3.1 (Axiom of Choice)
page: 3.3 Countable Unions and the Axiom of Choice
content: Let \(I\) be a set, and let \((A_i)_{i \in I}\) be a family of sets such that \(A_i\) is non-empty for every \(i \in I\) . Then there exists a function \[ c \colon I \to \bigcup_{i \in I} A_i \quad \text{with} \quad c(i) \in A_i \ \text{ for every } i \in I . \] Such a function \(c\) is called a choice function for the family.

page: 3.3 Countable Unions and the Axiom of Choice

title: Theorem 3.3.2 (Surjections Have Right Inverses)
page: 3.3 Countable Unions and the Axiom of Choice
content: Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a surjective function. Then \(f\) has a right inverse: there is a function \(g \colon Y \to X\) with \(f(g(y)) = y\) for every \(y \in Y\) .

title: Corollary 3.4.3 (The Subsets of the Naturals)
page: 3.4 Diagonal Arguments: Uncountable Sets and Cantor's Theorem
content: The power set \(\powerset{\nN}\) is uncountable.

title: Corollary 3.4.5 (Transcendental Numbers Exist)
page: 3.4 Diagonal Arguments: Uncountable Sets and Cantor's Theorem
content: The set \(\nR \setminus \mathrm{Alg}\) of transcendental numbers is uncountable. In particular, there is a real number that is not algebraic.

title: Definition 3.4.1 (Decimal Expansion)
page: 3.4 Diagonal Arguments: Uncountable Sets and Cantor's Theorem
content: A digit sequence is a function \(k \mapsto d_k\) from \(\nZ_{>0}\) to \(\{0, 1, \dots, 9\}\) . For \(n \ge 1\) let \[ t_n \coloneqq \sum_{k=1}^{n} d_k 10^{-k} \] ( @def-sum-product ), where \(10^{-k} \coloneqq (1/10)^k\) ( @def-power ). The digit sequence is a decimal expansion of \(x \in [0, 1]\) if for every \(n \ge 1\) , \[ t_n \le x \le t_n + 10^{-n} . \]

title: Theorem 3.4.2 (Cantor’s Theorem)
page: 3.4 Diagonal Arguments: Uncountable Sets and Cantor's Theorem

page: 3.4 Diagonal Arguments: Uncountable Sets and Cantor's Theorem
content: The interval \([0, 1)\) is uncountable. Hence \(\nR\) is uncountable.

title: Definition 3.5.1 (Comparing Sizes)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. We write \(\card{A} \le \card{B}\) , and say that \(A\) is at most as big as \(B\) , if there exists an injection \(A \to B\) . We write \(\card{A} < \card{B}\) , and say that \(A\) is strictly smaller than \(B\) , if \(\card{A} \le \card{B}\) and not \(\card{A} = \card{B}\) : there is an injection \(A \to B\) , and there is no bijection \(A \to B\) .

For \(0 \le x \le 1\) we have \(1/4 \le u(x) \le 3/4\) , so \(u\) does map into \((0, 1)\) . (2) If \(u(x) = u(y)\) , then \(x/2 = y/2\) , so \(x = y\) ; hence \(u\) is injective. (3) The inclusion \(\iota \colon (0, 1) \to [0, 1]\) is injective. (4) So there are injections in both directions between \([0, 1]\) and \((0, 1)\) . (5) Therefore \(u\) is a bijection, and \(\card{[0, 1]} = \card{(0, 1)}\) . Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? title: Proposition 3.5.1 (Comparing Sizes Is Reflexive and Transitive)
content: For all sets \(A\) , \(B\) , \(C\) : \(\card{A} \le \card{A}\) ; if \(\card{A} \le \card{B}\) and \(\card{B} \le \card{C}\) , then \(\card{A} \le \card{C}\) .

title: Proposition 3.5.2 (Injections and Surjections)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets with \(A \ne \emptyset\) . Then \(\card{A} \le \card{B}\) if and only if there is a surjection \(B \to A\) .

title: Theorem 3.5.3 (Schröder–Bernstein Theorem)
content: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be sets. If \(\card{A} \le \card{B}\) and \(\card{B} \le \card{A}\) , then \(\card{A} = \card{B}\) .

title: Exercise (C2: The irrationals)
Exercise (R1)
content: Prove that every integer \(n \ge 1\) is a sum of distinct powers of \(2\) : there are an integer \(r \ge 1\) and natural numbers \(k_1 > k_2 > \dots > k_r\) with \(n = 2^{k_1} + 2^{k_2} + \dots + 2^{k_r}\) .

title: Exercise (R2)
content: Show that \(\forall x\, \exists y\, R(x, y) \nvdash \exists y\, \forall x\, R(x, y)\) by a counter-model whose domain is \(\nN\) . Say in words what the two sentences say when \(R(x, y)\) is read as “ \(x < y\) ”.

title: Exercise (R3)
content: For an integer \(n \ge 1\) , how many truth functions with \(n\) inputs are there? Prove your answer.

title: Theorem 3.6.1 (Infinite Sets Contain a Countably Infinite Subset)
content: Every infinite set \(X\) has a countably infinite subset. Equivalently, there is an injection \(\nN \to X\) .

title: Theorem 3.6.2 (Infinite Sets and Proper Subsets)
content: A set \(X\) is infinite if and only if \(\card{X} = \card{Y}\) for some proper subset \(Y \subsetneq X\) .

title: Exercise (P2: core)
content: (20 minutes.) Here is a derivation of \[ \begin{aligned} &\forall z\, \exists y\, G(y, z),\ \forall y\, \exists x\, F(x, y), \\ &\forall x\, \forall y\, \forall z\, \bigl( (F(x, y) \wedge G(y, z)) \to H(x, z) \bigr) \vdash \forall z\, \exists x\, H(x, z), \end{aligned} \] with four justifications left blank, marked (i)–(iv). Fill in the justifications (i)–(iv): the rule and the cited lines. Explain why line 13 sits inside both of the boxes that begin at lines 5 and 7, and why each of these two boxes may close where it does. Read \(F(x, y)\) as “ \(f(x) = y\) ”, \(G(y, z)\) as “ \(g(y) = z\) ” and \(H(x, z)\) as “ \(g(f(x)) = z\) ”, for functions \(f \colon X \to Y\) and \(g \colon Y \to Z\) . Write the plain-prose proof that this derivation encodes, that the composite of two surjections is surjective, with one sentence for each box.

title: Exercise (P3)
content:
(20 minutes.) For each argument below, answer three questions. Is the conclusion true? Does the argument prove it? If not, which line fails, which entry of @fd1:exm-not-allowed-catalogue does it fall under, and what is a counterexample to the illegal step (not merely to the conclusion)? Claim: \(n^2 + n\) is even for every \(n \in

N\) . Then \((n + 1)^2 + (n + 1) = (n^2 + n) + 2(n + 1)\) is even. By induction, the claim holds. Claim: if \(A_n \subseteq 
R\) is bounded above for every \(n \in 
N\) , then \( igcup_{n \in 
N} A_n\) is bounded above. Proof: For each \(n\) , let \(M_n\) be an upper bound of \(A_n\) . Let \(M\) be a number larger than every \(M_n\) . Then \(M\) is an upper bound of the union.

title: Exercise (P4: core)
content: (20 minutes.) Let \(a_0 = 0\) , \(a_1 = 1\) and \(a_{n+2} = 3a_{n+1} - 2a_n\) for \(n \in \nN\) . Say which result guarantees that these equations define a sequence. Prove that \(a_n = 2^n - 1\) for every \(n \in \nN\) . Suppose instead that \(a_1 = 2\) , with \(a_0\) and the rule unchanged. Compute \(a_2\) and \(a_3\) , and say exactly which line of your proof in (b) fails.

title: Exercise (P5: core)
content: (20 minutes.) Let \(f \colon X \to Y\) be a function. For a family \((B_i)_{i \in I}\) of subsets of \(Y\) , prove that \[ f^{-1}\Bigl( Y \setminus \bigcup_{i \in I} B_i \Bigr) = \bigcap_{i \in I} \bigl( X \setminus f^{-1}(B_i) \bigr), \] with the intersection taken in \(X\) . Prove that \(f(X \setminus A) \subseteq Y \setminus f(A)\) for every \(A \subseteq X\) if and only if \(f\) is injective.
